narrative: I was the Student Pilot in command of this flight receiving dual instruction from a CFI. I was on the controls for the entirety of the flight. We took off out of ZZZ1 at XA:15 and departed west towards ZZZ. The lesson was a cross country flight with an instrument approach. We got VFR flight following from ZZZ1 Approach then ZZZ Approach. We executed the RNAV XX at ZZZ. On decent into ZZZ; I observed a low thumping feeling at low RPM. I asked my instructor if she felt or heard anything unusual and described what I experienced. After roughly 10 seconds it went away. We continued our descent and executed a touch and go at ZZZ at XB:45. Upon reaching cruise altitude of 3500 at XB:50 we attempted to run the cruise checklist. When leaning the mixture we did not see any rise in RPM. We went back to full rich as we started to slowly and progressively lose 10-30 RPM at a time. We each checked the throttle friction and attempted to lock it at a particular RPM as we observed it fall below each RPM setting we tried; we decided to navigate to a nearby airport; ZZZ2. We notified ATC that we would like to cancel flight following and land early at ZZZ2. We started a descent and flew past the airport to have appropriate time to descend. We noted that the throttle was further in than it normally was for the RPM we needed to maintain and we had to continuously adjust for greater RPM as it lowered. We entered the pattern and reduced throttle to descend for landing. We decided to maintain 1700 RPM rather than 1500 (what we would normally use). I noted on base leg that I was having to add RPM to arrest descent rate. We continued in for Runway; XY; flaps 10 degrees; floated slightly; and made a safe landing. Upon clearing the runway we attempted an after landing checklist and observed no RPM rise when attempting to lean the mixture. We taxied to the ramp and made contact with the maintenance team at the ramp who provided us with chocks for the tires. We immediately called Dispatch upon shutdown and described the incident. The maintenance team at ZZZ2 stated that they would move the aircraft to a different parking spot and tie it down until company could come get it.
narrative1: We left ZZZ1 for a cross country flight to ZZZ and back to ZZZ1. On the approach course for RNAV XX; during descent into ZZZ; student asked if instructor felt engine roughness; later reported as a low thumping noise at low RPM; instructor did not hear anything or felt anything; engine instruments did not show any changes. We did a touch and go at ZZZ; engine instruments were verified in the green on the takeoff roll by both student and instructor. At cruise altitude; after completing the cruise checklist and leaning the mixture; we noticed that the RPM kept slowly dropping 20-30 RPM at a time every few seconds. Student increased throttle to maintain airspeed. Engine instruments were checked; no large changes were noted. Instructor ran floor to door; setting mixture back to full rich; fuel pump on to check if that helped. Pitot heat on in case of icing. RPM still maintained slow and steady drop. We did a slow climb to 4000 ft at about 85- 90 kts for more altitude as we searched for nearest airport on our path to ZZZ1 while monitoring the RPM and engine instruments. Cruising at 4000 ft; while maintaining altitude; given the RPM continued the slow drop; and we were about 1NM from ZZZ2 at that point; we decided to divert there. We told ZZZ1 Approach that we were cutting our flight short and landing at ZZZ2; we did not declare an emergency. We landed XY at ZZZ2; maintained higher RPM than SOP (about 1700-1800 rpm) once we started the descent from pattern altitude since we were not sure we would be able to get more RPM back if we reduced it to 1500. When landing was assured; we added flaps 10; and slowly reduce the power on final. Student noted later that he had to increase the throttle setting on base to maintain airspeed. After we cleared the runway; we completed the after landing checklist; noted that there were no RPM rise when we leaned the mixture. We taxied and secured the aircraft and called school Dispatch for notification.
synopsis: C172 student pilot and flight instructor reported that during cruise flight they experienced a loss of engine RPMs resulting in the flight diverting to the nearest airport.

They weren't on ADSB when I had checked and cleared the area of traffic nor were they advising on CTAF that they would be overflying the field at any altitude. They were at 500ft AGL. As I leveled off at 200ft AGL and followed the shoreline westbound; the Captain made repeated calls on CTAF in an attempt to hail the military transport if they were on CTAF. I had no communication from the military transport before; during; or after the incident. Captain and I assessed the situation; climbed back to 4500ft; setup the aircraft for cruise and continued the flight home to ZZZ. Captain then contacted HCF center to get flight following and then over to HCF approach for arrival into ZZZ. On approach; we advised them as to what had happened and gave a detailed report to the controller. They then said they handed off the information to the supervisor on duty. We talked to ATC; requested priority handling and began our return. The FO (First Officer) did a great job flying the airplane; managing the icing conditions while returning back to ZZZ. At that time I paused that checklist; we had good engines; lots of fuel remaining and ZZZ just ahead of us; and with the plane stabilized in a shallow descent; the FO (First Officer) and I started more discussions; and that led us to the IMBAL checklist. Underweight landing with a smooth touchdown; we exited the runway and stopped for fire rescue inspection; and we were told there was no sign of leaks and everything looked normal. Uneventful taxi as we continued to the gate.

Next; I then followed my diversion checklist in the Dispatch Tool and sent the proper paperwork and forms and added the single engine MEL and sent the calculated landing data. I then called ZZZ Tower to see if they had indeed requested priority handling and to make sure we had emergency services available for them. The aircraft then landed on the ground with no issues.

narrative: The flight was ZZZ1-ZZZ; it was the last leg of a 3 leg day for us on day two of a 4 day trip. The only thing of note up until the event started was maintenance discrepancy 'Company Maintenance stations only' because of multiple write ups for ENG 1 FADEC. So we are at cruise at FL350 and get an ECAM for AIR ENG2 Bleed Abnorm PR. As we are beginning to run the ECAM procedure the warning goes away. I then pull up the BLEED systems page on the lower ECAM and notice that the #2 system still isn't operating quite correctly and told the FO (First Officer) I bet we get the ECAM again. About 10 seconds later we do get the ECAM except now it's AIR ENG2 Bleed Fault. We run through our ECAM procedures and then I notify Dispatch and Maintenance Control via ACARS; they respond and said to put in a logbook deferral sheet for it which I did. At that point I am still not feeling great about the engine and bleed system. I told the FO I was going to get on the Crew Phone and call Dispatch and Maintenance Control to talk to them directly about this just to make sure. Maintenance Control and I talked; and I explained everything and he said what we did was correct procedurally. So I disconnected with them and pressed on. At this point my ears were constantly plugging and popping. I asked the FO if he had the same feelings and he said no. I had a sense or what ever you want to call it that something wasn't right. ATC then asked us to slow from Mach .78 to .75 for sequencing to ZZZ. The FO selected .75 in the FCU (Flight Control Unit) and as soon as the #2 engine got to about 50% N1 we started getting very violent buffering and loud repetitive bangs coming from aircraft right. We immediately got ENG2 STALL ECAM. As we were starting the procedure the FA (Flight Attendant) in the back called to ask about the noise and buffering; I quickly said I'd call her back. As we completed the procedure I asked for; I believe; FL280 and told ATC what was going on. They gave us priority and cleared us to FL280. ECAM actions were complete and QRH follow-ups said we could slowly try and push the thrust back up if engine parameters were normal; which they were. I told ATC what we were doing and that both engines now appeared to be operating normally. They asked what we wanted to do and at this point ZZZ was our closest best option in my determination and with both engines operating normally I said we would like to continue to ZZZ. I asked for slow controlled descents so as to not cause large fluctuations in thrust settings; which ATC accommodated. I informed the FAs of the situation and explained a precautionary landing" in ZZZ is what we were doing; along with a PA to the passengers explaining everything. I told Dispatch of the ENG2 STALL ECAM. We landed in ZZZ with no further events and taxied to park under our own power.Cause: I believe that the shutting off of ENG2 Bleed from the first ECAM; coupled with our relatively high altitude of FL350; and a large power decrease going to idle by the autothrust when slowed to Mach .75 may have caused the compressor stall."

The gravity cross flow switch was opened and I crabbed the plane to try and get fuel from the left tank to the right. Additionally; Captain was using differential thrust to regulate the fuel flows between the tanks. This worked and we contacted dispatch and agreed to proceed to ZZZ1 while monitoring the fuel balance. Once the fuel was balanced; it did not have any problems. We landed in atl; maintenance came to the plane and the Captain and maintenance agreed that the plane was good to fly. THE STUDENT CALLED THE TOWER ON THE BASE LEG AND INFORMED THEM HE WAS GOING AROUND. AT THIS POINT INSTEAD OF TURNING TO ALIGN WITH THE RUNWAY HE CONTINUED FLYING STRAIGHT HEAD ON THE BASE LEG. THIS PUT HIM IN CONFLICT WITH ANOTHER AIRCRAFT ON A EXTENDED LEFT BASE. I WAS STILL ON THE PHONE WITH THE TOWER (GROUND CONTROLLER) AT THIS POINT; THE CONTROLLER BEGAN BERATING ME FOR TEACHING MY STUDENT TO FLY LIKE THIS AND THAT HE WAS NOW GOING HEAD ON WITH ANOTHER AIRCRAFT. I EXPLAINED THAT AT NO POINT HAVE I EVER INSTRUCTED THIS STUDENT OR ANY OTHER STUDENT TO DO WHAT HE WAS DOING AND THAT HE NEEDED SOME ASSISTANCE.TOWER WAS ABLE TO DE-CONFLICT THE TRAFFIC AND TURNED THE STUDENT OUT BOUND FROM THE AIRPORT. THEY TURNED HIM BACK TO THE AIRPORT WITH ABOUT A 3 MILE FINAL. THE APPROACH WAS NORMAL UNTIL SHORT FINAL. AT THAT TIME IT SOUNDED LIKE THE STUDENT WAS CARRYING EXTRA POWER AND WAS NOT AT IDLE JUST PRIOR TO FLARE OR TOUCH DOWN. JUST AFTER THE PLANE TOUCHED DOWN I NOTED THE RIGHT MAIN LANDING GEAR LIFT OFF THE RUNWAY 1 FOOT OR LESS. WHEN CLEARED TO LAND TOWER ADVISED WINDS WERE 120 @ 6 (RUNWAY XX WITH A MAGNETIC HEADING OF 076). WE DISCUSSED ALWAYS BEING READY FOR THE GO AROUND AND THAT IF AT ANY POINT SOMETHING IS NOT RIGHT TO EXECUTE; AND NOT 'WAIT AND SEE' WHAT HAPPENS. FOR THE SECOND AND THIRD LANDINGS WE IDENTIFIED THAT EVERYTHING WAS NORMAL UNTIL THE TRANSITION FROM THE DESCENT TO LANDING (THE FLARE). narrative: On a clear night; both 1st and 2nd party were returning north after doing various (presumably) training work to the south. The 1st party; Aircraft X; a high wing trainer; was returning to TIX. The 2nd party; Aircraft Y; a low wing trainer; was returning to COI.The weather was clear and a million; a great night for VFR or IFR training.1st party was cruising at 3000 feet; flying direct to LILAZ for return to TIX. 2nd party had been roughly paralleling 1st party at 4500 feet; a bit to our west; en route to COI.The site of the near-midair was west of COF airport/VOR. The 2nd party initiated a turn and descent towards COI. Being abeam and above our (1st party) wing; we were unable to spot them visually; however our graphical ADSB-IN display had allowed us to keep tabs on them as we cruised. Accordingly; the ADSB data broadcast from 2nd party -- including the descent and velocity data -- enabled us to realize that the 2nd party was forming a high risk conflict to us. Their intended descent cut directly across our course; and the angle of descent had them right at our altitude exactly as they crossed our course.Therefore; we initiated evasive action perhaps a minute before the would-be collision. While  we were turning roughly 270 out of our 360; they crossed our would-have-been course at our altitude a bit over a mile ahead of where we began our turn.We cannot be sure; but if we had been unaware of the traffic; which we were only aware of thanks to ADSB-IN; there was a distressingly high probability of invisible collision (neither party seeing the other). We were doing roughly 100 kts at the time; so we would have been roughly a mile and a half further along our course (compared to 'a bit over a mile' ahead of our turn). Optimistically; it would have been perhaps 3000 feet total separation; pessimistically zero feet. We can't know for sure without a detailed dynamics analysis of the mutual ADSB data.We are deeply thankful we had ADSB-IN to save our bacon.As stated; they were above our high wing so we couldn't see them; and we were probably below their low wing so they probably couldn't see us. We had good position and anti-collision lights; and most probably they did as well; but this was probably irrelevant. We only were able to avoid the situation; take evasive action; because of ADSB-IN. If we did not have ADSB-IN we would have been a critical event; or worse.Based on the fact that the 2nd party chose a descent path that generated such a high risk of conflict; most probably the 2nd party had neither visual contact (on account of us being under their low wing) nor ADSB-IN data. (That; or they were ignoring their ADSB-IN data.) Only the fact that we had ADSB-IN prevented a (very high risk of) midair; in my opinion. See-and-avoid failed; essentially; due to the low-wing-above-high-wing phenomenon. As far as I can figure; see-and-avoid could only have been made to work if clearing turns were required before all changes in course or altitude; which is of course a non-starter in the real world.The only way this would-be midair was prevented was ADSB-IN. We had it; they apparently did not.As far as I can tell; there is no immediate corrective action; other than encouraging further adoption of ADSB-IN by any means practical in all aircraft flying in busy airspace (such as where we were). ADSB-IN clearly proved its merit in my eye; and should be embraced further. (Not 'required'; since edge cases exist everywhere; but in the typical case; ADSB-IN is clearly beneficial.)Night-vs-day was not a factor; I believe. If anything; I find it easier to spot traffic at night; and as stated; all the lights on the planet could not have enabled us to have seen each other thru our wings; only clearing turns could have achieved that.

narrative: I took off from my home airport at ZZZ1 to fly to ZZZ with the possibility of continuing on to the ZZZ2 Airport; depending on weather conditions. I did a very long briefing with Leidos before departing primarily discussing the impact of an event on air traffic and the area's airports. The briefer was not sure what restrictions were in place for ZZZ but did advise that some of the local airports were not allowing for landing by any aircraft without a prior reservation and a code. Leidos also told me that despite the forecast for VFR conditions at ZZZ2 by XA:00; he did not think that was likely to happen given what he saw on the radar. So I made plans to meet my husband at ZZZ and decide then whether to fly on to ZZZ1. Before I took off I called ZZZ to determine the situation with landing and parking there during the event. I was advised that transient parking for VFR pilots had been moved from the spot in front of the terminal building to the ramp to the north and that only IFR flights needed a reservation. I took off from ZZZ1 and got flight following from ZZZ Center. I was having problems with com2 which was very static-y so I was just using com1 and switching its frequency when instructed to go to a new frequency. Com1 was coming in loud and clear. I was able to get the ATIS at ZZZ on com2 without static but any transmission to me or between ATC and other pilots could hardly be heard. I was switched to ZZZ [Approach] just about ZZZ3 although on com1 I had a hard time hearing him. I had to ask him to repeat transmissions as they came through very broken. There was considerable traffic. I was coming up to the golf course when ZZZ announced 'traffic; but the transmission was broken. I heard '200 feet' but could not make out direction or altitude. I heard another aircraft announcing  an intended landing at ZZZ but by then I was approaching ZZZ airspace. Then I heard ZZZ say 'Tower' with my call sign and assumed I was clear to go to Tower. By this time I was quite concerned about the situation given the lack of clarity in instructions caused by the radio not working properly; my proximity to the ceiling of the ZZZ airspace and the aircraft I knew was behind me. Tower came in loud and clear fortunately. I was told to make a straight in for Runway XX and I thought was left. I repeated it back but do not remember if I said XXL or XXR. I do know that my brain was visualizing and seeing XXL and that it the runway I was heading to. I was then cleared to land; and again; I repeated the instruction but I don't know about this time if Tower said left or right and I was still visualizing left. I came in a little high and was quite occupied with flying the plane; slowing down; pitching properly and engaging flaps. I knew other aircraft were also in the area coming in to land and one was about to take off on XXL in front of me. My usual practice of repeating the landing clearance twice was not followed either. As I recall I was still shaken by the issue with the radios. I was also thinking about the change in parking spot; not sure exactly where to go and trying to figure out how I would get there from XXL. I was on short final; full flaps and entering the runway environment when I received an instruction to go around. and to make right traffic from XXL for XXR. I powered up; pitched up; released flaps; set trim and climbed. I noticed and aircraft had just taken off on XXL and was on the upwind; but they had lifted off before I got into ground effect and I wondered if that was the reason for the go around. I executed the maneuver and was cleared to land XXR. After landing I asked Tower what had happened. Controller said they were reviewing the tapes but that they thought I had been instructed to land XXR and instead was attempting to land on XXL; which I admitted I was. Ground cleared me to taxi and park at the normal transient spots in front of the terminal. I advised Ground that airport operations had told me VFR pilots were to park elsewhere. He then took a minute to check and came back on to tell me VFR pilots were to park to the north and he cleared me to taxi straight ahead and park. This was a singular event caused I think by a set of unforeseen circumstances; primarily the distraction of the radio not working properly; my concerns about the clarity of the instructions; parking spot changes and the confusion over same. I cannot explain why my brain translated what I heard into 'left' when I must have heard 'right.' Because I was thinking about all the other factors at play; I relied on that image that first went into my head of landing on the left and proceeded to make it so. It was completely inadvertent. No that this had happened to me; I know it will never happen again.

At that point; we elected to divert to ZZZ2 which allowed us to remain VMC with ideal weather conditions for landing. I continued the ECAM actions deselecting the blue hydraulic electrical pump and then successfully resetting both FAC (Flight Augmentation Computer) 1 and 2 which restored Normal Law. I observed the Captain conducting the flight deck oxygen mask test and heard a prolonged; loud hissing sound. I initially suspected a stuck switch or regulator issue. I had the system page displayed and monitored the oxygen pressure; which was approximately 1870 psi and decreasing rapidly (1820; 1780; then about 1720).The Captain stated that we needed to call maintenance. Two mechanics came onboard. The Captain disconnected his mask and the mechanic replaced it. At that time I had not yet performed my oxygen mask test. A mechanic then asked if my side was normal. Then I conducted my test and it was normal. Shortly afterward; while passengers were onboard and we were preparing for route verification; my oxygen mask began leaking with the same loud hissing sound suddenly.The Captain instructed me that the mask be pulled and disconnected. I did not disconnect it myself; someone reached over and disconnected my mask following the mechanic's direction while they were still in the process of servicing/refilling the system. I just confirmed the Relief Pilot disconnected my mask directed by the mechanic. Almost simultaneously; both Relief Pilot's O2  masks were leaking. I then smelled what seemed like burning protein and realized the tip of my hair had burned. I looked back and observed smoke; sparks; and heard a loud explosion.Due to the high concentration of oxygen in a confined area; I was concerned about the potential for a fire and wanted to evacuate the flight deck immediately. However; the Relief Pilot was positioned behind my seat and I did not want to block the escape route by moving my seat aft; nor did I want to move closer to my oxygen mask cavity. I attempted to exit by squeezing between the center console and my seat. My right ankle became caught in the narrow space; causing me to lose balance and sustain a scratch to my right arm. I was able to move clear. The Captain directed the #1 FA to initiate a rapid deplaning of passengers.Cause: Follow SOP. Do not conduct any procedures outside of established protocol unless specifically directed to do so.
narrative1: After entering the cockpit; I settled in for my pre-flight checks. Ensuring a proper initialization of IRS panel. I then moved to the O2 panel to begin my flow. I removed the mask to  take a breath; hoping to re-seat the pressure demand function. again; to no effect.With O2 venting from the mask; uncontrolled; and bottle pressure dropping; I disconnected the mask; hose coupling; a simple procedure; which stopped the O2 loss; and obvious threat. I called maintenance right away; and the interest of an on-time departure. I wrote the item/faulty mask up in the maintenance logbook.Any individual having an issue with myself or any other Captain; simply uncoupling an O2 mask as the only way to stop an incredibly dangerous environment on an aircraft with over 300 souls on board; and a full tank of fuel; should consider it done under Captains; emergency authority.When maintenance technicians arrived; all procedures/actions from that point on were conducted by maintenance.As far as causal factors are concerned; the maintenance department at ZZZ should be consulted.  A simple observation from myself might be that anyone concerned should reference the AOM for servicing limits under environmental conditions as to temperature and bottle pressure. The system seemed to have been grossly over serviced at a very high pressure. A quick note. Cockpit crew members observe the tank pressure during pre-flight after testing the mask and THEN conducting the O2 mask microphone check. Not before.

narrative: On approach into ZZZZ airport; we were descending to 7000 and noticed traffic flying towards us from below that was climbing out of ZZZZ. The crew had briefed prior to arrival that there would likely be lots of GA traffic in the area that may or may not be transmitting on radios. We had the TCAS mode set to above and below to allow us to see all traffic around us; so we spotted the aircraft that was headed towards us at least 20 miles out. After observing the clouds with the understanding that we would have to descend into the airport VFR and remain clear of clouds; the crew came up with a game plan to make a slight left turn where there was much more blue sky versus the broken layer to the right; and after the left turn; proceed to fly over the airport above traffic pattern altitude and enter the left down for Runway XX. After we had the airport in view within 50 miles; we requested to cancel IFR with ZZZ Center; and before they approved our cancellation; they notified us of the traffic that we had on TCAS; but were not talking to them and did not have an idea where they would be going. We did not have them insight at this point; but decided to continue with the IFR cancellation and focus our efforts on traffic avoidance with what we could see on TCAS while also looking for the traffic visually. As soon as we canceled IFR; I initiated a descent to 3000 feet and started a left turn to avoid the traffic; as they were climbing out and at this point; were about 5 miles ahead of us and about 1500 feet below our current altitude. We could not initiate a right turn due to the cloud layer that would not allow us to descend to the airport VFR. The left turn would give us plenty of clear sky to descend; while also taking us away from the oncoming traffic. Soon after we initiated the left turn and the decent to 3000; we both noticed that the traffic started a right turn towards us; and we attempted to continue more to the left to avoid the traffic. We then got a TCAS TA; and soon after received an RA to climb; noticing that the aircraft was 400 feet below us at this point and still heading towards our direction; even though we had started the turn away from their anticipated path. I immediately and promptly disconnected the Autopilot and initiated max thrust and a pitch up attitude to comply with the RA that was commanding between a 1500 and 2000 ft./min. climb to avoid the traffic that was climbing below us. As I pitched up (we were at 210 kts. at the time in clean config); we experienced the stick shaker for one second which I respected with a slight relief in pitch up to stay below shaker AOA while keeping climbing. This happened in the few seconds that it took for the engines to spool up to APR thrust; and once thrust was achieved; there was no issue with maintaining the climb to meet RA requirements. The RA only lasted a few seconds as we climbed up to 7600 feet from 6500 feet. After we were clear of conflict; the First Officer (FO) got a short visual on the traffic out his right window below us. We were tuned into the AFIS at this point; but they did not provide any traffic avoidance. The First Officer let them know that we had performed a traffic avoidance maneuver and had been giving position reports to them since we were 60 miles out from the airport periodically. After we were clear of the conflict; we reset our altitude to descend to 3000 as planned to fly over the airport and eventually enter the pattern on the left downwind. All three pilots in the flight deck were fully strapped in via five point seatbelt; and did not feel that the maneuver was overly aggressive; but instead was an appropriate reaction to the RA. About one minute after the maneuver; we received a call from the cabin that the First Officer answered. The Flight Attendant called and asked what had happened; and the FO responded that we had performed a traffic avoidance maneuver. The FO asked if everyone was OK; explained that we would be landing in five minutes; and asked how the flight attendants were doing. The flight attendants mentioned that they had taken a stumble; but that they were OK at that point and they occupied their jump seats for landing. They also mentioned that all of the passengers were seated; and there were no reported injuries. At this point; we were glad that everyone was OK; and continued into the airport and landed uneventfully. We did not declare an emergency; since at this point everyone was doing OK and we were clear of any conflicts. After parking at the gate and starting the deplaning process; the forward Flight Attendant Person A let us know that he was feeling dizzy and was having some pain in his ankle and requested to sit down. We also got a better picture of how Person B was feeling; and she said she fell against a wall and had some scratches and soreness on her body from the maneuver. Person A said he had fallen and hit his head during the maneuver; and twisted his ankle. I asked them if they would like to be evaluated by medical personnel; to which they both responded that they would. I immediately asked Operations if they could arrange for medical personnel to give the flight attendants an evaluation on any injuries they may have sustained; as well as to hold boarding for the next flight. There were no customer reported injuries; but the flight attendants said that they felt unable to continue to work back to ZZZ. The station felt that the quickest and safest way to arrange medical personnel to see them would be to have a taxi service take them to the nearest clinic; which they done promptly. Myself and the line check airman that was with us riding the jump seat down to ZZZZ stayed with the plane; while the First Officer went with the flight attendants to the clinic. Over the next hour or two; I as the Captain talked with the Dispatch Coordinators; Maintenance; Operations personnel; and the FO talked with the chief pilots; providing a rundown and answering any questions that they had. We followed the procedures outlined in the FOM; and the airplane required further inspection due to our abrupt maneuver after FDR download. I made a write up in the AML (Aircraft Maintenance Logbook) and logged it with Maintenance Control; making sure to explain that we had achieved APR thrust in the maneuver. We continually received updates on how the flight attendants were doing; despite the poor facilities in the area and lack of good cell service. The flight attendants were given some pain medicine for their muscle soreness; but were not diagnosed with any serious injuries besides what has been described as soreness and bodily scratches. The entire crew was on the same page that the maneuver was necessary to avoid the oncoming traffic; and everyone worked extremely well and professionally together; including Dispatch; Scheduling; Maintenance and management teams. The ZZZZ Operations Station was extremely helpful throughout the whole process in arranging all of the logistics. There were no customer reported injuries during this entire incident.
narrative1: While we were on approach to ZZZZ airport on Day 0 coming through around 7000 feet we had noticed traffic who had just departed ZZZZ; and was headed roughly in our direction. We had discussed how there would be a lot of GA traffic due to it being non radar; and that they may or may not be communicating on frequency. We knew due to the location of the cloud layer off our right that we would need to maneuver left with the descent to get below any potential occurrence of IMC as we had to maintain VFR. Our game plan was simple. We had the airport in sight; and would begin a left turn descending to 3000 which is above pattern altitude; then over fly midfield for a left downwind entry for runway XX. I had also been making position reports on Comm 2 throughout this hand off to cancel IFR with center. ZZZ Center told us to cancel IFR when the airport was in sight and once we had located it we stated we were ready to cancel. As the controller was handing us off he advised us of traffic which was the same target we had on TCAS; no one was talking to them as they were VFR so we acknowledged the traffic and canceled IFR. Once canceled we began the left turn and the descent to 3000. The left turn was also sufficient to avoid the traffic on its current trajectory. The target was roughly 5-7 miles away and about 1750 feet below us. We had briefed and planned this move both for the protection of traffic avoidance and maintaining VFR.  Once the turn and descent began we almost simultaneously noticed the target had also turned further right now placing them headed towards us. We discussed slowing the descent to provide spacing and increased the left turn to provide even more spacing. Shortly after came the TA followed very quickly by the RA with the target showing about 400 ft below us. The CA responded immediately clicking off the AP and going Max Thrust with a pitch attitude to initiate the escape. I believe due to being at almost idle power setting due to the intent on descending it took a few seconds to get the engines to spool to max power. I think we were around 200-210 knots when this began. The stick shaker occurred very briefly followed by a reduction in pitch and achieving max power which allowed the aircraft to reach what was commanded by TCAS for resolution. As we cleared the conflict I believe I saw that last bit of the tail of the aircraft pass behind us as I had not been able to see him through the entire maneuver. We leveled off and I announced on AFIS (Airborne Flight Information System) of the RA with the intent to recommit to the descent and approach for runway XX. Around this time the Cabin called asking what had happened in which I explained the situation; they stated they had taken a tumble but were ok. I asked multiple times during this conversation to ensure they were ok as well as if the Pax were ok. They assured me they were able to continue. We completed the flight as normal. Upon parking and opening the flight deck door we were made aware that the FWD FA Person A was dizzy and needed to take a seat. The CA upon talking with Person A asked Ops for medics to check him out as it appeared the symptoms were not improving; it was also determined that the AFT FA Person B had gotten some scratches from the fall. A taxi was called to take the FAs to the clinic. The captain and I got together to game plan the situation; and we determined I would go with the FAs as I had a working phone and he would stay and tend to the aircraft and dealing with Maintenance; Ops; Scheduling. I was at the clinic for a couple hours where I was sure to call the on call chief and give a brief statement and update as to the current situation and to answer any questions he had. After a short while I returned to the aircraft to assist as needed. The Ops at ZZZZ were extremely professional and truly helped along the process as best as possible. I also commend my Captain for handling everything extremely professionally.We believed due to the proper entry into the pattern and the position of the outbound traffic from ZZZ1 we had best set ourselves up by making the left turn to descend under the deck for our turn inbound to enter the pattern. The jet that departed never spoke to anyone; turned into our track and continued a climb right into us.
synopsis: CRJ-900 flight crew reported an NMAC with a departing airplane at destination. Crew took evasive action and continued to a landing.

narrative: This aircraft had a right Air Conditioning (AC) pack that was inoperative. The release had several steps associated with configuring this panel during several phases of flight. The MEL required takeoff and landing to be bleeds off.The operation was normal until the after takeoff checklist. Following the steps for the right pack inoperative; there was a short period of time that the aircraft was climbing while depressurized.Maybe Boeing did a copy/paste and didn't think about reversing switches? The left pack inoperative would have a slightly different procedure; however; because the isolation valve remains open. So it's not exactly a mirror image procedure.Following the MEL steps for the right pack inoperative; the isolation valve is closed; so when I turn the engine 2 bleed air on; it doesn't do anything. The next step is turning the APU bleed air off; which is what started the depressurization. I paused for a couple seconds to allow some stabilization like would be done in a normal bleeds off takeoff.After realizing the issue; I quickly turned the engine 1 bleed air switch on. The aircraft began pressurizing again; and there was no further issue.For the right pack inoperative after takeoff checklist; the engine bleed air switches should've been reversed. Yes; engine 1 bleed air and APU bleed air would be on at the same time potentially causing the dual bleed air light. However; this is addressed in the notes of the MEL already so Boeing is aware and is OK with this light for a few seconds that it might be illuminated.The risk here is something like this happening at a high elevation airport and triggering the CABIN ALTITUDE warning.There's one other minor issue that could be addressed as well. For the landing checklist; it tells us to turn the APU bleed air on. However; there's no mention of turning the APU on prior to that point. So here's another potential of depressurization.
synopsis: B737 Captain reported the right pack was inoperative and while following the after-takeoff checklist with the bleeds off as required by the MEL; the aircraft was depressurized for a short period of time while climbing.

We asked to use the ILS but the controller notified us that ILS approach end tower visibility was reported as being poorer. We accepted the RNAV and briefed and set up for the approach. This was compressed due to our closeness to the field and the fact that the approach was now straight in vs opposite direction. However; we completed required checklists and briefings and upon reaching the FAF altitude everything seemed to be in order and the aircraft was properly configured. I remember seeing the autopilot capture the FAF altitude at 8700MSL; at which point the captain rolled in the missed approach altitude. We verified GPS APPR at 2 miles; computed a groundspeed at 1 mi; and at .2 prior to the FAF the captain rolled in a VSI and began his descent. I noticed that the VNAV snowflake was at full top deflection already; at which point I cross checked our altitude and noticed that we were already quite a bit lower than FAF altitude; in the vicinity of 8200MSL. At first I told the captain to level off; but I quickly realized we had probably been below FAF altitude since before the FAF; almost simultaneously the GPWS issued a 'Terrain; Terrain' alert; so I called for a missed approach. The captain executed the missed and we took vectors out to check our fuel and elect whether or not to try another approach. After discussing the incident and thoroughly preparing for another approach; we attempted the RNAV again. This time it proceeded without incident; though we did not see the runway at minimums due to poorer than reported visibility and performed another missed approach; ultimately diverting to our alternate. Cause: I believe causal factors included being rushed on the arrival/approach; which gave us little time to set up and probably caused us to become task saturated and more likely to miss errors. We did not complete all checklists until on the approach; which tied up our attention on non-flight path items. Also at the time; due to rapidly changing conditions; tower was not recording the full ATIS which required us to receive the complete weather report from the controller once on tower frequency; another source of distraction during a critical phase of flight. We probably became too fixated on the 3-2-1 checks prior to the FAF at the expense of a more complete cross-check. Although I do not know exactly where the descent below FAF altitude was actually initiated; I suspect it was slow and gradual; making it easier to miss.Suggestions: We could have built time for ourselves on the approach by requesting delay vectors or slowing earlier; which would have eased the pace and given us mental headroom. We should have considered discontinuing the approach when we were still running checklists while commencing it. As flight path management is always primary; we should have been incorporating the altitude more regularly into the crosscheck just prior to the FAF to detect a deviation; and were probably too trusting that the autopilot would keep us at the previously captured altitude (assuming we actually captured it and did not misinterpret indications).
synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported during their approach in IMC conditions descending below the FAF altitude resulting in a GPWS terrain alert and the flight crew executing a go around.  The flight crew's second approach also resulted in a go around and the flight returned to the departure airport.

Prior to commencing his flight; I reviewed his cross country planning and determined that the entire route would be VFR; and the winds would stay well within his demonstrated capability. It is not unusual for incidents such as this to occur in the training environment; especially at a student pilot level. However; I plan on taking corrective action by having him file a report; obtain further training through the WINGS program; and extensive flight training focusing on maintaining directional control on landing; with and without a crosswind component.

narrative: Climbing through 16;000 feet the First Officer's (FO's) airspeed indicator failed with a red flag. After checking all my instruments I determined my airspeed indications and engine indications were completely normal. I then told the FO that I had the flight controls and the radios and to get out the QRH and go to the back of any tabbed page and look for 'AIRSPEED'. The only checklist for our situation is the known as the 'AIRSPEED UNRELIABLE' checklist. Having done many sim sessions I am very aware of this 8 page checklist that covers a myriad of possible airspeed malfunctions and things can get extremely confusing when trying to navigate this checklist; and how our relatively stable situation could be easily rectified by doing a simple test. I have seen the exact malfunction on the ground perhaps over a hundred times during my career.It is a very common maintenance issue. Maintenance will be called out to the plane and will simply recycle the airspeed circuit breaker. My intention was to return to ZZZ regardless of whether the First Officer's airspeed was working or not and then write it up upon arrival. But if we could get the First Officer's airspeed indicator working again I would most likely not need to request priority handling. So; I instructed the First Officer to find the First Officers airspeed circuit breaker but not to pull it yet. When the circuit beaker was found and we both agreed that that circuit breaker was; absolutely in fact for his airspeed indicator; I instructed him to pull it and reset it. The result was exactly what happens on the ground. The airspeed indicator reset and went to the appropriate airspeed. In our case it went to 296 kts.; the same as my airspeed indicator. I then tested if his airspeed indicator would follow mine by simply accelerating to 320 kts. As we accelerated my airspeed indicator increased normally and his stayed frozen on 296. I knew immediately that we would need to request priority handling. Moments later; due to the discrepancy between our airspeeds; his airspeed indicator again flagged out.We requested to return to ZZZ and requested priority handling. We landed on Runway XXR with no incidents; returned to gate and wrote up the maintenance issue in the logbook. I recognize; as a Captain I am to simply followed the QRH checklist; however; given the circumstances; I was very concerned about making a relatively simple problem far worse by trying to navigate a very complex checklist in our QRH and end up possibly making our situation more dangerous.

narrative: Flight diversion recovery flight to ZZZ. On the recovery flight to ZZZ after landing poor taxi conditions lead to very slow taxi to the gate. Approaching gate XX the Captain lined up with what we thought was the lead in line for the gate as the ground crew scrambled to get vehicles out of the gate area. The line was completely obscured by snow and ice. Once we were lined up we started to taxi into position almost immediately the left wing walker threw up an X with his wands because they had missed a baggage cart that was in the safety area. The Captain stopped and we waited as two of the walkers tried to push it out of the way by hand. They moved it and signaled that we were clear to start pulling in again. We were moving super slowly; cautious of the ice and trying to find the line the whole taxi but especially when entering the gate area. As we were pulling in the Captain noticed the wing walker on his side throw up the X again as we had gotten close to the baggage cart they attempted moving. The Captain stepped on the brakes in an attempt to stop the aircraft but we started sliding on the ice and slid to the left bumping the baggage cart.The aircraft only came to rest after the Captain cracked the thrust reversers. After investigation and coordination with the ground crew and airport ops with clearance we decided it was best to have the tug back us out and tow us in rather than doing it under our own power. Which was a good decision because even the ground ops tow vehicle was not able to get traction with us. The ramp was sprayed and sanded twice before they got the grip to get us to the gate. After we arrived to the gate we ran all procedures as necessary. On post-flight walk around it was found to have a cracked nav light cover with no other damage to aircraftI believe the cause for this event was primarily the poor ramp conditions first and foremost. Had the ramp not been icy; or snow covered the aircraft would likely have been much closer to centerline to start and would not have slid further towards the cart during braking. I think that had either the ground or flight crew stopped and said that the ramp needed to be cleared first that would have saved this event from happening. This is very easy in hindsight but is something I will pay more attention to in the future and not be afraid to refuse a parking spot. I think a secondary cause was the ground crew giving little to no directions as we were entering the ramp area while having better reference to where we should and should not have been; the marshaller had sticks up and was waving straight in until the walker signed the X.In the future I will be more forward about refusing a parking spot if ramp conditions are poor or at minimum request extra caution from the ground crew.  Better training for ground and flight crews about what are and are not acceptable ramp conditions would also likely result in better safety and fewer events like this happening in the future

narrative: During a landing rollout in a Piper PA-32R (Saratoga); the aircraft experienced a violent; high-frequency vibration and a sharp pull to the left; resulting in a low-speed runway excursion into the grass. No damage was sustained to the aircraft or airport property.Initial Assessment. Initial symptoms; including a 'humming' noise during taxi and an apparent lack of symmetric braking; suggested a mechanical hydraulic failure or master cylinder bypass.Post-Event Analysis and Corrective Actions. I have taken the following proactive steps to ensure this does not happen again:Technical Consultation.  I consulted with a certified A&P mechanic to inspect the braking system. While the hardware was found to be within limits; the inspection highlighted the extreme sensitivity of this specific aircraft's braking system compared to other models in the fleet.Diagnosis of Human Factors. Through diagnostic taxi testing with the mechanic; I identified that a subconscious 'left-leaning' posture during the flare; combined with an off-center seating position; led to unintended 'brake pressure' on the left toe brake.Instructional Intervention: I have scheduled additional proficiency training with a flight instructor recognized as a subject matter expert in this specific airframe. SOP Implementation: I am incorporating a standardized 'Cockpit Stance Checklist' into my landing flow; which includes seat positioning. Ensuring specific seat-track notches for optimal leg angle.Neutral Position Check: A 'heels-on-the-ground' verification callout during the flare to ensure zero brake engagement. Conclusion. This event was a combination of aircraft-specific sensitivity and a subtle ergonomic error in pilot posture. By standardizing my 'stance' and enhancing my tactile connection to the machine; I have mitigated the risk of future directional control issues. And currently doing instruction with the CFI that is also most proficient with this particular type of aircraft for proficiency and familiarization before I use this particular aircraft for personal uses. My goal is proficiency and safety. I took the time to fully investigate the matter cooperatively with the club; A&P and other CFI; to address the issues and make sure that we resolved the problem.

narrative: During a CFII training flight in my aircraft; I was teaching my student how to give vectors to final for the RNAV XX approach into ZZZ with WAAS (Wide Area Augmentation System) disabled. We; Aircraft X; a Piper PA-28 gave ourselves VTF (Vectors to Final) at 2000ft MSL approximately 8nm NE from the airport. We turned into and captured the FAC (Flight Augmentation Computer) of RNAV XX with no other traffic on an approach into ZZZ for runway XX. We descended 500fpm until reaching 1500ft MSL; the FAF altitude listed on the approach plate. We were driving to the final approach fix; level at 1500msl approx 6nm from the airport when Aircraft Y made a 10nm final call over the ZZZ CTAF frequency. The Citation did not appear on our traffic map on the G1000 nxi MFD (Multi-funcion Flight Display)  until he was nearly 1000ft above us and I saw the traffic on the MFD display a downward arrow; indicating the Citation's descent. In a matter of less than 30 seconds; the Citation was approximately less than 1 mile behind Aircraft X; and 500ft above me. This is when I got the TCAS alert and immediately grabbed flight controls and took evasive action; banking the aircraft nearly 60 degrees and turning 90 degrees to avoid a collision from the Citation.My airspeed at the time of the evasion was 78kts and the citation; Aircraft Y was 201kts according to ADS-B exchange data. I started the evasion at XA:36:30. If I had not taken the aggressive and immediately maneuver; I confidently believe the Citation would have crashed into me; Aircraft X and killing myself and my student. No radio contact was established with the pilot of Aircraft Y  outside of his initial 10nm final call over CTAF and a short final radio call that I could pick up. After rolling wings level I made a radio call telling the pilot of Aircraft Y that I had to break off the approach to avoid being hit by him. He never replied to the radio call. I gave VTF again for the approach into ZZZ and landed safely. Prevailing conditions of the flight were VFR; cloud ceilings were approximately 3000-4000AGL. My aircraft; Aircraft X maintained VFR cloud clearance requirements of 500ft below cloud layers at all times during this flight. I do not believe the pilot of Aircraft Y ever saw us on the approach. IF the pilot of Aircraft Y was on an IFR flight plan shooting an approach into an airport with a known flight school; with pilots making radio calls at every phase of flight; I question why he would shoot an IAP going that fast; or why ATC would clear him for the approach while my aircraft is on the final approach segment.
narrative1: Aircraft: Cessna Citation CJ3+ (Aircraft X)Operation: Part 91 IFRDeparture: ZZZ1Destination: ZZZI departed ZZZ1 as PIC of a Cessna Citation CJ3+; Aircraft X; operating under an IFR flight plan to ZZZ. The clearance was direct ZZZZZ; then direct ZZZ; maintaining 3;000 feet. We picked up our IFR clearance at approximately 1;500 feet after departure.Weather conditions were IMC above approximately 2;500-3;000 feet MSL. While level at 3;000 feet in IMC enroute to ZZZZZ; we were handed off from ZZZ Center to ZZZ Approach Control. ZZZ Approach instructed us to climb to 3;400 feet and cleared us direct ZZZZZ for the RNAV (GPS) Runway XX approach into ZZZ; with a crossing restriction of at or above 3;300 feet at ZZZZZ. We complied with all instructions.Multiple aircraft were observed operating in the traffic pattern at ZZZ via ADS-B; and we had been monitoring this traffic since departure. One aircraft in particular appeared aligned with Runway XX and possibly flying the same RNAV approach. Upon reaching ZZZZZ and beginning descent; we broke out of IMC at approximately 2;800-3;000 feet MSL.At approximately 10 miles from the airport; we reported a 10-mile final for the RNAV Runway XX approach. ZZZ Approach issued a traffic advisory for an aircraft approximately four to five miles ahead of us and below; descending. We had already observed this aircraft on ADS-B and acquired it visually after breaking out of the clouds.Based on closure rate; we determined we were overtaking the traffic ahead and that continuing straight-in would likely reduce spacing. ZZZ Approach was not in communication with that aircraft; and it appeared to be operating VFR.To improve spacing and integrate safely with pattern traffic; we elected to cancel IFR and continue visually. Approximately 5-6 miles from the airport; we initiated a left turn to maneuver toward the published ZZZZZ1 visual reporting point; which is identified in the enhanced operating procedures as the preferred VFR entry for a 45-degree downwind to Runway XX.As we began the left turn; the aircraft ahead also initiated a left turn. At that time; we were approximately three miles behind and slightly above that aircraft. No prior radio transmission was heard from that aircraft indicating its intentions. The turn resulted in a temporary converging flight path.Upon assessing the geometry and maintaining visual contact; I determined the safest course of action was to discontinue the left turn and re-establish on the extended final approach course. We remained in visual contact at all times.During the convergence; a momentary TCAS Resolution Advisory was generated. The advisory was brief and consistent with the converging geometry. Visual separation was maintained; and the RA cleared as lateral spacing increased. No maneuver beyond normal course correction was required.The other aircraft continued turning away from our course and was no longer a factor. Shortly thereafter; the aircraft transmitted that it was breaking off the approach. Another aircraft on downwind stated that he would extend his downwind to provide spacing. We reported a 4-mile final and landed uneventfully at ZZZ. Visual separation was maintained at all times; and the flight concluded without further incident.Contributing Factors:IMC-to-VMC transition during approach phaseHigh volume of VFR training traffic at a non-towered airportMixed IFR arrivals and VFR practice approach operationsClosure rate differences between turbine IFR traffic and training aircraftLimited radio coordination from some aircraft in the patternHuman Factors: Situational awareness was maintained through continuous ADS-B monitoring and visual acquisition upon breakout. The combination of IMC-to-VMC transition; closure rate on slower traffic; and multiple aircraft in the pattern created compressed decision-making during a high-workload phase of flight. The brief TCAS RA reinforced the importance of conservative spacing when integratingmixed IFR and VFR traffic.Safety Consideration: This event highlights the operational challenges of mixing IFR arrivals with high volumes of VFR training traffic in marginal VFR conditions at non-towered airports. While conditions were legally VFR; arriving aircraft descending from higher altitudes and higher speeds may require instrument procedures for descent; which can compress spacing when pattern traffic is established ahead.Increased emphasis on communication clarity and conservative spacing during such mixed-traffic scenarios may help reduce similar occurrences.Corrective Actions / Lessons Learned: Consider earlier speed reduction or spacing adjustments when overtaking slower traffic on instrument approaches into busy training environments.Continue proactive ADS-B monitoring and early visual acquisition during IMC-to-VMC transitions.Maintain conservative lateral and longitudinal spacing when traffic intentions are unclear.Exercise heightened vigilance when integrating IFR arrival profiles into active VFR pattern operations.

narrative: This topic could have been raised before but I thought I would bring it to your attention. In Day 0 the FAA issued NOTAM for the CLT RNAV (GPS) Y Runway 36C. It is a NOTAM telling you to disregard the note about LNAV procedure NA during simultaneous operations. The issue I have is imbedded later on within the same NOTAM text it indirectly addresses a totally different approach; the ILS 36C. It says the I-DQG ILS or glideslope out of service. There are at least 2 or 3 other NOTAMs for Runway 36C but none of them call out the glideslope except for the RNAV NOTAM. You do not use the I-DQS ILS for the RNAV approach.Last night we were given a late runway change to the visual to 36C after setting up for and briefing the approach to 36L. The standard is usually to back up a visual approach with an ILS. We quickly reviewed the NOTAMs for 36C and the FO set it up and we briefed the visual backed up by the ILS 36C. We were vectored across the field coming in from the north to a right downwind for 36C. In the downwind vector; from a previous flight; I remembered there was a trick" with 36C. As I re-reviewed the NOTAMs I caught the imbedded ILS glideslope note within the RNAV 36C NOTAM. We changed the approach again in the box to the RNAV 36C; re-briefed; and except for the Tower Controller talking to us during the touchdown and high speed rollout; we made an uneventful landing.My question is; why is this not a separate NOTAM for the ILS 36C highlighting the ILS or glideslope out of service and how can this concern be relayed to the FAA?Cause: The ILS 36C I-DQS ILS or glideslope out of service should be its own NOTAM for the ILS 36C; NOT imbedded within the RNAV 36C NOTAM."

narrative: The First Officer (FO) and I had completed the Before Push Checklist and were waiting to hear from the tug driver that they were ready for brake release. I said to the FO; it seems like they're having headset issues... it looks like they're ready for brake release; why don't you call for push. I then held my hands up for the ramper to see my clenched fists and I opened both fists to show all 10 fingers and I released the aircraft brakes.  saw the ramper repeat my hand signal to the tug driver. I then noticed the ramper who was giving me hand signals move hurriedly toward the tug driver. I immediately moved my feet up on the toe brakes and gently applied pressure to slow the aircraft movement and bring it to a stop. If I had to guess; the aircraft moved somewhere between 5 and 8 feet before I brought it to a stop.I set the parking brake and we waited until the ground crew found an operable headset. Upon completion of our ensuing pushback; I asked the ramper to submit a safety report to document this event and told him that I would do the same.

narrative: - This was a two Captain flight crew operating flight #XXXX; with service from ZZZ to ZZZ1. This was the second flight of the day in the airplane and no major mechanical abnormalities were experienced during the first flight. The only notable event was a TLO light (Left Side) that illuminated during cruise. Person A  served as the First Officer and Pilot Monitoring during both the first and second flights. I had not flown in 18 days as a result of a previous reported incident and Person A  was helping me regain proficiency in the airplane.- In ZZZ; the aircraft started up normally and we taxied to the runup area on the 1 taxiway. Upon completing the Before Takeoff Checklist; and with both engines within all parameters; we were given taxi instructions to RWY XX and then cleared for departure. - Both engines eventually developed full power at 103 percent and we rotated around 72 knots. I noted that the engines were surging at times but appeared to smooth out with more airspeed and prior to rotation. When we were around 200 feet above the runway; the left engine began to make a loud popping noise and the power reduced to around 70%.- There was a substantial amount of runway left in front of us as RWY XX is 10;400 feet long. Since we had a headwind and variable crosswind gusting to 22 knots; I initially pulled back power in order to land back on the runway. This is what I had briefed in the Takeoff Briefing.- At this point; Person A stated that we should keep flying and to continue our climb straight ahead. I considered it and then moved both throttles back to full power. We started climbing again. The engine popped one more time but did not lose power. - We were able to climb without incident to 1;000 ft and Person A  notified ATC that we needed to return to the airport for landing. ATC was able to accommodate us immediately back for a left pattern for a return landing on RWY XX. The landing and rollout were uneventful and we notified ZZZ Ops that we had returned. We also informed them that Aircraft X needed maintenance attention and was not airworthy. We also told them that we would need another aircraft to fly our passengers to ZZZ1.- Person A contacted Maintenance Control while I wrote up the incident in the Aircraft Maintenance Log. Person A  then contacted Operations  to inform them of the situation. He was then instructed to contact Person B; the On-Call Duty Manager. He did so and we both chatted with Person B on speaker phone. He supported our decision to return and guided us through the process.- We obtained another aircraft and were able to fly our passengers to ZZZ1 without incident. We remained in our same crew positions for the second attempt of this flight; with myself as Pilot Flying and Person A  as Pilot Monitoring.

narrative: While at the gate in ZZZ the aircraft displayed a L OIL LVL LOW status message; with the left engine at shut off prior to blocking out. We (the first officer and I) checked the oil level on the menu page. It indicated that the left engine oil level was at 51%. After referencing the CRJ 900 QRH 0-XX Table 0-1: Oil Level Indication and Duration Table; we determined to be in the 10 hour flight range and above the Do not dispatch" minimum. We continued with the flight as normal. The APU was deferred on this flight so we executed a right engine start at the gate using ground supply air and electrical power. After the right engine start was complete; we pushed back from the gate and taxied to the XXR deice pad on a single engine using all standard procedures. Completed Type 1 deicing process and then began our taxi to runway XXL for departure via Taxiway 1. While on Taxiway 1; the First Officer and I completed a cross bleed start to the left engine using bleed air from the right engine as directed by the QRH. Once the left engine start was complete; all normal delayed start and before takeoff checklist and procedures were completed. In addition to that; the oil level of both engines were check via the menu page and found to be at an acceptable level for departure. Departed runway XXL at ZZZ with no adverse indications. Completed a normal climb to our cruise altitude of FL310 with no adverse indications. Following standard procedures and checklist at every phase of flight. Sometime after reaching our cruise altitude; about 10 minutes after level at FL310; I (the captain and pilot flying) checked the oil levels once again via the menu page. Upon checking the oil levels I found that the left engine was at 15%. We began monitoring the left engine indications as directed by the CRJ900 QRH 0-XX Table 0-1. At that time I began turning to the L ENG OIL PRESS checklist in the QRH just in case it would be needed. About 2-3 minutes after the First Officer and I began monitoring the left engine indications; we received a L ENG OIL PRESS warning message; chime and aural alert. At that time I handed the QRH to the First Officer; I remained the pilot and took over radio communication control; and we began running the CRJ 900 QRH 1-XY L ENG OIL PRESS and subsequent CRJ 900 QRH 1-XZ ENGINE FAILURE/INFLIGHT ENGINE SHUTDOWN checklist. Because both pilots confirmed that the L ENG OIL PRESS warning message was present and the oil pressure was below limits we continued with the intentional shutdown as directed by the checklist. All the while we remained in constant contact with ATC. Primarily ZZZCenter. After the left engine was brought to ideal the aircraft was unable to maintain FL310. So; with clearance from ATC; we descended to FL250. By the time we reached FL250 the left engine was fully shutdown. The aircraft was able to maintain FL250 with right thrust set to tracking. But I elected to descend lower to FL210 in an effort to "take it easy" on the operative engine. Once at FL210 all checklist were completed and that is when I requested priority handling with ZZZ center; informed dispatch and maintenance control via ACARS; and notified the flight attendants of the situation. We did try to contact dispatch through ARINC (Radio) frequency XXX.XX; but had no reply from City X radio. When informing the flight attendants; I told them "the left engine was intentionally shutdown by us to prevent damage. The aircraft is still flying perfectly normal. We are counting to ZZZ1 as planned. We are going to land at ZZZ1 and taxi to the gate just like a normal flight. At this time; the is no need to inform the passengers. If there is need I will inform them. You don't not need to prepare for an evacuation. If anything changes to the situation I will update you". After the flight attendants were informed; the First Officer and I reconfirmed the decision to continue to ZZZ1. We completed all briefings and checklists as we made our descent into ZZZ1. While talking toZZZ approach control; we requested to land on runway XY due to favorable headwinds. Upon switching to tower control; they informed us that fire and rescue would be standing by on the ground. The aircraft was landed safely on runway XZ and made a right turnoff at 2. After landing fire and rescue asked if we needed assistance. I informed them that no assistance was required and they replied by saying they would follow us to the ramp and then head back to the station. We taxied to gate XX; parked; shutdown the right engine and passed the aircraft over to station maintenance personnel.Cause:  The conditions that led to a loss of oil pressure inflight are unknown to me at this time. The post flight inspection revealed a large oil stain under the cowling of the left engine. Indicating a possible oil leak that possibly led to the loss of oil pressure."

narrative: During engine start; we received ENG1 GEN FAULT. We followed ECAM procedures and it came back online. I entered it in the ELB (Electronic Logbook); called Dispatch; and finished the procedure with Maintenance Control. We called for taxi; was cleared to Runway XX; taxied out; and departed. At approximately 1500' both the FO (First Officer) and I noticed a sort of shimmy; as though the gear was still down; flaps were down; or maybe the speed brakes were out; but all was normal. It did not seem to me like an engine vibration and we didn't notice any parameters showing high vibes; so we continued. On climb out; beginning at ~3000'; received multiple transient ENG 1 THRUST LEVER DISAGREE ECAMs. All engine parameters were normal on both engines and the thrust levers were perfectly aligned; so I felt that continuing was the best plan. On the 4th or 5th ECAM; it stayed up almost long enough to run the full procedure; but then it went away again. It came back again as we were passing ~23;000'. It was no longer transient and I decided we needed to start back to the field. I asked the FO to pass the info to Dispatch. They messaged back that they would get the ball rolling. ATC turned us back and began our descent. The ECAM cleared; but we had already started turning back so we continued. We requested priority handling in the turn back to ZZZ. To this point; both engines had been performing normally and it seemed like it may have been an indication issue. On level off; ENG 1 did not spool up; staying at flight idle. The plane commanded LEVER MCT (Maximum Continuous Thrust); and performance went into EO (Engine-Out). At this point; I asked the FO to request ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) support upon arrival. They said the trucks would be ready. We revisited procedures and both agreed that everything had been completed; to include a report to the (LFA) Lead Flight Attendant. We were vectored to the ILS XX; but the tailwind during the return pushed us too much and we were vectored around for further descent. Upon the next vectors; I thought ATC had requested a ten degree turn to the left; which I did and then our course was promptly blown too close to the localizer - apparently they had given me a RIGHT course correction. They vectored us out once again and gave us much more room to catch the localizer. We commenced the approach; and landed without any further issues. At some point; when were exiting the runway I smelled something odd; so I requested ARFF scan ENG 1 just in case there was something internal to the nacelle. ARFF completed the entire aircraft scan and reported no further issues with the FLIR. I requested to continue into the terminal; to which we were given clearance. At this point; a passenger got up and used the bathroom before the FAs could stop them. Once they sat back down; we continued to taxi to the gate; shut down normally; and deplaned the pax. I'm fairly certain; with everything going on and the previously transient ECAM; something was missed in the approach. We revisited the procedures; although we briefed the passengers later than I would have liked; making sure all the information was covered. I feel like everything was covered; maybe poorly and out of sequence; but so many things were happening that I was doing a lot just staying in front of the problem and making sure that I was prioritizing flying the aircraft. We were constantly checking in with each other to make sure each of us were up to speed and also SA.
narrative1: After ENG 1 started and stabilized; we received an ECAM: ENG 1 GEN FAULT. We completed the ECAM procedures; and the generator came back online. We contacted Dispatch; completed the ELB (Electronic Logbook) entry; and cross-verified the information with each other. We were cleared to taxi to Runway XX and subsequently departed.During climb; at approximately 1;000-1;500 feet AGL; we noticed a brief irregular vibration; similar to what it would feel like if a gear door were open or the speed brakes were partially extended. All system parameters appeared normal; and the vibration lasted less than 10 seconds. We elected to continue the climb.Beginning at approximately 3;000 feet; we received an ECAM: ENG 1 THRUST LEVER DISAGREE. The message cleared few seconds later. We verified engine parameters; thrust lever positions; and associated indications; all were normal. We assessed it as a transient condition and continued the climb. The same ECAM message reappeared multiple times (approximately 4-5 times). Then the ECAM remained long enough to begin and finish the ECAM procedure; but it cleared again.At approximately FL230; the ECAM returned. We requested ATC to level off to properly accomplish the checklist and assess the situation. While leveling at approximately FL280; we decided to return to ZZZ. We immediately notified Dispatch via ACARS of the ECAM message and our decision to return to ZZZ. We requested priority handling with ATC and advised them of our intention to return; including souls on board and fuel remaining. ATC cleared us direct to ZZZ.Until and during descent; both engines initially displayed matched parameters within normal limits. However; while descending; ENG 1 remained at idle and did not respond as expected. The system prompted us to set the thrust lever to MCT (Maximum Continuous Thrust). Considering the ENG 1 condition and the overweight landing; we requested ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) support from ATC.We completed all required coordination with ATC; Dispatch; the flight attendants; and passengers. After setting up for the approach and completing the approach briefing; we requested vectors to allow time to accomplish the overweight landing checklist. Upon completion; we cross-verified all checklist items to ensure nothing was missed.We were vectored for the ILS Runway XX but were unable to intercept the localizer. Requested another vector; cleared for the approach.We landed on Runway XX and vacated the runway. We stopped on Taxiway 1 to allow fire trucks to inspect the aircraft. ARFF reported no abnormalities. We contacted Operations frequency to advise them of our situation and assigned gate. We then taxied to the gate; shut down the engines; and the passengers deplaned without further incident. Being only approximately 50-60 miles from the departure airport; the repeated ECAM messages and evolving situation created a high workload environment. It was not a comfortable experience operationally. In hindsight; I could have taken additional time to review the Manual more thoroughly and attempt to gain a deeper; more systematic understanding of the malfunction. We also could have delegated tasks more efficiently to better manage workload and reduce task saturation.This report serves as a reflection on the event and improvement. While we strive for precision and professionalism; we recognize that we are not immune to human limitations.
synopsis: A320 crew reported numerous transient 'ENG 1 THRUST LEVER DISAGREE'  ECAMS during climb-out. During descent for return to departure airport ENG 1 failed to accelerate when commanded; but the flight continued to a safe landing.

I; as the FO and pilot flying; disconnected the autopilot in an attempt to halt the climb and descend to 10;000 feet. I did not reset the altitude selector to 10;000 feet; and the aircraft briefly accelerated to 325 knots while descending from 11;500 feet to 10;000 feet. Captain A then held the throttles at idle to assist with deceleration and directed me to set 10;000 feet in the altitude selector. The aircraft returned to a normal speed; and the over-speed condition lasted approximately 3-5 seconds.ATC asked about our intentions three times; we confirmed that we would remain at 10;000 feet while we assessed and addressed the issue. After the third inquiry; ATC vectored us to our assigned heading. Cabin altitude subsequently returned to normal; and we continued the flight without further incident.Cause: I am providing a cause narrative for the ferry flight from ZZZ to document the factors that contributed to the cabin pressurization event and to outline corrective actions. Vent flaps on the three non-primary cabin doors were not closed and secured; a condition that went unidentified prior to departure. This oversight stemmed from a lack of ferry-specific checks and limited experience; which led to the misinterpretation of EICAS messages as indicating slide arming rather than the actual vent flap status. The situation was further stressed by limited ferry-flight experience and delayed identification of the vent flap closure issue and misreading of cues from the EICAS system. A positive exchange of controls allowed me to close the vent flaps on the remaining doors; after which cabin pressure returned to normal and the flight proceeded without further incident. Another jet taxiing from the ramp to Runway 35; Myself in overhead left traffic for Runway 35 having clearly called number 1 for landing during coordination with the small aircraft on the other downwind and the jet holding short for takeoff; and last----Aircraft Y coming straight-in to Runway 35 making distance calls inbound to 'Cochran.' I didn't clearly hear the jet make a radio call. But I don't doubt the word of the other crew at debriefing given the factors described below. In any case; the crew did not recognize that the pattern was full at the airport they were approaching; and they did not coordinate their plan to come straight-in with any of the other aircraft using the airport.As I was descending from base to final; I was a bit high on approach. I received a TCAS TA while turning final. After rolling out on final the displayed threat aircraft was 100 feet directly beneath me (solid-yellow circle -100).No TCAS RA was issued since both aircraft were configured for landing below 1000 feet. This situation was something like a perfect storm that somewhat defanged the TCAS. Since the initial TA showed yellow and stayed yellow (20-48 seconds); the urgency of the situation was confused; and my initial reflex was to think that there was another aircraft in the vicinity of the airport; but not one on approach. It took me a moment after establishing myself on final to note that the threat symbol; and myself were collocated on the TCAS screen with only 100 feet of separation.Since I did not have full SA or visual contact with the threat aircraft; I was sufficiently confused by the situation to abandon the approach. I executed a go-around and re-entered the left downwind as Aircraft Y landed and rolled out on the runway.A second approach was safely completed without incident.All local traffic were coordinating using the phrase 'Thermal area traffic' to identify the airport and operations. This is normal at this airport even though the airport is called 'Jaqueline Cochrane Regional' airport. The word Thermal contains 2 syllables. The official name of the airport contains 7. This CTAF frequency is often very congested due to the uncontrolled traffic volume at this airport. It was congested at the time of this event.The crew was unfamiliar(first-time to the airport); and did not associate 'Thermal' with the airport they were landing at. As a consequence; they didn't participate in coordination efforts with the other aircraft using the airport. They rightly pointed out on debriefing that 'Thermal' is not printed on any of the airport plates. Thus; local habituated knowledge and telephony understandably contributed to all affected crews' loss of SA.Also a contributing factor was the inhibition of a TCAS RA at low altitude. The yellow-circle symbol did not reflexively indicate the proximate danger present during this event. Even so; without the TA advisory; I am confident that a catastrophic collision would have occurred. This can go up as a TCAS save----if a somewhat confusing one.The traffic situation surrounding this event; and every day at this airport during the snow-bird season can produce a situational-picture that is way too much for any single-pilot in a jet to safely keep track of. I'm a pilot not an air-traffic controller.At 100 feet of vertical separation; and no visual contact made; this was a very close call. This is my second traffic related go-around at this airport in X years due to jet-aircraft coming straight-in to a full-pattern without participating in effective self-coordination.This airport needs an Air Traffic Control Tower----like yesterday!
