narrative: I had a flight scheduled with a student pilot. The plane was Aircraft X. We both completed a preflight and had a full tank of fuel. Everything seemed normal. We taxied to the runway at ZZZ1 and did our run up. The magnetos showed around 50rpm drop each; as expected. Fuel pressure was normal; oil pressure was in the green arc. Immediately we both felt a sputter in the engine and I called for an aborted takeoff. We exited the runway on taxiway 1 and returned to the run up area. I wanted to try to diagnose the issue. I triple checked everything and went through the run up checklist another time. I completed a fouled spark plug checklist just in case that was the issue but I did not believe it was. I concluded that the sputter was due to the aggressive application of the throttle. We agreed to attempt the takeoff again with a smoother application of the throttle but if there was any sign of an issue; we would cancel and taxi back. The second attempt was normal and the engine had no issue so we took off. We took off. The rest of the flight was uneventful. We stayed on flight following while we did a cross country to ZZZ with the plan to return to ZZZ1 after. Based on traffic and our direction of flight; we elected to do a straight in for runway XY. We started our descent checklist and began descending to pattern altitude. We transferred over the ZZZ [CTAF] and began announcing our position. When we had just passed a 1 mile final; we were a little low for the approach and I instructed my student to add more power. I looked at her hand and noticed she had already added power but we weren't getting much power out of the engine. I didn't look at the tachometer but could tell based on the sound that we did not have a high RPM. Additionally; we were not gaining altitude and were still descending. I realized we had an issue and immediately say 'my controls' while trying to do quick troubleshooting. I checked the mixture and the fuel pump were both full rich and turned on. I attempted different throttle settings but had no change in RPM and heard more sputtering in the engine. I hadn't heard this before on this flight but sounded similar to when we aborted takeoff. The engine was still making noise and the propeller was still spinning but we had a partial power loss and would not be able to make it to the runway. At this point we were descending toward trees. I made a right turn for a field and did a soft field landing in this field. There was not more than 30 seconds from telling my student to add throttle and then landing in the field. There was no damage to person; property; or aircraft.

narrative: Yesterday shortly after takeoff from ZZZ we had what I was told by the purser was a near miss. Meaning the pilots had to abruptly pull upwards in order to avoid being hit by another aircraft. We were still seated due to turbulence but we had already passed 10;000 ft because the purser was in the middle of his announcements when this happened. I remember myself and the other flight attendant in the back looked at each other in shock and held onto our jump seats. It felt like a roller coaster almost so we automatically knew it wasn't turbulence. It felt like when you are driving and have to swerve quickly in order to avoid hitting something/being hit. The pilots pulled upwards bringing the aircraft higher in such a quick manner that we were instantly concerned. After finishing the inflight service announcements the purser called us and asked if we all felt that and if we were okay. We told him yes we felt it and luckily we were all still seated so we were physically okay. Later on towards the end of the flight the purser came back and told us that during a lavatory break the Captain had told him that we had a near miss with another aircraft and that's why they had pulled up like that so abruptly. The Captain also told him not to mention anything in front of the passengers. The purser then told us not to say anything to anyone and to keep it between ourselves/the crew. We were both stunned and couldn't believe what we were hearing. After landing I was expecting the pilots to at least debrief us since all passengers had deplaned and we were keeping the aircraft for our return flight to ZZZ but they did not. I even waited in first class for them to open the flight deck and come out to and talk to us but they never did. I was still in shock and shaken up so I just went to the lavatory in the back and just cried. I was so scared and feeling so many emotions and didn't want anyone else to see me cry. I am grateful that the pilots were able to get us there safely but it was off putting when nothing was said about the incident after the flight. It does not make me feel safe or comfortable knowing what happened and not being able to discuss it with the pilots after the fact.

narrative: Aircraft X was dispatched with MEL 28XXX for the #2 spar valve light; which stayed bright (indicating 'in transit') when the cutoff lever was moved to cutoff. I've had several deferred valve lights recently; this one caught my attention. The MEL allows dispatch but requires a mechanic to verify operation of the actual valve 1x/day. I called the dispatcher; who patched in maintenance control then the Chief Pilot and a Lead Mechanic. None was able to give greater technical insight than my ground-school understanding of the fuel feed system. All of them reasoned that Boeing; the FAA; Air Carrier X; and the union have all signed off on this deferral; and the chances of the valve failing to begin with are pretty small; not zero; but small. With all due respect; no one disagreed with my concern; that just because the valve worked when a mechanic checked it doesn't mean it will work now - and while that is always the case; the lack of an indicator light could lead; in the event of an engine fire; to the possibility of the loss of redundant shutoff valves between the fuel tanks and the burning engine. Not having that information during an emergency could cost the pilots critically. I accepted the aircraft; but in retrospect; not being able to verify the position of the valve seems like unnecessary risk. The analogy I offered is that I would not accept an aircraft with no gear-down indicator light even if the mechanics verified operation of the gear down-locks before every flight. Sure; the valve probably won't fail; and the gear will probably come down; not being able to verify it is the problem. Our first mandate is safety. Everything else comes after.

narrative1: Departing gate XX in ORD; aircraft was ready for block out. Flight crew called ground personnel ready for brake release. Ground informed flight crew they were ready but our tug died so we'll have you release the brake then reset it; and we'll hook up the other tug." Captain released the brake getting an out time 1 minute early; then reset brake. During this release the aircraft rolled back approximately 2-3 feet as the aircraft was on a downslope and the tug was never connected; this is the only aircraft movement of the entire event. Flight crew queried the ground personnel as to why the aircraft rolled and were informed ground personnel did not connect tug because "it's slippery with de-ice fluid on the ground." The second tug was then connected and push commenced as normal. Cause: Multiple causes of this event contributed to the roll. First cause is captain being complacent and trusting ground personnel instead of verifying the ground crew connected the tug. Second cause is the operational pressures put on employees to always get flights out on time; if this pressure was less the second tug would have been connected a minute or so after scheduled departure but this roll would not have occurred. Third cause is the operational norm of the ground personnel that ask for brake release quite often when they are not fully ready so the flight will not take a delay. Suggestions: As captain I always should be verifying all actions are done in the correct way and not allow the aircraft to move unless it is in the safest way possible. Ground crew should also verify the aircraft is in a safe state before asking for any brake releases and have a tug hooked."

I continued to fly the aircraft and I instructed the FO to run the QRH; as he had stated he flew this aircraft last week and had the same issue. After selecting the ice detector override knob to "all" and I advanced the thrust; the caution went away for approximately 60 seconds. Upon the caution's return we continued the next steps of the QRH and the I advocated to request priority handling. We quickly agreed as a crew and requested priority handling with ZZZ [TRACON] approach control to allow us to receive priority in exiting icing conditions and so I could have the ability to request whatever I thought we needed to safely arrive in ZZZ; as well as having a failure of an aircraft system. The next QRH step required us to push out then push in the wing anti ice button. The caution disappeared for approximately 60 seconds before returning. At this point; I decided we couldn't rely on the indication and to run the QRH as though the message persists. We requested minimum vectoring altitude and a wider base to final from ATC to avoid icing conditions and remain within QRH limitations of 30 degrees of bank and 190 minimum airspeed for flaps 0 and 9 degrees. After transmitting this request the caution went away. We were on our final vector for final when it returned. We agreed that there was no ice accumulation to warrant the "ice accretion" steps and we continued with the approach. Around this time; I had my FO notify dispatch. Due to the possibility of icing; I did not delay the approach and talk to the flight attendant; as we were already below 10;000' and we were more focused on getting the aircraft on the ground.The airport did set up priority handling vehicles as a precaution; and the FO gave them all pertinent information while I contacted maintenance.We landed without incident. narrative: Flight was normal and vectors to ILS XXL was programmed into the FMS as usual. The flight was vectored to final and intercepted the final approach course.  The crew was advised to maintain 3000 until ZZZZZ which is 9 miles from the XXL threshold. Normally the Proline 21 avionics automatically switches from long range nav (pink needles) to short range (green needles); but for some reason this did not occur when expected.  Because vectors to final was selected; only ZZZZZ1(point prior to the FAF) and subsequent fixes were displayed on the moving map.  The FMS generated glidepath came down and the Captain asked why the autopilot did not intercept the glidepath.  He then initiated a descent to capture the glidepath.  Shortly after; the tower called with a low altitude warning and a go around was initiated.  We were vectored around for another approach and landing which was uneventful. I as the non-flying pilot knew something was wrong but could not determine what was causing my confusion.  Both pilots lost situational awareness regarding our exact position ultimately as a result of selecting vectors to final.Neither pilot referred to the moving map display on their ipads and neither pilot looked  at the standby Horizontal Situation Indicator which was presenting ILS information.  Even more importantly; DME position was not compared to the approach chart.There were several lessons learned from this experience. Always program the full approach so that all points on the approach will be displayed on the map. Don't depend on cockpit automation.  Manually select short range nav if this information is needed  before automatic switching occurs.Always use any available information to ascertain position.  Bottom line; get back to the basics and listen to that uneasy feeling.  Don't continue a bad approach.

narrative: On Day 0 at approximately XA:30; IP Person A and student Person B were inbound to land at Mankato (MKT) from a flight lesson in ZZZ; flying in Aircraft X. Runway 33 was the active; and we had entered the pattern via a midfield cross. Flying the pattern was uneventful until the final leg.As we turned on final; my student made a radio call stating our position. We had traffic in sight (Aircraft Y) that was holding short of Runway 33. It was a calm and clear day so our groundspeed was probably around 70-80 kts. We heard Aircraft Y make a call stating that they were departing on Runway 33. In my mind I thought 'Wow that's cutting it close but they could probably make it'; but then; I didn't see the aircraft roll across the hold short line after making their departure call. I then thought 'Maybe they just now saw us on final and are waiting for us to land'; but I still maintained vigilance that they might depart anyways. Right after I had that thought; they rolled past the threshold line onto the runway for takeoff. By that time we were less than a mile on final. I had Person B stay on the controls and fly the plane while I watched the traffic outside. We saw them start their roll; but determined we would not be able to land safely without creating an incursion; so we executed a go around. We side-stepped to ther right to avoid catching up to or overflying the departure traffic; but could only side-step so much as there was other traffic on the upwind leg of the pattern (Mankato has an upwind leg for traffic sequencing reasons). At one point we were only separated by 100 feet; and I could no longer maintain visual contact with Aircraft Y due to our nose-up attitude for the go around and our spacing being so close. I'm not sure what our altitude was when we executed the go-around; as I was keeping my eyes outside watching for traffic.As soon as it was safe to do so; my student and I opted to break out of the pattern rather than turning crossdwind in order to recollect and re-assess the situation. When we landed; we each submitted a safety report. We also discussed the situation and determined that we had the right of way. We agreed that something we could have done better was make the go around decision sooner; which would have provided better spacing.

narrative: While operating a Part 135 charter flight in Aircraft X at SFO; we were instructed to taxi from the ramp to Runway 1R. Ground Control issued progressive taxi instructions; however; due to frequency congestion and perceived pressure from the controller to expedite movement; the taxi clearance was delivered rapidly.The airport surface environment at SFO is complex; with numerous closely spaced and angled intersections. Taxiway markings in the area appeared faded and were difficult to distinguish; particularly at high-workload intersections. Signage and painted surface identifiers did not provide clear situational awareness in the moment.While attempting to comply promptly with ATC instructions and maintain flow; we inadvertently taxied onto the incorrect taxiway at one of the intersections. The error was recognized shortly thereafter through cross-checking the airport diagram and outside visual cues. We immediately corrected course and notified Ground Control. No loss of separation or runway incursion occurred.Contributing factors included: Complex taxiway layout at SFO. Faded or unclear taxiway markings. High workload during taxi phase. Congested frequency. Perceived ATC pressure to expedite. Time pressure associated with Part 135 operations. Crew resource management was utilized to identify and correct the deviation promptly. After recognizing uncertainty; we slowed the aircraft and verified position using the airport diagram before proceeding.Human Factors: Time pressure. Communication workload. Expectation bias. Reduced situational awareness due to environmental complexity.Corrective Actions / Recommendations: When operating at complex airports such as SFO; request progressive taxi instructions early and advise ATC if unable to comply promptly. Reduce taxi speed in high-density ramp and intersection areas. If any uncertainty exists; stop the aircraft and clarify position before proceeding. Airport authority should evaluate taxiway marking visibility and signage clarity in the departure areas.

narrative: Aircraft X; a C172; was on an approach to Runway XX at ZZZ. The radar controller assigned a climbout of runway heading for Aircraft X. Aircraft X was cleared for the option and executed a touch-and-go. Once Aircraft X was on the go I initiated a rundown for Aircraft Y; a C68A; on a heading of 170. The rundown was then acknowledged by the radar controller and I switched Aircraft X to their frequency when Aircraft X was about a half a mile off of the departure end of runway XX. I observed on the radar scope that Aircraft X appeared to be drifting a couple of degrees slightly east of the runway heading that he was assigned; possibly due to wind. As a result; I called down to the radar controller on the recorded shout line with an approval request for a 150 heading for Aircraft Y to ensure more separation between Aircraft Y and Aircraft X. The radar controller then said that he was going to 'crank Aircraft X on a 090' heading. This did not make sense to me as a 090 would create even more of a conflict with Aircraft Y who was already on a 170. Thus; I reiterated my approval request of a 150 heading for Aircraft Y and the radar controller replied 'approved.' I then switched Aircraft Y to the radar controller about a half mile off of the departure end of runway XX on a 150 heading. After both aircraft were switched to the radar controller's frequency I observed Aircraft X; who was at this point about 2 miles south of the runway; turn directly towards Aircraft Y with targets appearing likely to merge at co-altitude. Ultimately; a 170 heading was coordinated in the rundown for Aircraft Y and another more eastbound heading of 150 was coordinated and approved by the radar controller. The radar controller decided to turn Aircraft X directly towards Aircraft Y creating a near mid air collision. Lastly; I think that it is worth noting that the radar controller is a supervisor who is certified only in one position in the facility and received that certification with zero recommendations from a CPC in the building. narrative: This aircraft had a L engine exceedance and engine swap prior to report time. This was the first flight after engine change with a MEL deferral It required an ETOPs verification flight (1 hour cruise; all systems normal per FOM 5.60.2) before legal to enter the ETOPs area of operation.  Showing at aircraft about an hour before departure; three Maintenance personnel were working in the cockpit.  The crew gained cockpit access around the departure time. After a few maintenance issues were resolved on the ground (L thrust REV status message; Auto Spoiler EICAS; and previous exceedance that wasn't cleared); we pushed about an hour late.  All was normal until takeoff roll.  Around 80-100 knts; the left engine N1 vibration indicator was higher than normal and the box inverted to white with black digits in the 4.0 range.  Takeoff was continued (no EICAS indications) and vibrations weren't felt on the throttle and airframe until past the low-speed abort phase and into initial climb. One of the Relief Pilots also thought he smelled something not normal.  The FO noted an additional vibration surge above 5.0 occurred during power reduction at 1500 AGL. The non-normal engine indications made ETOPs entry illegal; so the decision was to hold over water and dump 200;000 lbs. of fuel or land overweight   Dumping fuel would delay landing an additional 45 minutes.  AAs the engine was not working normally on its first flight; I decided landing overweight to be the safer option to get on the ground sooner with long runways available back in ZZZ.  This had been coordinated previously with dispatch regarding the ETOPs verification options.  After initial climb out; we completed the After Takeoff checklist as I wanted to clean up and get some altitude to discuss the issue.  The crew concurred to return to ZZZ per our plan with Dispatch on the ETOPs verification.We requested a level off with ATC and were assigned 14;000MSL on the ZZZZZ SID; then a request to return to ZZZ.  ATC cleared us direct ZZZ and descent to 11;000 MSL and to expect the ILS XXR.  While I (PF) and the FO (PM) prepared for the approach; the Relief Pilots assisted by getting a SATCOM with Dispatch.  I had them inform the FAs and Passengers of our plan to return to ZZZ.  We run the electronic Overweight Landing checklist and determined we had to use Flaps 25 for landing as the target speed was over 161KTS.  I believe the final target speed was 167KTS.  The FO pulled up ACARs landing data for RWY XXR that we knew was slightly longer than the takeoff RWY XXL.   Brakes 4 selected.  Approach was brief and Descent checklist completed.  ATC vectored us similar to a ZZZZZ1 STAR down the bay as we slowed and descended.   The approach was uneventful on the ILS to XXR.  Landing checklist and callouts per SOP.  Touchdown was smooth rolling to the end and exiting RWY XXR.  After crossing XXL on Taxiway 1; the brake temps began to increase; so we coordinated with ground to hold on taxiway 1 and have the ear inspected for hot brakes.  APU was started and engines shutdown to allow the parking brake to be released with no aircraft movement.  Brakes began to cool and we verified no fire or fuse plug issues from fire rescue vehicles. We requested to be towed back to gate to avoid using brakes or need to restart engines. After the brakes had cooled around 30 min and began going from amber back to normal; Maintenance and tug crews connected and towed aircraft back to gate XX.  Normal checklists completed at gate and passengers deplaned.  Maintenance write-ups for the engine vibration experienced on the left engine and the BRAKE TEMP EICAS.

narrative: While on the STAR inbound to ILS29R at FAT the weather dropped below CAT1 minimums. I was pilot flying; but the Captain would have to fly the CAT3 approach now required.  We requested and entered holding at the point outside the FAF (SANGO). I continued to be pilot flying until the Captain had completed the CAT3 ILS and associated briefing guide. With the Captain as pilot flying he selected flight change for a pitch mode and set the altitude for SANGO (2800) in the MCP (Mode Control Panel) altitude window. He and I have a discrepancy in what we remember being set in the altitude window.  I remember confirming 2800 and he remembers setting the altitude for the FAF (1800).  The best way to fly this segment of the approach would have been to stay in VNAV to ensure the altitude restriction at SANGO was protected. I didn't realize the wrong altitude was in the MCP until approach gave us a low altitude warning.  At this time we climbed and corrected the altitude deviation.  I reset the appropriate altitude in the MCP and the rest of the approach was uneventful. Lessens learned are taking more time in holding to prepare for approach; verifying what you see; and use of VNAV.

narrative: A series of systems failures led to an engine fire shortly after takeoff.Just after raising the landing gear after lift off we; the crew; heard and felt a vibration that was very much like a nose wheel rubbing on the scrubbers; and we smelled what we thought was burnt rubber.  We all thought that a nose tire had perhaps failed and was disintegrating against the scrubbers.   Each of us had experienced this before.  However; this vibration went on too long.  At this point we were at around 1000 AFE and the #2 hydraulic system lost all quantity.The #2 hydraulic system lost all quantity to the standpipe level; but we still had hydraulic pressure.  I decided to wait until we were in a lower threat phase of flight to deal with this issue.  We were perhaps now at 1500 AFE and I noticed that the #2 engine vibration was very high.  I called this out to the crew.  I don't remember the exact number.  All other engine indications were normal; and the N1 and EGT matched the other engines (as far as I can recall). Then; the #2 engine failed. The Relief Pilot called out #2 engine failure.  I decided to run the engine failure checklist.  The FO advised me to wait until flaps were up.  This is the correct procedure following a V1 cut; but I felt that in this case we were high enough to begin the checklist.  However; I agreed to the FO's suggestion.  At this point we were probably 2000 AFE.  I notified ATC and the engine caught fire. The #2 engine caught fire and I ran the fire checklist while the FO flew.  At this point the vibration was gone and we knew what the problem actually was.  The fire went out after the first fire bottle.I now took over pilot flying duties.  We returned to ZZZZ for a landing and the fire department checked the aircraft while we were on the runway.  The fire was out and we had the necessary hydraulics to taxi back to the ramp so we taxied back and shut down.Maintenance later showed me that we had multiple bird strikes all over the aircraft and much damage as a result; including a hole in the right wing root.Perhaps I could have ran the severe engine damage checklist before the engine failed.  However; all engine indications except the vibration were normal.  I would have expected a high EGT; surging N1 and banging noises if we had severe engine damage; and we had none of these.
narrative1: Upon gear retraction; we heard what we thought was nose gear scrubbing. The sound persisted; and grew louder; and we even commented how none of us had ever had a nose gear make that sound for that long. We then smelled what we thought was burning rubber. Passing through 1500; we got engine vibrations indications on the EICAS engine display. Shortly after; HYD QTY 2 LO caution alert. As Relief Pilot; I kept an eye on number 2 engine indicator; and shortly after called out that #2 was rolling back. We then got ENGINE 2 FAIL alert. Captain notified ATC; called for checklist; but FO (PF) recommended we wait until cleanup. Capt agreed. Shortly after; we received OVHT ENGINE 2 NAC; then subsequent FIRE ENGINE 2. At this time; we were around 3500; climbing to 4000; and decided to run Engine fire 2 checklist. We reported engine failure with ATC; and began immediate vectors back to ZZZZ for an approach to RWY XXL. Being below max landing weight; we had no concerns with the relatively quick vectors; Captain and FO ran checklists and set up the FMS; I ran landing performance; and we reported to ATC our information and Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) requirements. Still suspecting nose gear and hydraulic issues causing the fire; we discussed stopping on the runway for inspection. Capt flew the approach; and we landed uneventfully. We stopped on the runway; ARFF trucks inspected and saw no further damage or fire; and we opted to taxi to parking under power. Upon parking; maintenance teams discovered significant bird evidence and damage. We had discussed birds during the CRM/threat briefing. However; suggestions the future include caution against confirmation bias. The timing of the vibrations and noise were perfectly coincident with what we thought was a nose gear spinning in the wheel well; and further confirmation bias from what we thought was burning rubber. Aside from that; we all acknowledged external factors; such as the recent similar accident; caused a little extra stress that might not otherwise exist. However; this incident certainly cemented the importance of having a full crew; as we all worked together and each was able to contribute to bringing the event to a safe conclusion.
synopsis: B747-8F Captain and Relief Pilot reported an engine failure; engine fire; and hydraulic failure EICAS messages during the climb. The flight returned to the departure airport and landed where maintenance identified bird damage to the engine.

narrative: During transition into DFW from FL310 we executed the appropriate 'Descent Checklist' and set the altimeters to 30.57. Throughout the arrival there was no indication of error from ATC. Upon reaching DELMO at what we believed to be 12;000 MSL we were given a frequency change to 118.42 and instructed to continue our descent to 6000 MSL. During the descent we were instructed to expedite and given additional clearances to 5000msl while turning base; 4000 MSL on base; and 3000 MSL on base to final. While rolling out on a 160 heading to intercept the 18R LOC for the visual approach. ATC asked us to verify our altitude. At this point we were still descending to 3000 MSL indicated. ATC then verified the altimeter setting of 29.57 and instructed us to level at 2300 MSL. Nearly simultaneously ATC issued a 'low altitude alert'. I immediately disengaged the Auto Pilot and pitched slightly nose high to level and reduce speed from 210 kts. While maneuvering the aircraft the  PM was able to get the appropriate altimeter setting and we were able to use his PFD (Primary Flight Display) to verify altitude. Once acceptable altitude and heading for the approach was achieved I was able to set my altimeter to the appropriate setting and proceed with a stable approach to landing. Cause: Multiple factors contributed to causing this incident. Pilot complacency with higher altimeter settings associated with cooler climate therefore not being alerted to the significant change when arriving in a warmer environment. Misinterpretation of the ATIS altimeter setting; failure to verify the altimeter setting; and lastly a lack of warning from ATC that previous altitude restrictions at altitude had been missed by nearly 1;000 MSL. Suggestions: Apply common sense when returning to warmer climates after conducting consecutive operations in cooler weather.
narrative1: When descending on the boove7 into DFW passing 18k we set the wrong altimeter setting. 30.57 instead of 29.57. We descended down to 12k indicated with approach and when handed off told to descend to 6k and expedite. We continued to descend and were told to continue down to 5k and turn 15 degrees right eventually. We continuously descended from 12k towards our final cleared altitude of 3k as we turned final. Approach asked if we were going down to 2300 because we were cleared to 3000 and I replied were at approx 3300 going to 3k. ATC responded we were already below that and gave us the correct altimeter setting. Fo flying disengaged autopilot to stop descent and begin climbing. We reset the altimeter to the correct setting and were cleared for the approach and handed to tower. FO continued to hand fly the visual to landing. Cause: Usually an altimeter that high would cause a second glance but with this weeks cold front that had been a typical setting. Checking the ATIS against the setting an additional time would have also caught the error. Our printer was having clarity issues and we read our takeoff v speeds off our EFB to verify they were correct due to a misprint. ATC never noticed or alerted us that we had been low on the arrival even when leveling off at the bottom altitude then we were given a continuous descent down until the lower than assigned altitude was noticed. When approach gave us the altimeter on initial contact it wasn't noticed that it was different than what we had set. Suggestions: Double check the ATIS printout more regularly and if ATC notices an aircraft below the level off final altitude it is indicative of an incorrect altimeter setting.
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported receiving a low altitude alert from ATC on initial approach to DFW because their altimeter was improperly set.

Communication was made with the passengers and flight attendants before the tug pushed us back about 20 feet. This was enough for us to then disconnect and move under our own power. We then back-taxied down the runway and finally to our gate.Cause: I think both my Captain and I could have done a better job of confidently identifying the taxiway before making the turn using the taxiway lights as cues. narrative: While operating as PIC from FAR to ZZZ; we prepared for push. We had good communications with ramp crew. During pushback; we were cleared to start engines. My FO started the right engine. The push crew pushed us; stopped; and continued the push several times. I had been told my previous trip to Fargo that they were still creating the proper procedures to push aircraft off of the new gates; so we attributed the several stops to the push crew being unfamiliar with the new area and push procedures.At one point; we stopped for a longer period of time. I asked the push operator if we were complete with the push; but got no response. I then noticed we seemed to be moving forward. I asked why we were moving forward and got no response. I looked further down below the nose while trying to determine why we were getting no response and saw what looked like people working near the nosewheel while my FO announced that we were definitely moving forwards.I chose to slam on the brakes to avoid possibly running over the ground grew who appeared to be near the nosewheel. I then told the tug operator to stop everything and tell me what was going on before we continued. He informed me that they had disconnected my aircraft from the tug without telling us or asking for the brakes to be set. After reminding them that communicating this with the crew was a vital safety measure; the tug operator apologized for forgetting and admitted it was his first time pushing an aircraft. There was no training supervisor present.Fortunately; my FO and I were paying attention during the push and I was able to stop the aircraft and prevent anybody from being hurt or any equipment from being damaged.This incident reinforced to our crew the importance of keeping high situational awareness and not relying on the ground crew; even when using reliable headsets. In the future; we will be even more alert during pushback having seen how quickly a bad situation can develop.

narrative: On day 0 I was put on the engine change crew to continue with the remove & replace of #2 engine on aircraft x. My first job was to apply the protective coating on the bottom of the aft engine mount due to corrosion that was found during the after removal of engine lower pylon inspection. Upon first application of the primer i noticed that the bottom outboard mating surface of the aft engine mount had in my opinion a substantial amount of pitting. I ceased operation and notified the inspector of my finding. The inspector did a visual of the area and told me that it was ok to continue the application of the second coat and the area was within limits.the initial found fault of corrosion found during the engine inspection was already documented and signed off as removed corrosion per the applicable aircraft maintenance manual (amm). I initially took his word for it and continued because i was just coming to a somewhat extensive and lengthy job and assumed that everything had been researched and performed per any applicable amm or structural repair manual (srm). While waiting on the paint to cure enough for work to be performed i did start research in the srm to look for limitations on corrosion in certain areas. I found a few items in the srm that went over engine mounts and brought it to the inspectors attention. There were some limits that we went over and came to agreement that .020 was a max allowable limit on certain areas. I do recall looking mainly in the srm i did also eventually look in the amm and found a ref for the inspection of the aft engine mount. At this point i was still taking into consideration that he is a quality control inspector and that he has  more extensive training in limits and expectations of repairs of damaged areas on the aircraft as well as the experience of seeing discrepancies like this on a more regular basis. After we had hung the engine and installed engine mount bolts i looked back at the task card and noticed that the engine install( the task the inspector said was used for the inspection) referenced the removal of corrosion amm for both the inspection of the lower pylon fwd and aft fittings as well as the lower longeron and the remove corrosion if found item. In my opinion i could not see how you can use a reference to remove corrosion as a reference for doing an inspection. I went to the amm for the inspection of the aft engine mount and found that it calls out for the removal of the mount itself to do the inspection. I then brought it up to everybody i believe and pressed the issue until we were instructed to remove the engine by our manager. We subsequently found a substantial amount of corrosion in the pylon bolt holes at the point where i went off shift. I was questioned as to why; if i believed that the pitting corrosion was not in limits then why would i assist in the engine install up to the point of where i called for the removal. The only answer i can give is that i was trusting of the judgement of my fellow mechanic/inspector but for my sake and the safety of the aircraft/lives i was still going to continue research until i was either satisfied with the inspectors signoff or i found documented evidence that disputed him. I was concerned about flight safety and my fellow union members that were working on it and was willing to call for the engine removal no matter what step of the install we were on. For the human factors i believe i can attribute: 1: lack of communication on my part by not communicating my concern to someone outside like technical support/engineering/maintenance control; 2 lack of knowledge: not knowing the corrosion limits and stopping the job until everybody was in agreement that the aircraft was safe in a timely manner; 3 lack of assertiveness: not injecting my concerns severity sooner.;  this report has been submitted in good faith and the events/timeline that happened have been reported to the best of my recollection.

No fuel was added given that there was a line at the fuel pumps and the fuel truck was not available. The next flight was scheduled right after the end of this flight. The next flight was an aircraft transition training flight with Pilot A (Instructor) and Pilot C (PPL only with about 240hrs). Three laps in the pattern were completed. The first lap was Go Around due to a gust during flare making the aircraft climb. Pilot C initiated a Go Around. The second lap was a normal landing and takeoff (touch and go). During the third lap; Pilot C completed a GUMPSS flow: fuel selector BOTH; mixture FULL RICH; light switches ON and seat and seat belts SECURED. Once abeam the numbers; Pilot C reduced the power and aimed for 1500 RPMs. The RPMs showed 1200 RPMs. Pilot C realized the difference and slightly added power. The MFD (Multi-function Flight Display) displayed 1700 RPMs. Pilot C was distracted by the RPM settings and started to extend the downwind leg while descending. Pilot A noticed a change in propeller sound different from the usual increase in RPMs and similar to an rudder only turn during cruise. Pilot A checked the position of the 'ball' in the PFD (Primary Flight Display) and confirmed it was centered. Pilot A then noticed the altitude of about 600' MSL and prompted a turn to base. Pilot C noticed higher than usual RPM changes and asked Pilot A to take over to rule out Pilot C's improper throttle changes. Pilot A took controls during the base turn and confirmed the propeller sound was still present and decided to do a full stop landing to troubleshoot on the ground. Pilot C agreed. Pilot A turned final and confirmed the fuel selector was BOTH; fuel shut off was IN; mixture was FULL RICH; and magnetos were on BOTH. Oil pressure was in the green arc; oil temperature was in the green arc and fuel flow was still in the green arc. When Pilot A confirmed the aircraft could glide to the runway; he reduced the throttle to IDLE. The propeller slowed down more than usual. Over the numbers; Pilot A set the flaps to 20 degrees (10 degrees already added on downwind). After touchdown the propeller stopped windmilling and came to a complete stop. Pilot A used the energy remaining to let the aircraft roll to the first exit; ([Taxiway] 1) and called [clear of the runway attempting to roll all the way clear]. After crossing the taxi intersection; Pilot A applied brakes and brought the aircraft to a complete stop. Pilot A called Pilot B and reported the issue. Pilot A restarted the plane without prime and the aircraft started without a problem. The aircraft was taxied to its parking spot and shutdown. A magneto ground check did not show any issues. Pilot B met the aircraft with a representative of Maintenance. The aircraft was secured and was not refueled. What I believed caused the problem:I believe the throttle control settings may caused the problem. After repeated use of the throttle controls the settings inside the cowling may have come loose and caused the engine to stop. I believe something was not properly secured during the 100hr inspection. No debris or water was found after inspection of the fuel sumps (left; right and engine). There were no changes in the mixture during flight. The aircraft restarted and taxied without problems on the ground. Not sure what can be done to prevent the recurrence

FO had a 2 mile ring around CORDE for SA; and as a spot where he briefed he would drop the gear and call for flaps 15. FO armed the approach but we did not set a lower altitude. CORDE altitude is 7000' or above. Just outside of the 2 mile ring from the FAF I mentioned that we were high and needed a lower altitude set with the autopilot on; did he want 7000?  We then set 7000' and the plane began a shallow descent; but we were still high. Just inside the 2 mile ring (1.5 miles from CORDE) we were 600-700' high and going higher on the path. We lowered the gear; he called for flaps 15; and began to slow to his target speed of 160. We were now over 800' high; and I mentioned that it would be helpful to keep his speed up to lose the required altitude. He responded by increasing the MCP speed back toward 170 with the autopilot on. When I saw that we were over 1000' high on the path deviation scale I told him we that wasn't going to do it; we needed to get the nose down and increase our rate of descent; whereupon he disengaged the autopilot and pitched down a bit. We also went flaps 25 at this point. I assessed that we were too high to use V/S to capture glideslope from above in time to make the stabilization windows; but we were nearing glideslope as he hand flew the plane; at between 165-170 kts. I told him that the 1000' window was coming up; we should reduce the descent rate from what I recall was reading over 1800 fpm.Big failure on my part was that; as I was distracted with helping correct the descent rate and glideslope; I failed to mention that we still did not have final flaps at the 1000' window.FO was able to arrest the rate of descent; but; as we were nearing 600'; I recall that the PAPI was displaying 4 red (low); and we got a couple of 'glideslope' calls. As we were still slowing to our target speed I felt that by leveling off he would recapture glideslope from below about the same time we would hit our target speed; so I figured we'd be able to achieve the 500' stability window. However; as we neared the 500' window we received a 'too low; terrain' call and went around. The 'too low; terrain' call surprised me; as we were completely VMC and nowhere near dangerous terrain on final; but I then realized that we were not at flaps 30. I know that will sometimes cause a 'too low; terrain' call instead of a 'too low; flaps' call; which would've been more obvious as to what was wrong.In hindsight a 'too low; terrain' callout should be followed by a terrain escape maneuver instead of the go-around that we did.The go-around was uneventful; as was the subsequent landing on RWY35R.
narrative1: Upon receiving final vectors and being cleared for our approach to runway 34L; we were at 9000 MSL. This was 2000 ft above the FAF altitude leaving us high for the approach. I failed to notice this in a timely manner and did not request a lower altitude. This resulted in us being; high; fast and not fully configured as we approached our stabilization gates. I disconnected the autopilot in an attempt to capture the glide slope. By 1000 ft AGL; we had gear down; flaps 25 and were on speed but had not yet fully configured. By 500 AGL; I inaccurately stated that we were stable. We heard an aural callout as we descended below 500 AGL stating that we were too low. As we continued descending; we were still at Flaps 25 and had not completed a landing checklist. My CA then called for a go-around which I immediately initiated.
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported an aural terrain warning during a visual approach to DEN. Crew executed a missed approach.

I looked on the hydraulics page and there was no hydraulic pressure in system 2. The Captain requested ATC assistance and advised approach that we had XX souls on board and 4900 pounds of fuel. The Captain requested vectors so that we could stay out of the way of other aircraft and could run the checklist per the QRH. Once the Captain located the checklist he started going through it and while doing it; we also got the SPOILER FAULT EICAS message. The Captain completed the HYD 2 LO PRESSURE checklist items and HYD 2 LO PRESSURE remained annunciated; after that he worked on the SPOILER FAULT checklist and once that was completed; SPOILER FAULT extinguished. The Captain then calculated the landing numbers to get the appropriate V-speeds and landing distance. Once he got those numbers we transferred controls and he became the flying pilot and I became pilot monitoring.When the Captain called for gear down I moved the gear selector and the gear did not come down and we got the LG LEVER DISAGREE EICAS message. After completing this checklist; it called to go to the Alternate Landing Gear Extension Checklist which we completed and the gear came down.  After this; we notified ATC that we were ready to come in for landing; they gave us runway XX L which is up sloping. This was the most ideal choice as it would aid in stopping the aircraft. The landing was successful and soft but the plane did not have nose wheel steering; so differential braking was used to keep directional control. The Captain was able to slow the aircraft enough to make the high speed exit and clear the runway and make a slight right turn onto taxiway 1. Once on taxiway 1; the aircraft was stopped and we notified tower that we would need to stay there until we could get tugged in.Once tower was notified; the Captain notified the passengers; operations; and dispatch of the issue. narrative: On Day 0; I; Captain A; was operating flight ABCD from ZZZ1 to ZZZ as Pilot Monitoring. While on the ZZZZZ X arrival into ZZZ; at around 10;000 to 11;000 MSL; HYD 2 LO PRESS appeared on the EICAS. I looked at the Hydraulics page on the MFD (Multi-function Flight Display) and noticed that there was no hydraulic pressure within system 2. I requested priority handling with ZZZ Approach; notified the controller of the fuel on board; which I believe was roughly 4900 pounds of fuel at the time; and that there were XX souls on board the aircraft. Because I was not the only operational aircraft arriving at ZZZ at the time; I requested with the approach controller to be vectored off the arrival procedure to stay out of the way while I began working on the QRH checklist items. I located the HYD 2 LO PRESS checklist within the QRH and began going through the listed items. While completing this checklist; SPOILER FAULT also appeared on the EICAS. I continued with the HYD 2 LO PRESS checklist items and completed the checklist. Once completed; HYD 2 LO PRESS remained annunciated. I began working on the SPOILER FAULT checklist. After completing the checklist items; SPOILER FAULT extinguished from being displayed on the EICAS. Following this; I used the non-normal section of the ERJ landing app to set the appropriate Vspeeds for landing. At that point I took control of the aircraft as Pilot Flying from First Officer Person B and had him run the Loss of Hydraulic System 2 QRH checklist.Once the landing gear was extended and all checklist items were complete; ZZZ ATC was notified that we were ready to come in for a landing. The landing runway that we were using was XXL as it is an upsloping runway. It was decided that this would be the best course of action to aid in stopping the aircraft. Additionally; I had also requested that emergency services follow the aircraft up the runway after we land. The landing was successful and soft. Because I had no rudder control or nosewheel steering upon touchdown; differential braking was used to keep directional control of the aircraft. I was able to slow the aircraft enough to make a slight right turn onto Taxiway 1; clear the runway; and make another slight right turn onto Taxiway 2. At that point; I stopped the aircraft; communicated with the tower controller that I would need to remain in the current position; as I was unable to make larger right or left turns and would have to be towed into the gate.After communicating with the tower controller; I informed the passengers; operations; and dispatch of the issue; and that the airplane would have to be towed to the gate. I left the aircraft in the landing configuration; started the APU; and left both engines running until the tug arrived roughly 25 to 30 minutes later. Once the tug arrived; I secured both engines; the tug was attached to the aircraft; and the aircraft was successfully towed to gate XX. Once at the gate; all passengers were deplaned; dispatch transferred me to a supervisor to notify them of the event; and I conversed with Maintenance Control in the logbook entry for the event.Cause: Aircraft loss of hydraulic system 2.Suggestions: According to the HYD 2 LO PRESS QRH checklist; if the HYD 2 LO PRESS remains annunciated on the EICAS; after turning the associated HYDRAULIC ELEC PUMP to the OFF position; the HYD 2 LO PRESS checklist is complete; and I am supposed to complete the LOSS OF HYDRAULIC SYSTEM 2 checklist. Instead of doing this; I went ahead and completed the SPOILER FAULT checklist instead. Had I continued with the LOSS OF HYDRAULIC SYSTEM 2 checklist; as I should have; I would have known that it is stated not to accomplish the SPOILER FAULT checklist.Additionally; because of the feeling stress; I failed to inform the dispatcher; the flight attendants; and the passengers of the situation at hand. Looking back at the situation; I had plenty of time and fuel remaining that I could have accomplished communicating with dispatch; the flight attendants; and the passengers.
synopsis: EMB-175 Captain reported loss of a hydraulic system on descent. Flight landed successfully.

narrative: In cruise; we noticed lightning on the horizon across a very wide area and activated the on-board radar. The tops were stratiform in all directions. The stratiform layer rose as we progressed; so we requested FL360 to maintain the ability to corroborate what we were seeing outside with the weather radar. The radar began painting a few isolated cells in the vicinity of ZZZZZ when we were 160nm away. The cells appeared well-defined and reasonably dispersed. We discussed a preliminary plan for diverting around the weather and agreed to proceed unchanged until we were approximately 80nm from the cells where we would have a more clearly-defined understanding of the weather as depicted on the radar. We also coordinated with center to verify the information we were seeing. At approx 80nm from ZZZZZ; we began a left deviation with the intention to later turn right direct the ZZZ VOR and then direct ZZZ. According to on board radar and center control; this was a safe path well clear of cells. As a matter of caution; I turned on the seatbelt sign and ordered the flight attendants to take their jump seats. We were still in smooth air; but conditions began to deteriorate to occasional and then to continuous moderate. The FO said to take over the airplane if I felt it necessary. Suddenly; airspeed dropped precipitously by approx 30kias. I said;Power! Power!" to the FO. He rapidly responded by applying TOGA power and asked if APR was necessary. I said no as airspeed was rapidly recovering. It is important to note the weather radar had previously showed no weather at or beneath the location where this happened at any point leading up to or at this location. Moments later; the autopilot disconnected as the airplane lurched suddenly into approximately 20 degrees of left bank and 7 degrees of pitch up accompanied by a rapid loss of airspeed. I took control of the airplane and called;"My aircraft." I leveled the nose immediately and leveled the wings while simultaneously reapplying TOGA thrust. Focused on maintaining attitude; I allowed deviations in altitude but remained very conscious of airspeed as it fell. I ordered the FO to call a descent to FL340 to ATC as a means of maintaining airspeed as the airspeed was initially completely unresponsive to the increased thrust and I felt a descent necessary to stay on the correct side of the power curve. In approximately negative 2 degrees of pitch; the airplane initially began descending to approx FL355 and then rapidly climbed to approx FL365 while still pitched down as the airspeed rapidly recovered before the FO could inform ATC. The airplane came back under positive control and I modified my instructions to the FO; 'Inform ATC of a severe turbulence encounter with deviations +/-500 feet.' The airplane remained under positive control thereafter; although for 5 or 10 minutes a very high thrust setting (CLB) was frequently necessary to maintain .75M; which we had been flying at before; during; and after the encounter. I returned control to the FO and the rest of the flight proceeded as normal except for a later STALL FAIL caution message in the descent to ZZZ. No one was injured and there was no apparent damage to the aircraft."
narrative1: In cruise at FL340 we notice build up from weather ahead; our radars indicated widespread perception in direction of our flight. After talking to ATC with the information they made available to us we requested to climb to FL360 and received the clearance to do. Looking at the on board radar and talking to center about what they're seeing up ahead; we determined it was best to deviate left of course where there weren't any radar echos on the MFD (Multi-function Flight Display) or what ATC was seeing on their side. We request a deviation left of course and receive the approval. A few minutes into the new cruise altitude; we start getting moderate chop to moderate turbulence with airspeed fluctuations requiring me to put in TOGA thrust to get back up .75 Mach. When then hit severe turbulence getting major altitude and airspeed fluctuations disabling the autopilot. Captain took over pilot flying duties and I took over pilot monitoring duties during the upset recovery from the severe turbulence. We alerted/requested ATC that we were descending from FL360 to FL340; for a greater buffet boundary as we were having a hard time maintaining airspeed and altitude due to the turbulence. After leveling at FL340 the fluctuations continued with moderate chop to moderate turbulence. The turbulence stopped approximately 3 minutes after leveling at FL340; we determined with the radar and ATC that it was clear ahead. I called in the back to talk to the flight attendants to make sure everyone was okay and no one was hurt. The captain gave me control of the aircraft back and rest of the flight proceeded as normal; except for receiving a STALL FAIL caution message in the descent into ZZZ.
synopsis: CRJ 700 flight crew reported temporary loss of aircraft control due to moderate to severe turbulence encountered during cruise.

narrative: After closing the doors and pulling the jet bridge back; we made contact with the ramper crew who was just off the right side of our nose. I (Captain) asked for the phraseology to allow us to release brake. The ramper told us all secure below; FOD walk complete; steering disengaged; ready for brake release." I then released the parking brake and responded with "parking brake released; clear to capture; we are calling for the push now." The aircraft then began rolling backwards at an unusual rate. An operations manager in a truck off the right side of the nose then yelled and told us to set the brakes. Both the First Officer and I applied pressure to the toe brakes however they didn't actuate so I instead pulled the parking brake and we came to a stop.The cause is most likely due to lack of communication between flight crew and rampers; ramper's fatigue; and complacency. After making initial contact via headset; I believe the ramper just instinctively gave his whole prior to pushback brief without fully confirming everything he stated.Suggestions: I recommend rampers to be more thorough with their instructions; making sure that each topic they speak about is true by visually confirming it. As a pilot; we could also start using a double confirmation before changing configurations; such as releasing the brake of disconnecting inter-phones."
narrative1: Once jet bridge was pulled Captain called for rampers via operations since no one had answered our calls down below. Operations manager pulled up in a truck and spoke with the crew chief who then looked at us. I pointed to my headset and that established comms between the flight deck and ramp. Captain asked if they were ready for brake release for which the crew chief responded with all secure below FOD walk complete ready for brake release." At this point Captain disengaged the parking brake. The aircraft started to roll a little as it normally does but soon it rolled a lot more than usual. Operations manager yelled and we were already trying to stop the aircraft from moving. I used the toe brakes but due to no hydraulic pressure they were ineffective. Captain then engaged the parking brake to stop the aircraft. After that the crew chief walked back over to the aircraft and secured the airplane to the tug. Everything from there proceeded as normal however it took calling ramp twice to get them to push the airplane once cleared.Cause: Lack of proper communication and complacency by ramp crew. We released the parking brake when the ramp agent gave his brief and stated ready for brake release.Suggestions: I should've made sure that the ramp agent was actually focused on the act of pushing the aircraft. By waiting until he was done talking to the operations manager we could've prevented a situation in which the aircraft was in fact not secured to the tug."
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported a lack of communication with the Crew Chief led to the aircraft rolling backwards at an unusual rate after brake release and the Captain had to engage the parking brake to stop the aircraft.

narrative: While enroute to ZZZ at approximately 4000 ft. and about 8 miles to the west of the airfield we're cleared for a visual approach to Runway XXL. We had the visual approach to XXL with a 5-mile final; loaded into the FMS for reference. I knew the airport elevation was 800 ft. so that would give us a pattern altitude of 2300 ft. From our position relative to the field we decided to enter the pattern on a left base for the runway. After being cleared for the visual approach I began a descent to pattern altitude. While descending and at approximately 2500 we heard the alert from the GPWS warning us of terrain. I was hand flying at the time so I immediately added power and arrested the descent and then initiated a climb. We climbed up to approximately 3000 ft and continued on a heading that coincided with a left base for XXL. As we approached final; maybe 1 mile prior; I again began a descent for pattern altitude. Once on final a higher than normal descent rate was needed to get on profile; but we were able to get back on profile well before our 500 ft. stabilized call out. The rest of the approach and landing were normal.Alerted by GPW System. Cause: Unfamiliar with terrain west of airport as this was my first ever approach and landing in this direction. Also; night time darkness. Immediate level off and climb to higher altitude. Suggestions: More awareness / respect for first time landing on this runway.

narrative: On Day 0 while operating from ZZZ to ZZZ1. We experienced a pressurization issue shortly after departure. During the climb; the cabin was not pressurizing as expected and cabin altitude indications were not responding normally.we had a rapid rate of cabin altitude ascent. We proceed to stop the climb out and stop at 7;000 feet to stop the cabin from climbing.Prior to departure we did write up that the N1 gauges were showing a big split between each other on the ground at the gate. Maintaience came and looked at the issue which was written up a similar way for this aircraft earlier. Maintaience put the right pack back on Mel even though it had been cleared in ZZZ2 just prior to this flight. I questioned that choice and spoke with the dispatcher; duty pilot and Maintenance Control. Maintenance Control went through the previous write up and looked to see what was done. I was informed that the problem the aircraft had for the pressurization issue prior was not related with the pack and that they performed tests of pressurization in accordance with Boeing standard procedures. After speaking with Maintenance Control my FO and I were comfortable taking the aircraft as they said what test and checks were done by maintenance and the plane was safe to continue for service.Once we leveled off and communicated with ATC. I immediately directed my attention to the abnormal indication and the FO and I accomplished the applicable QRH procedure for pressurization malfunction. The aircraft was leveled off as required and we began coordinating a return to ZZZ.Given the proximity to the departure airport; ATC coordination; aircraft configuration considerations; and time compression associated with the abnormal condition; my focus was primarily on safely flying the aircraft; completing the QRH; and setting up for the return and landing. The decision was made to return to ZZZ.During this period of high workload and compressed timeline; I overlooked referring the FOM for additional considerations related to overweight landing and did not formally declare an emergency with ATC. ATC was informed about what the situation was and that we were doing a checklist and our plans to return to ZZZ. The QRH checklist was followed for the overweight landing and what to expect and to do a landing assessment. In that QRH under additional items which was after checklist completion it had a few lengthy paragraphs about overweight landing characteristics and a line about going to the FOM for more guidance which I overlooked about the FOM. In retrospect; referencing the FOM would have prompted a formal emergency declaration due to the overweight landing condition.The approach and landing were uneventful. The aircraft landed safely without injury to passengers or crew and without aircraft damage. After clearing the runway; we coordinated with maintenance and completed the appropriate write-ups in the aircraft logbook regarding the pressurization malfunction and overweight landing.Upon reflection; this event reinforced the importance of deliberate consideration of administrative and procedural follow-through such as emergency declaration requirements even when the operational outcome appears controlled and manageable. In the future; I will ensure that; workload permitting; I take a moment to cross-check FOM guidance when abnormal situations involve potential overweight landings or other criteria requiring formal declaration.Safety was maintained throughout the event; and all required documentation was completed.Cause: Aircraft had recent pressurization-related write-up. The Right pack was re-MEL'd after being cleared.Although maintenance stated issue was unrelated; prior history may have increased system vulnerability. There is also a potential normalization of repeat discrepancy.I think to mitigate this would be to not dispatch an aircraft with a repeat item in the same day with similar write up issues and investigate the problem closer.
narrative1: While completing fms preflight tasks; I noticed that the takeoff N1 settings were mismatched and fluctuating. This mirrored a similar maintenance issue the previous crew had with this aircraft; that resulted in a loss of pressurization. Maintenance was already at the aircraft due to other write ups; and they were notified right away. Eventually; an MEL was applied to the right pack; but as the captain and I were noticing that this event felt very similar to the events leading up to the previous loss of pressurization; the captain called both the duty pilot and Maintenance Control to express our concern. Ultimately we felt convinced that the aircraft would be safe after a thorough explanation from Maintenance Control; explaining that a leak test was conducted; and that the right pack MEL and N1 differential was most likely not associated with the cause of the pressurization issue earlier in the day. After an hour from when maintenance was first called we pushed back. On departure we noted that the actual takeoff N1 settings were not within .5 percent of the performance data setting; but we interpreted that to be in accordance with the pack inoperative MEL. The taxi and take off went normally; but on the initial climb out we noticed cabin altitude climbing at around 2000 feet per minute; and our ears were popping. We leveled off at 7000; and the captain transferred radios to me(I was already pilot flying); and then notified dispatch. The bleeds were set in accordance with the MEL; with the right pack off; the left pack on; and the isolation valve closed. It was then determined that we should return to ZZZ; which was coordinated with dispatch and then ATC. The captain ran the overweight landing checklist; and the non routine landing considerations checklist; while I flew the aircraft and set up the aircraft for a landing in ZZZ. The cabin altitude warning checklist was not completed; as we never received a cabin altitude warning. Unfortunately both the captain and I missed that an emergency needed to be declared when landing overweight. We landed safely; and returned to gate XX; and all passengers were deplaned right away.Cause: I believe that a more thorough investigation by maintenance could have prevented this incident. Both myself and the captain continuously expressed concern about the similarities of our situation and the event described to us by the previous crew. With hindsight I wish we would've held more firm in not accepting the aircraft.
synopsis: B-737-800 flight crew reported returning to departure airport after the aircraft failed to pressurize during climb out.

narrative: After getting pushed back from Gate XX and with one engine running; I released the brakes to start single-engine taxi. I was expecting the aircraft to start moving forward without adding any thrust because we were not that heavy. I was getting ready to test the brakes when I realized that the aircraft was actually rolling backwards. The brakes worked; and the aircraft stopped. I confirmed with the FO that the aircraft was indeed rolling backwards; and it was not an illusion I had. He confirmed that he also felt that the aircraft had started rolling backwards. This was the first time that I've had the Airbus roll backwards from what seemed like a flat surface.I had the FO start the second engine; and this time I was able to taxi forward with minimum thrust. There's construction in the vicinity of Gate XX; and it wouldn't have been safe to taxi out single-engine from that spot using anything more than idle thrust.Cause: I am a big proponent of single-engine taxi when surface conditions are not icy and/or wet and slippery. I will be adding sloping ramp areas to that list. But the only way to know if the ramp area slopes is if that information is provided to the pilots at someplace; like in company pages. narrative: This report is documenting a flight did not operate event for an airplane without an APU that we were scheduled to fly for two legs (ZZZ-ZZZZ-ZZZ1). The day before this; I operated Flight ABCD from ZZZZ1 to ZZZ without an APU. Although the APU was listed as inop in the MEL. ZZZ ops was not aware of the APU inop on arrival. Although we called ops on the ground in ZZZ to ensure power and air would be available at the gate (XX); they failed to have a jetway driver at the gate (so no ground power) and ground personnel were unaware that we would be leaving an engine running for en extended period of time; leading to an unsafe situation with the wing walker moving towards an operating engine and no control of vehicle traffic behind the aircraft.Report narrative of flight did not operate.Just prior to closing the aircraft door for departure out of ZZZ; the APU automatically shutdown. Maintenance accomplished a restart and the APU automatically shutdown a second time for high APU oil temperature. Maintenance informed me of their intentions to MEL the APU as inoperative for our next 2 legs through ZZZZ to ZZZ1. The temperature in ZZZZ was forecast to be 84 degrees; and I felt that would have caused uncomfortable cabin temperatures at the gate and on departure. In addition; my experience with issues of not having a gate agent/jetway driver upon arrival (for ground power from the jetway) as well as potential of having inexperienced ground personnel around a running engine; and language issues complicating communication; had me concerned about safety issues on arrival at these locations. For those reasons; I placed a flight did not operate entry in the logbook. Report narrative of Flight ABCD Day 0.Prior to boarding in ZZZZ1 with no ground power or conditioned air available at gate XY; the APU automatically shutdown. We accomplished the APU fault checklist and coordinated for maintenance; ground power; conditioned air for the cabin and for the potential need for pneumatic air cart. With coordination from maintenance and Maintenance Control we conducted an APU restart and the APU again automatically shutdown. The APU was MEL'd and we proceeded with appropriate supplemental procedures and coordination for departure. The weather in ZZZZ1 was 84 degrees and cloudy. We had conditioned air prior to boarding and all necessary ground equipment standing by. At the time; I felt ZZZ should be a competent station to safely receive an aircraft without an APU. The cabin temperature got uncomfortably warm during the crossbleed start but cooled relatively quickly in flight. The APU was in the MEL and we felt ZZZ should have been aware of the aircraft status for arrival. After an uneventful flight and landing on Runway XX in ZZZ; we called ZZZ ops on the short taxi to gate XX. The FO asked ops if power and electrics would be available immediately on arrival at [gate] XX. Ops said something like 'understand you are asking for power and air; does that mean you have an issue with your APU?' The FO responded that the APU was inop and we would need electrics and air conditioning at arrival. Ops told us power and air would be available but I don't recall their exact words.We taxied to the gate and set brakes. I looked towards the operating engine and saw the wing walker walking from the wing tip towards the operating engine. She took about four steps then stopped briefly before taking another step or two towards the running engine. I opened my window and motioned for her or someone on the ground to get her away from the left engine. I was prepared to shut the engine down if she continued moving towards it. A supervisor yelled in her direction and she moved outboard of and aft of the wing to stop traffic on the road behind us.I then looked at the jetway and realized we didn't have a jetway driver; and therefore had no ground power available. The FO called ops and asked for a jetway driver. The response was that an agent was on the way. The agent arrived at the gate a few minutes later and we waited for the jetway to be positioned before ground power could be provided to the plane.I felt the entire process of receiving an aircraft without an APU was handled without urgency or an understanding from ops or ground personnel of the potential dangers involved. I felt like we were communicating the situation but we weren't understood. To make matters worse; we had an FAA representative on the jump seat witnessing the entire event.
synopsis: B737 Captain reported a deferred APU during pre-flight. Captain refused aircraft.

narrative: We took off XXC in ZZZ. It was a flaps 5 bleeds on NADP (Noise Abatement Departure Procedure) 1 DEP. After calling flaps up after takeoff checklist; my FO noticed during the checklist that we had a R DUCT pressure of 80 psi and that the L DUCT pressure was only at 40psi. We then told ATC that we wanted to level off. They gave us 15000ft to do so. At that time I transferred the controls over to my FO as well as the radios and I started to focus on the issue. I remembered from previous flights that there is no real guidance on this issue other than a brief paragraph in the limitations section from the FM. Which states '  A duct pressure difference of more than 8 PSI may indicate a mechanicalmalfunction. If a duct pressure split is observed after bleeds are configured forflight; and the lowest indication is approximately 18 PSI or less; contactMaintenance. ' we had exceeded those numbers. when we leveled off at 15000 the duct pressure equaled out and seemed stabilized; but not having more info I had dispatch call us to get Maintenance Control on the radio. Maintenance Control did not have more guidance for us after verifying where gauges were saying at this time. They said that it would be ok to continue.  FO and I talked and agreed to try. We got clearance immediately to climb to FL230. Once power was added to initiate climb; the duct pressure needles again split with R DUCT going all the way to 80psi. Maintenance Control was still on the radio and we told them what happened. At that moment we decided to head back to ZZZ. Knowing that we were going to be very overweight we requested priority handling and had personnel waiting for us. We briefed each other; the FAs and passengers of the situation. We got the airplane ready for landing in ZZZ and landed without any incident. We exited the runway and had personnel verify our brake temps before entering the terminal area. Everything was normal and proceeded to the gate.

Both me and my first officer called 'Upset' simultaneously; and I hand flew the upset recovery procedure. I believe we lost around 400 feet of altitude in the recovery before I was able to get the wings level and the aircraft stabilized.
