narrative: On Day 0; I departed ZZZ to ZZZ1 for the purpose of practicing tower operations at an unfamiliar airport. After two landings at ZZZ1 with a couple hours of leisure flight in between the landings; I departed ZZZ1 for my return to ZZZ. My eta at ZZZ was approximately XA:00; and; based on the weather data available through my EFB; my expectation was an arrival on RWY XX at ZZZ. The flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ was unremarkable in all regards. Approximately 10 miles east of ZZZ; I obtained the weather via the ZZZ AWOS system; which indicated winds from 020 at 9 kts. As expected; the winds favored an arrival on RWY XX; so I set up for a slightly wider than normal righthand base entry for RWY XX. There was no local traffic in the pattern; and the only radio traffic was from a single inbound plane approximately 10 miles out for RWY XX.I descended to pattern altitude at approximately 5 miles from ZZZ; added 10 degrees of flaps; and entered the right base for RWY XX pitched to approximately 90 kts. Upon turning north for final; approximately 2-3 miles south of ZZZ; I noted the winds aloft at pattern altitude seemed brisker than the AWOS report and I felt slight gusting; which was consistent with my prior experience at altitude and generally unremarkable. Because of the ground level crosswind and the gusting at pattern altitude; I decided to make my landing with 20 degrees flaps; rather than my normal 30 degrees; and adjust my final approach speed up from my normal 65-70 kts to something in the low to mid 70 kts range.During final approach; I added the second 10 degrees of flaps approximately one mile from the threshold and I maintained a crab angle into the wind; which meant my heading was east of the runway heading; as expected. I adjusted my pitch after adding the second notch of flaps and was holding a pretty steady 72 kts airspeed with 20 degrees of flaps. Upon reaching short final; I added left rudder to transition from a crab heading to runway heading using a 'right wing low slip technique' and continued to hold approximately 72 kts. The slight gusting I had experienced at pattern altitude was no longer evident at short final altitude. Overall; the final approach felt stable and my airspeed and heading varied very little from the initial turn final until the threshold; except for the intentional airspeed adjustment associated with adding the second notch of flaps.As I crossed the threshold; I pulled power to idle; compensated for the slight nose down action associated with the 182 when power is brought to idle; and entered the ground effect. Flight in the ground effect was stable; and my runway placement was slightly left of center but certainly within the middle third of the runway.When my airspeed dissipated sufficiently; I began my flare for touchdown. At this point; I experienced a gust (presumably) that caused the plane to yaw noticeably and abruptly to the left; which resulted in me being in a 'right wing low' bank with the right main leading the left main. I was expecting to touchdown any moment; so my reaction was to correct the left yaw by adding right aileron to bring the nose to the right and toward the center of the runway. In doing so; I believe I overcorrected for the left yaw and ended up pointing too far to the right when I touched down; which occurred immediately after making my correction.The touchdown led with the right main; which would have been oriented farthest to the south at this point due to the overcorrection. After the right main touched down; the left main and nose gear followed; either at the same time or perhaps with the left main slightly ahead of the nose. The touchdown itself was not particularly hard; although I wouldn't hold it out as my smoothest landing by any means.At this point; elapsed time became a little difficult to judge; but it seems like within a second or two after touchdown; I felt a force acting on the plane that I hadn't experienced before; and that caused me to pause for another second or two in order to evaluate what I was experiencing. I determined the force was sideloading toward my left; and I also noticed the left wing of the plane was dipping and the right main had come off the runway; resulting in the plane rolling only on the left main and the nose gear. I responded to the side loading by adding what little remaining right aileron I had left and pressing the left rudder pedal aggressively. Unfortunately; neither control input seemed to help; and I believe the sideloading actually caused the nose wheel to turn to the right because the plane began rolling across the runway in a right arc. The tilt to the left gradually increased to the point where I actually leaned to the passenger side of the plane in an attempt to offset it. At some point; I heard a rubbing noise I didn't recognize; and my first reaction was to look out the left window to see if the left wingtip was dragging the ground. It did not seem to be close to dragging; so I assumed the rubbing noise was coming from the nose gear being in a bind or something along those lines (I later learned the noise was the prop contacting the runway surface).After arcing to the right across the runway for a couple seconds (which felt like an hour) with all the right aileron and left rudder I had to provide; the plane leaned back to the right and settled on all three gears. At this point; I engaged the brakes pretty aggressively and came to a stop about three feet from the right edge of RWY XX with the engine running smoothly at idle. I'm guessing at this point; but it seems the nose of the plane was pointing about 040 or 050 at the time. Suffice it to say; the rightward arc I traveled across the runway was significant in any event.I looked out the windows of the plane and noted a runway light less than a wing width away toward my left; and; based on my proximity to the runway edge; I didn't think I had enough room to attempt a left turn on the runway without risking an impact with the runway light. As a result; I elected to exit the runway to the east; make a lefthand arc through the RSA; and reenter the runway between the next set of runway lights; so that's how I proceeded. The exit and reentry of the runway was smooth and uneventful; so I proceeded north down RWY XX to the next taxiway intersection and exited the runway. While taxiing down the runway; I heard the plane behind me call a five-mile final; so I announced myself upon exiting the runway and noted the traffic was on short final at that point.I taxied uneventfully back to the hangar and shut down the engine; and when the propeller came to a stop; I realized the tips were all curled; hence the unexplained noise I heard while arcing across the runway. This was the first time I realized a prop strike had occurred.At the time of the occurrence; I held a private pilot license with an instrument rating; as well as high performance and complex endorsements. I had 314.9 hours of total time; with 287.2 as PIC. Specific to C182 time; I had a total of 81.0 hours and 100 landings; 40 of which were night landings. In the last 180 days; I had 20.8 hours in a C182 and 18 landings; 7 of which were night landings. In the last 90 days; I had 5.6 hours in a C182 and 11 landings; 6 of which were night landings. Eight of the eleven landings in the prior 90 days; including all six of the night landings; took place one week before the occurrence; and those practice landings took place at ZZZ in nighttime crosswind conditions comparable to the date of the occurrence.I believe the occurrence was ultimately caused by pilot error; and better pilot actions at a couple different points in time could have potentially avoided the outcome. The initial opportunity could have been when I first experienced the gust (if it was a gust) and the resulting left yaw immediately before touchdown. Had my reaction been to add full power at that point; rather than attempt to correct the heading; the outcome might have been avoided. Likewise; had I not overcorrected with right aileron / under corrected with left rudder during the correction; I may have touched down aligned with the runway and avoided the sideloading upon touchdown. Additionally; had I immediately recognized the side loading force when it occurred and added the remaining available right aileron and left rudder without a couple seconds of delay; I may have timely offset the force and corrected the track of the rollout before the side loading became so strong that the right main gear left the runway pavement. In terms of future corrective actions; I plan to schedule some instructor time under crosswind conditions so the instructor can make a fresh evaluation of my crosswind landing technique to see if there are deficiencies I haven't recognized. As an additional step; I believe I'm going to obtain a tail wheel endorsement because I've heard and read that tailwheel training really enhances rudder skills during landing and taxi operations.

narrative: Potential electrical hazard in the BK117C2/C2e. While checking aircraft battery voltage; I noticed the Caution and Advisory Display (CAD) had asymmetrical caution lights with the left side BUS TIE OPN caution not illuminated. After troubleshooting; I was able to determine the #1 Main Bus was hot when it should have been cold in this state. The cause was determined by Maintenance after extensive troubleshooting and effort to be a failure of the Bus Tie Control Relay in the Overhead Panel as it was generating power at all times causing the Bus Tie Relay to be closed at all times and rendering the BUS TIE switch inoperative. My concern is that our base pilots operating per the checklist for everyday operations close both bus ties and never noticed; nor should they have noticed; the anomaly with the aircraft. There are multiple electrical emergency procedures that would be affected by such an anomaly and I feel Airbus should consult as to whether or not they wish to change their guidance for preflight procedures as they did when they added the DC System Check" to the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) for the EC135 in the early 2000's. They should add a step in the normal procedures section of the RFM to pause when turning power on via the BAT MSTR switch in the "ON" position until the Central Panel Display System (CPDS) self-test is complete and ensure both BUS TIE OPN caution lights are illuminated before cycling the switch to the "Engage" position."

narrative: On Day 2; I was assigned to build Pratt & Whitney 4060 HPT (Hight Pressure Turbine) module. There were three cardboard boxes stacked on a wooden pallet. The lowest box contained the T2 rotating airseal; the middle box contained the T1 outer airseal; and the top box contained the T2 retaining plate. The boxes were not secured to the pallet; which has not been an issue in the past.Previously; on Day 0; I had opened the top box containing the T2 retaining plate (P/N XXXXXX); installed the plate and placed the empty box back on top of the other two. On Day 2; I opened the box containing the T1 outer airseal; visually inspected the part and noticed an area on the edge that was dented and had raised metal. Looking closer I noticed it was cracked. Inspection looked at the damage; rejected the part and placed the item on pending Engineering review. On Day 3; I removed the bottom box containing the T2 rotating airseal and immediately noticed a grey powder near the edge of the part. The edge had what appeared to be a dent approx. 2' long and a rough; jagged area about the same length as the dent. Inspection looked at the damage; rejected the part and placed the part on pending Engineering review. It appears that both parts suffered impact damage with a hard surface; probably concrete. All three items were made serviceable on different dates; so it is unlikely that they were damaged before or during their short stay in the stockroom. The logical conclusion is that the parts were pulled from stock; placed on the pallet and then fell off the pallet during transport from the stockroom to the build area. The cardboard box for the T2 rotating airseal had grey powder along the cut in the box; indicating the part came through the box; impacted; and then was pushed back into the box.Although having damaged parts is never a good thing; I am more concerned with the fact that someone knew these parts had fallen off the pallet and then placed them back inside the box and there was no follow-up to ensure the items were still serviceable. Was this accident brought to Management's attention or did the employee; fearing loss of his job; try and hide what happened? Once Inspection looked at the parts; it was immediately clear the parts were not serviceable; so I highly doubt anyone bothered to get Inspection involved. Furthermore; these parts still had serviceable tags on them; meaning the Inspectors who made them serviceable were placed in jeopardy by someone else's deliberate carelessness. Lastly; if I had not seen the damage and installed the parts; then my job would have been in jeopardy also. If I sound upset; it's because I am: hiding damaged parts is crossing the line and doing so endangers other employee's careers and puts our passenger's safety at risk.Suggested Resolution: The Company needs to do a better job communicating that damaged parts must be brought to the attention of Management; and Management must get Inspection or Engineering involved before proceeding. Early in my career it was drilled into me that you won't get fired for damaging a part; but you will get fired if you try and hide it. It appears the company is not doing a good enough job of ensuring this is well known amongst all employees.

narrative: We departed ZZZ on runway XXL with a clearance to 5000 with a heading of 110 degrees after takeoff.   I was the pilot flying and shortly after VNAV was selected at 1000 AGL the airspeed tape appeared abnormal as it showed yellow caution tape on the airspeed indicator while well above flaps maneuvering speed. All three airspeed indicators were indicating the same airspeed and it was reasonable but my airspeed tape was indicating yellow and an EICAS Message of Airspeed Too Low displayed. The First Officers airspeed tape was indicating correctly. We got a momentary stick shaker even though we were well above the flap maneuvering speed. Also during this time the Captains and First Officers flight director pitch bar disappeared. Cycling the Flight Deck switches brought them back but only momentary. Once the flaps were retracted and accelerated to 250 kts I selected the alternate air data computer which eliminated the airspeed too low message. We continued to climb and continue to a safe altitude to attempt to resolve the issue. At this point I suspected that the captain air data computer had failed but as we continued it was apparent there was more to the situation. The aircraft would level off about 150 low on every altitude captured. In addition to that the Autothrottle Flight Mode Annunciator (FMA) would indicate ALPHA at level off and then change to SPD.I transferred control to the First Officer with the Relief Pilot backing him up while I contacted Dispatch and Maintenance Control via satcom. After a discussion we jointly determined that a return to ZZZ was the best option. We then requested priority handling with ATC and were cleared direct to the airport. We planned for an overweight landing but it was only projected to be approximately 5500lbs overweight. During the descent we noted that using FLCH caused a aggressive nose down pitch and added power. The FMA for the auto throttles displayed ALPHA.  After some experimenting it was noted that with the auto throttles OFF and use of V/S the autopilot worked normally. We were vectored for the ILS Z XXR and landed with no further issues. Upon block in we were met by maintenance personnel and they informed us that the captain side AOA probe was broken. There was a previous write up from the inbound leg that the crew stairs hit the aircraft and the AOA probe was likely damaged but not detected. No one was aware that the probe had been compromised by the crew stairs.  It was likely cracked and not detected and once airborne it failed. The AOA vane was replaced by maintenance and we departed ZZZ with no further issues.The success of the safe return and landing rests on the tremendous job of the First Officer and Relief Pilot who were indispensable in making this happen.

narrative: ATC cleared us for 170 KIAS to the final approach fix. CA called flaps 2-to-3 at the fix; then flaps 3-to-full as we slowed toward approach speed. While flaps were transitioning from 3 to full at ~155 KIAS; the aircraft pitched down significantly- FO called out an instantaneous VSI of ~2;200 fpm. This happened as we descended through 1;200 ft AGL; with intermittent ground contact.By ~1;100 ft AGL; we gained intermittent visual contact with the runway and started correcting toward the glideslope (about 3/4 dot low). At ~800 ft AGL; tower issued a low-altitude alert; we acknowledged and continued. No GPWS warnings sounded--likely because the deviation stemmed from the earlier pitch excursion rather than terrain proximity.  Go around was not called at 1000 ft AGL because the aircraft was correcting and we gain visual reference.  The aircraft was stable with runway insight at 500 ft AGL.Cause:  It is believed the rapid flap extension from 2-to-full; combined with high deceleration; created a strong nose-down moment that overwhelmed auto pilot pitch control momentarily. In future;  especially in intermittent IMC conditions; earlier and slower flap transitions will help create better conditions for a smoother approach.
narrative1: ILS XXR at ZZZ: Told to fly 210 on final and subsequently told to slow to 170. Aircraft intercepted GS as we were still slowing to 170 and we selected flaps 2 (2000 ft) and gear down (1700 ft) as we intercepted the GS. After I called for flaps 3 and very soon after flaps full we got 1 dot above GS. The Autopilot rapidly lowered the pitch in response to being slightly above GS (coupled with the large flap configuration change). The excessive pitch down change resulted in slightly more than 2000 FPM descent rate and the aircraft going 1 dot below GS. I was milliseconds from performing a Go Around; I doubted the Autopilot would have remained engaged during the rapid pitch change and was preparing to disconnect the Autopilot and perform a manual Go Around. We had just broken out of the weather and the Autopilot was correcting back to GS with a normal pitch attitude and I decided to let it recapture the GS while monitoring it very closely. The Autopilot got back on GS and speed and we were stable before reaching 500 ft.  The Autopilot remained engaged and slowly corrected the pitch to recapture the GS and continue to slow to approach speed. The tower did alert us to a low altitude alert during the event - I'm not sure if that was a result of the Vertical Velocity Indicator (VVI) or the altitude.Cause: I should have put the gear down and selected Flaps 2 earlier (as soon as tower slowed us to 170). This would have given the Autopilot a better chance to stabilize on GS at a slower speed. The rapid flap change from 3 to full caused the Autopilot to get above the GS and overcorrect. I believe this rapid flap change (3 to full) was the catalyst to this entire event. This rapid flap change should have been avoided by being more stable with the gear and flaps 2 on GS earlier. Initially I was frustrated with the Autopilot performance and focused the blame on the aircraft. But I realize I was asking too much of the Autopilot all at once. *The decision not to Go Around during the high VVI/below GS event was based on my prediction of how disorienting the Go Around would have been and my doubt that the autopilot would've remained engaged during the subsequent rapid pitch up. We would have also went back into the weather; further adding to the disorientating effects. Regardless of those factors; I was still moments away from performing the Go Around (after debriefing with the FO he told me he was about to call Go Around as well - right around the same time as the Autopilot started recapturing the GS and stabilizing the pitch). The FO did a good job throughout the event calling out the excessive VVI. **I realize that once the Autopilot was correcting we were still technically unstable on the approach...and should have performed a Go Around. I elected not to because we were below the weather and the Autopilot was leveling off and predictably correcting back to GS. We were very rapidly getting back to the stable criteria.
synopsis: A319 flight crew reported an unstabilized approach and a low altitude alert from ATC when the autopilot reacted with an excessive pitch down moment below the glide path after a late flap configuration change. The autopilot recaptured the glide path; stabilized; and landed.

narrative: I had purchased a Cessna 340A on Day 0. The same mechanic who performed the annual inspection also performed the pre-buy inspection as well. Everything appeared to be in order and we took ownership and ferried the aircraft from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. Over the next few months I had accumulated approximately 27 hours in the aircraft from training and familiarization flights to and from various airports. All were uneventful. However; as I continued to log more and more time in the aircraft; I endeavored to continue to familiarize myself with the specific maintenance requirements of the Cessna 340A as well as keeping track of relevant Airworthiness Directives; that I would need to accomplish to maintain airworthiness of the aircraft. However; in my studies; I discovered a discrepancy a few days ago with the propellers - I found that both propellers are listed in an AD - which indicates that the lag screws; which are a vital component in securing the propeller blades to the propeller hub; are defective in certain MT composite propellers manufactured/installed between certain years. As it turns out; both of the propellers on Aircraft X are flagged under this Airworthiness Directive as having the defective lag screws. Under certain high-load conditions such as heavy turbulence or maneuvers; these defective screws can fail; leading to potential inflight blade separation and severe damage to the engine and airframe. Continuing to go through the propeller logbooks; there is no evidence that this AD was ever complied with whatsoever. The aircraft mechanic who performed most of the maintenance on Aircraft X in the 4 years prior to our purchase of the plane; made no mention of it either.Because of this; the aircraft is not airworthy and has not been for several years at the earliest; and the previous owner flew it during this time as well. Immediate corrective actions had begun the moment I discovered the propellers had an outstanding AD. The aircraft was immediately grounded. First; the aircraft will have its propellers removed and shipped to an authorized repair facility; and the aircraft will have another annual inspection performed to rectify these issues. I exercised poor judgment in assuming that everything was in order with the aircraft and did not do enough due-diligence on the aircraft logs or AD records; as I perceived the aircraft to be in excellent shape with everything else in order on the pre-buy inspection. Ultimately; it falls to the pilot in command to ensure the aircraft is airworthy; and I incorrectly placed the entirety of my faith in the mechanic that did the annual and pre-buy; as well as the previous owner. Said corrective actions will continue as swiftly as possible to correct this oversight and return the aircraft to a fully airworthy condition. In addition; going forward; I will heavily scrutinize and cross-check any and all maintenance performed on this airframe; ensuring everything is in order for each flight and not allowing any assumptions to fall into place.

narrative: This incident occurred during takeoff at ZZZ at approximately XA:24 on Day 0. I was taking off runway XX with calm winds; >10sm visibility; and skies clear. Once airborne; I encountered mist; but it did not impact actions on the ground during takeoff. I initiated a rolling takeoff and accelerated to my published Vr speed of 86. I rotated and leveled the aircraft to accelerate in ground effect per my company's pilot training. Once established in my level acceleration; I retracted the gear. Either as the gear retracted or shortly after retracting; the cockpit door on the right side of the aircraft popped open. Prior to takeoff; I had verified the door was secure twice: once before taxi (personal technique); and again short of the runway in accordance with the before takeoff checklist.Due to the increased airflow and noise within the cockpit from the door popping open; I lost situational awareness of the aircraft and failed to continue my climb out. The nose of the aircraft dropped; and the airplane lost altitude over the runway. When my attention returned to flying the aircraft; I recognized the nose-low attitude and pulled back on the yoke to resume climbing; but had lost enough altitude that resulted in the right propeller struck the runway; causing damage. Indications of the ground contact were a spark-like flash and a scraping sound loud enough to be heard over the engine and airflow noise.Following the ground contact; I recognized that my gear was retracted and there was insufficient runway; so I continued my takeoff and executed a left traffic pattern to land back on runway XX. I did not receive any cockpit warnings; cautions; or advisories. While in-flight and during my deceleration to land; I noticed a mild vibration that further indicated damage to the propeller; but I felt no significant loss in controllability or performance. Upon landing; I immediately taxied to the FBO ramp and shut down the plane.After parking; I completed a thorough inspection of the aircraft. I found that all three blades of the right engine propeller were damaged; curled up about 3-4 inches each; with some pieces of the propeller broken off. I found the passenger's footstep aft of the right wing was bent upwards with a crack in the tubing and abrasion damage on the bottom. Additionally; I found punctures to the fuselage skin on the right nose; inboard of the right nacelle; and below the nose baggage compartment; moving towards the leading edge of the right wing. I did not find evidence of the right wing; or any part of the fuselage; including the nose; belly; and tail; making contact with the ground. The left propeller also appeared free of damage.I immediately notified my flight controller; who notified the Director of Operations; and then notified my Director of Maintenance; who initiated recovery. After debriefing my company's safety officer on the events; it was determined that the takeoff profile I used did not align with published procedures; but was corroborated by other BE58 pilots as what was taught in our training. Contributing factors: This was my first time flying in and out of this airport. Runway illusions induced by an unfamiliar runway at night may have given me the perception that I was higher off the runway surface than I actually was when I retracted the gear during my level acceleration.Human Performance Considerations: I had received approximately 16 hours of rest following my previous duty; and about 7-8 hours of broken sleep in the preceding 24 hours; but had been awake for approximately 11-12 hours by the time the event occurred. An additional factor affecting performance was that the cargo pickup was delayed by an additional hour; resulting in almost 2 hours of waiting on the ground at ZZZ in the dark and cooler weather. Actions/Inactions: I failed to maintain aircraft awareness and was distracted by the door pop event; despite knowing from training that it could not be resolved while airborne. I also believethat the pitch trim; set during ground checklists; had been set slightly nose-low within the takeoff range indicated on the trim indicator wheel; which required more effort to keep the nose up; rather than nose down during the takeoff; so when my focus was pulled from flying; the nose was able to dip. After the takeoff; while returning to the airport; I assessed the condition of the aircraft; mostly certain of the propeller strike; but unconfirmed; and determined the aircraft was still flyable and therefore did not shut down the engine to avoid complicating the scenario and requiring a single-engine landing.

We did note a brief but apparent smell of burning electrical cable or wire; which dissipated within several minutes. There was no associated smoke or fumes beyond that. After querying the cabin crew if they saw anything irregular they also noted the brief smell but otherwise cabin and occupants were not experiencing anything out of the ordinary during our descent. Given no aircraft faults; we were able to continue the arrival and landing uneventfully and arrived at ZZZ for a normal shutdown and deplaning. The maintenance team was able to meet us at the aircraft shortly after the cabin door was opened and we described the incident and they conducted their exterior inspection. The conditions at the time were light periodic rain; at night with marginal ramp lighting. I also conducted a thorough inspection during my routine exterior walk-around to see if I could find evidence of a lightning strike. With our limited visibility from the ground using only handheld flashlights; both the maintenance personnel and myself were unable to find specific evidence of a strike with only a visual inspection. So we continued our preflight; maintenance cleared the forms and we planned to continue the next leg ZZZ-ZZZ3.However; during the flight deck preparation; shortly before our preflight checklist and briefing; an ECAM fault appeared that was either TCAS or RA related. Some of these were cautions and several were warnings including 'All Engines Failed' with a continuous bell ringing in the cockpit (during boarding); in addition to 'Stall; Stall; Stall' and other significant warnings and aural alerts. This was all while we were still completing boarding; with passengers walking right behind us. Upon power up; the aircraft did not seem to have any faults noted; so maintenance again cleared the forms and gave us a clean release. Shortly thereafter; we got one additional ECAM fault (at XA:36; picture attached); reducing our confidence that the issue was fully corrected or otherwise absent. At this time we suspected there might be something deeper within the avionics that got damaged but without a further inspection we could not be certain. narrative1: Aircraft refusal of flight ABC is due to events occurred on flight ABCD ZZZ2-ZZZ on Day 0.While on the arrival phase of the flight; passing 13000 ft at 280 kts on the ZZZZZX RNA's arrival; we went through an area of thunderstorms when a sudden bright light and an immediate thundering sound were perceived; followed by a pressure wave felt by both pilots. The FO was flying pilot; we immediately acknowledged the lightning strike and we kept monitoring the aircraft systems during the descent. No indication of system damage or alerts were present. Shortly after a faint electrical burnt smell started appearing; we called the flight attendants to make sure the situation in the cabin was under control and they reported the lightning strike and the burnt smell; but reported no irregularities in the cabin. The smell dissipated quickly; approximately 2 minutes after the strike. We sent an ELB report requesting a lightning strike inspection. Given the proximity to the destination airport and the regularity of all systems we continued to ZZZ; where we landed and taxied to the gate without issues. Maintence met us at the gate; performed an inspection and the FO conducted a detailed preflight inspection. No strike marks were noted on both inspections. After preparing the plane for the next leg; flight ABC to ZZZ2; with boarding almost complete; we had a NAV RA 2 fault message appear; and approximately a minute later; all systems were faulting. We had GPWS warnings; Stall warnings; Engine failure warnings; wind shear alerts; many more and we had to press the emergency cancel to silence the warnings. Photos of the warnings are available if needed. Maintenance was called; and while they were on the way; the warnings cleared themself. Shortly after; NAV RA 1 fault presented itself. Maintenance run a system diagnostic and all systems presented no fault. A supervisor was called and advised to run a full aircraft reset. A PA was made to the passengers to advise them that the aircraft would go dark for approximately 3 minutes. After the system reset; no faults were noted. Approximately 20 minutes later; NAV RA 1 fault message appeared again. Maintenance run their diagnostic and no faults were found. In the meanwhile; I called the chief pilot to explain the situation and obtain new informations that could aid the resolution. Maintenance cleared the aircraft and issued a new release. At this point; after consulting with the first officer and chief pilot; I communicated my decision to be unable to operate the aircraft. Given the shared experience in the flight deck; corroborated by the flight attendants in the cabin; we knew a lighting strike had occurred. The sudden appearance of all systems warnings and aural alerts told us there was something wrong with the aircraft. The fact that maintenance couldn't find any faults at the moment didn't give us the peace of mind it wouldn't happen again in flight; at night; through the thunderstorms surrounding the ZZZ airport. narrative: Almost immediately after takeo' from Istanbul; we experienced GPS jamming. By top of climb; we suspected GPS spoofing. The checklist was run and GPS updating was turned o'. I had the first rest so I went back to the bunk. When I returned later and signed in as PIC I reviewed the status of the aircraft and noticed that the FMC time was four minutes and 36 seconds faster than the aircraft clock time. At about four hours into the flight we started to receive a GPS signal; but it was unreliable showing the GPS position between 38 to 45 nautical miles ahead of our IRU (Inertial Reference Unit) position with DME/DME updating (this position was also checked against land based VOR signals). By the time we crossed into the Astana FIR we were receiving a reliable GPS signal to the captain's iPad the FO's iPad started to receive a reliable signal about an hour later. We kept GPS updating turned o' and let ATC know about our situation. With our 3 IRUs updating our ANP was between 0.38 to 0.45nm. Crossing position SARIN entering Chinese airspace (Urumqi FIR) we began a turn to TCH on airway A368. We then received the EICAS caution message UNABLE RNP. Our ANP was noted at 15.4nm and fluctuating. I was about to call Urumqi control when they called with a heading of 130. Again we let ATC know of our spoofing encounter. Within two minutes our ANP showed 0.39nm. After a few minutes on the heading; Urumqi control asked if we were able our own navigation and gave us direct position SALMO. About 25 minutes later we were alerted to the EICAS caution message AUTOPILOT; with LNAV and VNAV faults shown. We also noted an ANP of 12.3 that almost immediately decreased to 0.43nm. We selected HDG (Heading) SEL and FLCH and the re-engaged LNAV and VNAV; with no disruption to the flight path. The flight continued to destination with no other anomalies.
narrative1: As per note on release and activity in the area we experienced GPS interference on our route.  Earlier we had run through the GPS data unreliable QRH and had GPS update off.Approaching SARIN and in the turn to our next position TCH we received an UNABLE RNP EICAS message. SARIN was our entry point into Chinese airspace and ATC issued us a HDG (Heading) 130 after the turn. Not too long after issuing the heading ATC cleared us own navigation to our next point. We notified them that we had been having GPS issues. They said to notify them if we had any further issues and couldn't maintain our own navigation. The PF mentioned he had noticed the RNP jump way out in the turn. ANP was now back in limits. In the GPS unreliable QRH is mentioned we may get this. We then ran the UNRELIABLE RNP QRH and continued as normal. We presumed that we may have had some lateral deviation during the turn hence the heading from ATC. 25-30 mins later we got AUTOPILOT EICAS message. FMA (Flight Mode Annunciator) showed LNAV and VS with a line through. I had noticed that the ANP had gone out to 13.2nm then went back to .38-.40 where it was sitting most of the time. We ran QRH which just mentions degraded autopilot and roll mode or pitch mode failure. PF cycled through different mode and then reactivated LNAV and VNAV and we continued as normal. We continued to monitor RNP/ANP without further incident during our flight. Cause: GPS jamming in the Middle East. Ground based navigation not too accurate in certain areas. Suggestions: Just have to pay closer attention to navigation accuracy during turns and overhead waypoints. Keep ATC updated if necessary.

narrative: Time: Day 0; Approx time of event XA:45Weather: Night IMC; navigating rain storms with minor convection imbedded.Location(s): Approximately at waypoint ZZZZZ on the ZZZZZ1 departureAirspeed about 300 KIAS; Altitude FL260Aircraft: Aircraft XCA: Person A (PF)FO: Person B (PM)FO's Narrative:Departing out of ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 at FL260 crew experienced a dual generator failure.  CA retained control of the aircraft by using the standby instruments; he remained on altitude and maintain a safe airspeed; manually adjusting the thrust and 'hand flying'. He also turned on the DOME light immediately.  FO; referenced the QRC and stated this is not a 'Quick Action Item or an ECAM exception'.  The crew had to wait as the RAT (Ram Air Turbine) deployed and this took approximately 2 to 5 minutes to provide emergency power.  When the upper ECAM became available; the crew was reassured the engines were operating normally; which was evident in the ability of the CA to maintain altitude and airspeed; and the crew had situational awareness that the aircraft control was being maintained in ALTN LAW (Alternate Law) with no auto thrust.  After the audio panel initiated a boot up sequence; the FO requested priority handling with ATC and began coordinating with ATC to proceed back to ZZZ1. Weather at ZZZ1 was received from ATC and reported OVC 200' 1/2 mile visibility.  CA instructed FO to get weather at ZZZ; which was better with OVC 600'; with light easterly winds.  CA instructed FO to begin coordination to divert to ZZZ.  After the aircraft was safely moving in the direction of the divert field; the FO began ECAM actions which regained generator 1 after one attempted reset and did not regain number 2 generator after one attempted reset.  ECAM did not direct the crew to disconnect the bus tie to attempt a second generator reset on the number 2 generator.  Other ECAM actions were to reset the FACs (Flight Augmentation Computer) and ENG (Engine) N1 MODE OFF (1/2).  The autopilot was functioning now in direct law after the FAC reset but the auto thrust wasn't functioning after ENG N1 MODE was selected OFF; as expected by the crew.  At this time the crew elected to not address any ECAM follow ups due to conditions and crew workload.  During system initialization; after restoration of aircraft power; the FO didn't have a map on his side and primary instruments were unreliable.  The CA regained full functionality of the PFD (Primary Flight Display) and Map; and the FO regained PFD; but the Map did not function on his side.  This condition persisted for the reminder of the flight.  CA/FO elected to not run the APU because the crew was satisfied with the electrical power being supplied from the RAT and gen 1; and the cause of the ELEC malfunction was unable to be immediately identified by the crew with the information presented.  The crew didn't want to introduce another electrical component to the system if they didn't know the exact cause of the malfunction.  Additionally; no immediate procedure drove the crew to turn on the APU; it is in the ECAM follow ups.  During the decent into ZZZ; the crew addressed all remaining non-normal and normal checklist; ran the land app using the 'normal' tab for the overweight landing.  In the land app the non-normal tab; under the failure tab; did not have an 'additional system failure...' selection that fit the current condition.  Additionally; the crew accomplished the overweight landing checklist in its entirety.  The only communication with Dispatch was through the ACARS diversion message; which the FO accomplished.  The CA maintained PF duties for the whole duration of the event and the rest of the flight. The FO maintained PM duties for the event; and briefed the FAs about the nature of the event and the crew's plan to divert into ZZZ.  Of note; the #1 FA has enhanced systems knowledge of the Airbus fleet and understood the RAT was deployed because she heard the 'humming' of the Turbine.  She knew the flight crewwas dealing with an electrical problem and/or a hydraulic problem and was able to relay to the FO during this conversation of her situational awareness.  This is above and beyond for her position and her actions need to be commended.  She enhanced the other FAs awareness of the gravity of the situation and maintained passenger confidence that the pilots had the situation under control.  The CA directed the FO to address the passengers that we experienced a 'power interruption' and brief them of our plan to divert into ZZZ where there will be company assistance to continue their travel to ZZZ2.  The crew was vectored by ATC to 4;000' MSL on final for RWY XX at ZZZ.  The crew set up and briefed the ILS to RWY XX after a few turns in holding on final.  This gave the crew time to reassure themselves the aircraft was in a safe configuration to accomplish a safe recovery to the runway and taxi to the gate.  Additionally; this low holding help reduce the aircraft weight.  The crew flew a non-eventful ILS to a min rate of descent to touch down; and taxi to gate with no additional malfunctions. narrative: While working the flight there was a situation that arose from ground crew-to-flight deck communications. Upon reaching the gate; the ground workers gave us the 'stop' message with the batons in the shape of an 'X.' The manor in which we received this signal was abrupt and nonchalantly given. Our original thoughts in the flight deck were about the idea that we had rolled too far on the parking job and that it could potentially be possible that a tug would have to push us back. We deducted that this was a possibility due to the nature in which we were told to stop. The abrupt order to stop from the ground crew helped us draw this as a potential conclusion. The head ground personnel had given us the 'x' and stood stationary for almost 2 minutes while the captain and myself later assumed he had forgotten to give us a 'chocks-in' signal. We proceeded to run shutdown flows and checklists because of the ground workers approaching the airplane for post flight duties despite the forgotten chocks in gesture. It was at this moment that we received hand signals from the lead ground Marshaller; to disconnect our parking break. This was later found out to be the ground controller signaling us about the beacon light still being on. The hand signals he gave us were incorrect and were interpreted as a 'release brakes' message.In some scenarios; it had been known that being pushed back from the stopping point is a possibility at some airports because of the lack of motion in some gate docking devices. We assumed this was the case; and that a tug had been hooked up as well to the nose; to also prepare for the next quick turn on this aircraft.With the assumptions made; that we were asked to release brakes; and that the tug could be connected; like it possibly; and many times is after shut down; we elected to turn the parking brake off after the shutdown checklists. Our thoughts were that we had received word from ground that we were too far forward and needed a small push from ground crew to correct this. So we complied with what we thought was happening; which was a small pushback correction. We had wing walkers come to the wings as if we were actually pushing back from a gate to fuel the idea that this was a serious possibility. So as the brakes were disarmed; the captain and I were attentive to the controls. We were ready to act at any moment in this sterile environment.We were both under the impression that we were in an active push back discussed via the common sign language used between flight decks and ramp crew. It was at this moment that we also realized the wing walkers followed us back as if we were getting pushed. At about 10 feet back from where we had originally stopped; we became alarmed to see that the tug was still at the stopping line at the gate; and began to immediately question why we were moving and why there was crew doing nothing to stop us or explain what was occurring. I had opened my window on the first officer's side to inquire about why were still moving with ground crew if there actually was no tug attached. The same moment; we came to an abrupt stop; which was a required action as we had realized that the plane was rolling backwards with no indication from ground crew that; that was our reality. The parking break was pulled in an effort to immediately stop the potentially dangerous roll; and thankfully; no damage; injury; or potential to put someone else in serious danger had occurred. The seatbelt sign was unfortunately off due to the shutdown flow being completed. The events that had unfolded happened in a very short time frame; that the primary consideration was with what was happening to the state of the aircraft.The nature of this entanglement with the parking situation was grounded in miscommunication from the start. The nonchalant nature of the ground crew made it near impossible to realize that we were in an entirely dangerous scenario where we thought they signaled to push in a non-controlled ramp. We were able to quickly act by stopping the aircraft; and having a direct verbal conversation with ground personnel to get towed back in to the gate.Cause: Miscommunication; no action taken by ramp workers.Suggestions: To avoid this event again; my suggestion would be to emphasize the need to not move the aircraft until absolutely certain the message received was correct and based on fact. It would be beneficial to also emphasize the idea that ground ramp personnel can't always be trusted and that a pilot's judgement needs to be separate from what ramp may indicate.
narrative1: The issue began in the parking phase of the flight at the gate. The marshaller ushered us forward until he showed the 'X' signal with the wands indicating us to stop and set the parking brake. He did so very abruptly which made us believe there was potential the aircraft had been parked too far forward. With the parking brake set; I began my Captain Shutdown Flow. I was waiting for the chocks in signal from the marshaller for what seemed like almost 2 minutes. The marshaller then signaled to us with an open hand then closed fist which at the time was interpreted to us as a 'Brake Release Signal' and confirming our original thought that the aircraft was parked too far forward. Later; we realized the signal he was trying to communicate to us was that the beacon was still on; and that he could not attach the chocks until the beacon was turned off. Me leaving the beacon on was my mistake; and the one and only item that I missed on my shutdown flow. Complying with the marshaller; I made the decision to release the parking brake; and after a few seconds the aircraft slowly began rolling backwards. We had assumed a tug was already attached as it often is right after parking the aircraft. We were a bit confused as to why we were being pushed without further coordination from the ground crew. The wing walkers also walked back with us indicating at the moment that everything seemed ok and the aircraft was indeed being pushed by a tug. This all happened very quickly and both me and the FO were very unsure about what was going on and instantly began questioning what was taking place. About 10 feet back I realized the tug was still at the gate and the marshaller; and other ramp personnel near the aircraft essentially stood there with zero urgency not letting us know that the aircraft was abnormally moving backwards. The ramp personnel didn't wave to stop; they weren't yelling at us and one ramper even looked at the aircraft moving backwards and then nonchalantly walked back in to the office as if nothing was wrong. All seemed completely unalarmed which led to further confusion about what was transpiring. When the aircraft was very clearly past the E-175 mark and we were not conducting a small correction push back on the parking line I sensed that something was very wrong and made the decision to pull the parking brake. The parking brake was pulled in an effort to immediately stop the potentially dangerous roll and to maintain aircraft control. Unfortunately due to the Shutdown flow being completed the seatbelt sign was off at the time. The aircraft came to an abrupt stop. I immediately contacted the flight attendants to verify everyone was ok. They mentioned one passenger had fallen down; but that they reported they were ok and did not require any further assistance. The ramp personnel came up to the front of the aircraft; connected the headset and began communicating with us via interphone. A tug was then brought over to pull the aircraft back into the parking spot. With no damage to the aircraft and all passengers disembarked safely we handed the aircraft off to the next crew.Cause: The failure to turn off the beacon during the shutdown flow which led to what was interpreted as a brake release signal from the ramper; which then began rolling the aircraft backwards. Furthermore; an inadequate display of urgency and alarm from the ramp personnel lead to further confusion about the nature of what was occurring; or if a tug was connected to the aircraft..Suggestions: To avoid this happening in the future; first off the beacon needs to be turned off as required by the captain shutdown flow. Secondly; some other means of communication to let us know that the beacon was still on would have helped in this situation. The flashing fist' signal from the ramper's hand looked almost identical to a brake release signal. Prior to the parking brake being released there should have been explicit; preferably verbal; instruction from the ramper. Furthermore; an inadequate display of alarm or that anything was wrong from numerous ramp personnel as the aircraft slowly rolled back is cause for concern and I would have immediately stopped the aircraft had I known we were not undertow or that something else was wrong.
synopsis: EMB-175 flight crew reported a situation where ground personnel used non-standard signals while the aircraft was attempting to park at the gate. The flight crew released the brake resulting in the aircraft rolling backwards. The flight crew regained control of the aircraft and was tugged back to the gate.

narrative: While flying the HYDRR ONE Arrival into PHX; we were following a heavy Aircraft Y. The FO was the PF and the CA was the PM. When becoming aware that we were following an Aircraft Y; 5 miles in trail; we requested to sidestep upwind in order to mitigate the threat of wake turbulence. ATC was unable to accommodate since we were not yet experiencing the wake turbulence. The CA and the FO created a shared mental model that if we experienced wake turbulence we would use emergency authority to deviate upwind and away from the wake turbulence. Along with that; the CA made an announcement to have everyone seated; including the flight attendants; as a preemptive measure. Once passing JUDTH on the arrival; ATC cleared us direct GEELA and to descend via the arrival. While descending through FL230; the aircraft began to experience minor oscillations similar to light turbulence. The FO put their hands on the controls and shortly after the aircraft experienced the full wake of the Aircraft Y; banking left between 15 and 20 degrees and slight nose up attitude. The FO disconnected AP (Autopilot) and recovered by pushing the nose down; rolling the wings level; increasing thrust; and stabilizing the aircraft. During the recovery; the CA requested priority handling and stated that we were experiencing wake turbulence and deviating course to evade the wake. Once stable; the FO flight upwind which was left of course and leveled the pitch in order to stop the descent into further wake. The FO then called for heading; altitude; and autopilot which the CA armed on the FMA (Flight Mode Annunciator). Once fully recovered and away from the wake; the CA called the flight attendants to see if there were any injuries; which there were not as everyone was seated and buckled in. ATC clarified if we still needed priority handling and if there were any injuries. We responded negative; cancelled priority handling; and continued on course with the arrival begin directed to fly direct GEELA and to continue the arrival descent. We created space between the Aircraft Y and ourselves and landed uneventfully. Debriefed on the ground.Cause: The cause of this was due to lack of separation from a heavy Aircraft Y and lack of accommodation when preemptive actions were requested by the pilots.  Suggestions: In order to avoid this in the future; further separation from a heavy Aircraft Y is needed. If ATC will not accommodate; we must be more assertive in how it is necessary for safety.
narrative1: On Day 0; at approximately XA:55 while conducting an arrival into PHX on the HYDDR1 arrival we noticed an Aircraft Y; 2000 feet above and 5-10 miles ahead. Course was transversing ours. We requested a sidestep to the up-wind side of the heavy's course to avoid wake. ATC said unable to the right; but you can go left; but that would put us in the wake. so; we stayed where we were. Me and my FO created a shared mental model. If we were to encounter wake turbulence we will request priority handling and deviate as safety dictates away from the wake turbulence.It was at that time was getting a little choppy I had the seatbelt sign on and I made an announcement for the flight attendants to prepare the cabin and take their jump seats. Once passing JUDTH on the arrival we no longer had contact with the Aircraft Y; we then thought it was no longer a threat. No advisory was given by ATC that we would be following the heavy on the arrival into PHX.We were then cleared direct GEELA and to descend via the HYDDR1. While descending through FL230 the aircraft started getting some light chop and oscillations. My FO then guarded the controls and shortly after we experienced the wake. The right wing up; banking left 15-20 degrees with a pitch up attitude. I then requested priority handling as my FO disengaged the auto pilot and recovered. We then deviated off course to the northeast away from the wake upwind and were told to Descend and Maintain FL190.Once the aircraft was stable; I called the flight attendants; and they reported the passengers were seated and flight attendants were in their jump seats. There were no injuries. At that time; we repopulated the FMA (Flight Mode Annunciator) and re engaged the auto pilot.  I then at that time cancelled the priority handling request and we said we were able go back on course. We were then cleared direct GEELA.We then advised ATC that we will be creating space between us and the Aircraft Y. We landed uneventfully and debriefed at the gate.Cause: ATCs lack of communication that we would be following a heavy into PHX. As well as lack of spacing on the arrival.Suggestions: ATC needs to communicate with pilots when following a heavy not sometimes but all the time and provide adequate spacing and accommodations for deviation requests that aircraft request while following a heavy.
synopsis: ERJ-175 flight crew reported an inflight upset resulted when they encountered wake turbulence on descent into PHX in trail of a heavy aircraft. ATC was not helpful when they requested a track deviation prior to the encounter.

The nose settled on to the extended NLG. Ops and Airport Rescue and Firefighting inspected the aircraft; pinned all landing gear before exiting runway. narrative: Previous flight that we flew in for assigned (737 NG) aircraft Y had a pneumatic maintenance issue. I was unhappy with maintenance effort to rectify problem. They cleared the warning electronically and did a leak check of right ACM (Air Cycle Machine) bay. Basically; they turned on APU and told us to call them back if light came on again; but would not check the wing strut or leading edge despite our requests and explanation of system. After a discussion with Dispatch; she agreed it was a problem; and offered a solution of another aircraft; Aircraft X; that was scheduled to ferry to ZZZ with two pilots we had deadheaded in. This plan was put in motion. I was told the ferry paperwork needed to be changed to a revenue flight and aircraft brought from hangar. Deadheading crew was to fly back with us.While we waited; we reviewed the aircraft history. Apparently on Day 0 Aircraft X (737NG) experienced a #2 engine failure that tore up the turbine blades and sent debris into the horizontal stabilizer. The logbook documented that the engine was replaced at ZZZZ; ground run only; and horizontal tail holes speed taped. FO and I discussed concern on putting revenue pax on aircraft with new engine that had never been flown; and concluded this was indeed FAA approved company policy and all paperwork appeared in order.When we arrived at aircraft; it was clear it had never flown; and cockpit was in configuration of last single engine landing (flap inhibit up; trim adjusted). Duty day was beginning to become concern due to delays and it was brought to my attention that customs closing was an issue. At some time dispatch notified me that customs would stay open; but we needed to hurry up. The usual delays of switching aircraft (bags and catering) occurred; and I was notified some bags had to come off for pax that had not re-boarded. Start up and push was normal; but upon After Start check we discovered that EECs (electronic engine controls) were in ALTN. Called dispatch and conferenced in Maintenance Control to discuss (item is flight crew placardable). Discovered EEC were not on; FO said he must have missed on pre-flight flow (very easy to do). Maintenance Control could find no reason they were off; but I asked about ground run test card that was in logbook and on a hunch she got the actual mechanic that did the ground run (he was still in ZZZZ) who admitted it was part of the test and that he left them off. Maintenance Control then cleared us to turn them on and proceed and with concurrence with dispatch; FO did so. Dispatch then had to check to see if customs would still stay open at ZZZ for our late arrival; which they did and she gave clearance to proceed.Taxi; takeoff; and initial climbout was normal for night VMC at ZZZZ. We had just negotiated a isolated line of thunderstorms that were putting out a little light turbulence and FO as PF had slowed the aircraft for turbulence when he decided to speed up to ECON speed at about 31000 ft. I felt a rumbling vibration and a slight yaw as PM and asked 'did you feel that?' Before he could answer I felt more vibrations and looked over to the engine instruments to see #2 engine rolling back and 'ENG FAIL' displayed. He said 'MY Aircraft' at same time I said 'your aircraft' and clicked off autopilot as aircraft was slowing and yawing. I realized that we would immediately be drifting down; and requested priority handling with ZZZZ Control asking for lower and a return to ZZZZ (we were 20-30 min out and this was closest suitable airport). Immediately started getting calls from back of aircraft saying they had seen a flash and 'sparks'. Executed QRC Eng Severe Damage or Separation checklist due to prior vibrations; and subsequent One Eng Inop Landing and Nonroutine Landing checklist while FO navigated back through weather towards ZZZZ and I followed along with charts monitoring minimum safe altitudes (low chart and 20-1 page) as identified threat was also terrain. Communication was difficult dueto constant communication with cabin and language barriers with ATC. ATC told us to expect ILS Y XX which is a teardrop turn from ZZZ VOR to the ILS XX. Neither the FO nor I could get it to load without placing a discontinuity in the middle of the approach. We tried numerous techniques but it kept leaving a discontinuity in middle of approach. Normal checklists also completed sometime in here. I am familiar with ZZZZ and knew they vector on one side of the airport; so asked for vectors for the ILS Z which they approved. This removed a major distraction. FO flew the aircraft on FD1 (Flight Director) and AP1 (Autopilot) (CMD 1) to downwind as I briefed the approach; and set up for Flaps 15; brakes 3. I decided to fly the approach as I had just done a flaps 15 in there that morning and was more experienced in the aircraft. Took aircraft on base leg and intercepted LOC on vectors at 2;500 ft. For some unknown reason; I saw flight director disappear in HUD and looked down at PFD (Primary Flight Display) to see lateral disappear and shortly after vertical to disappear. Immediately transitioned to HUD raw data and continued hand flying while asking FO to troubleshoot by resetting FDs. Field was in sight and PAPIS operational.Flew overweight landing to a smooth touchdown about 1;500-1;700 ft down and stopped short of a taxiway (1 maybe) about 8;000 ft down 10;500 ft runway. FO moved flaps 40 and spoilers down while I spoke to people in back. ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) rolled up to inspect aircraft. We quickly discovered we had no contact with ARFF and tower wanted to relay all communications to them which became really awkward as we relayed our condition; what we wanted checked; and tried to warn them to stay clear of operating #1 engine. Additionally; we checked brake energy and discovered for our weight and speed were in 'caution zone'. Through a series of awkward communications (language barrier and 'pass the message' barrier) we asked tower to have fire chief aware and eventually we got back info that one tire/brake was indeed smoking. I asked tower to have ARFF chock nose so I could release brakes with a plan of allowing brakes to cool some and eventually taxi to gate. This seemed to not be understood or confusing to those on ground. FO at this time was also trying to get hold of OPS for gate assignment and to notify maintenance. We attempted visual signals but mostly just got quizzical looks. At some point a random individual showed up on FO side and he believed this individual (which was not a uniformed fireman) was asking us to shutdown. Since we had not gotten hold of anyone at company yet and fire chief had not cleared us off; I was reluctant to do so. I told him to signal the fellow to come over to my side and tried to communicate to this very animated individual who was not responding to my chocks signal either. Had to shut down in order to hear him. Turns out he was company maintenance of some sorts and basically just took over from Fire Chief telling me he would get tug to tow us in. I told him we had hot brakes (assuming he might not want us immediately in a gate area) but he did not seem to care. Tug showed up and we towed to gate area. Once at gate and checklist complete; I sent FO down to ensure wheels were chocked twice and released brakes to cool. FO told me that maintenance got a bit aggressive downstairs stating he was in charge and how we should have listened to him immediately (even though we had no idea who he was or why he was there). My FO says he corrected him in the conversation as to who was in charge-us and ARFF at that point in the situation. Later I found out that they had run from hangar straight out to us; but had no headsets; radio; or chocks with them. I am not sure they were communicating at all with Fire Chief on ground. Ops never answered on radio. I called dispatcher; who had gone home; asked replacement for chief pilot; who could not be found; so called safety. Filled out logbookfor engine failure and overweight landing. After that; things seemed to move along. Through ops coordination and the app eventually secured 8 rooms for crew. Assigned to fly Aircraft Y (original aircraft) home next morning. My original refusal write-up as signed off with requested inspections when we showed up.Cause: What started out as a simple 'turn' ended up being very long day. The length of day and darkness exuberant the 'startle affect' for all involved; but front and back end of crew worked well together. Terrain; weather; and communication barriers were a constant distraction. FO and I reviewed/debriefed with safety software. I discovered a few errors and pointed that out for us both to learn. I found out that when I asked for flight directors to be reset; he did not turn his off (just mine) as he was afraid he would lose his flight director. I suspect had we recycled; that problem would have gone away. We are not sure why approach would not load. I suspect it was some combination of direct to IAF and constraints somewhere. The next day I was able to put in the FMS for Aircraft Y no problem.Maintenance in ZZZZ seems to have a bit of attitude working with aircrews and ARFF. If they are going to insert themselves with ARFF they really need comm gear (radio/headsets) and if planning on towing; chocks. ARFF at ZZZZ really needs comm capability with priority aircraft. Finally; I really don't think the first flight after an engine change needs to be with revenue pax on board.
narrative1: On climbout from ZZZZ approaching 31;000 ft MSL I felt and heard two distinct high frequency vibrations. I immediately looked at the engine gauges and saw the #2 engine N1 RPM rapidly winding down. The EGT maintained at this point. I verbalized this to the CA and called My Aircraft. We analyzed what was happening and I clicked off the Autopilot to fly the aircraft. My focus was to keep the aircraft in coordinated flight; maintain speed with minimal altitude loss. This was at night and I knew there was mountainous terrain underneath us. ZZZZ1 was to our left around 30 miles or so and my thoughts were that returning to ZZZZ was the best option since it was low altitude and was clear of terrain to the west and south. The #2 engine N1 wound down below idle and ENG FAIL showed on the EGT. Since we had engine failure with associated vibrations the CA pulled out the QRC for Engine Failure or Shutdown and followed the path for Airframe vibrations with abnormal engine indications. We followed the QRC and QRH and shut down the #2 engine. The CA requested priority handling and asked for a return to the ZZZZ airport. I maintained the flying role while the captain then ran thru the checklists and took care of the people and flight attendants. I turned the aircraft back to the airport; turned the autopilot back on and flew back to vectors to downwind for an ILS to runway XX. The CA had flown a flaps 15 into this airport that morning so he took that aircraft and flew the approach and landing. This return to the airport; approach and landing was mostly uneventful except for two minor avionics oddities which didn't affect our ability to safely return and landing the aircraft. The first was that we could not get the ILS Y Rwy XX to fully connect without discontinuities. We tried a couple different methods to fix this but to no avail. We simply executed vectors to the south of the airport and picked up the final portion of the ILS. We were able to get this approach to load the next day without issue on a different aircraft. The other issue was that when the localizer was captured the CA's flight directors (FD) disappeared. Everything else appeared normal - generators on the APU; radar altimeter reading correctly and the FO had normal FD and indications. This also didn't affect the approach and landing since we were VMC and had PAPIs; HUD; raw ILS data; etc but it is noteworthy. Landing was over max landing weight and after coming to a stop I set the flaps to 40 and we used the brake cooling tables to assess that we were in the caution zone. 'Wheel fuse plugs may melt.' 'Delay takeoff and inspect after 1 hour.'The fire trucks and emergency personnel were in position to check us over but the only way to communicate with them was with replay comm thru Tower. I was able to tell Tower what we needed from the emergency crews etc and they would relay that to the emergency crew. The crew would then relay what they see back to Tower and Tower would then tell us. Realize that there is a bit of a language barrier due to accents and terminology. I was able to clear the emergency crew; thru Tower; that they are cleared to inspect the plane. I informed Tower at least twice that the right engine was shutdown; the left engine was running and asked to tell the crews to look for damage; debris on the runway; damage to the engine; wing and tail and to stay clear of the running engine. This took a significant amount of time to relay to the emergency crew to get in there and inspect because there was no way to talk to the ground crews via direct radio contact.The CA and I were also concerned about the hot brakes. I asked Tower to get them to look assess the brakes as well. From what I remember there was indication from Tower that the brakes were hot or abnormal; and nothing else abnormal with the engine; FOD damage - so in the CA and my mind our priority now is to get the nose wheel chocked so we can release the brakes. I communicated this to the Tower numeroustimes and there was basically no action from what I could see from the crews to chock the plane. They were walking around but no chocks. At this point a new person to the scene was waving at me and trying to get my attention. He was not part of the emergency crews and he eventually yelled to the CA that he was a part of company maintenance. I opened my window to be able to yell or get my 'chocks in' signal more clear. He gave me the shut down the engine signal. I went back and forth with him a few different times trying to get him to confirm that the chocks were in. He held up his finger to indicate 'not yet - wait for it' I was trying to get Tower to give me confirmation that the chocks were indeed in but there was no winning comm at this point. Since it was dark and the crews were looking confused we couldn't tell what they accomplished or didn't accomplish. From what the Tower indicated was that the emergency crews were trying to find chocks somewhere. The maintenance person was telling us to shut down the #1 engine but was not part of the fire crew so I was confused on what exactly was happening. Again no radio comm available to anyone on the ground. The CA and my priority since we were told everything was fine by Tower was to get the plane chocked so we can release the brakes. Our overall plan was to let the brakes cool; have the fire crew inspect and then - as we are trained to do - decide to taxi or not single engine back to the gate. The maintenance person went to the CA's window and they were able to yell back and forth. He said we were to be towed in to the gate. I was also talking with Tower and they told me that our company was going to tow us back to the gate. During all this I had tried to call ops on their freq but no answer - late at night or out here at the jet - unknown. The CA and I were happy to be towed back to the gate but the big issue was that maintenance was aggressively trying to get us to shut down the other engine without understanding our situation. This was highly frustrating but we worked as a team to eventually get the plane chocked; shut down the engine and get towed back.The main issue we have is the lack of ability to communicate with the emergency crew. The second is that as far as we were concerned the emergency crew is the ones to be handling this aircraft especially considering the hot brakes situation. The maintenance person just popped in to the situation and tried to take command of what we were doing and it added negative value to this situation.I spoke with him on the ground at the gate and I explained that we had hot brakes and were not going to shut down the engine without being chocked. Additionally we were told by the emergency crew - thru Tower - that there was no danger so why was he trying to get us to shut down the #1 engine. He said that in order to inspect the aircraft we had to shut the engine down. I said we were never trained to do that and additionally if there wasn't a fire or some more severe issue that we weren't going to just shut down the engine without chocks or a signal from the emergency crew. I told him our plan was to chock the nose; assess the brakes and then taxi back; get towed back or evacuate if something bad occurred. The previous flight experienced the same #2 engine failure but with material failure and shredding of turbine blades which caused damage to the engine; wing and horizontal tail. The removed and replaced the engine; testedit on the ground; but never test flown. We were the first flight to fly this jet with passengers with a new engine.

narrative: Experienced a traffic conflict (TCAS TA) due to another airport's traffic while circling to land in PVU. Commenced a VMC circle maneuver from the RNAV Runway 13; to land Runway 31. Winds required landing Runway 31; and the RNAV Visual Runway 31 was not an option due to marginal ceiling that would have prevented us from maintaining required visual contact and cloud clearance. While maneuvering base-to-final for Runway 31; we received a TA; and the target appeared to be within 2 miles (possibly closer) and less than 700 feet below us. Shortly after the TA sounded; we heard a traffic call on the other airport's CTAF; which we were monitoring in accordance with company chart recommendations. As we were in a very high workload moment; I don't recall how close the target ultimately became. We never acquired visual contact with the conflicting traffic. Already in a turn away from the conflicting traffic; we continued the circling maneuver to landing. Cause: Spanish Fork Municipal (SPK) lies less than 5 NM from the approach end of PVU's Runway 31; with a similarly-aligned runway. PVU's Class D airspace has a cutout for this airport; such that the only way to keep a circling maneuver within the Class D would be to fly less than a 2.5 NM final to Runway 31. Utilizing the protected circling radius of 4 NM; we were well outside of PVU's Class D during the maneuver; placing our base-to-final nearly over the departure end of SPK's active runway. The layout of these two airports; especially with one being uncontrolled; presents a unique risk of midair collision.Suggestions: For my part; I would have made a traffic call on SPK's CTAF during the circling maneuver; though doing so would need to be carefully balanced with the need to manage the flight path during a high workload situation. Having monitored the CTAF since well before commencing the approach; I would have hoped for a traffic call from the other aircraft before they were airborne; but it seemed that their first CTAF call was made after departing. Besides mutual CTAF communication; I'm unsure how to mitigate the risk of midair collision between these two airports; but there must be an in-depth discussion of how to do so. Of all the places I operate; landing on PVU Runway 31; especially when the RNAV Visual 31 is unavailable; presents a unique risk. Enough repeats of this flight's circumstances; in my view; will eventually lead to an accident.
