narrative: Date: Day 0Location: Practice area east/northeast of ZZZ near the ZZZZZ fixAircraft: Aircraft X; Aircraft YOther Aircraft Involved: RV-4 On Day 0; during a training flight operating in the practice area northeast of ZZZ; a near midair collision occurred between our aircraft and an RV-4  near the ZZZZZ fix. The conflict developed as both aircraft converged while climbing and maneuvering in the same airspace. Evasive action was required to avoid the other aircraft.During a training flight on Day 0; I was instructing my student pilot departing from ZZZ. They are working on their Private Pilot Airplane Single Engine Land training in the Cessna 172 Skyhawk. They have nearly 100 hours and was doing one last flight to prepare for their end-of-course progress check. After departure; we transitioned northbound from ZZZ and proceeded into the local practice areas commonly referred to as City X and City Y at 7;500 MSL. These practice boxes are below ZZZ1 class Bravo.We remained in the practice area for a short while; conducting normal training maneuvers for a private pilot. After completing those maneuvers; we transitioned eastbound; positioning ourselves slightly south of ZZZ2.While in this area; we conducted two ground reference maneuvers: turns around a point and S-turns across a road. These maneuvers were performed at approximately 1;000 feet above ground level. Which; for this given area; was roughly 5;900 MSL. We were making routine traffic calls on the North Practice area frequency of XXX.XXX throughout the entire flight. We made sure to comply with 91.119 and maintain an altitude allowing for an emergency landing without power; without undue hazards to person or property on the surface. This is a sparsely populated area consisting mostly farmlands underneath the ZZZ1 class bravo.Upon completion of the ground reference maneuvers; we began a climb to 6;500 feet MSL while turning westbound to return to ZZZ. This put us roughly 1;500 ft AGL.While en route westbound at approximately 6;500 feet MSL; shortly after; I observed a traffic advisory on the aircraft's MFD (Multi-function Flight Display) indicating traffic off our right side. The traffic was identified on ADS-B; an RV-4; and was initially displayed approximately 500 feet below our altitude.Because I did not yet have visual contact with the aircraft; I instructed my student to initiate a climb to 7;000 feet MSL in order to increase vertical separation. The student began the climb; and the aircraft reached approximately 6;770 feet MSL when I observed the aircraft passing below. I pointed out the traffic to my student and notified them that it should soon be passing under the nose and appearing on their side (left) of the aircraft. We continued climbing to increase separation. I monitored the traffic information on the MFD and observed the altitude separation decreasing rapidly. The traffic indication changed from 500 feet below to 400 feet below; then 200 feet below; and eventually indicated the same altitude and the same position.At that point; it became clear the other aircraft was climbing directly toward our altitude. I immediately took control of the aircraft and initiated a right-hand evasive turn to the north.As I initiated the right turn; the RV-4 also began a right-hand turn toward the north; indicating the same altitude the whole time; further reducing the lateral separation between the aircraft.Based on the maneuvering and flight profile; it appeared the RV-4 was performing aerobatic maneuvering in the area and was likely unaware that we were operating nearby.I personally did not obtain visual contact with the RV-4 during the conflict. However; my student; who was seated in the left seat; did acquire visual contact and estimated the aircraft passed approximately '3-5 feet off our wing'. They told me; 'They are right next to us and turning into us'. I then steepened the bank to roughly 50 degrees and pushed the nose forward to accelerate us to 129 KIAS.We lost roughly 1;000 ft attempting to break away from this aircraft and were still indicating the same altitude throughout the evasive action. This lasted almost a minute.Following the evasive maneuver; we successfully separated from the traffic. We then continued east briefly before turning northbound to reestablish our route back toward ZZZ while maintaining separation from the other aircraft. We then went north of the class Bravo and climbed up to 8;000 MSL. The aircraft continued to the south. We attempted to contact the aircraft on both practice area frequencies of XXX.XXX and XXX.Y. We received no communication back from the traffic. No further traffic conflicts occurred during the remainder of the flight.This event is concerning because the practice areas northeast of ZZZ are routinely used by student pilots from multiple training organizations. Many students conduct solo operations in these areas and routinely transition through the same airspace.The behavior and maneuvering of the RV-4 suggested the pilot was likely conducting aerobatic maneuvers and may not have been aware of other aircraft operating nearby. The lack of apparent situational awareness by the RV-4 created a hazardous situation in an area that regularly contains high volumes of training traffic.Given the frequency of student pilot operations in this region; this type of maneuvering presents a significant risk for future conflicts. Given the maneuverability of the RV-4 and the spontaneous maneuvering; it was extremely difficult to decipher which direction/altitude would clear us of traffic. No contact was made with the aircraft.

narrative: On Day 2 at approximately XA:00 prior to aircraft door closure I was informed by the ground crew that they had observed an uncontrolled fuel leak coming from the right main wing tank on the outer edge of the tank towards the winglet.Immediately I grabbed my safety vest and air protection; exited the flight deck; and went out to the ramp to confirm that yes indeed there is a pencil width sized leak coming from the vent hole on the fuel tank. This leak was uncontrolled; could not be stopped; and required immediate attention. I returned to the flight deck and made a PA and told the passengers the situation and mentioned that because it was a fuel spill that had not been contained yet it was advantageous for everyone to grab their belongings and exit the aircraft as soon as possible. I then called my dispatcher and told them exactly what I had done and the event that had occurred outside. He was in agreement; deplaning the aircraft was a good idea. In the meantime; the ZZZ Ground crew flawlessly contain the spill so that there is minimal impact to ramp safety.I got off the phone with the dispatcher so that I can make the appropriate entries into the aircraft electronic logbook. My first entry into the logbook; stated that there was a new leak coming from the main wing tank. This issue had previously been written up and addressed on Day 0.After making the logbook entry; I called back dispatch and asked to be connected with the maintenance desk. The tone of the maintenance technician on the phone sounded frustrated; but eager to help. They simply said without any investigation or asking me any questions that I had just been over fueled and the situation was normal. The situation was not normal. We were already at our recommended fuel release load. Between us inspecting the leak and approximately 10 minutes later we had lost almost 200 pounds of gas due to a leak. When I advised the technician of this they did not change their judgment. They simply said yes that happened because you were over fueled; even though we are at the correct fuel load given our flight conditions as a matter of fact; we took off out of ZZZ1 with a higher fuel load on the previous flight and never encountered a leak.Once I was finally able to make my point across the technician on the other end of the phone; they decided it would be worth calling contract maintenance to come out and look at the aircraft.Roughly about an hour later maintenance arrived to the aircraft and began inspecting the wing for leaks . Maintenance personnel asked me to fully extend the flaps and slats so that they can fully inspect the wing to find other leaks. The contract maintenance technician then asked me to move fuel from the fuel control panel inside the aircraft to different tanks. I told him I was not comfortable doing that because it violated our SOP's. And I was not fully taught how to do this. Less than one month prior to this incident I remember an email being sent to all pilots asking us not to perform maintenance functions on the aircraft.The contract maintenance person was frustrated with me after I politely told him that I would not be able to comply with that request. I offered him my seat so that he could do it himself. The contract maintenance personnel moved roughly 1000 pounds from the right main wing tank to the left main wing tank and told me that the leak has stopped and that we were good to go. He became very frustrated with me when I told him that that doesn't comply with Company SOPs. And that we are not allowed to take off with a 1000 pound and balance between the wings. I also informed him that both main tanks had to be full of fuel before the center tank could be filled. The leak simply stopped because we moved gas away from the hole not that we did not actually solve the problem or find the source of the leak.After this diagnosis and attempt to fix the problem; I refused the aircraft and made a corresponding info item notation in theelectronic logic book. I had lost faith that this problem was gonna be solved to a satisfactory and safe nature and I elected that it would be best to remove myself from the situation. And not fly an unsafe aircraft.I then received a call from the chief pilot. The chief pilot did not give me their name and immediately became a line of questioning that seem to escalate and tone and speed; spinning a tighter and tighter web trying to find a fault in my story and trying to find a weakness in the narrative that I had told them. The told me not worry; the aircraft was actually fine and I was being overly cautious. I was told we had just been over fueled and it happens sometimes. For the record; I have almost 6;000 hours in this aircraft and that has never happened. I also informed them that we were at the correct few release number. This fuel release number is also not very large and it's very normal for this route and altitude.Their line of questioning seemed to invalidate my concerns for safety. Had I not been so confident in my judgment and prior experience; I could've easily been manipulated into making an unsafe decision that merely would've only benefited the company by moving an aircraft. This line and reasoning for questioning is very concerning to me. It seems unsafe; unprofessional; and against the norms that I had become to expect from Company.Thankfully; the first officer had taken a video of us finding the leak. I sent the video to a number that texted me saying that they were with the management team and they needed to talk to me immediately. I wanted to also let it be known that every contact attempt by the company did not include the dispatcher. I found that very concerning because any communication with the dispatcher is on a recorded line.I talked to a new maintenance control supervisor named Person A. He told me that the contract maintenance personnel also found a fuel leak coming from the fuel service panel on the right wing. Person A then asked me to perform more function checks on the aircraft. I told him I did not feel comfortable doing that. Although Person A seem frustrated; he did not seem frustrated with me. Merely just at the situation. I fully understand the inconvenience and impact this maintenance issue caused; but unfortunately the facts are undeniable. Taking an aircraft off the ground full of people that is leaking fuel is unsafe.A new contract maintenance personnel member came out to the aircraft approximately 2 1/2 hours after our initial report of the fuel leak at this point the leak had stopped; but we had lost approximately 400 pounds of fuel. The maintenance technician went to the flight deck; asked to sit in my seat and begin working with the fuel panel. The technician moved fuel from both wing tanks into the center tank and claimed that he had fixed the leak and that everything was good to go. I asked him how he fixed the leak and he said he had moved fuel from the wing tank to the center tank and you should be fine while both tanks were balanced. The center tank was grossly overloaded. This goes against Company standard operating procedure of fueling the wing tanks first then fueling the center. I asked if the hole and leak had been located and fixed he said no.Despite and obviously known outcome; I remained on duty to ensure that the maintenance situation was dealt with accordingly; I was fearful that another pilot would be given this aircraft with it fully not fixed and have an issue. I just wanted to call and see why things were and how things were going.'I informed him that nothing really changed. There is still a leak. I then told him for a third time I am still refusing the aircraft. I will not go into crew rest only to come back out to the airport and fly the same aircraft home if nothing had been fixed. I noted that I had said this for three times; and put it according info item in the electronic logbook hours ago. It was at that point we were finally released from duty given a min rest overnight and a new aircraft to fly home the following morning. Cause: Safety can at times be inconvenient; however should not cut corners to find a substandard resolution.

narrative: During the pushback sequence from gate XX; engines 4 and 3 were started in accordance with approved company procedures. Ground handling personnel failed to adhere to standard operating procedures in several critical respects:-They did not issue any verbal instruction to the flight crew to set the parking brake prior to initiating disconnection of the tow bar and tug.-Without prior authorization from the Pilot in Command (PIC); and while engines 1 and 2 had not yet been started; they proceeded with disconnection of the towing equipment.With the parking brake unset and the nose wheel steering bypass pin installed (disabling hydraulic steering); as engines 4 and 3 stabilized at idle thrust; the aircraft began to move forward and yaw uncontrollably to the left.Ground personnel immediately shouted instructions to 'release the parking brake;' to which the PIC promptly responded; 'parking brake is released.' Shortly thereafter; ground personnel urgently directed the crew to 'set parking brake.' The PIC applied the brakes without hesitation upon observing the aircraft's forward and leftward movement.Despite the immediate brake application; the aircraft's residual momentum caused the nose landing gear to strike the tow bar; resulting in damage to the scissor link (torque link).Immediately following the incident; the flight crew overheard; via the interphone; the headset operator (ground personnel) state: 'I [expletive] up.'Upon return to the gate and subsequent opening of the aircraft door; the flight crew promptly disembarked to inspect the damage and assess the situation. The headset operator involved in the pushback was no longer present in the vicinity.The root cause of the incident was procedural non-compliance by ground handling personnel; specifically:Failure to follow the standard pushback sequence; including the omission of any instruction to the flight crew to set the parking brake.Initiation of towing equipment disconnection without clearance from the PIC.Premature disconnection attempt while two engines (1 and 2) remained unstarted.No injuries were reported.Suggestions: Reinforce ground personnel procedures and communications.
narrative1: After completing all ground checks on either; crew side and ground crew side; we started the push back procedure from gate XX in ZZZ; first by the broadcast where aircraft Y behind us was pushing back first. After aircraft Y started taxiing; we then proceeded to make another call on the broadcast frequency and receiving no reply; determined it was safe for us to initiate the pushback. The ground crew initiated the pushback at XA:00. During the pushback; the PIC; using standard phraseology at all times; requested from the ground crew the authorisation to start engines; after an initial 'stanby by;' the clearance to start came while the aircraft was still in towing motion. While starting engine 3 and 4 on autostart; the plane came to a stop in what appeared to be an intermediate position; far from aligned with the taxiway 'aircraft offset on the left of the taxi lane with nose in by 20 to 30 degrees.' While monitoring the engine start; we heard nothing from the ground personnel nor any commands from them prompting us to think that the tow was still in progress to the final start stop 'E2 in that case.' The crew then felt a motion forward that would be similar to a tow then came again to a stop. Still awaiting any commands from the ground staff; we then finished to monitor engine 3 and 4 starts. The aircraft then sustained a mid to strong shake; again happening sometimes during a tow; came to a stop; to then a violent shock and a stop followed by a motion forward and yaw to the left.The ground personnel then eventually start talking ;shouting on the headset 'realease the brakes; release the brakes;' command that both startled us as not being able to have any idea of what was happening downstairs. Looking at the EICAS showing no 'parking brake set and the PIC feet that were not commanding any brakes; we asked the ground staff to confirm if he wanted the brakes to be set; where he simply yelled back "Brakes; brakes.'The PIC then set the parking brake and seeing the motion stopping; we realized that the ground personnel disconnected the equipment and the motion forward was induced by the engines and not commanded by the tug. During all that time; the mic of the ground staff remained open and we could eventually hear the staff on the headset verbally confirming 'I [expletive] up man; i [expletive] up' to his co-worker driving the tug. Following this; the ground supervisor came to take charge of the tow; assess the situation and tow us back to the gate. It is important to note that at this moment while we are still waiting in the cockpit to clearly understand what happened; that the towing personal in charge of the headset left the scene; and the tug and tow bar involved in the incident also were removed and swapped from the scene. After confirming damages to the NLDG; the new staff then proceeded to tow us safely back to the gate to asses damages. Notes : - After confirming that a report on their end will be completed; the ground supervisor 'who promised to come back with the involved staff;' never came back to the aircraft. - The crew nor the onboard mechanics; never had a chance to see the involved tow bar. - Nor the crew or the onboard mechanics had a chance to see or talk to the involved personal.Potential causing factors. - Lack of standardization from the ground personal using wrong phraseology in normal and under pressure situation. - Heavy breach of SOPs on the ground crew side that did not respect the standard actions and calls on the following :     - Never asked for the parking brake to be set nor confirmed or established communication about this subject with the flight crew.    - Initiated a disconnection of the tug and tow bar; during engine start while SOPs assert that a disconnection cannot be initiated without consent and positive contact from a flight crew member after the parking brakeis set and all engines are started and stabilized; with parking brake confirmed by the PIC 'verbally and on the EICAS' and visually confirmed by a light on the NLDG.    - Used under panic; incorrect terminology; making the situation worse.    - ultimately damaged the equipment by incorrect actions.It is important and fortunate to note in this situation that nobody on the ground got injured by what could have been; really fast; a life threatening situation and/or causing further damages to neighboring aircraft's or equipment. Reinforce the strict adherence to SOPs and sequences at all times and circumstances to mitigate potential risks. While it is impossible to judge at that precise time in the process; if a motion of the aircraft is provoked or unwanted; the only solution would have been a clear communication from the ground staff.Suggestions: Review and reinforcement of SOPs and safety procedures for all ground personnel during towing operations; with an emphasis given to the fact that flight crew on specific aircraft cannot see the ground crew operate."

Additionally; avoid turns inside of other traffic; even if sufficient space is available.Brief the importance of a sterile cockpit for ICS communications with passengers to avoid blocked radio calls from other traffic; Emergency calls only.Even though in the landing phase minimize overflight of airport hangars and buildings. Normally; when an aircraft responds in an unexpected expected manner I immediately disconnect the autopilot and hand fly; but in this case I wanted to gain insight to what the jet was doing in this situation.  The initial sensation of the event mimicked a configuration change from flaps 2 to full flaps and then progressed to a steeper descent.  There was no configuration change taking place. narrative1: Landed Runway 18; Tallahassee International Airport; at XA:21 on Day 0 in VFR conditions with slight mist forming in calm winds. Tower was closed as was Runway 9/27 per NOTAMs. Noted numerous vehicular warning lights at the approach end of Runway 09. Called the approach and exiting the runway on CTAF (118.7). Taxied to ramp; refueled and filed IFR flight plan utilizing Foreflight. Originally filed: ZZZZZ VXX ZZZ VXY ZZZZZ1. Foreflight notified that the flight plan had been alter to: ZZZZZ2 ZZZZZ3 TXXX ZZZZZ4 which I acknowledge and received notification that the later routing had been filed with an ETD of XB:30 and altitude of 11;000 MSL. Started aircraft and typed in my expected flight plan in my Garmin 430W and autopilot. Announced on CTAF that I was taxing from the ramp to Runway 18 and activated runway/taxiway lighting. Taxied via taxiway A11 then A to A1 - holding short of the runway in such a manner that I could clear taxiway A. Still calm winds and increasing mist - but could see the lit taxiway and runway lights to end. Accomplished engine runup and tried to contact clearance on 126.65 - was unsuccessful as tower was closed. Then attempted to contact Tallahassee Approach via phone as per the Chart Supplement at XA:23. This too was unsuccessful; Then tried to reach Jacksonville ARTCC - but failed as I had misdialed the number. I the dialed the FSS Clearance Delivery at - directed me to contact Jacksonville Center on 128.625. I attempted contact; but received no answer nor did I hear any radio traffic on that frequency. I again contacted FSS Clearance Delivery who instructed me to try again and then was able to hear radio traffic but had considerable trouble contacting the controller. The net result was that I was off the Tallahassee CTAF from XA:23 until XA:52 until I got my clearance. The clearance received was not that which Foreflight had said was filed. More scrambling to enter the data to this revision of my flight plan. I finally received clearance to take off at XA:56; called on CTAF that I was taking Runway 18 for takeoff; lined up and started rolling. After some 2500 plus feet of takeoff roll I noted white lights on the east side of the runway which I determined to be another aircraft back taxiing on Runway 18. These lights blended in with the runway lights and the lights at the approach end of Runway 09. There was insufficient time/space to do anything except maneuver to the west side to the runway - thereby avoiding a collision. I never heard any call from that aircraft - either before or after we passed each other.Being off the CTAF for some 30 minutes contributed to this almost mishap. During this time I probably missed the call from the other aircraft that he was taxiing - as he probably turned his radios on during that 30 minute period and; not hearing any conversation from me on the CTAF was not aware there was another aircraft moving on the airdrome. Possibly we both assumed we were the only aircraft active at TLH.I am not aware to the RCO situation at TLH; but it appeared that initially; no one was monitoring/transmitting through the local RCO until a second phone call from my cockpit got Jacksonville Center to start transmitting through whatever RCO was being used at THL. This might be an equipment or manning issue - and I am definitely not blameless in obtaining my clearance (though I have done it successfully many times before).Pilot controlled situations (like tower closed and with only CTAF to control aircraft actions with reduce visibility at night) demand the participating pilots adhere to set procedures. Back taxiing on a runway when a well lit taxiway is available to move to the number one position incurs additional; unnecessary risks. If the other aircraft had used taxiway A the entire conflict could have been avoided. If one is in a back taxi situation under pilot controlled conditions; one must monitor the CTAF for any unexpectedincursion or use of the runway. I never heard a call fromthe other aircraft when I announced my departure on Runway 18 nor when I passed close by the other aircraft. If the crew was using the back taxi to coordinate their departure - it was the wrong time.

narrative1: We were cruising at M.80 at FL450 in the vicinity of ZZZ VOR when we encountered some moderate turbulence. As this turbulence was forecasted at FL450 for the next hour; we asked the controller how the rides were at FL470. The controller asked the traffic passing by us in the opposite direction at FL470 and pilot reported the ride to be smooth. We chose to climb to FL470 hoping for a smoother ride. Once we reached FL470; it was smooth for about 5 minutes before we encountered the first mountain wave. It was relatively light with the usual gain/loss of airspeed ranging from M.76 to M.83 and very little turbulence associated with it. As we continued at FL470 at M.80 for a few more minutes in smooth air; we hit the second mountain wave which initially gave us an increase of about 100 feet in altitude; immediately followed by a sudden loss of airspeed from M.80 down to M.72 with a decreasing speed trend on the tape within a second or two. I immediately pushed the throttles full forward and grabbed the yoke. Realizing that a high altitude stall was imminent; I feel like I instinctively disconnected the autopilot and pushed forward on the yoke to initiate a stall recovery. I am not sure if my recovery or the 'stall' and shaker came first but we were immediately in a nose down attitude trying to recover from the high altitude stall.As we proceeded in the recovery procedure; the PNF reported the loss of altitude to ATC and he cleared us to a lower altitude; eventually clearing us all the way down FL300; noticing a rapid descent from our aircraft. Eventually; after a couple thousand feet of altitude loss; the red low speed tape cleared and we were able to gradually level the aircraft and gain positive control. narrative: I was the PIC and pilot flying a Learjet LR-60 departing RWY XX at ZZZ. We obtained our IFR clearance via telephone from ZZZ Departure and were released for departure with instructions to climb and maintain 5;000 MSL. Weather at the airport was MVFR with strong gusting winds (270/G40+); snow flurries; and very cold temperatures (later determined to be approximately ISA -18). Based on the conditions; I anticipated entering IMC and encountering turbulence shortly after departure. My SIC and I conducted a thorough briefing of the takeoff and climb profile. I executed a crosswind takeoff on RWY XX without incident. After takeoff I established a climb at 250 KIAS. The SIC completed the after-takeoff checklist. Moderate turbulence was encountered shortly after departure.At approximately 2;500 MSL; just prior to entering IMC; I engaged the autopilot in heading mode (laterally) and level change (vertically) to continue the climb at 250 KIAS to the assigned altitude of 5;000 MSL. We entered solid IMC and continued climbing in moderate turbulence. Approaching the assigned altitude; I observed that the aircraft climb rate had increased to approximately 3;000-4;000 FPM and was continuing to increase. The increase in climb rate occurred without a corresponding pitch increase or thrust change; suggesting the aircraft had encountered strong vertical air movement. It became apparent that the autopilot would not capture the assigned altitude. I reduced thrust and disconnected the autopilot to manually level the aircraft. Although airspeed decreased as expected; the aircraft continued climbing at a significant rate. I reduced thrust to flight idle and lowered the pitch attitude; however; the aircraft continued to climb while the speed decreased to about 170 KIAS. The aircraft was experiencing moderate turbulence and control responses seemed atypical. I suspected a strong updraft or unstable air mass. Due to concern about imposing excessive negative-G loads on the aircraft structure; I elected not to force an abrupt level-off and instead allowed the aircraft to 'ride it out;' and stabilize. We subsequently exceeded the assigned altitude. The ZZZ Departure controller queried our status and I advised that we were 'correcting.' ATC then issued a climb to 8;000 MSL. At approximately 7;000 MSL the rate of climb began to decrease and the aircraft stabilized. I re-established a normal climb profile. As we approached 8;000 MSL I re-engaged the autopilot; however; the autopilot again failed to capture the altitude.  In retrospect I suspect this occurred because I engaged the auto pilot too close to the level off; not allowing sufficient time to capture. I again disconnected the autopilot and manually leveled the aircraft as we exited IMC into VMC on top. The aircraft leveled at approximately 8;500 MSL. ATC again queried our status and I advised that we appeared to be experiencing an autopilot issue and were working the problem. We were instructed to climb to 10;000 MSL and proceed on course and were then handed off to ARTCC. The ARTCC controller asked if we required assistance or had an emergency. We advised that we were not declaring an emergency and that the aircraft was under control. We were subsequently cleared to climb to 17;000 MSL. I hand-flew the aircraft to that altitude and leveled off.After completing the cruise checklist and confirming that all systems appeared normal; I re-engaged the autopilot. The autopilot then appeared to function normally for the remainder of the flight. Lessons Learned:  This event caused me to give serious consideration to the fact that; in conditions involving strong winds; turbulence; and cold temperatures; significant vertical air movement may be present even outside of convective activity. This highlighted the importance of more closely monitoring climb performance and autopilot modes before; during; and after altitude capture. If the aircraft energy state becomes excessive or automation behavior is unexpected; transitioning more promptly to manual control and managing the aircraft more conservatively would help prevent future altitude deviations or structural loading concerns.  The SIC and I debriefed this incident at length after the flight and discussed strategies for prevention of such occurrences in the future.

narrative: Below is a summary of the unforeseen malfunction with the Autopilot/Trim that caused the pilot deviation while transporting 6 passengers to include infant today. This event occurred after takeoff on the initial climb out of ZZZ VFR. As I proceeded to climb to 1000ft under the Bravo shelf; I received a blinking Trim Error notification on the autopilot display panel and the plane began gradually porpoising. I followed the standard operating procedure by disconnecting the autopilot to reset the system. It worked initially; however; after 10-15 seconds and activating autopilot again; the Trim gave an error indication; once more; and the plane began an abrupt nose up pitch. After disconnecting the Autopilot again; in an attempt to recover the aircraft; the Trim wheel was still rolling aft and the plane kept increasing the rate of climb. I ran the system reset flow and recovered the aircraft after approximately 2-4min. While regaining full control of the aircraft by hand flying; I attempted to make contact with ZZZ App on XXX.X to inform them of my flight deviation; however due to the high volume of radio calls they were handling at the time because of severe weather; I never got a reply from ATC. After receiving no response; I switched frequencies and contacted ZZZ App XXY.XX to explain what had just occurred. This can be verified by the squawk code that I received to get VFR flight following. By this time; I was able to resolve the issue with the trim and eventually land the plane safely . After deplaning the passengers; I immediately contacted our lead mechanic to inform him about the event that had just occurred while in flight. I explained that this was my first time experiencing something like this and he recommended additional measures to take in the event that this ever happens again. I; in no way; had any intention of this happening and sincerely apologize for the deviation or possible inconvenience this may have caused. I pray this type of malfunction or incident does not occur again. Thank you for your time.

narrative: We were level at FL330 after descending from FL370 and the cabin altitude warning started sounding. Both pilots accomplished their memory items for the associated checklist. Communication was established quickly. When I looked at the cabin altitude indication; we were indicating 10;000 ft. cabin altitude. We initiated an emergency descent to 10;000 ft. MSL and requested priority handling with ZZZ Center. During the descent; I did notice at one point in the descent the PF had gone from LVL CHNG to VS and our IAS was increasing. I commanded the PF back to LVL CHNG and to reduce speed back to 280 kt. IAS as that is when the warning occurred and I knew the checklist would later say not to increase speed if structural damage is suspected. We had not reached that point in the checklist yet and had not made that determination. The cabin altitude warning checklist did not regain pressurization. According to the cabin altitude needle; we remained at 10;000 ft. cabin altitude. Later on when we were level at 10;000 ft.; the cabin altitude needle indicated as high as 50;000 ft. The cabin altitude needle changed multiple times during the rest of the flight making indications that didn't make logical sense and I suspected it was an indication problem. My theory was further reinforced that prior to the event; there were no physiological symptoms reported by any crew member. Regardless of this theory we still treated the problem as an actual depressurization. Physiological symptoms of ear and sinus pain did occur for some crew members as a result of directions for manual control of pressurization from the checklist. The cabin oxygen masks never deployed. An uneventful approach and landing occurred. Emergency personnel followed our aircraft to the gate.
narrative1: At cruise; as pilot flying; I briefed the Captain (CA) per the briefing card for our arrival into ZZZ. Weather was discussed as a possible threat that was northwest of ZZZ; as well as some gusty winds and possible choppy rides for descent. The ZZZZZ Arrival to the ILS XXL was briefed and descent checklist completed. The passengers were seated and seatbelt sign was turned on by the CA and flight attendants (FAs) were instructed to prepare the cabin prior to descent. We descended from our cruise altitude of FL370; with an intermediate level off at FL330. Shortly thereafter; the cabin altitude warning sounded and cabin altitude annunciator illuminated. Both the CA and I performed our associated memory items. We both saw a cabin altitude of 10;000 ft. The CA relayed the situation to ATC and we were given a clearance to descend to 10;000 ft. Priority handling was requested with ZZZ ATC and an urgent descent was initiated down to that assigned altitude. The CA ran the associated QRC and QRH checklists for the cabin altitude warning. The checklist never recovered a lower cabin altitude; from the 10;000 ft. cabin until below 10;000 ft. MSL. At one point while level at 10;000 ft. MSL the CA pointed out the gauge became erroneous and pegged out to the maximum cabin altitude of 50;000 ft. No passenger injuries were reported. FAs were briefed prior to arrival. Dispatch and Maintenance were notified as time allowed.A normal approach and landing ended the flight and emergency vehicles followed us to the gate; as a precaution. The CA and I debriefed at the gate.

narrative: At approximately 90 minutes prior to touchdown; we completed the descent checklist and briefings. At about 40 minutes out; while maintaining FL360; I reached for the sun visor to detach and stow it. The visor fell inadvertently and landed on the aft section of the center console. While the visor struck the left start lever; neither pilot immediately realized the lever had been moved to the cutoff position.We noticed a discrepancy a few seconds later; a thrust lever split developed and the autothrottle disconnect light began flashing. Initial diagnosis suggested a mechanical issue with the left thrust lever; I attempted to prevent the lever from retarding and tried to re-engage the autothrottle; but the system would not engage and the lever would not maintain its position.The FO identified that the left start lever was in the cutoff position and verbalized the state while I observed the airspeed dropping. Recognizing the engine loss; I reiterated that I had control of the aircraft and radios; and commanded the FO to perform the appropriate checklist. We requested priority handling and initiated a descent. When the FO requested to return the start lever to idle; I concurred; however; upon observing an engine EGT over-temp; the FO correctly returned the lever to cutoff to protect the engine.While the FO was waiting for the APU to start; he contacted the flight attendants (FAs) to inform them of the engine shutdown; they were instructed to wait for further guidance; though no brief was conducted at that time. We both agreed to delay the passenger announcement until the results of the engine restart were known.In accordance with the checklist; once we descended below FL240 and accelerated toward 300 kt.; we initiated the engine restart. The engine restarted successfully at FL220 and 300 kt. Once the engine stabilized and checklists were complete; the FAs were updated and a passenger announcement was made stating that we had experienced abnormal engine indications which were successfully resolved.Dispatch was notified of the engine shutdown and subsequent restart. I transferred radio communications back to the FO and directed him to cancel the priority handling. We continued for an uneventful landing in ZZZ. Following the shutdown checklist; we conducted a crew debrief. Maintenance received a full briefing on the flight deck; and an entry was made in the Electronic Logbook (ELB). We then briefed the Chief Pilot and Dispatch. Although we initially felt fit to continue our deadhead to ZZZ1; the Chief Pilot later informed us of a schedule change for review; and we were released to go home.
synopsis: B737 Captain reported the flight crew did not notice the left start lever inadvertently moved to the cutoff position during cruise flight but was able to successfully restart the engine for an uneventful landing.

narrative1: While at Gate XX in ZZZ rampers had us keep brakes on while they hooked up the tug. After we were secured to tug rampers gave us the all secure below; FOD check complete; steering disengaged ready for break release. We released brake and called for push. Ramp cleared us for push; rampers notified us that the tug was broken and they would need to get a new one. Ramper told us standby he will let us know when to set the brake. Both the FO and I agreed that we heard the ramper  say to hold on he will let us know when to set the brake. We heard rampers working below the aircraft. I continually over the headset asked ramp if they were ready for the brakes with no answer. We could hear them banging on something below the nose. We heard the interphone disconnect as the plane was lowed from the tug and felt the plane move back slightly. I had my feet on the brakes and applied slight pressure to come to a stop. We saw rampers below move the broken tug back. I kept giving hand signals to the ramper that came into view to set brakes. He gave me the set brake signal and I set the brakes. Another ramper came onto the headset and told us we had a rollback event. She also stated that she saw the green light illuminated after the rollback happened. Rampers said they did not see any damage and we did not roll back far. I called Maintenance Control and asked if we need to have anything checked out; we had no indications and ramp saw no damage; Maintenance Control said we were good to go. We elected to get hooked back up and push back to continue the flight with no issues.Cause: There was a miscommunication from ramp on setting the brakes. The FO and I agreed we heard the ramper say hold on I'll let you know when to set the brake. We could hear the rampers on the headset doing something below the nose but they did not respond to my repeated questioning if they needed brakes set.Suggestions: Need better communications with ramp to verify brakes were set when they needed to be.

narrative1: During descent to the initial approach fix we entered into IMC with moderate precipitation and continuous light with pockets of moderate turbulence. As we continued on approach; we were switched to tower and we were cleared to land. As we descended on the approach the moderate turbulence turned into severe turbulence. We decided to execute the missed approach around 10;000 MSL and let tower know. We were then switched back to ATC. At that point we also entered into wind shear. No wind shear warning populated on the Primary Flight Display (PFD) as we were above 1;500 ft. AGL. With excessive airspeed fluctuations; -3;000 fpm on the VSI; and 30-degree roll either direction; the captain (CA) elected to regain as much control of the aircraft as possible with two hands on the yoke and gave throttles to me. With the wind shear now a factor with the severe turbulence I pushed the thrust levers to max. We eventually climbed while focusing on maintaining control of the aircraft on the published missed track. As soon as we could we contacted ATC to report we had severe turbulence and we were going missed. As the turbulence started to turn back into moderate; we realized we still needed to put in an altitude. CA requested FL230; something that would be well above the turbulence; and to let ATC know. Examination of the flight data confirmed this. It also confirmed that all engine indications were normal through the run-up; takeoff roll; and early climb. I made a 45degree descending left turn down to 10;000ft until making visual contact with the aircraft. Due to the aircraft proximity during the evasive maneuver I did not have high fidelity situational awareness of the other aircraft's location until making visual contact. Aircraft Y had been enroute VFR from ZZZ to SBP on what appears to be a direct course at 12;500ft. Aircraft Y began its decent into SBP; at 174kt. At this time Aircraft X was 1.6NM ahead; 1000ft below and at 130kt. Aircraft Y accelerated to 210kt in the decent; making the closing speed at the incident 80kt.Aircraft X made an evasive descending right turn. There was a less than 200ft of vertical separation; less than 200ft of horizontal separation and Aircraft X was unable to make contact with Aircraft Y on 121.5. The evasive action allowed visual contact to be made; and both aircraft arrived without incident to SBP. In summary: Aircraft Y began an enroute decent; and accelerated during the denent. Uncertain of obstruction or telemetry inside the Aircraft Y aircraft; the pilot was likely unaware of the high speed overtake on the same course and position. Aircraft X was only able to identify the situation through ADSP and Garmin 275 display; and made evasive action avoiding a mid-air collision. narrative: The aircraft operated was under MEL for a failed B fire detection loop. A loop only selected per the MEL and tested ok on preflight. Shortly before reaching cruise altitude we noticed the fire loop A FAULT light flashing intermittently. A message was sent to dispatch and we were patched through to Maintenance Control. After some confusion in relaying the system failure due to poor radio connectivity we sent an ACARS to Maintenance Control explaining that we had a failed B fire loop and now a fault in the remaining A fire loop.  Maintenance Control advised it was Captain's discretion whether to continue the flight or not. After conferring with the FO we decided it would be better to divert back to ZZZ because we had no working engine fire detection system on either loop. Our thinking is that we had another 4 hours of flying ahead and it would be bad to continue since it would be possible to have an engine fire with no flight deck indication. We coordinated with ATC for a return to ZZZ and ran the appropriate checklists. Flight attendants and passengers were notified. We ran the checklist for overweight landing and opted to land on the longest runway; XXL; with auto brakes 2 to avoid hot brakes. We advised ATC that we wanted fire and rescue to examine the aircraft after landing to verify no smoke or fire on the brakes and no signs of an engine problem. ATC advised that if we wanted the trucks they would have to request priority handling for us. We agreed out of an abundance of caution to have fire and rescue look us over after landing. Subsequent approach and landing were uneventful. Upon exiting the runway post flight inspection showed no signs of engine problems or hot brakes. We taxied uneventfully to the gate. Maintenance entries were made for an overweight landing at 174;000 pounds and the failed fire detection loops.

narrative: ZZZ was meant to be a fuel stop on our trip. When we fueled up and departed ZZZ; called for gear up; the gear handle raised but the gear did not retract.  We continued to climb to a safe altitude of 6000 feet and get vectors from the controller while we ran the checklist. The gear handle would not go back down to the 'gear down 'position for some time. Upon reaching the point of the 'gear will not retract' checklist; it called for gear handle down and with some force; the handle finally moved to the down position. The gear indicators throughout the entire time remained 'three green' down and locked. There was never a 'gear unsafe' red light illuminated. There was never a hyd pressure light illuminated to indicate pressure to gear . Never received any other abnormal indications.  Once sufficient fuel had been burnt off to make landing weight; we returned to ZZZ with Airport Rescue and Firefighting positioned   just in case. The landing was uneventful. Two days later we ferried plane for maintenance on a ferry permit. Crew was fine and passengers were sent another aircraft for remainder of their trip.Suggestions: The checklist for 'gear will not retract' addressed some of what we were seeing but not everything. Our concern was that the gear handle being left in the up position might cause a gear collapse on landing if left in that position. Luckily; we were able to move it back to the down and locked position.  With the gear handle down and the gear never having retracted; the checklist was complete.  I believe that ultimately the entire gear handle mechanism got replaced but would like to know for sure what failed in the system to cause this problem.
synopsis: Citation Excel Captain reported a landing gear handle malfunction where the gear would not retract during the climb; then the handle would not return to the down position. The handle was forced into the down position; then returned to the departure airport and landed safely.

narrative: During climbout from ZZZ; #1 engine vibrations fluctuated wildly; oscillating between 2.0 and 3.5.  High vibrations continued until power was reduced to maintain cruise altitude.  I contacted dispatch through VHF radio and we did a 3 way call between myself; dispatch; and Maintenance Control.  Maintenance informed us during the conference that the #1 engine had a recent history of several writeups for high vibrations and that there was a technical item assigned to that engine to track its performance.  I expressed my concern that this aircraft was assigned to a destination like ZZZ1 (our original destination) given its history.  The three of us agreed that it would be prudent to return to ZZZ given the limited contract maintenance available in ZZZ1 and the high terrain in the area that places a high demand on the engines  in the event of a go-around or takeoff from runway XX.  At the time we were about 6;000 lbs over max landing weight; so we coordinated with ATC to hold until we were under max landing and we returned to ZZZ.  Known history of bad performance on an engine that was also assigned to a destination which has limited contract maintenance.Aircraft with engines that have a recent history of questionable performance should not be assigned.  The lower display in the 737 should be turned on during the after takeoff checklist so that all secondary engine indications are displayed to catch this and other engine situations that slowly creep up on the crew.  The time to be prepared and do something is early before the situation arises; not when the display automatically pops up. This should be standardized across all Boeing fleets.
narrative1: I was performing PF duties flying Aircraft X from ZZZ Airport to ZZZ1. During climb out it was noticed that the left engine vibration was fluctuating. The CA; performing PM duties; and I each looked and noticed the engine vibration fluctuating in an erratic pattern. I noticed that the initial fluctuation grew from approximately 2.0-2.5 to 1.5-3.5 rapidly and unpredictably; while the right engine remained steady at approximately 0.2. As the PF; I scanned other instruments and all other indications seemed normal; we continued the climb while watching the engine vibrations. The CA opened and referenced the engine vibration checklist in the event we might need it; so that we would be prepared - however we did not perform the checklist as the fluctuations did not go out of limits.We had a brief discussion; which resulted in us not being able to say why the engine was vibrating like that; and that the captain could actually feel the vibration on his side of the cockpit. Shortly after the CA asked if I was comfortable handling the aircraft and radios so that he could try to call dispatch; to which I concurred.Around this time passing through FL280 and leveling at FL290; over Location X I assumed those duties. I noticed that the engine vibration fluctuations lessened but did not resolve at cruise power settings. As the Captain was working through his call to dispatch; I was focused on aviating; navigating; and communicating - having to work route deviations and climbs to avoid weather over Location X. I did note that when we climbed from FL290 to FL330 for weather; the engine vibration fluctuations increased at climb power as they had before - and settled a little lower but did not resolve at cruise power at FL330.I was able to hear a small portion of the conversation the Captain was having; most notably the discussion from the maintenance representative that this aircraft had some form of history of this engine vibration; and that there was a concurrence with dispatch that a return to ZZZ was prudent. The CA informed me after their call that we would return to ZZZ.It was my understanding having discussed with the CA after his call to dispatch that this return to ZZZ was based on there being a known history of fluctuating indications on the left engine for an unknown reason. Our discussions revolved around ZZZ1; the single engine profiles; performance; and potential for the engine to have some form of failure at the wrong moment on those complex departure procedures. After the decision to return to ZZZ the discussion was had weather to land overweight; or to burn down fuel to land under max landing weight. Based on: strong and gusty crosswinds; the potential to damage the aircraft landing heavy; the engine remaining within limits and settling lower at cruise power; I recommended to descend and burn down fuel in holding to below max landing weight; to which the CA agreed. We then returned to ZZZ uneventfully. An engine with a history of engine vibration presentation; which was fluctuating rapidly close to the upper limit. Engines with known issues such as this should not be dispatched. The lower display is turned off per SOP; however passing 10k this screen should be turned on to be monitored during the remainder of the flight.
synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported engine vibrations and return to departure airport.

He had me fly the aircraft and run radios while he dealt with this procedure. We elected to level off and enter a hold over ZZZZZ to develop and analyze a plan. We notified ZZZ tower we would be stopping on the runway and would need possible tow off runway as well as Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) to give a quick inspection. Joining final for RWY XXL; we turned on GREEN ENG 1 PUMP as directed by the STATUS page APPR PROCEDURE. We regained back all our inop systems and the aircraft was operating as normal. We landed as normal; came to a stop; and the captain made a PA to the passenger notifying that ARFF would be inspecting the aircraft out of caution. We were able to taxi back to the gate under our own power with no further issues. Event was caused by hydraulic abnormalities. Only mitigation is to continue to be proficient in emergency procedures.
narrative1: Enroute we received a HYD G SYS LO PR ecam and other subsequent ecams. We performed the ecam methodology as trained. We entered a holding pattern between ZZZ1 and ZZZ. FO remained PF while I spoke with dispatch; ATC; FAs; and passengers. The decision was jointly made to divert to ZZZ; only 45 miles away at that point due to the long runway; acceptable Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) and maintenance personnel. The FO remained PF during the duration of the flight and did a great job. Per the ecam we were able to turn the G pump back on and get the gear and flaps down normally using whatever fluid was left. We stopped on the runway; ARFF performed their inspection; and we we able to taxi to the gate on our own power. We took our time and were deliberate in our actions and decisions. Air Carrier X was a great resource and very helpful during the entire event as was ATC. We are trained very well such that two pilots who have never met or flown together until the day before can be professional and standard and work together in a setting like that.Nothing really from a flight crew perspective. Per the logbook closing actions looks like a faulty hydraulic drain valve and busted o ring. Not sure what we as flight crew could do different for a maintenance item like that

I could also hear the loud ambient noise through the intercom as we talked.I told the FAs that the door seal most likely failed or did not engage properly; and that the door was mechanically secure so there was no safety risk of it opening inflight. Ultimately a decision was made to return to ZZZ and that the airplane would be landing about 7500-8000LBS over the max structure landing weight. I had the FO coordinate with ATC new clearance to return to ZZZ and to request lowest altitude possible to burn off as much fuel as possible on the return as well as attempted to lower the Cabin ALT and reduce the ambient noise if possible. An emergency was not declared at the time.I did a Brief with the Purser; then made a cabin PA for the passengers explaining the situation. After referencing the 737 Flight Manual for overweight landing I ultimately decided that due to our landing weight being close to 8;000LBS over the max structure  the need for runway XXR in ZZZ (longest available) as well as the possibility of hot brakes after landing that requesting priority handling and having fire trucks on standby for the brakes was the most conservative plan of action. I informed ATC of the change of status to priority handling and why; then requested runway XXR and to have the fire trucks on standby for a brake check once clear of the runway. ATC passed along all the information and verified our FOB and SOB. I did another briefing revision with the purser due to the change to priority handling status. I then made a PA to the cabin about the reason for the fire tucks meeting the aircraft after landing.After the FMC was set up; Briefings and checklists were complete I took over PF duties of the aircraft. Maintenance techs met the aircraft and took the details from me after I sent in the Log Book reports for the door and overweight landing. Flight XXXX continued out of gate XX with a different aircraft 90 min later.

narrative1: Fifteen minutes into our climb; at 28;000 feet; the forward galley flight attendants called the flight deck to inform us of a fire. The Captain slid the phone halfway off his cheek; looked at me; and said fire". I asked; "Is it contained?" Given the panic in the galley; we initially believed the fire was not under control. Aircraft controls were transferred to the CA; who initiated a descent and a turn towards ZZZ. I informed ATC of our actions. Shortly after our turn towards ZZZ; the flight attendants called back with additional information. They reported that the fire was located in the forward galley oven and that one fire extinguisher had been used. I repeated this information to the flight attendants to ensure clear communication. The fire had been extinguished. I then relayed this information to the CA. Ultimately; since we could not determine the source of the fire and could not guarantee that it would not reignite; we decided to continue our diversion to ZZZ. We discussed the potential threats associated with an overweight landing and the increased pace of flight deck duties associated with a quick return. We prioritized the important threats appropriately; and trapped them with mitigation strategies. We performed an overweight landing and stopped on the runway until we could assess brake temperatures. The most incredible moment of this flight unfolded when we arrived at the gate. To our astonishment; all of our wheelchair passengers walked off the airplane."

narrative: In the interest of safety; I am writing this report to help pilots be more aware of the risks of improper fuel planning. On Day 0; a passenger and I made our way to ZZZ for a joyride. When we arrived at the airport; I immediately began my preflight with Aircraft X. My standard walk-around includes checking all control surfaces; propeller; tires; brakes; oil; and fuel. Fuel is always my last task. On this particular day; I visually verified that both tanks were full. I also strained the fuel to ensure no contaminants were present. Since this was a day VFR joyride; I calculated the distance and time we would be flying; and it was agreed we would just go where we wanted to.The flight was uneventful for the first portion as we made our way from ZZZ to ZZZ1 at 4;500 feet; where we conducted a landing and then flew up to Location X for pictures. We then flew from Location X to ZZZ2; where I flew the RNAV XX approach. At that point; I decided not to stop and check the fuel and performed a low approach; believing I had plenty of fuel to make it back to ZZZ.I knew the aircraft held 38 gallons of usable fuel and estimated a burn rate of 8 GPH. At the time we executed the low approach at ZZZ2; we had only been flying for approximately 3 hours; which I believed was sufficient to return to ZZZ.I then began setting up for a practice RNAV XY approach into ZZZ. After crossing ZZZZZ on approximately an 8-mile final and descending through about 2;500 feet; the engine began to sputter. I checked the total flight time; which was approximately 4 hours and 5 minutes. I immediately looked for the nearest airport on the GPS and initiated a 180-degree turn to attempt to return to ZZZ3; which was approximately 4 miles behind us.The engine continued to sputter and then completely lost power shortly after leveling the turn. At that point; it was clear we did not have the altitude or power to reach an airport. I immediately began running the emergency checklist and pitched for best glide and began looking for a suitable field.Around 100 feet AGL; I noticed the airspeed decreasing and added full flaps. The selected field was clear of crops; and I executed a soft-field landing. There were no injuries and no damage to the aircraft.Upon review of the aircraft; it was determined that both fuel tanks were empty due to higher-than-expected fuel consumption during the flight. Even though we departed with full fuel; I did not adequately calculate the fuel required for the flight we ultimately conducted.Additionally; the mixture was not properly adjusted during portions of the flight; which likely contributed to increased fuel consumption. The decision to continue from ZZZ2 without verifying fuel quantity was also a contributing factor and; in hindsight; could have prevented the situation.As PIC; I take responsibility for the outcome of this flight and the planning decisions that led to this situation. This experience highlighted a lapse in judgment that resulted in a scenario I had not intended.I am proud of how the situation was handled. I remained calm; followed established procedures; and relied on my training to safely land the aircraft without injury or damage.I learned more from this experience than any single flight lesson. It reinforced the importance of thorough planning and disciplined decision-making.In the future I will ensure fuel requirements are properly calculated; including legal reserves; even on shorter or 'joyride' flights. Properly adjust the mixture throughout all phases of flight. Stop and verify fuel status rather than relying on assumptions.This is an experience I will not forget; and it has reinforced the importance of completing all calculations thoroughly and maintaining situational awareness throughout the entire flight.

Before drones; law enforcement helicopters were deployed for this type of surveillance. Drones should be required to have a highly reflective surface in addition to higher intensity anti-collision lights. narrative1: On Day 0; I was pilot monitoring of Aircraft X as first officer with scheduled service from LIR to ZZZ. The captain and I arrived to the airport well-rested after a 23-hour overnight and the arrival to the airport and airplane was standard. We were given clearance for push back and start from gate XX; which was accomplished normally and we joined the line for taxi to the departure end of the runway. The airport had been on runway 07 operations for the entire time we were there; so a full-length back taxi was required. Upon reaching the runway; we waited in the turnaround for arriving traffic behind an aircraft. There was an arriving Aircraft X that landed a few minutes after the aircraft departed that; once past us; we were issued a line up and wait clearance; which we accepted. After waiting in position for approximately two minutes; we were given a takeoff clearance by the tower. Initial power up and acceleration was normal. I called 80" and almost immediately after; tower calls "Aircraft X; cancel takeoff clearance." The captain and I were a bit confused as there was nothing hazardous immediately apparent in front of us; but we initiated a rejected takeoff. The deceleration was smooth; and callouts were standard. Once stopped; I started a timer and dropped the flaps to 40° and the captain retracted the spoilers and made an announcement to the cabin to remain seated. Once slowed; we were asked if we could make a 180 on the runway to return to the departure end; which we were able to accommodate. I was instructed to perform an after landing flow; and the captain and I began to discuss the requirements for a rejected takeoff and brake cooling requirements from the table in the AOM. The auto brakes did not fire; so we knew we were below 90kt when the reject was initiated; however with the adjustments for the length of taxi and the headwind; we determined that the most conservative cooling time was 45.9 minutes. We were not in the caution or melt zone; so we set the parking brake when coming to a complete stop.When queried the reason for the rejected takeoff clearance; the tower responded that an airplane had not fully cleared the runway. They tried to issue us a second takeoff clearance while we were calculating cooling times and contacting dispatch and maintenance control; and ultimately we were instructed to return to the gate for a visual inspection. We were caught in a lot of traffic; but made our way back to the gate and maintenance was waiting on us. We elected to not give the opportunity to deplane given the efficiency with which we were parked and accommodated by maintenance. The airplane was determined to be safe to continue on; so we closed the main cabin door; and pushed back for a normal flight arriving to ZZZ about an hour and a half late. No injuries were reported and no further problems with the airplane were experienced. Cause: We were issued a late cancellation of takeoff clearance for a runway incursion that was impossible to see from the departure end of the runway. Flight and cabin crew followed SOPs to mitigate injury or escalation of the event."

As part of the deferral; we were restricted to FL250 (originally FL360) and since this was an MEL affecting our performance and fuel consumption calculations we needed to call dispatch and see if we have enough fuel; and if so; get a new release. Upon calling dispatch we were able to continue with our current fuel on-board; and obtain a new release. After getting our new release we rejoined the departures and the taxi-take off was completely uneventful. The take off was normal until the climb portion where I had noticed the EICAS message 'ENG 2 BLV VLV CLSD' during my after take off flow. I consulted the Captain on the appropriate QRH procedure and conducted the QRH procedure. Upon completion of the procedure the message had cleared and we continued. As we leveled off at FL240 (our final filed altitude); I smelled a burning smell; simultaneously the Captain had noticed the same thing. As we looked at each other; I noticed smoke coming above the Captain's head. We then dawned our O2 masks; and we informed ATC that we needed to immediately return to ZZZ due to 'smoke in the cockpit'. The flight attendant also contacted us about a burning smell. We then descended and received vectors back to ZZZ; we joined the localizer for XXC. Since I was not fully caught up on setting up approach/speeds; I informed the Captain that I 'needed more time' we informed ATC. We continued on that heading for a brief minute; then the Captain determined that the safest course of action was to continue for XXL instead of delay vectors; as we did not know the source; nor the severity of the possible smoke and fumes. narrative: I decided; for the safety of Flight; and perhaps a good discussion; to post a little educational rant about a very close midair my student and I watched happen on Day 0 at XA:20 at ZZZ. We were holding short of RWY XX and watched a prior plane on a somewhat long final make a touch and go. A Cherokee then turned their base behind them appropriately and I pointed out to the traffic to my student. Interestingly; we then noticed a subsequent Cessna turn a very low tight left base. The Cherokee by this time was already on final; and had made their call. They then asked if the Cessna had them in sight. They replied in the affirmative and that they would 'extend their base.' For the record; they were already on their base leg. I watched as both planes continued on a collision course right above the Street X intersection with the Cherokee finally climbing and side stepping and the Cessna staying low and flying due south probably about 50 feet of separation between them; then making a radio call 'that was close!' I spoke to the Cherokee pilot afterwards and fortunately they did have the Cessna traffic in sight throughout the incident; so I suspect while it looked close that it would have had a safe outcome regardless of how it looked from my vantage point. A few thoughts for all of us to ponder. I am convinced that the Cessna never had the Cherokee in sight. I presume; perhaps falsely; that they were looking at an ADSB return rather than out the window. We all need a reminder that ADSB is NOT visual separation. When ATC asks you if you have traffic in sight; they mean with your eye balls. Not on your 'fish finder'. Please; for the love of God; do not call it that. Even more importantly; when another pilot asks if you have them in sight; do not reply in the affirmative if you do not. Instead; take action immediately to increase the separation between you. In formation flying when you lose sight of your wingman; you immediately call blind and increase the separation between the aircraft. This isn't checkers; it's flying. And a simple screw up will kill you; or much worse; someone else. ADSB isn't perfect. It has a lag. Sometimes a fraction of a second and sometimes 20 seconds. Are you using a third party device that then wirelessly connects to your foreflight app to show you? Are you holding a phone in your lap? Or is your system installed in the plane and displayed on a Multi-function Flight Display (MFD)? Even primary radar has a lag. Nothing is perfect. More importantly  not everyone has ADSB. It's not required. I don't have it in my plane. It is for situational awareness. It is not meant to replace your eyeballs. When someone on the frequency calls a position you should look outside the plane first; not at your panel or your phone. I presume we all know 91.113 about right of way. Read it again if you haven't this year. Landing traffic has the right of way. If someone is already on final; turn your left base once they are at your 9'o'clock; not while they are still at 11 o'clock. The C210 on Day 0  turned their base low at least a half mile before the Cherokee. In the left seat; low; with a high wing; they had no chance of seeing that Cherokee. Why then did they say traffic was in sight? And what does extending your base leg even mean when you are already on your base?The question I pose to myself; sitting at the threshold; is should I have been empowered to play ATC and demand a go around? My thought was to not clog the frequency while these two worked it out. However in hindsight; there was no negotiation between them. I would have felt very guilty if I had not said something. Kudos to both pilots afterwards for being kind and professional. Neither of them got nasty on the radio (something that I hear too frequently these days) and neither of them chastised each other. The Cessna exited the area and the Cherokee got back in the pattern. I presume both had honest debriefs when they got home. However; the rest of us can stand to learnsomething from this close call before the flying season gets busy. Every year in our country someone dies due to this situation because of two reasons: 1.) they misinterpret 91.113 or 2.) they are too hard headed to realize that even though they are in the right; they neglect to knock off their approach and create separation because - dang-it - they have the right away!!! I argue that this Cherokee; due to the fact that they could see the Cessna making a mistake; could have aborted their touch and go 30 seconds earlier. They could have sidestepped on an upwind to keep the Cessna in sight and learned a valuable lesson that being courteous; even when you were the one that was wronged; is the right thing; and the safe thing; to do. Don't think this thing happens a lot? How many classic 91.113 see and avoid mishaps come to mind right off the bat?  DCA accident?  Centennial accident between the metro liner and Cirrus. Or maybe all of us need to have a little common sense and remind ourselves to be courteous. This means if you are working with a student on instrument work and the pattern is really full; it's not the time to do your circling maneuver. This means if it's clear and a million and you're on an instrument plan in a single engine piston; you shouldn't fly a 10 mile straight in and you should join the pattern in a VFR manner - even if your bladder is about to explode! It means if a turbine is arriving; that the rest of us make way and let them land. We only have one sand box to play in. We should keep it pleasant for every user…we all have a right to be there.

narrative: Aircraft X upon reaching cruise altitude of FL350 received an ECAM for CAB PR SYS 1 FAULT. Ran ECAM; QRH; Follow ups (none) and ECAM Supplemental. Item was listed as 'Crew Awareness;' as suspected. Wrote up the ECAM as it was listed in the status page as an INOP system. Logbook Deferral Sheet #XXXXXXX. Continued to ZZZ without further incident. Maintenance met the aircraft at the gate in ZZZ. They needed to run resets and computer checks so flight crew exited the cockpit. Item was cleared with a Final Action of OK; Message Cleared. Upon returning to the flight deck; I reviewed the sign off in the log book. The troubleshooting took some time and we were about done boarding. I checked the status and the INOP system; CAB PR 1 in Amber was still in box 4 of the ECAM. I called station maintenance and asked for the mechanics to return. The junior mechanic came back to the aircraft and I showed him the status message. He then saw that the system was indeed; not fixed. He said he needed to run the resets again. First Officer stayed in the cockpit while I vacated the area so the mechanic could use my Multipurpose Control Display Unit (MCDU) and seat. He proceeded to troubleshoot the same issue for about 45 minutes. After some time passed; the more senior mechanic arrived back to the aircraft and joined his partner in the cockpit. The first officer exited the aircraft and joined me on the jetbridge. He was listening to the mechanics talk about the issue and basically realize that the system that they signed off; message cleared was in fact; not cleared. They were essentially attempting to fix the system this time without entering anything else into the maintenance logbook to cover up the fact that they didn't actually clear my write up. Eventually; they gave up and decided to MEL the system. Something that should have been done from the very start so that we could have had an on time departure out of ZZZ as this system was allowed on the MEL. They wrote up a new discrepency of CAB PRESS SYS 1 FAULT Logbook Deferral Sheet #XXXXXXY and applied MEL 21-XXX. They pulled and collared circuit breaker D9 and X23. We waited for the sign off to clear the logbook and reviewed an procedure that needed to be accomplished during pre flight to satisfy the MEL. Upon review of the procedure; I saw that we needed to open circuit breaker X23 that controls the Residual Pressure Control Unit (RPCU) on step 1. Step 6 states to close circuit breaker X23. This circuit breaker had been pulled and collared by ZZZ station maintenance. At this time I had lost all faith in these two mechanics. They were rushing to complete a task. I called Air Carrier X Maintenance Control and conferred with them about what to do. I asked if I had permission to remove the  circuit breaker collar since the pre flight pilot procedure was to manipulate the circuit breaker and that it needed to be in the closed/in position for flight. After looking up the MEL and procedure; Maintenance Control agreed with me that the circuit breaker collar needed to be removed and left off to remain in compliance with the MEL. Maintenance Control  mentioned that they station maintenance might have been using an old revision of their repair manuals. At this point; neither the FO or I trusted that station maintenance complied with the maintenance procedures listed in the MEL so I had Maintenance Control go over them with me and he confirmed that by having circuit breaker D9 pulled; the Aircraft Maintenance Manual (AMM) procedures were in compliance. At this same time; the station maintenance called up to the flight deck using the ramp head set and told us to remove the circuit breaker collar at X23 and that they were using the wrong AMM repair manual. He apologized. After reconfiguring the aircraft to the state that was in compliance with the MEL and performing the pre flight tasks associated with it; we deemed the flight safe to continue and left for our destination without further incident. I take this event to be a serious safety infraction as an expired manual was used in the application of an MEL that required circuit breakers to be pulled for flight. Station maintenance's attempt to cover up the fact that they had cleared the write up instead of issuing the MEL was unacceptable. Cause: Use of expired repair; AMM; and MEL manuals by ZZZ station maintenance. Rushing to complete the task by ZZZ station maintenance. Signing off a write up that shouldn't have been signed off. Applying the wrong MEL procedure by ZZZ station maintenance. Air Carrier X's pressure of middle managers to push mechanics; pilots; and other staff to rush; overlooking a safe operation such that they achieve their quarterly bonuses is an egregious causal factor. It should never have come to the pilots needing to check the work of mechanics and fixing these mistakes as the last barrier to safety. These mistakes should never have been made and it shakes the foundation of safety culture and our trust in our peers' ability to perform their jobs safely and correctly. I do not appreciate being pushed to the limits of safety in the name of on time performance. I have a life outside of flying as a father and husband and I take those jobs extremely seriously and they are more important than any job flying airplanes. I intend on making it home to them every time I leave for work. This airline needs a serious look at other work group safety; I'm so tired of the onus being laid upon us time after time; risking our licenses and lives; for what? Bonuses and stock prices. NASA; the FAA; and whomever else has a stake in safety needs to have a look at practices here at Air Carrier X and really push safety first. We say it every day; it's time everyone actually lives it.
