narrative: During the climb; around 20;000; the PIC and I heard and felt a 'bang'. I looked back and noticed that the aft seated passenger appeared to have just shut the lav door and I thought he slammed the door shut; thus causing the 'bang.' I glanced at the cabin pressure differential gauge and noted there was a split in the differential pressure and that it appeared normal.Just after leveling off at 38;000 the Crew Alerting System (CAS) message 'CABIN ALTITUDE' appeared. We donned our masks; requested priority handling; and started to descend. I pulled out and began to run the checklist. The PIC took the radios and requested a lower altitude and a clearance direct back to our home base. After running the checklist; I took note that the cabin pressure differential gauge still showed a split in differential pressure; and that cabin altitude showed 10;000. The PIC advised the passengers of what happened and one passenger requested the oxygen masks; which the PIC then manually deployed.Once we descended below 8;000 the CAS message 'CABIN ALTITUDE' shut off. We canceled priority handling request and landed uneventfully back at our homebase.What I believe really caused the problem is that the outflow valve or some of the pressurization piping malfunctioned or blew a seal during climbout. To better respond to this issue in the future we could have requested priority handling soon after hearing the 'bang'. I now plan to monitor the cabin pressure differential gauge more closely during the climb and more frequently during level off and cruise.
narrative1: On our climbout; somewhere around FL200; we heard a bang and felt a pressure wave in the cabin. My first reaction was to look at the cabin pressure differential gauge to see if we had lost pressure. Upon looking at the cabin pressure differential gauge; everything looked to be normal. We had a cabin pressure differential; and our cabin altitude appeared to be at the correct altitude. I also looked for any lights near the cabin pressure differential gauge to indicate a failure of the automated system; and I observed none. I then looked for any Crew Alerting System (CAS) messages on my Multi-function Flight Display (MFD) and did not see any. I then looked back at the passengers to see if I could see anything wrong with the aircraft in the cabin. I noticed that one of the passengers closed the lavatory doors and thought that he might have just slammed it shut. With no issues found; I elected to continue our climb to FL380.Shortly after arriving at our cruise altitude (FL380); we received a CABIN ALTITUDE Master Warning. Both pilots quickly put on their oxygen masks and established communication. I was the flying pilot; took control of the radios; and the pilot monitoring started running the QRH procedure for CABIN ALTITUDE. I requested priority handling and requested an immediate descent. ATC cleared us to FL300 and asked for the number of souls on board and remaining fuel. I responded to those questions; requested a lower altitude; and stated we wanted to return to ZZZ. We were cleared directly to ZZZ and to 10;000 ft. We deployed the passengers' oxygen masks and asked for 8;000 ft. At this point; the pilot monitoring completed the QRH procedure. Upon reaching 8;000 ft.; our master caution cleared; and the QRH procedure was complete; so we advised that we were no longer needed priority handling. We decided to return to our departure airport; ZZZ; and landed safely without further issues.Upon landing; we looked at the aircraft and found no obvious problems. Currently; maintenance is looking at the aircraft to determine the issue. I assume that it is something to do with our outflow valve. We did not have a rapid decompression; and the aircraft was still maintaining a little bit of cabin differential pressure; but not enough to keep the cabin altitude where it should have been. That is why it is my assumption that it has something to do with the outflow valve.  Lessons learned and things we could have done better. After landing safely and discussing the event with my copilot; I found some things that I could have done better.-Upon hearing the bang and feeling the pressure wave; my copilot and I should have been paying closer attention to the cabin pressure differential gauge. We could have potentially caught the issue sooner and descended before we needed to request priority handling.-Secondly; it was hard to hear ATC with the oxygen mask on; and I had to ask them to repeat some things. I could have turned my vox off to eliminate the breathing noise; and I could have turned the volume up more so I could hear better. -Lastly; I could have deployed the oxygen masks sooner for the passengers. I should have deployed them when both me and the copilot donned our oxygen masks.

narrative: I was flying with my friend in his airplane during a VFR sightseeing tour through the Grand Canyon Special Flight Rules Area (SFRA). We were northbound in the corridor when we observed traffic at our altitude on an eastbound heading from our left on the ADSB; resulting in a converging situation. The other aircraft subsequently turned southbound while remaining at the same altitude. Per the applicable section of 14 CFR pertaining to this SFRA; direction of flight within the Grand Canyon SFRA corresponds to specific altitude assignments.As the traffic continued to close; We attempted multiple times to establish radio contact with the other aircraft on the CTAF to determine if they had us in sight. No response was received. The applicable section of 14 CFR requires all pilots operating within the SFRA to monitor the designated CTAF frequency.As the closure rate increased and radio contact was not established; I disconnected the autopilot and began maneuvering a descent and right turn to create separation. At that moment; the right seat pilot called 'my controls.' To avoid a dual-input situation during an already time-critical event; I relinquished. The right seat pilot executed a left descend turn. The other aircraft passed at very close range. To my knowledge; I was the only crew member with a visual on the traffic throughout the encounter.Following the incident; I recommended discontinuing the tour and landing. I also attempted to conduct an informal debrief with the other crew members on board; the conversation did not take place at that time.The next day; I identified the pilots from the other aircraft and approached them to discuss the incident and review the applicable SFRA regulations. One pilot engaged in the conversation and indicated they had been receiving flight following services and had been attempting to descend at the time of the encounter. The remaining pilots from that aircraft did not engage in the discussion.Contributing factors were the converging traffic at the same altitude within the SFRA; no radio communication established on CTAF prior to close proximity; cockpit workload and crew coordination dynamics during the avoidance maneuver.Continued pilot education on the Grand Canyon SFRA requirements is recommended; particularly altitude assignments under the applicable section of 14 CFR and CTAF monitoring requirements. Review of CRM protocols for dual-pilot operations during traffic conflict situations; including clear pre-flight agreements on control transfer procedures.
synopsis: Light twin pilot reported during cruse flight in the Grand Canyon SFRA encountering another aircraft not flying at the appropriate altitude for direction of flight resulting in taking evasive action to avoid a collision.

narrative: At approximately XA:00 local at ZZZ; my student and I were departing for a fly-in event at ZZZ1. The student had approximately 10 hours of private pilot training at the time.Preflight and taxi to Runway XX were uneventful. After receiving takeoff clearance; the student began the takeoff roll and applied power. During the roll; the aircraft began drifting to the right--either due to excessive right rudder input or a crosswind from the east causing a weathervaning effect.In an attempt to avoid departing the runway into the grass; the student rotated early and aggressively; placing the aircraft in approximately a 15-30 degree nose-high attitude.I verbalized; 'I have the controls;' and attempted to lower the nose to reduce the angle of attack for a standard climbout. The student was unresponsive; his fight-or-flight response appeared fully active; and he was fighting me on the controls with both hands.I had to physically remove his arms and hands from the controls in order to regain control. I was then able to lower the nose enough for the stall warning to cease.The remainder of the flight was uneventful.Contributing factors may have included slight complacency during the takeoff phase. In hindsight; more active rudder coaching--such as prompting or assisting with left rudder during the takeoff roll--may have helped prevent the initial deviation.After the flight; we conducted a debrief. The student understood what occurred and recognized that he had placed the aircraft in a potential power-on stall situation.After further discussion with other instructors; an alternative technique was suggested: temporarily blocking the student's visual reference (e.g.; covering their eyes) to interrupt the startle/freeze response and regain control of the aircraft. I plan to evaluate this technique and incorporate it into future training as appropriate.The purpose of this report is to recommend that flight instructors incorporate a mandatory simulated takeoff upset prevention scenario; including techniques to ensure the student releases the controls when necessary. I believe this should be a required task in the CFI ACS (Airman Certification Standards).Lighter or less physically strong instructors may be at a disadvantage when a student resists. A DPE could simulate early rotation and/or poor directional control during the takeoff roll; transitioning into a high but still safe climb. The instructor should emphasize a clear positive exchange of flight controls; and be prepared to take immediate; decisive action such as covering their eyes to regain control of the aircraft if the student does not comply.

narrative: I was entering a straight-in approach to runway XX at ZZZ; intending to practice crosswind landing. I believe winds were 300 @15kt; and knowing it was a strong crosswind I wanted to test this specific airplane in those winds. This was the first contributing factor; not having done crosswind landing in some time; and not in this airplane. I was not strongly considering my minimums.I had significant right-rudder input; as well as moderate left aileron; lined up with the runway and doing fine until I hit a strong downdraft over the highway. I had expected this downdraft having flown this approach before; but the downdraft felt much stronger than what I'd prepared for and I elected to go-around. Not having a solid plan for the go-around and aerodynamic effects of full power from the crosswind landing configuration into a climb was my second contributing factor. I knew I may go-around; but I hadn't visualized it and prepared for it sufficiently. As power was added; I failed to maintain left aileron and the plane began to yaw to the right. I failed remove rudder and maintain runway heading; and panic started to set in. I failed to notice my right leg was still mashing the right rudder for several seconds.At this point I was doing everything I could to maintain airspeed well above stall; instinctually pushing the nose down and for some reason I let the airplane turn to the right as I struggled to maintain level flight and airspeed. I realized my foot was heavily or possibly full right rudder once I had significantly deviated from runway heading and neutralized the rudder after at this point. I stabilized the climb and headed south; maintaining separation from the tree line south of the airport. At this time I was close to heading 140; roughly 2000ft to the West side of the XY approach; low; headed downwind. I elected to head straight back to my departure airport ZZZ1 and end the flight.My performance in this flight was definitely inadequate. I did not take appropriate action to train on this specific flight condition in my aircraft with a CFI; or refresh with a CFI in recent months on higher crosswinds; and my skillset has obviously diminished; or I overestimated my minimums for this aircraft; a C150D with a horton STOL kit. My judgement to take a leisurely scenic flight and 'throw in some crosswind practice' on my way North created risks due to insufficient planning and contingency planning for 'whatifs' and I was not prepared to react properly in my go-around. I hope my experience will help others to not make the same mistake. Practicing crosswind landings is crucial; briefing phases of flight; and their resultant phases of flight; whether it be landing or going around; is crucial. I made a decision to challenge myself; without preparing myself. I had to work VERY hard to recover from what should have been an ordinary crosswind practice approach and landing; and this is largely due to the startle effect and subsequent panic when my right leg became frozen subconsciously. I'm happy nobody was hurt.In the future I will practice in a simulator and with a CFI; and refresh my personal minimums to better judge what I can do safely. I will review proper crosswind technique; and go-arounds in crosswinds. I will also research what I can do to avoid freezing any particular control in urgent situations. I think making sure I am in the best condition to fly is also imperative; as being dehydrated; tired; or less than optimal overall can have dire effects when stressors are added.

narrative: While conducting a flight for the purpose of completing a Certificated Flight Instructor (CFI) Practical Test; the incident aircraft (PA28R-200) experienced retractable gear malfunction/collapse and erroneous indications. While approaching the right downwind for RWY XXR and after contacting ZZZ Tower; both the Designated Pilot Examiner (DPE) and CFI candidate on board the incident aircraft witnessed the two main gear lights illuminated and the nose-wheel indicator light OFF after setting the gear selector switch in the 'DOWN' position. Both pilots onboard immediately established appropriate CRM and began troubleshooting efforts. These efforts included: Several pass-by's for a controller/tower visual inspection of the landing gear; multiple usage of the 'emergency landing gear extension' checklist and yawing maneuvers; and one final tower confirmation that the gear was down prior to landing. Throughout the 'troubleshooting' phase of the flight; the 'gear in transit' light would remain illuminated and a whining noise (suspected by the pilots to be a hydraulic pump) was audibly heard. After the incident aircraft made the several low passes; the ZZZ Tower Controller stated that the gear appeared to be down and that he was unsure the gear was locked. Ultimately; the decision was made between both pilots on-board to make a landing on Runway XXL (longer and wider runway). Understanding that the nose wheel indicator light remained OFF; the landing was briefed in the flight-deck by the pilots. It would be a smooth landing (using similar techniques as required for a soft-field landing) and the aircraft would be allowed to 'roll' with no braking as necessary in order to prevent the nose gear from collapsing in the event it was not locked and uncontrollably-lowered by itself. Priority handling was [given] by the tower and fire-emergency services were requested by the pilots prior to landing. Approximately 20-30 minutes after first responders were contacted; emergency vehicles and airport personnel were ready. It was decided that the DPE would land the aircraft on Runway XXL and the CFI Candidate would operate the only exit door located at the right side of the aircraft. Upon landing; the aircraft's main landing gears touched down smoothly and within seconds of landing the right main gear slowly collapsed by itself. Upon feeling this unexpected condition; the DPE corrected by deflecting the control wheel to the left in an effort to prevent the hard impact of the right (lowering) wingtip with the runway. Eventually; the right wing/wingtip would impact the runway causing the right wing to drift aft and the aircraft to veer off the runway and into the dirt just off the right side of Runway XXL. As the aircraft came to a stop; the engine was immediately isolated/starved of fuel and the aircraft's right door was opened. An immediate evacuation was initiated and no injuries or fire occurred. Emergency services and airport personnel responded in a quick manner and were ready to assist pilots as necessary. In retrospect; this incident showed me how critical Crew Resource Management (CRM) is in the event of an emergency. despite having large differences in experience between the DPE and CFI Candidate; both pilots communicated; split tasks; and assessed the situation continuously. Aside from the CRM found in the flight-deck; it is my opinion that the assistance/communication that ZZZ Tower Provided was concise and necessary to the outcome of the best case scenario of this incident. With this in mind; it was emphasized/learned that communication and clear actions both inside and outside the flight-deck are necessary in the event of an emergency.

This began a period of just 3-4 seconds where everything happened; starting with a very firm touchdown mains first. The plane either bounced or fully extended the gear shocks; but movement was definitely upward and I called for a go-around. As the aircraft settled back down onto the runway I looked down at the thrust levers and in that instant it appeared that the FO had started the reverse process part of the landing sequence; and then went up to TOGA mode after my Go Around call. Since I thought I had seen Thrust Reversers activated; I said something like 'forget it. I have the aircraft'; and control was immediately relinquished to me. I went into full reverse with approximately 7000ft of runway remaining and the aircraft was fully settled and under control. Again; this sequence of events happened very quickly; just a couple of seconds; during which I was working off of outside visual cues and a brief glance at the thrust levers. I did not see the VSI or Primary Flight Display (PFD) and cannot say what they were reading at touchdown; but got some info after parking from the jumpseater who helped us debrief and break down what went wrong. Rollout and taxi-in were normal; and after the parking checklist; the FO and I debriefed the landing and requested input from the jumpseater; who was performing a FAA Line Operations Safety Assessment (LOSA). Knowing that LOSA observers don't normally debrief; I felt like this event was important enough to request his input just as a fellow air carrier Captain. He pointed out two things that in the moment I did not even realize had occurred: our touchdown pitch had approached 10 degrees; and we got the 'pitch pitch pitch' aural. In those few seconds where everything was coming at us fast; I must have had a tunnel vision effect that did not allow that cue into my thought process. Had he not told us; I would not have know that occurred. After the debrief; the FO and I went outside to check for any indications of a tail strike and found none.

narrative1: Flight was conducted normally from departure to landing. No issues or abnormalities during this time. Upon landing XXL we had a normal landing; rollout; and turn off. Once we acquired our taxi clearance from tower we were cleared to taxi from intersection 1 down 2 to our gate XX. Once we were clear of the runway and were heading down 2; CA called for Flaps Up" triggering after landing checklist. Once that was completed I offered to start the APU for the short taxi; CA agreed. Upon starting the APU as N1 reached approximately 75% the aircraft AC power shutdown. The flight deck went dark and the EICAS populated numerous messages. CA brought it to a stop and set the parking brake. I advised ground we need to stop for a moment before checking in with the FAs to make sure they were alright while the aircraft finished running through the EICAS messages. The FAs advised passengers had started getting up so I made a PA to remain in their seats. CA had communicated with ATC to advise that we did not need assistance at that time. narrative: Began taxi before receiving All Clear salute; with tug and marshallers below field of vision. Preconception that a salute was received.  No damage or injuries.  Stopped airplane.  Completed salute. Remainder of flight completed without issue.Cause: Received 'clear to start engines' immediately after Clear to Push instructions given.  This caused both engine starts to be completed relatively early.  As occurs regularly in ZZZ; when I don't immediately see the salute; marshallers sometimes return to the gate - usually before engine starts are complete.  Ran the After Start tasks and checklist.  FO and I did not see the marshaller or Lektro cart (my seat is in the highest position while in ramp areas.  This operation was run with one Lektro cart driver and one Marshaller.  FO sent taxi request command.  Waited some time and did not hear from ramp; so FO radioed for taxi and we received a taxi clearance.  We cleared left and right sides; turned on taxi light; and began to move the airplane in a right turn.  The Lektro cart driver ran out from under the airplane giving the stop signal; and I stopped the airplane - realizing we had not actually received an all clear salute.  The marshaller also moved to a visible position with the headset bag.  I opened the window to confirm that we had not hit the tug or a marshaller; which was confirmed that we did not.  Lektro cart driver moved the cart to a visible position and we received the all clear salute.  Notified ramp that we needed 5 minutes in position; and received the ok.  We called for and received a new taxi clearance and proceeded to the runway.  Remainder of flight completed with no issue.  Suggestions: One Marshaller to remain visible between 10 and 2 o'clock positions.  Lektro cart driver retrieve the headset if there are only two marshallers. Preferably use three marshallers.  Use a pole or lighted antenna on low/small Lektro carts; to remain visible from flight desk.  Confirm via call-out with FO that both of us have seen the salute.  Avoid distractions until the all clear salute is received.  If unsure; stop or open the window to see below.
narrative1: I was first officer acting as pilot monitoring during pushback; engine start; and taxi out.  Captain coordinated successful nose wheel capture with ramp crew via headset.  I sent ACARS silent push request; received push clearance from Ramp tower; and captain relayed clearance to ground crew.  Two ground crew members began moving aircraft and almost immediately cleared us for engine start; captain directed me to start engines one and two.  I started both engines over the course of approximately 1.5-2 minutes during push back and release from tug; ground crew movement was not visible to me during this process and me responsibility was to monitor the engine start rather than push back progress.  I stated 'normal start' after completing the second engine start and captain called for the next flow; we completed this and he called for the after start checklist; which we ran and completed.  At this point I had not seen or heard ground crew in some time and believed they had disconnected and given the all clear salute while I was heads down during engine start; as the after start checklist is called for following the salute in normal ops.  At this point we would normally be ready to taxi; so I sent ACARS silent taxi request.  Ramp tower did not respond via VHF after .5-1.5 minutes; so I called for taxi via VHF. During that period there was still no sight or sound from the two ground crew; which the captain and I both believed had disconnected and cleared the aircraft.  We received a taxi clearance from Ramp tower after the second request; the Captain visually cleared left and I visually cleared right for the tight 180 turn we would be making; neither saw any issues; I turned on the taxi light; and the captain began a tight right 180.  After moving the nose about 20 degrees the captain abruptly stopped the aircraft and was looking down out his left window. He then opened the window and began talking to ground crew who were apparently disconnected from the aircraft but not yet clear of the area.  The captain confirmed there were no injuries; no damage to the aircraft; and that the two ground crew would immediately clear the area. Seeing no issues and having coordinated with everyone we thought was relevant we departed and completed the flight.Cause: The ground crew and tug were not physically visible from my seated position after initial capture with the tug.  There were two rather than the usual three ground crew members; so no one on the ground was standing in a visible position to coordinate ground crew movements with the cockpit after headset disconnect.  There were no raised flags or wands from the tug to make its presence known to anyone in the cockpit.  I do not recall the voice interaction between captain and ground crew during push back and disconnect; only that everything was being coordinated normally while I was heads down starting the engines; but in our Standard Operating Procedures the FO's indication that ground crew is all clear is that the Captain calls for the after start checklist.  Had there been any visual; voice; or checklist/flow confirmation or even slight suspicion on my part that the ground crew was not clear; I would have delayed the taxi request; told the captain the aircraft was not clear for a turn; etc; I simply was not aware the ground crew was under the aircraft even after a delayed clearance to taxi.Suggestions: Tugs should have a raised wand; flag; light bar; etc. so that from the cockpit there is an indication that the tug is below or directly in front of the aircraft.  Three ground crew should be utilized with one between the 10 and 2 o'clock positions so that signals can be relayed between the ground crew members directly below the aircraft and the cockpit; when headsets have been disconnected.  The Standard Operating Procedres should include confirmation that the FO has seen the ground crew salute or some other verification step that they acknowledge the ground crew is clear; rather than the captain being the sole crew member confirming this.
synopsis: Air carrier incident Captain reported beginning taxi from gate prior to salute from ground personnel. Reports from flight crew thought to be the incident flight crew reported they did not taxi before salute.

narrative: Upon arrival at the aircraft; I was advised the aircraft had experienced a significant maintenance event involving the hydraulic system. While reviewing the aircraft status in the Logbook; no MEL had yet been issued; and I was awaiting clarification on which MEL; if any; would be applied in order to properly evaluate its applicability and associated safety margin.After discussing the discrepancy with the previous Captain who made the original write-up; as well as dispatch / Maintenance Control; I developed concern that an incorrect MEL could be applied to the discrepancy; potentially masking the actual system involved. Specifically; Maintenance Control referenced the yellow hydraulic electric pump; while the original discrepancy involved the yellow engine-driven pump; indicating a possible misalignment between the reported condition and the anticipated MEL application.Given the potential for an incorrect MEL application to inappropriately authorize dispatch of an aircraft with an unresolved or non-deferrable condition; I determined it was necessary to delay boarding until the discrepancy and maintenance action could be fully verified.I proceeded to the gate area and instructed the gate agent; Person A; to hold boarding until I could verify the maintenance status with local maintenance; Dispatch; and Maintenance Control.The agent responded that boarding would continue; stating; 'No; the tower instructed us to board.' I reiterated my instruction to stop boarding; emphasizing the need to confirm the aircraft's airworthiness. The agent again refused and stated that I was 'not in charge of boarding.'I issued a third and final instruction to not board the aircraft; then returned to the flight deck and contacted Station Operations via radio to request a supervisor.A supervisor subsequently arrived at the flight deck and acknowledged concerns regarding the gate agent's conduct. I requested a reassignment of the gate agent; which was completed.Following coordination with Maintenance Control; it was confirmed that an incorrect MEL had been applied to the discrepancy; and the actual system affected was not eligible for MEL deferral. As a result; the aircraft was removed from service and a replacement aircraft was assigned. The flight was completed successfully. As of the time of this Report submission; aircraft X remains out of service for the hydraulic system discrepancy; now exceeding approximately 34 hours; further reinforcing the significance of the original maintenance issue and the importance of delaying boarding pending proper evaluation.This event highlights multiple breakdowns in communication; coordination; and adherence to established authority during an active maintenance situation:The gate agent's immediate refusal to comply with direction to hold boarding introduced undue time pressure to accept a maintenance action without proper evaluation. This type of operational pressure can lead to rushed decision-making by flight crews. Given that this was a known recurring issue from the prior leg; which manifested shortly after takeoff; there was a credible risk that proceeding under these conditions could have resulted in an in-flight abnormal or escalation.The gate agent's behavior became a distraction from a higher-priority safety issue; specifically the need to correctly diagnose and resolve the hydraulic discrepancy. This diverted attention and resources away from critical troubleshooting.The agent's unwillingness to follow direct instructions from the Captain raised concern regarding reliability in time-critical situations; including the ability to execute essential duties during an emergency (e.g.; evacuation or emergency deplaning).Local ZZZ maintenance demonstrated a misunderstanding of the original discrepancy and appeared to pursue a path focused on expediency rather than full verification of the write-up in the Logbook. This created risk of applying an incorrect MEL to an unrelated system.There was a lack of direct communication from local maintenance to the flight crew. I spent approximately 15-20 minutes attempting to gather information independently; as no maintenance personnel initially made contact at the aircraft to discuss the discrepancy.Initial coordination with Maintenance Control was also ineffective. Maintenance Control declined to engage in discussion regarding MEL applicability; citing local maintenance authority. This was inconsistent with standard practice; as Maintenance Control is typically involved in MEL evaluation and troubleshooting coordination. After further effort; I was able to establish direct communication with the responsible A320 Maintenance Control team member; at which point it was confirmed that the incorrect procedure was being considered.Overall; these combined factors--external pressure to board; lack of coordinated communication; recurrence of the discrepancy; and misapplication risk of maintenance procedures--significantly increased operational complexity and reduced safety margins during a critical phase of aircraft evaluation.Cause: 	•	Breakdown in adherence to Captain's authority: Gate agent refusal to comply with explicit instruction to hold boarding during an active safety evaluation.	•	Operational time pressure ('get-there-itis' at the gate): Immediate push to board created pressure to accept a maintenance action without adequate verification.	•	Maintenance misdiagnosis risk: Local maintenance did not fully verify the original discrepancy in the Logbook and appeared to pursue an expedient corrective path; increasing the likelihood of incorrect MEL application.	•	Ineffective communication and coordination: Lack of timely; direct communication between flight crew; local maintenance; and Maintenance Control; initial reluctance from Maintenance Control to engage in MEL discussion further delayed accurate assessment.	•	Distraction from critical task: Gate agent interaction diverted attention from troubleshooting and evaluating a known recurring hydraulic issue from the prior leg.	•	Lack of standardized escalation: No clear or immediate pathway to pause operations (boarding) while resolving conflicting maintenance information.	•	Reinforce Captain's authority: Ensure all gate/customer service personnel understand that boarding must stop when directed by the Captain for safety-related reasons.	•	Establish a formal 'boarding hold' protocol: Create a standardized procedure that clearly pauses boarding when an aircraft is under active maintenance review or airworthiness uncertainty.	•	Improve maintenance verification procedures: Require local maintenance to validate discrepancies against the original write-up prior to MEL application; especially for system-specific issues.	•	Strengthen Maintenance Control involvement: Reinforce expectation that Maintenance Control actively participates in MEL determination and troubleshooting coordination; regardless of station-level activity.	•	Enhance communication standards: Require direct; timely communication between maintenance and flight crew during active discrepancies before operational decisions (e.g.; boarding) proceed.	•	Training on operational risk awareness: Educate gate and maintenance personnel on the risks associated with time pressure and recurring discrepancies; emphasizing safety over schedule.	•	Standardize escalation pathways: Ensure flight crews have a clear; At that time; our airspeed was at or slightly above the maximum allowable speed for landing gear extension; so we made the decision to delay extending the landing gear until the aircraft slowed and continued with the rest of our checklist.As we continued toward the airport; our workload increased due to pattern entry; radio communications; and configuring for landing. During this time; although the checklist had been initiated earlier; we did not complete a final verification that the landing gear had been extended.On final approach; both my instructor and I were focused on maintaining a stable approach and landing. We did not visually or physically confirm gear extension prior to touchdown. Another pilot attempted to alert us via radio; however; we misunderstood the transmission and did not recognize it as a warning regarding the landing gear.The aircraft touched down with the landing gear retracted. After landing; we secured the aircraft and exited safely. There were no injuries.Upon reflection; I recognize several contributing factors; including initiating the before-landing checklist too early; delaying gear extension without establishing a clear follow-up trigger; increased workload in the pattern; and a breakdown in final verification procedures. This resulted in a loss of situational awareness regarding the landing gear status.This experience has reinforced the importance of strict adherence to checklist discipline and redundant verification of critical configuration items. Moving forward; I will ensure that landing gear extension is verified multiple times during the approach; including on downwind; base; and final; with a positive confirmation of 'gear down; three green' prior to landing. narrative: Our flight was from ZZZ.  We boarded Aircraft X and found the flight deck and forward galley in a bit of disarray; with gear pins; papers; and rags on the cockpit floor and a mechanic's headset and pitot tube covers in the galley.  The aircraft had been sitting in ZZZ for what I recall was a few days from the logbook.  We requested that a mechanic come to retrieve any items that didn't belong on the airplane and ensure that everything that was required to be onboard was accounted for; which they did.  My FO verified that no gear-pins; collars; reverser locking pins; etc. were in place on the exterior of the aircraft.We departed on time and taxied to runway XXL for takeoff.  The takeoff was normal and we received a vector of 230 and clearance to 10;000 feet from ZZZ departure.  Passing through approximately 6;000 feet; an ECAM message appeared; ENG 2 EGT OVER-TEMP" with engine parameters in agreement.  I was the pilot monitoring and began the non-normal plan strategy; which led us to reducing thrust to see if the EGT would come below the high-limit.  It did; but after a brief discussion of our situation and about how such a reduction in thrust didn't make flying all the way to  our destination seem very practical or wise; we decided that returning to ZZZ would be prudent.  This discussion was cut short by a second ECAM; "ENG2 EPR MODE FAIL"; so the plan strategy began once again.  The ECAM action led us to a reversion to N1 mode of thrust control and subsequent loss of auto-thrust; and that went smoothly.  My FO; whose capacity to fly the aircraft extraordinarily well and handle high task-loading with apparent ease (while I was quite busy with QRH followups; STATUS page updates; the ECAM Supplemental manual; diversion notification; etc.); was able to observe that increasing the thrust on the affected engine close to climb would cause another over temperature condition while decreasing the thrust to idle also caused a sharp increase in temperature up to the limit.  Unusual.  I notified the flight attendants and passengers of the need to return to ZZZ for a mechanical discrepancy.  We notified ATC for a more immediate return to the airport; although the situation was quite under control; the strange behavior of the EGT on the affected engine gave us enough reason to think being on the ground sooner than later would be a good idea.  We performed an overweight landing checklist for what would be a landing at approximately 4;000 pounds over maximum landing weight.  During landing the #2 engine thrust reverser didn't deploy; and displayed amber when selected to reverse.  After clearing the runway we noticed that the #2 engine; when at idle; was approximately 150 degrees hotter than the #1 engine at idle; but within limits.  After shutdown; we also noted an "ENG2 FADEC" Class 2 status message.  Before I had the chance to pick up my iPad to begin making all of the necessary logbook entries; we were greeted on the flight deck by two mechanics who noted that they weren't very surprised by our return because the airplane had "quite a history".  They mentioned that the work done on the airplane over the last day or two involved replacing pieces of a wiring harness; but the reality was that the airplane simply needed an engine change.  I can't speak to the veracity of that statement; but it was said to me.  I spoke with our dispatcher; Chief Pilot.  We swapped to another A-320 at the neighboring gate and departed about 2 hours late for a successful flight.Cause: The specific causal factors; at least in so far as what caused the EGT to over-temp in such a way with the follow-on failures (Engine Pressure Ratio mode failure; thrust reverser failure; Full Authority Digital Engine Control fault) aren't available to me at this point; so I could only speculate.  My decades of experience flying turbine engines would lead me to believe that the engine's turbine tolerances had become excessive and the engine was simply out of time.  That would agree with the statement the mechanics made to me; but I can't verify that.  As I sit writing this; it's not immediately apparent to me why an EGT exceedance (at least one that's not severe) would cause the other issues; too.  Concerning this; I don't have any recommendations for this situation to be prevented; but I can speak to the effectiveness of the planned strategy and of course recommend the reinforcement of its teaching.  An EGT over-temp on a high-time engine for a brief period during takeoff isn't exactly unheard of; and in fact is even allowed in some cases with a maintenance discrepancy item; but this event unfolded in a rather unexpected way after the over-temp occurred; and the planned strategy is indispensable in such a situation."
synopsis: A320 Captain reported returning to departure airport after experiencing an engine EGT over-temp on climb out.

narrative: On departure out of ZZZ we received an engine exceedance Crew Alerting System (CAS) message briefly. PM observed the message and called for the low speed abort. We cleared the runway and taxied back to ramp to contact maintenance and company.Cause: Tail wind component was within limits and winds were variable in direction. We believe the tailwind component may have shifted which generated the momentary CAS.Suggestions: Crew will be even more conservative below the published tail wind component maximum to help ensure the possibility a shifting tail wind component does not necessitate another low speed abort.
narrative1: We were attempting to fly from ZZZ after landing on runway XX. We deplaned our passenger; fueled; and prepared to takeoff on XY. We had collectively decided that runway XY was the more favorable runway due to the local ceilings as well as the fact this was the only runway where a Departure Procedure existed. We had shifting and gusty winds for our landing and departure; but had made a determination that we had not exceeded the 10kts tailwind limit for the CE-700. We also determined that the performance assessment and associated limitations were met for this strategy. We lined up on the runway; ran up the engines for static takeoff; checked the engine instruments; and began our takeoff roll. My role was PM at the time; and as we proceeded in the low speed section of the takeoff roll. we received an amber Crew Alerting System (CAS) message stating that one of the engine limits was being exceeded. I believe the CAS message was 'ENG EXCEEDANCE'; which engine I cannot recall. I immediately called for an aborted takeoff; and the PF complied. We exited the runway; called clearance to cancel our release; ran our checklist and called maintenance to proceed with whatever they needed. We waited for maintenance to get back to us; and they determined that we were released to attempt another takeoff. We never did; as there was no legal way to depart the other runway; so we taxied back to the ramp.Cause: I believe that this was likely caused by the winds at the time of the event. While we had determined that the aircraft's tailwind component limitation was respected; the wind was highly variable as it gusted through the mountains near ZZZ. I believe that what happened was that during our takeoff roll; there was a change in wind that either caused a momentarily exceedance of the tailwind component or a change in crosswind loading on the engines. Either way; the change in engine intake airflow likely caused the engine to momentarily near an exceedance. The checklist for this CAS message explains that it appears when the engine N2 is in the transient region and close to exceeding an operating limit.Suggestions: While I believe that we were within the limitations of the aircraft; I also think that this instance is a great example that the limitations we fly with are legally defined sharp lines; with a good side and a bad side. In reality; the equipment's ability to perform is not as sharp as the limitations that try to define the ability to perform. While we were legal to attempt takeoff; it is clear that between the gusty and shifting winds and the existing tailwind component; we had managed to find an area where the machine was unable to perform despite what the book says. Perhaps the wind momentarily gusted past 10 kts of tailwind; but we will never know. What we both seem to be taking away from this instance is that we need to consider the totality of the situation a bit more in-depth before simply relying on exactly which side of a limitation we are on. We should have taken into account all of the wind shifting and gust factor as well as the tailwind component and simply declined the takeoff. I will be more cautious of these types of situations in the future; and will be ready to discuss with flight support why we were unable to take off even if we seem to be in limitations on paper.
synopsis: Cessna Citation flight crew reported receiving an ENG Exceedance CAS during take off. Crew rejected takeoff and returned to the ramp.

Very quickly; the HYD synoptic showed a steady decrease in hydraulic quantity on the left side at a loss of .01 every 8-9 minutes.If that rate were to remain steady; we calculated that the left hydraulic quantity would read 55% by the time we reach ZZZZ1. Complicating the matter was that the Flight Plan Release included a ZZZZ1 Field Report that indicated a wet runway; with a 500/500/500. As a restricted Captain; I am not authorized for a CAT III approach. If those conditions had persisted; we would have been eligible for a CAT II approach using the exemption. I made radio calls on CTAF 122.7 announcing my intention to taxi onto and depart Runway 09. After lining up at the Runway 09 threshold; I observed Aircraft Y move from the parking area to the runway edge at midfield (2100' ahead from me); then taxi onto the runway and proceed toward Runway 27 -- the opposite end from where I was positioned. No radio calls were made by the aircraft at any point during this time. I made multiple calls to the aircraft and multiple radio checks; no response was received. I elected to abort my intended takeoff and vacate the runway rather than risk departure with an aircraft of unknown intent on the runway.After I vacated; the Aircraft Y pilot then disclosed he had been on the wrong frequency the entire time. Aircraft Y appeared unaware that Aircraft Z had passed overhead. Aircraft Z subsequently called on CTAF to apologize; disclosing they had also been on the wrong frequency throughout their approach and pattern.Contributing Factors:Two of three aircraft at the airport were simultaneously tuned to the wrong CTAF frequency; rendering the standard self-announce separation system ineffective.W28's runway configuration requires prolonged runway occupancy to reach thresholds; increasing exposure time and collision risk.The Aircraft Y pilot; after discovering his frequency error; did not pause to assess the traffic situation before proceeding with departure.The narrow runway (40 ft) with no parallel taxiway significantly reduces margins for error.What Prevented a Worse Outcome:I visually detected Aircraft Y before initiating my takeoff roll and held position.I elected to vacate the runway rather than assume the other pilot's intentions.Aircraft Z's go-around (likely triggered by sighting Aircraft Y on the runway) provided vertical separation.Recommended Preventive Measures:Encourage pilots who discover a frequency error to pause; listen; and build situational awareness of the existing traffic situation before taking any further action.At narrow runways like W28 where no parallel taxiway exists; hold-short lines should be positioned to provide greater lateral clearance from the runway edge; and pilots should be explicitly encouraged -- through signage or Chart Supplement notes -- to perform a thorough visual check for aircraft already on the runway before entering.

narrative: Chain of events and discovery: During an introduction flight I followed checklist usage; however after the run-up I demonstrated to the student that it is important to lean out the mixture while waiting to take off to prevent the spark plugs from fouling. I aggressively leaned the mixture as prescribed; but forgot to re-apply the appropriate mixture for takeoff (full in this case with a density altitude in the negatives). As the aircraft began to accelerate with the student's full application of power; the engine stuttered and stopped on the takeoff roll. I scanned the cockpit and noted the problem. I immediately felt a sinking feeling in my stomach; but was simultaneously struck with fear for how dangerous that situation could have been if we were off the ground. I notified other airplanes on the CTAF that we were stopped on the runway; re-started the engine and taxied off the runway. This event shook me up. As a new instructor; it was a wake up call that it is harder to diagnose issues without my hands on the controls. It was also a shock for how fast everything occurred. I have replayed the event many times in my mind and considered what I should have done differently. I am so thankful that we both walked away safely; and for the instructors that demonstrated aggressive lean procedures to me. This technique caused the engine to stop on the ground rather than in flight.Contributing factors: As a new instructor I was undoubtedly focused on the new students performance during the takeoff. The previous mental space that I would have devoted to re-applying mixture was now distracted with my student. This inadvertently and unnecessarily lowered my situation awareness. Another causing factor was lack of a final flow or adequate takeoff checklist before applying full power.Correcting actions: A learning lesson for me from this was to always use the demonstrate / performance method. An external factor at play was me trying to make the introduction flight as fun as possible by letting the student takeoff. In retrospect; I should have simply let the student put his hands on the controls to feel the correct application. If I would have focused on the demonstrating the correct configuration; the next time the student would also have knowledge of the correct mixture configuration. Additionally; my attention would be less on the students control inputs and more on an overall scan for improved safety. Another learning lesson is two fold: 1) Updating the takeoff checklist in the airplane to include mixture configuration (3rd party checklist and manufacturer's didn't include this). 2) performing a final takeoff flow in all airplanes to cover the most important items; especially ones like mixture that might have changed. For example; once on centerline; I will callout as I confirm: mixture set; props forward (if applicable); throttle forward. Closing notes: This was a very humbling event for me. I feel thankful that nothing serious happened; and I hope to do the most learning I can do from this to prevent another occurrence like this from happening. I also hope that others can learn from my mistake. I apologized for/debriefed my mistake hope that it does not negatively influence his training.

They instructed me to turn left and join the left traffic pattern for Runway 32L and cleared me for the option on 32L. I acknowledged 'cleared for the option 32L.'While on the base-to-final turn for 32L; I heard Tower clear another aircraft for takeoff on Runway 19L. The other pilot acknowledged the clearance. On short final for 32L; I observed the departing aircraft beginning its takeoff roll on the intersecting Runway 19L. (XA:30) To avoid a potential collision at the intersection; I immediately initiated a go-around.Tower then instructed me to 'continue downwind for 32L' and said they would call my base. I replied 'negative; I am on short final 32L; going around.' Tower responded with 'sorry' and stated they 'did not see where I was.'After the go-around; I re-entered the left pattern for 32L and completed two uneventful touch-and-goes.Later; while on the upwind from Runway 32L; I heard a jet request landing on Runway 1L and receive clearance to land on 1L. narrative: I was operating Cessna 150. Prior to the flight; my scheduled flights were canceled because the owner/operator stated that the aircraft needed a 100-hour inspection. Based on that explanation; I understood that the aircraft would be unavailable until the required inspection was completed and the aircraft was confirmed airworthy.However; during the same weekend when I was told the aircraft would be down for the 100-hour inspection; the aircraft was operated for approximately 40 additional hours. This made me question whether the 100-hour inspection was actually performed at that time; whether it was properly completed before the aircraft was returned to service; or whether the aircraft was being operated beyond its inspection status. No clear maintenance log entry or inspection signoff was provided to me before I flew the aircraft.During the flight; the aircraft experienced an engine failure or serious engine malfunction involving a cylinder failure. I monitored the available engine instruments. Oil pressure and oil temperature indications appeared normal; including after the event when troubleshooting was performed; and the engine was restarted; but only limited to 2100 RPM under full throttle. However; the aircraft's cylinder head temperature indication was not available to the pilot because the CHT system had reportedly been disconnected. There was no clear cockpit indication available to me that would have warned of the developing cylinder problem.After the incident; I was informed that a mechanic had previously heard the aircraft backfire on the ground and attempted to stop it; but the aircraft was not stopped before the flight. This information was not communicated to me; the pilot; before departure. If I had been told that the aircraft had backfired or showed signs of abnormal engine operation; I would not have accepted or continued the flight without further maintenance inspection and written confirmation that the aircraft was airworthy.My safety concern is that the aircraft may have been released for flight even though the stated 100-hour inspection was not performed; not properly completed; or not properly communicated to the pilots. If the inspection had been performed correctly; the cylinder condition; compression; ignition system; spark plugs; and related engine components should have been checked before the aircraft was returned to service. The later cylinder failure and the report of prior backfiring raise concern that an existing mechanical issue may have been missed or not addressed.Another safety concern is cockpit instrumentation and placarding. If an engine monitoring system; such as CHT; is installed but disconnected; the pilot should have clear information on its status; including proper INOP placarding if required. In this event; the normal oil pressure and oil temperature indications did not provide warning of the cylinder-related failure; and the unavailable CHT indication reduced my ability as pilot to detect abnormal engine conditions before the failure became serious.In addition; the aircraft was operated under a dry lease structure; where operational control should rest with the renter. However; scheduling and maintenance availability were controlled by the owner/operator. My flights were canceled for the stated purpose of maintenance; but the aircraft was reportedly still operated by others during the same general period. This created confusion about who had operational control; whether the aircraft was actually down for inspection; and whether the aircraft had been properly inspected before being released.The main lesson from this event is that a pilot should not rely solely on verbal statements about maintenance status. Any required inspection; especially a 100-hour inspection; should be clearly documented and communicated before the aircraft is returned to service. Any reported engine abnormality; including backfire; rough running; abnormal sound; or suspected cylinder/ignition issue; should be immediately communicated to the pilot; documented as a discrepancy; inspected by qualified maintenance personnel; and resolved before further flight.In the future; I will personally request confirmation of the maintenance log after any major inspection or maintenance-related cancellation; verify the status of any inoperative instruments before accepting the aircraft; and decline the aircraft if there is any report of abnormal engine operation that has not been clearly inspected; documented; and resolved.To prevent recurrence; aircraft owners; lease operators; and maintenance personnel should establish a clear process that requires written confirmation when a required inspection is completed. Aircraft should not be released for flight based only on verbal statements. Any abnormal engine operation observed on the ground should be immediately communicated to the pilot and entered as a maintenance discrepancy. The aircraft should remain grounded until the discrepancy is inspected; corrected; and signed off by qualified maintenance personnel.
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported the engine malfunctioned during a flight and was possibly flown without required maintenance inspections.

narrative: Got to the airplane about an hour before a scheduled departure and Maintenance was on board fixing a problem with our Elevator Aileron Computer (ELAC) system. This caused a delay of about an hour. Flight was not very full but we were boarded up and had to stay at the gate until Maintenance finished their job and paperwork was signed. We eventually pushed back and everything was normal. 2 engine taxi out to runway XXR for departure. There were 2 other planes waiting at the end to takeoff but we were given a takeoff clearance by tower since they were waiting for en-trail spacing. I remember thinking that our takeoff clearance was given a little early; as we were still probably 500'-800' or so from the end of the runway. CA was PF and I was PM on this leg; our first flight together. CA pushed the throttles up and we began the takeoff roll. Everything was normal up until about the 50-65kt range when the Takeoff Hold Lights suddenly changed from green to red. At this point I was looking at the engine pages but I remember seeing the change from green to red happen out of my peripheral vision. I also remember looking down the runway and even though it was dark; I saw an airplane crossing downfield. The captain immediately used MAX braking to slowed the plane to a stop. We skidded a little bit due to the wet runway. He set the parking brake and made a PA in the back. At the same time; I advised ZZZ Tower that we were aborting the takeoff on the runway. They seemed a little confused but one thing that stuck with me is that they NEVER asked us why we discontinued the takeoff. I asked Tower to roll the fire trucks in case our brakes were hot or locked up or there was any other outside damage they were able to see. We were able to taxi so we decided to turn off the runway on an upcoming taxiway and that's where Airport Rescue and Firefighting met us. They could see no such damage and our brakes were not on fire or anything like that. We sat on the taxiway for a while to gather ourselves and to run appropriate checklists. We decided that it was best to go back to the gate because we were getting close to our min fuel for takeoff and we also wanted Maintenance to do a quick inspection of the plane in case one of the wheels locked up since we skidded during the abort. We taxied back to the gate without issue and myself and the captain walked up to the terminal to debrief what had happened.In my opinion; there needs to be better communication between controllers and pilots. I'm still not sure if this was a case where ZZZ ground cleared a plane to cross XXR while ZZZ Tower cleared us for takeoff; or if the crossing plane did so without a clearance; or what exactly happened. It was very strange (in my opinion) for tower not to ask us a reason for the abort. They NEVER recognized the reason why we had to abort the takeoff or maybe they did and said nothing about it. Either way; there was a massive communication breakdown between ground; tower; us; and another aircraft.
synopsis: Air carrier FO reported a rejected takeoff was caused by another aircraft crossing the active runway.

narrative: I was the pilot monitoring for this flight. Toward the end of the climbout of ZZZ; somewhere above 2000 feet; flaps had been retracted on schedule and we were climbing at 240 KIAS. Weather was IMC. I was prompted to switch to departure; then we were given direct to ZZZ [VOR]. I was about to call '3000 feet' and prompt for the after takeoff when this occurred. After I had got confirmation and executed the direct; my FO said something about the autopilot being degraded. I then looked at the Flight Mode Annunciator (FMA) and saw 'ALT HOLD' with an amber line through it indicating a degraded vertical mode; then noticed our airspeed was quickly rolling below 200 kts and nearing 180 kts. We were in the amber airspeed band with the Performance Limiting Indicator (PLI) visible. There was a startle effect and a moment of disbelief or confusion in what I was seeing; but I called out the speed; and prompted the FO to accelerate as the PLI was floating near the limit. I remember saying something like 'lower the nose'. When the PLI contacted; I called 'STALL' took control; and rolled wings level to initiate the recovery. It took a few seconds for me to realize we were not accelerating at which point I realized I was unconsciously working against the auto throttle at which point I pushed the throttles all the way forward and clicked the autothrottles off. The aircraft began accelerating; the descent arrested and began climbing. During this I also had to tell ATC we were responding to a situation and we'd get back to them. They gave us a vector to 270 and to advise them when everything was okay. Airspeed reached approximately 270 kts as we were climbing again where I started to easy the climb and the airspeed to re-automate. I called for Autopilot Center Command; and once it engaged it resumed the turn to the heading we had been assigned (270). However we immediately got a 'bank angle' aural alert; which confused us because although the Autopilot was banking slightly beyond the Flight Director; the angle was not any higher than 25 degrees while at about 240 knots. Nevertheless; I disconnected the automation again; eased the bank and hand flew with the Autothrottles engaged at 240 kts. Once rolled onto our heading of 270 and steadily climbing to our altitude (we had gotten 7000 and then 11000 assigned during this); I called for the Autopilot again; and then never had another issue. I asked the FO if they were ready to retake the controls; and they took over just before 10;000. We then accomplished the after takeoff checklist. I did not notice at what point we went into altitude capture; when the vertical mode degraded; or when airspeed began rolling back as I was in the middle of ATC responses etc as is typical for this phase of flight. The events all happened very quickly. I only remember seeing the degraded mode; and then the pitch and airspeed which I was immediately fixated on along with the VSI and the altitude; the usual instrument scan. Automation modes were secondary to me at the time as they were being disconnected. I did not think to reset flight directors or try other autopilots since I was focused on the recovery and keeping the plane flying. We descended about 700' during recovery starting from about 3700' regaining altitude at about 3000' and climbing. We talk about; and practice upset recovery in every sim session. We talk about startle effect in CRM every year and in sims. We are trained to expect the unexpected; but it's not until it happens to you in the real environment where you fully realize the effect it has on you.

My copilot pulled the QRH manual and looked up the procedure for auto pilot failure and I flew the airplane manually while he troubleshot the issue. I was able to immediately engage the FMS and fly the command bars and keep the altitude and track constant; especially after the first unexpected incident; I was prepared for this potential issue. It disconnected several more times below RVSM on the way to ZZZ1. The airplane is at the service center currently; I spent time with maintenance going over the issues. I also downloaded the computer Data Storage Unit (DSU) of the flight and gave it to maintenance DSU so they could trace the cause of the autopilot failures.

The ground crew was already in place; and they marshaled us into parking where we set the brakes and shut down the remaining motor uneventfully. The maintenance representative came on board and told us that he saw a tailpipe fire as we were taxiing with a lot of oil underneath the number two engine on the ramp. We both concluded it was the oil that was dripping on the hot engine and exhaust area that caused the smoke and tail pipe fire. We had no indications of any type of fire or high EGT inside of the aircraft since the tailpipe fire was outside of the internal core of the engine. The maintenance representative left and returned telling us that the fire had reignited and he wanted to get everyone off of the aircraft quickly. We were already in the process of deplaning the aircraft; but I made an announcement over the PA that we had smoked coming from the right side of the aircraft and we needed to expedite the disembarking of the aircraft. Even without inching forward much; their left wing tip encroached; although slightly; the service road. I observed multiple catering trucks drive around the service road instead of stopping and waiting for the aircraft to exit. This is an incredibly unsafe situation that apparently has become normal practice for the ground handlers to drive in such a careless way in one of the most congested ramp areas in the world.

narrative: During installation of the RH engine upper outboard start fuel nozzle; the new nozzle assembly was damaged.  During installation of the new nozzle the mounting ears of the nozzle got bent due to an unseen misalignment of the nozzle.  It was found that either during removal of the old nozzle or during insertion of the new one that there is a tapered boss on the burner can internal to the engine that floats in a flange; this boss was shifted and causing the new nozzle to not correctly engage into the engine. The mounting nuts were run down and damaged the mount ears of the new nozzle during this process.  No damage occurred to the engine mounting boss. narrative: On Day 0; at approximately XA:20; I was pilot in command of Aircraft X; a Cessna 172S NAV III; departing Runway XXR at ZZZ on a personal flight with one passenger. I hold a Private Pilot certificate; ASEL; with approximately 163.5 total flight hours; all in Cessna 172 aircraft; and 16.6 hours in the preceding 90 days. I was well-rested; of sound mind; and had completed the IMSAFE checklist prior to flight with no concerns. No hazardous attitudes were recognized.The aircraft was rented from the FBO at ZZZ. Prior to flight; I taxied to the fuel tank where the FBO personnel topped off the fuel. A preflight inspection and walkaround were completed with no abnormalities. Fuel was sumped with normal results. Engine oil was observed at approximately 6.5 quarts; one quart was requested and added. A weight and balance computation was completed and confirmed the aircraft was within limits. The fuel selector was verified on BOTH. Aircraft loading was as follows: PIC at 180 lbs; one passenger at 255 lbs; and approximately 20 lbs of baggage in the rear seat area; with full fuel.ATIS Information 1 was current at XD:53; reporting winds 120 at 10 gusting 18; variable between 070 and 140; visibility 10 statute miles; ceiling broken at 4;000 ft; broken at 7;500 ft; temperature 27°C; dew point 17°C; altimeter 30.18. Increased bird activity was noted in the vicinity of the airport. The wind presented a right crosswind component on Runway XXR. Density altitude was elevated due to the 27°C temperature; however; the conditions were within the normal operating envelope for the aircraft type and loading.During the engine run-up at 2;000 RPM; a magneto check was performed. The left magneto dropped to 1;930 RPM and ran smoothly. The right magneto dropped to 1;910 RPM and ran rough. The idle check was satisfactory at 840 RPM. A second magneto check was performed; during which the right magneto ran smoothly. Both drops and the differential were within limits.I contacted ZZZ Tower and reported holding short of Runway XXR at Taxiway 1; ready for departure. Tower instructed line up and wait due to traffic on the downwind. Subsequently; Tower cleared me for takeoff on Runway XXR with an assigned heading of 080.I began the takeoff roll from the full length of Runway XXR. Full throttle was applied with mixture full rich; flaps up; and trim set for takeoff. Engine instruments were checked and indicated in the green. Airspeed was confirmed alive. The takeoff roll felt normal in terms of acceleration. I noticed the crosswind component during the roll consistent with the reported winds.Rotation was initiated at 55 KIAS with approximately 10 degrees of pitch. Immediately after liftoff; climb performance was sub-optimal and the aircraft was barely gaining altitude. At a few feet AGL; the stall warning horn activated. I reduced the angle of attack; but airspeed was not increasing. I observed the engine RPM between 2;400 and 2;500. The engine sounded smooth and was not surging or running rough. The aircraft drifted left of the runway centerline.Within a few seconds; recognizing the aircraft was not climbing and was drifting off centerline; I made the decision to abort the takeoff rather than risk running out of usable runway or being forced to land off-surface. I pulled the throttle and mixture fully out; shutting down the engine. The aircraft touched down on the remaining runway approximately abeam Taxiway 2; roughly 1;600 feet from the Runway XXR threshold. I continued on Runway XXR; slowing down and turning right onto Runway XY; where I came to a full stop.I transmitted to Tower that I was aborting the takeoff. Tower initially instructed a right turn at Taxiway 3 to contact ground; then corrected to exit on Runway XY and contact ground. I acknowledged and advised that the engine was off. I contacted ZZZ Ground and reported engine-off on Runway XY after the aborted takeoff. Ground asked if I needed assistance; I requested a moment to assess. After confirmingeverything was in order; I successfully restarted the engine and requested taxi back to the Southeast ramp. Ground cleared me to taxi via Runway XY and Taxiway 3.Upon return to the ramp; I completed a squawk write-up documenting the event. Maintenance was contacted. The aircraft is pending inspection and the cause of the degraded takeoff performance has not yet been determined. No injuries were sustained by either occupant. No aircraft damage was observed.Chain of Events and Contributing Factors:The problem first arose during the run-up when the right magneto ran rough on the initial check. Although the second check was smooth and within limits; this may have been an early indication of a fouled spark plug or developing magneto issue. The problem became apparent immediately after rotation when the aircraft failed to achieve a normal climb rate despite full throttle application; and the stall warning activated at a few feet AGL. Engine RPM was observed at 2;400-2;500; which; combined with the initial rough magneto; suggests a possible partial power issue such as a fouled spark plug or intermittent magneto malfunction.Human Performance Considerations:I was well-rested and had passed the IMSAFE checklist with no concerns. My perception of the initial rough right magneto was that it had cleared on the second check; and I judged the engine fit for flight based on the smooth recheck and all indications being within limits. In hindsight; the initial rough magneto warranted additional scrutiny. My decision to abort was made quickly once I recognized the convergence of poor climb performance; stall warning activation; and lateral drift from centerline. I prioritized remaining on the runway surface and bringing the aircraft to a safe stop over attempting to continue a climb that the aircraft was not performing.Corrective Actions and Prevention:The aircraft has been squawked and is pending maintenance inspection; which should identify the mechanical cause. In future operations; if a magneto runs rough during the initial check -- even if a recheck is smooth -- I will perform an additional magneto verification while holding short prior to takeoff to confirm the issue has truly resolved rather than accepting a single smooth recheck. This additional step adds minimal time and could catch an intermittent ignition issue before committing to a takeoff. I will also establish a more deliberate go/no-go gate at the hold-short line for any anomaly observed during run-up; treating an initial rough magneto with greater caution.

narrative: Aircraft X cleared for the RNAV-Visual runway 12C into IWA. Aircraft Y squawking 1200 not in communication with ATC maneuvering outside the Class B. In my opinion. Aircraft X came into an unsafe proximity to Aircraft Y. Traffic was issued; and the pilot had Aircraft Y in sight and maintaining visual separation. No TCAS-RA was announced. The RNAV-Visual approach into IWA barely touches the PHX Class B airspace. It provides minimal protection from VFR aircraft not in communication with ATC. The majority of this procedure is in Class E airspace. There is high intensity training activity in the area of the approach. This area is a known 'hot-spot' to controllers due to the frequency of TCAS-RA's and traffic alerts. Maneuvering aircraft routinely change trajectory and/or altitude placing them into unsafe proximity into airliners descending or departing from IWA airport. There is a huge risk currently of unpredictable; non-participating aircraft intersecting with high-speed traffic flows. I propose 3 solutions to help mitigate this safety issue. Listed from most effective to least effective:1) Implement Class C airspace at IWA. A standard Class C airspace design would fully contain the approach procedure. IWA meets the FAA requirements to become Class C. In 2025; IWA recorded 15;309 air carrier operations; presumably all of which were IFR; and 95;618 air taxi operations; unknown with publicly available information how many were IFR. The threshold is 75;000 IFR operations. Additionally; IWA had 2;036;218 passengers in 2025; dramatically above the threshold of 250;000 enplaned passengers. 2) Expand the Class B airspace to more fully encompass the approaches at IWA. This may be difficult because IWA is not the primary airport; but the airspace should be studied to more fully accommodate jet traffic in the Phoenix area. 3) Implement a Special Flight Rules Area (SFRA) or Special Air Traffic Rule (SATR). Mandate that pilots communicate with ATC near the IWA airport. 4). Charted Hot Spot on the sectional/TAC chart. We were descending to land at Long Beach 26L with VFR flight following; on SoCal Approach. Route of flight was direct from the southeast; descending through 3000 on a 303 degree heading; descent to 2500 authorized. ATC issued a traffic alert for a converging aircraft at 2500 feet indicated. I added power and held 3000 feet until further advised. I never saw the other traffic; so turning away was not an option. As the other aircraft (Aircraft Y) passed directly beneath us; my copilot snapped a ForeFlight screenshot showing the tracks crossing; the other aircraft was shown at 2600' on ADSB-in.The other aircraft was not in communication with SoCal so far as I could tell. It is possible the other pilot was on the practice area CTAF; though I was not. The near-miss happened very fast. Collision was avoided due to my evasive action of aborting descent in response to the ATC alert. My analysis is that my choice to use ATC flight following; and a quick response to the ATC traffic alert; likely saved our lives. My attention was divided between managing the descent; visually scanning outside; descent checklist; navigation; and communications. My iPad was not showing traffic consistently; as it would not maintain a steady WiFi connection to my Sentry Plus. Yet I should have been able to note the conflicting traffic on my own ADSB-in on the G1000 Multi-function Flight Display (MFD). Had the other aircraft been on frequency; likely there would have been ATC intervention to deconflict. Had I been monitoring the CTAF; I might have heard the other aircraft make a position announcement; but the extra radio work would have increased my workload and delayed my imminent handover to LGB Tower.See-and-avoid is a fantasy in situations like this one. Again; though I was actively looking; I never saw the other traffic. I will redouble my own efforts to maintain situational awareness of traffic using all resources available. I would support a requirement for all aircraft to transmit ADSB-out in all US airspace. I would also support a change in the FARs to allow general aviation copilots to log Second in Command (SIC) time; in order to encourage pilot-passengers to serve as Pilot Monitoring. Thank you.

I wondered if it was an aircraft on the runway or a single Runway End Identifier Light. I reported my position and intention to land on 32. A helicopter pilot responded and said they had been on the runway. I explained my frequency mistake and apologized. I saw the strobe light move off the runway onto a closed diagonal runway so I continued my downwind.Just before touching down another voice transmitted; saying he was the instructor in the helicopter and claimed we were just 10 feet above them when I initiated the go-around. The associated maintenance comment indicated the issue had been entered into the maintenance software; however; there was no clear documentation specifying the corrective action taken and if that was the current deferral we had. However; due to the ambiguity in the maintenance records and absence of a clear timeline or action history; uncertainty remained as to whether the correct loop had been deferred or if both loops were potentially inoperative.Given the possibility that both fire detection loops on ENG 2 could be non-functional; effectively leaving the engine without fire detection capability; we assessed this as a potential safety-of-flight concern. After additional review; Maintenance confirmed that the deferral was correct and that both fire detection loops on ENG 2 were inoperative; LOOP A having been placed on deferral a while ago; and LOOP B being inoperative now without deferral. The absence of clear documentation regarding when a system was deferred; what exact corrective actions were taken; or whether previous discrepancies were related to current deferrals. I realized my mistake; corrected my comm 1 volume; and taked with the aricraft that was on the go and going back into the pattern.
