narrative: Yet again I have to write a report because the safety culture of management; Traffic Management Unit (TMU); and the command center is severely lacking. The FAA does not have safety as its number one priority. They care more about efficiency and running plans to keep stakeholders happy than controller workload and safe sector flow.On Day 0 multiple areas in ZTL worked extremely high volume traffic that was not predicted or well managed due to the special event. I had already been working steady traffic flow at Spartanburg with CLT departures and arrivals; and ATL departures as well as numerous point outs on AGS/AIK/DNL/HQU arrivals going into East Departure. I was called by the Macon sector to say that East 16 had told them to hold AGS and I would need to hold one in my airspace; once I got them in the hold I called East to let them know ATL departures would be delayed climbing due to the holding pattern; East said we're not holding AGS put them on a 180" which I did. Not two minutes later Macon called again to say we are holding AIK; put another in the hold and then the supervisor said were running AIK but 25 Miles in Trail (MIT). I called East and they said that they had never been holding AIK. This was just the start of an extremely chaotic and unsafe 45 minutes where it became clear that TMU and OMs were not aware of the traffic volume and did not have a plan to appropriately mitigate it. The sector Spartanburg has a Monitor Alert Parameter (MAP) value of 14; we started at a 20 and briefly went up to a 24 which is absolutely not safe; an unacceptable risk for no reason.When I finished up with the holding mess I looked back to the east side to see about 8 AGS area departures flashing at me all looking for higher and with a mess over overtakes and bad speeds. All of these departures would cross the standard ATL departures with everyone wanting higher. I had to vector a few to maintain separation but this was an absolute disaster where my D-side and me were barely holding on to the sector. I left that session feeling extremely stressed and frustrated that we did not get support from TMU and ZTL management to stop sectors from being overloaded.This happened because the command center; facility management; and TMU do not care about safety and do not care about sector overload. Their number one priority seems to be keeping as many aircraft moving as possible; especially when it involves special events. TMU is forcing normal ATL and CLT traffic flows which already put our sectors near capacity and then adding significant event volume on top of that; is not a safe combination.Additionally we do not have the staffing to support overloaded sectors with D-sides and trackers. We had XX people on this shift and needed two more than that positions open but we couldn't do it.Recommendation: When there are special events regular traffic flow must be reduced to not overload sectors; even something like 30 MIT off ATL and CLT would have helped in this case. It is unsafe for a controller to work normal traffic flow plus 100s of additional flights for the special events.From what I can discern TMU has no tools to plan for departures pushes off of smaller airports; especially with a special event they need to be able to see these departures and meter them to manage sector overload. When a sector starts getting overloaded the first move should be shut off departures; re-evaluate the situation and then resume with needed restrictions in place; this did not happen in this event.Local facilities need more say on what restrictions to implement from the command center; especially when it involves safety. I can't count how many times I have told an Operations Supervisor (OS) or OM that some situation is unsafe but the answer is that's what the command center wants so we have to do it.Traffic volume needs to match controller staffing; we need to reduce traffic on low staffed days and this needs to be variable depending on numbers. If we have 9/12 then we should have 75% of traffic volume; this way demand can better meet capacity as opposed to the current method of we will put in a staffing trigger if you are at 50%."No notice holding" needs to be an absolute last resort; we should have the tools to see when too many aircraft will get to an airport at the same time and manage that well in advance to reduce last minute holding and vectors which increase risk.The MAP is a useful tool but it is too slow to update and does not properly capture departures from small airports. Today 32 Spartanburg was showing green for most of the day with the exception of the current block that was a red +5 - 10 above MAP. How can we use this tool to manage sectors if it can't accurately look at departures?Overall I cannot wrap my head around the fact that on a normal day if we are 1 over the MAP number on a combined sector they will split it; if a sector appears red on the board they will add a D-side but on a day like today where we exceeded the MAP values on multiple sectors we are just a "little busy" and managers say "well we made it through; thanks for the hard work" this is UNACCEPTABLE we cannot have it both ways. If exceeding MAP values is a big deal on a normal day than it also needs to be a big deal on special events and weather days. We cannot keep working sectors that are too overloaded to safely separate traffic; someday there will be an error that is unrecoverable."

narrative: While completing cruise duties at initial level-off and preparing for ETOPS entry; the PM checked the status page on the lower EICAS as part of normal system checks. It was then that both pilots noticed the status message 'AIR/GND DISAGREE'. After checking circuit breakers; we discussed the meaning of the message and the fact that status messages are not controlling in-flight and do not require crew action. However; we discussed the possibility of the issue developing into an 'AIR/GND SYS' EICAS Advisory which drives a non-normal checklist. We considered about 10 minutes into discovering the discrepancy that we may need to air return. We considered the weather forecast at ZZZ1; ZZZ2; and ZZZ. ZZZ1 and ZZZ2 were forecasting rainy and gusty conditions with thunderstorms in the vicinity; ZZZ was dry with light winds. We also considered that if we received the EICAS Advisory that our auto brakes; auto speed brakes; and thrust reversers would be inop all while navigating near thunderstorms approaching ZZZ1. We completed an HF phone patch to Maintenance Control to discuss the issue; attempt to gain more awareness about this message; and rope in dispatch to get their latest information about local weather. We researched more and discussed the risks which worked in our favor to burn more fuel to get our gross weight below max landing weight. At about 1+30 into the flight; we decided that the workload to take this potential issue into the islands with unfavorable weather would not be the safest course of action. Additionally; the MEL mentioned that the issue does not have MEL solutions once on the ground. We coordinated with dispatch; ATC; and flight attendants to start heading back to ZZZ. On the approach; we configured early including gear to see if the ground/flight mode anomaly would appear and force the AIR/GND SYS advisory. It was a normal approach; however; I noticed that the aircraft sank faster than usual while pulling power during the flare. This may have been because the jet allowed the engines to go to ground idle before touchdown; but I added power to re-establish a normal flare and descent rate then gradually reduced power to idle as the jet touched down. While deploying thrust reversers; the EICAS Advisory 'AIR/GND SYS' appeared and remained on until we cleared the runway. We passed all this info to maintenance who was able to capture it in the write up.
narrative1: Leveled off at FL330 waiting to accomplish a cruise check and begin departure using the ZZZZZ guide.  I noticed  a status message alerting us AIR/GND SYS.  FO continued flying while I looked up the status message approaching ZZZZZ1.  We had been radar service terminated from ZZZ CTR.  FM was not much guidance so we decided to contact ZZZ radio for a SELCAL check and position report as we elected to continue on the track.  After establishing contact with ZZZ radio; I requested an HF Phone Patch and was given a separate HF frequency at which time a phone patch to Dispatch and Maintenance Control was established.  The phone patch was limited and we could barely hear Dispatch and Maintenance Control.  Maintenance Control was not sure nor could verify if the aircraft was in air mode or ground mode.  We tried several times to check circuit breakers and EICAS to see if we could determine which mode the aircraft was in and what to expect when we put the gear down.  We were not sure if we would get Air/Gnd System which would affect braking and thrust reversers.  The Wx in ZZZ1 was gusty winds with rainy showers and wet runway.  The Wx in ZZZ2 (Mx base) was worse and forecasted to get worst.  We continued flying given we were tankering fuel with 14;000lbs extra which put us landing over weight with an air return and also landing heavier than normal with rainy weather and gusty winds with terrain.  Given these threats; we elected to continue towards the fix to burn fuel down.  The extra flying time would allow us to brief an air return; close out the HF phone patch by also notifying the company and dispatch; speak with FAs; and develop a plan.  We accomplished all; referenced the diversion guide in the FOM; and communicated our plan with ZZZ radio.  We executed a diversion from our track turning right flying directly North and returning back to ZZZ.  We requested an early descent while also encountering holding for traffic delays in ZZZ which was to our advantage to burn fuel down to help with our overweight landing.  We held for ten minutes at 10;000 ft and took delayed vectors landing runway XXR about 300 lbs overweight.  We put the gear down early to make sure no further issues or status/EICAS messages were present.  We received AIR/GND SYS on the EICAS upon putting the landing gear down.  In anticipation; we previously referenced the AIR/GND SYS checklist and had already prepared for non-normal landing distance and any configuration differences.  We accomplished the landing checklist while configuring early and landed with no issues.Of note; approximately 50-40ft above touchdown; we did notice the aircraft loose airspeed and drop unexpectedly to which the FO added slight power to arrest the descent due overweight landing considerations.  I briefed a shallow touchdown due to overweight landing as a threat and to use the entire runway for braking.  We landed and stopped turning off at taxiway 1 with no issues using minimal braking.  No emergency was declared.My decision to air return was based on several considerations; mostly unknown conditions from the air/gnd computer with bad weather in the islands.  The FO was excellent in executing the air return as the PF allowing me to coordinate the divert with no issues.

narrative: This was the last leg of a 4-day trip. Boarding was normal. We were completely full plus a Company X Pilot in the cockpit jumpseat. We were cleared for takeoff full length on runway XXL at approximately XA:06 UTC. We were cleared on the ZZZZZX RNAV departure out of ZZZ. Takeoff was normal. We were instructed to contact ZZZ departure at approximately 1000 ft AGL. I checked in with ZZZ departure; the controller instructed us to climb to 5;000 ft. As I was replying to that instruction I received a call from the cabin. I answered the call and the purser alerted me that they may have a fire in the cabin. The forward galley was filing with smoke and it appeared that it was coming out of one of the ovens in the forward galley. I told the captain what was going on in the cabin. At that time we began smelling a strong acrid odor as well as seeing a haze of smoke in the cockpit. The captain; myself and the jumpseater all donned our oxygen masks and established crew communications. The captain told me that they wanted to return to ZZZ immediately. I alerted ATC that we would like to stop our climb at 5000 and we would probably be heading back to ZZZ. ATC gave us a 280 heading to put us on a downwind for runway XXL and began giving us a descent to 4000 feet. As we leveled at 4000 feet we received an Off Schedule Descent light.I pulled the QRC down from the glare shield and looked at the immediate action items for Smoke/Fire/Fumes. I saw that we had already accomplished the steps of donning our oxygen masks and establishing crew communications. I pulled out the QRH from my side of the pedestal and was about to go to the fire protection section as it was the next step from the QRC but was distracted by the purser calling up from the back. She confirmed that the smoke was coming from the oven. She told me that she didn't want to open the door of the oven. She was afraid that it would make it worse. She told me that she shut the ovens off but there was still a lot of smoke coming out.  I instructed her to pull the circuit breakers for both ovens in the forward galley. We continued to receive transmissions from ATC. They wanted to know what the issue was; souls and fuel onboard. it was at this time that we received priority handling with ATC.At the captains direction; I began setting up the FMC for the ILS XXL at ZZZ. I loaded the approach; set the ILS frequencies and minimums. I also loaded VREF and target speeds for landing. The purser called up front again. I answered and was told that the smoke was starting to dissipate. I told them we were heading back to ZZZ and we would be on the ground shortly. I told the captain that the smoke was dissipating in the back. We noticed that we did not have the acrid odor or smoke in the cockpit anymore either. We decided it was safe to remove our oxygen masks. We had some issues communicating with each other. I remembered to close the oxygen mask door and test it on my side to return the audio to normal. I failed to remind the captain of this and they continued to have some issues with communication that I wasn't aware of at the time. I pulled up the divert page on the ACARS portion of the FMC and told the captain that I was going to send a divert notice to dispatch. I glanced over the page briefly and thought that I pressed the send button. I later found out that dispatch didn't know about the divert. So I either didn't press the button hard enough or it didn't go through. I began going into the ACARS section to get landing data as I knew we were overweight landing back at ZZZ. I typed in 161.0 for our landing weight and XXL for the runway and pressed send. I didn't see until we were on short final that I received an error for our landing data. I believe that I didn't enter ZZZ as our landing airport. The landing data page defaulted to ZZZ1 for the landing airport and the error was because there isn't a XXL runway at ZZZ1. At this point we were on downwind for XXL. The captain transferred the controls to me and they briefed the approach. I believe at this time the captain also made an announcement to the passengers. I transferred the controls back to the captain. ATC began turning us on a base leg and descending us further. The captain began to call for flaps and the gear down. We were given one more turn and then cleared for the ILS XXL. I pulled out the checklist and accomplished the descent checklist and after we were fully configured for landing I accomplished the landing checklist. When we were on short final I received the error for the landing data. I showed it to the captain. I can't remember if the captain acknowledged it or not. The captain later told me that they felt we had plenty of runway for landing considering the headwind and dry runway conditions.The landing was normal and uneventful. We cleared the runway to the right at taxiway 1. There was ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting ) equipment that was waiting for us as we cleared the runway. They followed us to the gate. I spoke to them on the frequency at one point and they told me that they would be on the jet bridge as we pulled in to make sure the fire in the oven was contained. There was about a 5 minute delay holding short of the gate as we waited for a ramp crew to guide us in. Parking and shutdown was normal. The captain called the fight attendants and instructed them to disarm the L1 door and allow the firefighter on the aircraft to look at the oven. We deplaned the passengers and our maintenance crew came out to look at the write-up for the smoke coming out of the oven as well as the overweight landing. Maintenance determined that there was a lot of grease all over the top of the foil on many of the meals. They think that the grease dripping off of the foil on our takeoff roll and climb out caused the smoke event.
narrative1: Climbing through 3000 the purser called reporting smoke in the cabin. She said it was either coming from the oven or behind the oven. Looking at the flight deck door camera we could only see solid white since the smoke was rising to cover the camera. At this point smoke began entering the flight deck so I commanded oxygen masks on and had the FO requested priority handling with ATC. I requested an immediate return to the airport. We were given a left downwind vector and subsequent turn to base. The flaps were already at 1 and I began configuring. Brakes were selected to 3 and an abbreviated descent check was completed to include speeds and gust factor. The purser at some point in this called to say the smoke was slowing down after they had turned the oven off and pulled the circuit breaker. I made the decision to continue our quick return rather than diving deeper into the smoke checklist. I made a quick announcement to the pax (Passengers) as to the plan of action and what to expect when we landed. My concern was that there was a fire that couldn't be seen and could reignite. Rescue vehicles were dispatched and followed us to the gate where fire personnel boarded the aircraft and used thermal imaging to make sure all was okay. The oven was taken out of service and an overweight landing inspection was completed. We departed again about 2 hours late with an uneventful flight to ZZZ1. As for TEM (Threat and Error Management) during the air return; VVM (Verbalize; Verify; Monitor) was done to the best we could with the challenge of oxygen mask use. Someone was always flying the plane. If I had the event to do over once I heard the smoke was decreasing I would have asked for a delay on the approach to readdress the smoke checklist. Everything was conducted safely but was more rushed than it ultimately needed to be with the smoke decreasing. I think total flight time was 12 minutes. It was a definite learning experience and has put additional tools in my 'toolkit'.

narrative1: I was PF and my FO was PM. Shortly after takeoff and climbing through approximately 3000MSL; we received a call from the cabin. We noticed a burning smell in the flight deck and executed immediate action items. We did not observe smoke in the flight deck and did not don O2 masks. After referencing the QRC; I gave flying pilot and normal ATC duties to my FO while I referenced the QRH for Smoke; Fire or Fumes. ZZZ approach asked us if we had a runway preference; and considering that we did not have any aircraft performance issues; I suggested any runway; not thinking about the fact that we were over maximum structural landing weight. narrative: While holding short of Runway XXR at Taxiway 1 at ZZZ Airport; I received a transmission that included flight following information (remain clear of Class B airspace; a departure frequency; and a discrete transponder code). At the time; I believed I was on the appropriate frequency for departure. Due to the high traffic volume; extended delay prior to taxi; and my position at the hold short line ready for departure; I misinterpreted this transmission and believed it was a takeoff clearance.I read back: 'cleared for takeoff Runway XXR; remain clear of the ZZZ1 Class Bravo; departure frequency; and squawk code.' The controller responded with 'readback correct.' I interpreted this as confirmation and believed it was a takeoff clearance. Believing I was cleared; I visually checked final approach and did not observe any traffic on final; and observed a Cirrus holding short at Taxiway 2 (full length); which I believed was the aircraft I had heard waiting for an IFR clearance to ZZZ2. I then entered Runway XXR from Taxiway 1. An aircraft was still on the runway but in the process of exiting; and after it cleared the runway; I started my takeoff roll.Sometime during the takeoff roll; I heard 'monitor tower;' which led me to recognize that I may not have been on the correct frequency or had not received a valid takeoff clearance. Around liftoff; I attempted to contact tower on the assigned frequency (XXX.X) but did not receive a response and then switched to the other tower frequency (XXX.XX) to establish communication. During this time; I heard another aircraft execute a go-around. I adjusted my climb profile by shallowing the climb to reduce the risk of conflict but still maintain a safe distance above the ground.The problem arose from a misinterpretation of flight following information as a takeoff clearance. I believe some of the contributing factors included high workload due to traffic volume; frequency congestion; extended ground delay leading to expectation bias; and the similarity in cadence between the transmission and a takeoff clearance. Receiving the flight following information while holding short of the runway; in a position normally associated with an imminent departure clearance; likely increased expectation bias and contributed to the misinterpretation. Additionally; in busy environments it is common for flight following to be delayed or unavailable; and because no earlier indication was given that flight following would be issued later; I did not anticipate receiving it at that point; which likely contributed to the confusion. My perception that I was on the appropriate frequency and ready for departure influenced my judgment and decision-making. The issue was discovered when I heard 'monitor tower' during the takeoff roll; which prompted immediate recognition of a discrepancy.Corrective actions included attempting to establish communication with tower; switching frequencies when necessary; and modifying my climb profile to maintain safe separation from other aircraft. No further conflict developed.To prevent recurrence; I will ensure I'm on the correct frequency prior to departure and will positively verify that an explicit takeoff clearance has been received from tower before entering the runway. I will also deliberately pause at the hold short line; particularly in high workload environments; to confirm clearance and reduce the effects of expectation bias.

My trainee and I worked on getting the flight manual open to the applicable non-normal checklist and open the flight in FPM (Fleet Program Manager); and I had my trainee look to see what ARINC frequency area the aircraft was in. The crew agreed to the patch and my trainee either mis-read or mis-typed the frequency to monitor. The crew responded that it isn't a selectable frequency; and if we meant a similar frequency. I direct dialed into the incorrect frequency and tried to raise the event flight several times; but didn't hear any verbal response. In the meantime; the crew reiterated THINKING ZZZ. At this point; I took over the desk and I saw that they had already sent the FMC divert message stating they were diverting to ZZZ. The FM (Flight Manual) directed the crew to land at nearest suitable due to the loss of 1 source of AC electrical power and the fact that the APU was not starting; leaving the aircraft in a state of single system redundancy. I saw the flight had ZZZ1 off to their right approximately 104 NM away. ZZZ was over 260 NM behind them at the time. I called ZZZ2 ARINC to try to connect me to the flight since I had no luck raising them and I sent the crew the following message:SHOWING ZZZ1 CLOSER. NOT HEARING YOU ON FREQI had the dispatcher at the next desk advise the Maintenance Dispatcher of the situation and that the flight would likely be diverting to ZZZ1. The ARINC operator connected me with the flight and the captain recapped what was going on. I advised that I had reviewed the FM checklist and saw that it didn't require using a non-normal landing distance table and asked if they concur; which they agreed with. I reiterated my recommendation to divert to ZZZ1. The captain voiced concern about the fact that they'd be well over max landing weight; which I acknowledged; and told them I was working on getting them ZZZ1 landing data to address their concern and updated  burn info but was having technical issues; so I would get Maintenance Control on the line while I continue to troubleshoot. FPM kept on giving me an error saying there was no PET (Point of Equal Time) between ZZZ3 and another airport; or something similar. Despite reactivating the current release; re-doing the CHG (Change) DEST (Destination) on the FPM Details tab; and deleting ZZZ3 in the quick EROPS box on the EROPS tab; it still wouldn't calculate the diversion to ZZZ1. The conversation between the flight and Maintenance Control was relatively short in respect to any systems recommendations. The event flight had already turned around to the west; and the captain stated to Maintenance Control their intention to go to ZZZ; with Maintenance Control responding they would notify local maintenance. I advised the crew that I was unable to get a calculation to go to ZZZ1; but that ZZZ4 was suitable; and closer than ZZZ. ZZZ4 was WNW (West North West) of their position; then off to their right; approximately 140 NM away; with ZZZ still at least another 100 NM further. I was able to calculate a diversion to ZZZ4 and recommended that they divert there; and stated despite their high landing weight concerns; they would still have enough runway distance available  even if the runway condition code were to deteriorate to 3/3/3 (which would be unexpected.) I didn't send the current ZZZ4 weather or NOTAMs to the crew at this point since we were still discussing on the call; but I saw that neither of these factors would prevent a safe landing there.The captain responded that they still wanted to return to ZZZ. I said to the captain So you are intending to continue to ZZZ under emergency authority? Since I had made several attempts to get the captain to land at what I considered to be the nearest suitable airport(s) at the time and the captain was not budging off their intention to return to ZZZ  despite me implicating that they would be continuing under captain's emergency authority to go there  I decided I could not continue to argue with them and would rather have them focus on getting on the ground safely. I told them I would work on calculating their diversion back to ZZZ; send them landing data; and asked them if they needed anything else from dispatch. I advised the crew I sent the landing data to their printer and asked if they needed anything else. narrative: During climbout; all indications were normal until right at 8;000 feet; at which point the cabin began to rapidly over pressurize. Initially; the condition was physically noticeable through ear discomfort and a message on the EICAS: PRESSN AUTO FAIL. We then referenced the Cabin Pressure Acquisition Module (CPAM) indications on the bottom of the EICAS and became fully aware of the situation.At one point; I observed approximately -3000 fpm on the cabin VSI. Eventually the Cabin altitude and Cabin VSI indications are dashing out yellow on the EICAS and the Delta Pressure rapidly went to 8.0 PSI. Due to the increasingly uncomfortable and mildly disorienting conditions; I elected to engage ALT HOLD before we even reached 8100 feet and stop the climb. At this point the First Officer took over the radios as well and began to inform ATC of our intention to hold 8000 feet and for the moment continue on course. Manual control of the digital controller was unresponsive and inoperative which led to a cabin dump. After completion of the QRH I knew we would have to return.We were in contact with ATC and advised them of the situation; stating our intent to return to ZZZ. We requested delay vectors in order to reduce weight and arrive within landing limits. The flight attendant had contacted the flight deck when we were still running the QRH and still in sterile; clearly recognizing that something was abnormal with the obvious ear pain and expressed concern from himself and the passengers. I advised him I would provide a special procedure shortly; as we were still managing a high workload at the moment. Once workload permitted; with the First Officer handling flying duties and radios; I provided the flight attendant with a proper report; explaining that we were experiencing a pressurization issue and would require approximately 30 minutes to land; because we needed to burn fuel; I instructed him to prepare the cabin for a normal landing and deplaning; with no special instructions or brace commands anticipated.I made a PA to the passengers advising that the situation was under control; that the aircraft was safe; and that we would be unable to continue to ZZZ1 and would instead be returning to ZZZ.No cabin aural warnings were triggered; as the event occurred at 8;000 feet. Passenger oxygen masks did not deploy. At no point did I or the First Officer declare an emergency; rather; we communicated to ATC that we were returning to the field and requested delay vectors to reduce weight. As this was not assessed to be a time-critical emergency; I exercised judgment to avoid an unnecessary overweight landing. We elected to drop flaps 9 and gear significantly early to increase drag and fuel burn to get on the ground sooner and there were no exceedances of any limitations.On final approach; I observed the fire trucks had rolled out. I queried ground regarding this; as no emergency had been declared from the flight deck. It is possible that ATC provided priority handling on our behalf; however; this was not communicated to us. After landing; we contacted the fire chief on their assigned frequency and advised that no assistance was required. We then taxied to the gate; parked; and deplaned normally.Suggestions: It would be nice to get confirmation from ATC on if priority handling was provided on their behalf.

We did not receive a briefing beforehand on hand signals.I saw the marshaller give the signal for remove chocks; the captain acknowledged. I then saw the captain signal for brake release. I did not see what the marshaller did in return; but the captain mentioned that we were good to release brakes. The captain then gave the hand signal to initiate the pushback procedure. I did not see what the marshaller did in return as I was heads down continuing to set up some of our radios. At this point I was heads up. The head marshaller then put his hands and wands behind his back; and watched the following unfold without giving us any indication that anything was wrong.The captain and I both believed that we were under tow at this point. We came back what I estimate to be 20 feet; and then came forward what I estimate to be 10 feet; we then came back maybe another couple of feet before coming to a stop. The Captain then gave the hand signal to set his parking brake; and the marshaller gave us the return hand signal to set our parking brake; and the parking brake was then set. We then sat there for a couple minutes for the ground crew to disconnect the tug; but couldn't feel or hear anything. Finally the captain opened his window to discuss with the marshaller if the tug had been disconnected. The marshaller responded; There is no tug here; you guys rolled back." The captain asked; "We rolled back? There was no tug?" To which the marshaller said; "Yes; most people here will either powerout; or rollback and then powerout." The marshaller implied that people before us had done the same thing; which I believe is a major safety violation; and we have no written procedure for.We then started both our engines and continued our flight to ZZZ without further incident.Cause: There were a few main breakdowns in communications between the flightdeck and the groundcrews. narrative1: On Day 0 I was the Captain operating SPI-ZZZ. Phase of flight was gate departure. Everything was normal leading up to door closing. After a minute of no response I look out in front of me while tapping my headset. The ground crew looked at me back pointing to his headset with a thumbs down. Nobody briefed me that this would be a push using hand signals. However; I looked out the window and gave him all the hand signals as a brief since the jet bridge was disconnected and door was already closed. Ground crew signaled for parking brake release to which I responded with the same hand signal. I then proceeded to release the parking brake. There was then a two way chocks remove signal. We then started what I presumed to be the push. We moved back about 20 feet then came forward 10 feet. We stopped moving so I signaled for parking brake set to which ground crew responded with appropriate hand signal. I set the brake and waited what seemed to be 2 minutes for the tug to clear. This didn't happen so I opened the dv window and looked down and yelled down I didn't see the tug clear the area is there an issue down there?" The gentleman said "there was no tug sir you rolled back". I was shocked by this for multiple reasons. The first being that the whole thing felt like we were getting pushed. There was no briefing from the crew chief that this was a power out gate or that there was no headsets. There was also no company page stating this was a powerout gate. The ground crew also just stared at us the whole time and watched us roll backwards without alerting us. Didn't wave their wands; didn't shout at us or signal something was wrong. When I had the dv window open I asked why they let us roll backwards without alerting us to which he responded "most crews just roll back or power out". We started engines and completed the rest of the flight with no issues. The first Officer completed the walk around in ZZZ and reported nothing wrong.Cause: I believe this all to be a result of lack of communication. Had the ground crew taken a few minutes to come to the flight deck and brief that there was no headset or briefed that it would be a power out gate; this all could've been avoided. Something in the company pages depicting it as a power out gate would have been a huge help as well. All this combined I believe was a perfect recipe for something like this to happen. I was extremely frustrated to find the ramp crew just watch us rolling backwards and not do a single thing to intervene. I did not like to hear the ramp crew after the fact state that this was a normal procedure. I also in the future need to look at the field report for remarks on power out operationsSuggestions: I suggest more communication from the ground crew in SPI. narrative: On departure we experienced Master Warning BRAKE OVHT at about 1000ft. We flew the plane to a safe altitude and ran the company procedures. We requested priority handling with ATC and had them send a fire truck out to meet us when we landed to make sure that there was no fire threat. We told dispatch and maintenance our situation. narrative1: After takeoff at approximately 1000 ft MSL; we received a BRAKE OVHT warning message. BTMS (Brake Temperature Monitoring System) temperatures for the right outboard brake were initially indicating a red '07'; spiked to a red '20'; displayed amber fault lines consistent with a sensor anomaly; and returned to '20'. The indication was non-decreasing throughout the event. The captain and I executed the Company Procedures. As BTMS indicators were non-decreasing; the QRH directed a return to the nearest suitable airport. We leveled off at 8;000 ft MSL and maintained 200 KIAS in accordance with QRH limitations while evaluating the indication. We requested priority handling; accomplished all remaining checklists; and determined the nearest suitable airport was ZZZ. We requested and were met with crash and rescue services upon landing. When we taxied off the runway we requested crash and rescue to inspect the right main landing gear for possible overheating -- they did not observe any abnormal heating of the brakes. We taxied back to the gate; documented the warning message in the Logbook; and deplaned the passengers to coordinate with maintenance; customer service; and company dispatch.Cause: There was a mechanical failure of a sensor part of the brakes that led to this indication - this was physically determined by maintenance after we had landed.Suggestions: The lack of QRH guidance for diagnosing this as a genuine overheating scenario resulted in the turn back to ZZZ. The BTMS indication behavior -- including an initial red '07'; spike to '20'; amber fault lines suggesting sensor anomaly; and return to '20' -- was not addressed by any available checklist or decision tree. If written guidance existed to diagnose indications as anomalous based on specific observable criteria; a continuation to destination could have been more easily justified with appropriate documentation. Development of a BTMS anomaly assessment decision tree within the QRH or Standard Operating Procedure manual  would provide crews with a defensible; procedure-backed pathway for these scenarios.

I found the airplane completely covered in oil; which appeared to be coming out of all openings on the engine cowl. With help from the rancher; I got the aircraft secured. narrative: The aircraft is used for flight training; but I am the owner and not a student pilot. We had a report of a C0 alert in the aircraft and so the PIC made a precautionary landing at ZZZ on the Day 0. When our mechanic was available; we went out to the aircraft on the Day 2 and I assisted in his repair of the issue; which was an exhaust manifold separating from the header due to the bolts coming off. We inspected the remainder of our fleet and discovered that the other aircraft also had loose or missing bolts also on the rear exhaust headers; these were accordingly tightened and will be routinely checked.After the repair; I performed a run-up and; satisfied that the engine was operating normally; obtained clearances to taxi out and depart Runway XX. Just after takeoff; I heard a noise from the engine; and almost immediately started seeing the C0 numbers climb and an alert warning (as the aircraft is equipped with a monitoring system). As the numbers were quickly approaching 100ppm (and did pass them before landing); I opted to return to the field immediately. I had been assigned a straight-out heading; and was unable to reach Tower due to communication congestion; but given the situation started my turn anyways; at which point Tower contacted me and asked the situation. I explained that we were having engine problems; as we did not yet know what they were; and he cleared me to land. I landed and taxied in without further incident.Upon examining the engine; we determined that the exhaust springs had stretched; allowing the muffler to separate from the right side exhaust headers when full power was applied quickly for takeoff (we believe the more gradual application of power in the run-up had not done this). The following day; our mechanic replaced all exhaust springs and re-sealed the system; we performed extensive run-up testing; and I flew the aircraft home without incident and returned it to service.Due to the occurrence of loose exhaust header bolts across all the RV12 aircraft; which we believe is being exacerbated by an existing gearbox issue impacting the Rotax 912is motor; we are implementing a regular inspection interval of 50 hours on all exhaust header nuts. I believe this should be expanded via an SB (Service Bulletin) or AD; as applicable; to all 912is-equipped RV12 aircraft; until the situation is better understood. The RV12 has an exhaust system manufactured by/for Van's Aircraft; and not the stock Rotax exhaust; so we have no reason to believe that this issue necessarily affects other models using the same engine.

narrative: Coming into El Paso landing east; runway 08R. Tower breaks us off the arrival and assigns a 260 heading for the visual. From the arrival and assigned vector; we were arriving on the north side of the airport. During the flight; I warned my FO of the threats involved with El Paso and being known for unstable approaches. This was his first time in El Paso; and my first time landing east. On downwind; we tried to slow but the winds at altitude kept us fast leading to the gear being dropped to slow down. Both pilots had the terrain feature pulled up for visual reference due to the blinding sun and low level haze layer obscuring the mountain directly ahead. Once the sun dropped below the mountain the fog immediate disappeared and the mountain was only several miles away. I recognize it and immediately start a mountain escape with vectors and altitude from ATC after I successfully escaped. We came around from the south side and had zero issues and landed 8R.Cause: GPWS message for terrain west of EL Paso airport.Suggestions: Being cleared the visual from the north side for runway 8R is NOT safe. I have lost sleep realizing how close I actually was. There is ZERO warning of terrain regarding El Paso; no published app procedures for 8R; (due to mountains); but no company pages for suggestions; the AOM suggests creating a PBD of 5nm (FAF) and 1500 AFE to keep a standard 3.0 glideslope. (This is the procedure of a visual approach per the book). That was what I followed; and due to the lack of general company pages on Jepp; I had no idea terrain was inside of 5nm. Due to the terrain feature being pulled up on my own; it saved us from the mountain. There was no warning; no prior training in visual app; no company pages; new pilots with no experience landing east; and sunlight blinding us as it set were definitely factors. I hope this almost crazy accident is investigated further to realize that landing from the north for Runway 8R is WAY too close for comfort.
narrative1: On approach into El Paso; ATC assigned us the visual for runway 08R. We accepted that clearance and they brought us in from the north instead of the south. While on approach on the left downwind for runway 08R we got a GPWS terrain warning because of the upcoming mountains. The captain executed a go around and we came in from the south on the second time around without issue.Cause: GPWS AlertSuggestions: My suggestion would be to create a suggested visual approach procedure for runway eight right coming in from the north. A detailed explanation of speeds to fly and markers to hit when we fly that approach would have helped us immensely on this specific instance. For any pilot flying into El Paso I would say be 160kts gear down flaps 3 at the maximum abeam touchdown point and start your turn 10 seconds after that point. That being said; the procedure from the north is very tight and if I had to do it again; I wouldn't do it at all.During the event; the captain and I both noted that it was hard to make out the distance to the mountains when the sun is setting over them; causing the backside of them to shade. It was only when the sun set behind the mountains that the captain and I noticed how close we were.

narrative: On Day 0; while operating Aircraft X from ZZZ to BOI; we were initially planning the RNAV (RNP) Z RWY 28L. My prior examination of the BOI notams were confusing for this approach as it stated procedure NA" and later provided adjusted specific altitudes for specific legs of the approach. During descent toward the end of the Kourt 4 arrival toward LITTL; ATC informed us that the RNP Z was out of service due to crane operations. The approach controller offered us a visual to 28L or the RNAV (GPS) Y 28L. The first officer quickly pointed out on our company arrival pages that the RNAV (GPS) Y 28L was not listed as an authorized procedure. Finding out it was completely out of service; given our location and workload in mountainous terrain; lack of destination framiliarity/procedures and the offered approach not being authorized; I elected for the radar vectors to a visual approach 28L given the favorable VMC conditions. We accepted radar vectors for a visual approach to RWY 28L. To ensure a stabilized approach and maintain terrain awareness in the mountainous environment; I elected to retain the HOBSI fix in the MCDU (Multipurpose Control Display Unit). I programmed a hard altitude constraint of 3;900 ft at HOBSI (the published FAF altitude for the RNP Z) to serve as a safety barrier and provide vertical guidance for a 3-degree glidepath. Again; we were being radar vectored on to the visual approach in VMC conditions with a final vectors of 260 descend to 3900ft. These vectors pointed us directly to HOBSI fix.We conducted the arrival using a managed descent profile toward HOBSI with 3;900 ft set in the FCU (Flight Control Unit). The aircraft was fully configured and on speed just prior to reaching HOBSI to meet FOM stabilized approach standards and to account for a lack of local airport familiarity. As we were in the managed descent approaching 4;000 ft; just prior to HOBSI; the EGPWS (Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System) issued an 'Obstacle' alert. I immediately verified our position visually and confirmed we were clear of all terrain while the aircraft leveled at the 3;900 ft FCU altitude. Shortly after; at or around HOBSI; the system issued a 'Terrain; Terrain; Pull Up' warning. Although we were in visual conditions and clear of obstacles; we immediately executed the full EGPWS escape maneuver in accordance with SOPs. At the start and during the maneuver; I noted that no prominent guidance was displayed on the PFD (Primary Flight Display) VSI.During the climb we made ATC aware of the go-around actions; received a heading/altitude assignment and cleaned the aircraft up. We then conducted a briefing to discuss the event and plan the next arrival. We subsequently flew the RNAV (RNP) X RWY 28L to an uneventful approach and landing. It is my assessment that the crane operations near the approach path likely triggered the EGPWS logic.Cause: A significant factor in this event was the late-stage transition to a visual approach in an unfamiliar; high-terrain environment; which was made more challenging by confusing NOTAM information. The decision to keep the HOBSI fix and a 3;900-foot altitude constraint in the system was a proactive effort to ensure a stabilized descent and maintain safety margins. The election for a visual 28L inadvertently brought the air carrier into EGPWS threshold for the temporary crane operations even though we were well clear with of any conflict. The limited selection of authorized backup procedures also added to our workload; as we had to quickly adapt our plan while navigating mountainous terrain. Based on the timing; unclear notams; mountainous terrain if we had more time at altitude with the issues at hand we could have researched the RNAV (GPS) Y 28L;  found it to be legal and optimum to fly. This was discussed post flight with the first officer on how and why we could have flown the RNAV (GPS) Y 28L. Again; he did a stellar job looking at the company arrival pages and I was focused on descent inmountainous terrain. It was my decision for the radar vectors to 28L approach based on workload; timing; terrain.To help manage these types of situations in the future; it may be beneficial to clarify ambiguous NOTAMs with Dispatch or ATC as early as possible. I looked left and spotted cranes up south of the aircraft course near some construction. That may have lead to the election to use an instrument approach instead of a visual. I incorrectly reviewed the approach authorization table as meaning that we could not fly the RNAV Y approach but after reviewing the charts post flight realized the RNAV Y was a GPS approach not an RNP approach and we could have flown that approach from the east successfully; that also could have lead to a better outcome. narrative: During this flight I was the Captain and Pilot Monitoring. On final approach to runway XX at ZZZ the departing aircraft on the runway began their takeoff roll; momentarily stopped; then began rolling again.  Tower cancelled their takeoff clearance and directed us to go around. The First Officer (PF) had disconnected the autopilot in the descent at 1000ft AGL and was hand flying the aircraft during the approach and go around.  The FO immediately initiated a go around at 400ft AGL as directed. All initial go around procedures were executed and call outs made. The aircraft was established in a climb; gear up; flaps 3.The aircraft had established a very high rate of climb and we were on the way to the published missed approach altitude of 3000ft. At 1000ft MSL the PF moved the thrust levers to the Climb detent. Also; at 1000ft MSL tower switched us to departure frequency. Immediately upon establishing radio contact with departure they told us to maintain 2000ft. Given our very high rate of climb; both of us immediately focused on altitude awareness and the need to level at 2000ft. Both of us reached for the altitude set knob to put 2000ft in the window. Eventually; it was set; and 200kts was set in the speed window. The PF began to lower the nose and rate of climb in an attempt to catch 2000ft. At that time; we heard the flap overspeed warning. I immediately set the flaps to 2 and the PF manually reduced thrust and raised the nose to control the speed. The aircraft slowed below flap overspeed and the PF placed the thrust levers back in the Climb detent. Shortly after that we reached 2000ft; still in a climb. The PF pushed the nose over at 2200ft and began a descent to 2000ft. The aircraft began accelerating again towards a flap overspeed.  I raised the flaps to 1 and the PF once again manually reduced thrust.  Once level at 2000ft and safely below flap overspeed the thrust levers were again placed in the Climb detent; and the autopilot was engaged.The flap overspeed was approximately 5 knots; which was confirmed by maintenance during their inspection.Cause: The causal factors for this event were a combination of Human Error; Automation Management; and Task Saturation.  The initial go around procedures were executed in accordance with SOP; but the maneuver got away from both of us at 1000ft with the radio switch to departure.  The unexpected level-off clearance at 2000ft was the first distraction that took my attention away from aircraft configuration and speed monitoring. It had the same effect on the PF whose full attention went to altitude control.  The high rate of climb and proximity to the new level-off altitude became the primary concern of both of us. So much so that the PF reached for the altitude knob to make sure 2000ft was set in the window as quickly as possible.  There was a moment where we both were reaching for the altitude knob and had to establish whose responsibility it was to set it. This momentarily took us both away from the primary flight instruments at a critical time. The result was that we did not configure the aircraft to flaps to2 on cleanup schedule.This failure to continue to maintain the normal configuration schedule was a direct result of task saturation and monitoring error on my part.  I allowed my attention to be drawn to the altitude issue and away from monitoring the aircraft configuration and aircraft performance.  So; task saturation led to an error in monitoring.Additionally; the PF's decision to hand fly the entire go-around with no autopilot added significantly to the workload for both of us. Not engaging the auto pilot earlier in the maneuver required significant attention to be paid to basic flight control and added to the task saturation.The first recommendation I have is to utilize the autopilot as much as possible during a busy maneuver like a go around. That allows both crew members to focus on aircraft trajectory; performance; and configuration; rather than monitoring basic aircraft control.The other recommendation is for me as PM to establish crew duties immediately as soon as it gets busy like that.  As Captain and PM I should have told the PF; since he was hand flying; to concentrate solely on the primary flight instruments and let me listen to departure; set altitude/speed window parameters; and keep him informed of any necessary changes.  Had I focused his attention back to flying the aircraft immediately; he probably would have caught the overspeed before it happened. I also should have recommended that the autopilot be engaged early in the process.The lesson learned for me is that I need to ensure a very thorough brief on pilot duties and automation management during a go-around.  I also need to take a more involved approach during the maneuver to make sure that the PF is solely concentrating on flying the aircraft and controlling its trajectory; velocity; and configuration.
synopsis: A319 Captain reported executing a go-around to avoid a traffic conflict with an aircraft on the runway; they then experienced a flap overspeed and altitude deviation.

narrative: During pushback I notified the push crew first to standby;" then when cleared by ramp I said "cleared to push tail north". I did not release the brake and I failed to say "brakes released."  An unusual sound was heard and I immediately realized that the brake was still set.  The push crew stopped the push and investigated for any damage - I informed him that the brake had not been released. They advised that tow bar and plane looked ok and were ready to continue the push. I released the brake and the push continued. About 50 yards into the push the crew stopped and had me set brakes. Something was not right with the tow bar and they had to swap it out. Once the new tow bar was attached we continued the push.  Nearing the desired drop point; the aircraft was stopped by the push crew and the left wing walker gave a hold brakes signal with his wands as I waited for the driver to advise me to "set brakes." Just then the tug and the aircraft began to roll forward and the driver said "Captain brakes brakes."  I immediately stopped the aircraft from rolling and set brakes and stated "brakes set; cleared to disconnect inter phone."  I had assumed the aircraft was still being positioned by the tug driver; but perhaps we had been disconnected without brakes being set.  On taxiout we entered the hardstand. The FO researched tow bar pin shear (FOM requires inspection) as we both began to wonder if that may have occurred. Since we were off gate we contacted Dispatch and were patched through to Maintenance Control. Maintenance Control did great work to coordinate with ZZZ Maintenance and OPs to find out if there was a shear.  While we waited in the hardstand the FO and I decided it best to taxi back to gate and get the nose gear inspected just in case there was a pin shear. We taxied back to Gate XX; shutdown and entered an logbook entry.  There was notably good collaboration at the gate from our Maintenance team including the original ground crew providing their inputs so that the inspection could be done properly. With the inspection complete we departed without further issue.Cause: Causal was my failure to release the parking brake prior to authorizing the push.  My normal habit is to say "standby" after receiving the guide person's "all secure below" advisory; which I did.  But when I reviewed the ECAM just prior to clearing the pushback I only noted the NW STRG DISC memo and failed to note the Park Brake memo. And I didn't state "Brakes released" nor did I release the brakes. I am going to add a technique of pointing to the parking brake handle and then to the ECAM prior to stating "brakes released; cleared to push."  This was suggested by the FO who has seen other CAs using this technique.  And while I didn't feel rushed; I think making this process a slower and more deliberate execution will do me well in the future. I'm certain that the drop point rolling issue was part of this cascade from the non standard pushback. The guide person was very quick to catch the issue and call for brakes."
narrative1: We were given the brief from the pushback crew but had not completed our Before Start Checklist and had not received our pushback clearance from ramp.  The Captain told the push crew to standby."  Then once we were cleared by ramp to push he informed the ramp crew  "cleared to push tail north".  At that point the parking brake was still set. (Normal call "brakes released; cleared to push (tail north)").  When the ramp crew went to push we heard an unusual noise.  Then we realized that the parking brake had not been released. The Captain then notified the ramp crew to stop the push and investigate for any damage.  Additionally; he informed him that the parking brake had not been released. After the ramp crew investigated; they advised us that the tow bar and plane looked ok and were ready to continue the push. The captain released the brake and the push continued. After about 50 yards; the push the crew stopped and had us set brakes. They informed us that there was an issue with the tow bar and it needed to be swapped out. Once the new tow bar was attached we continued the push. Nearing the desired drop point; the aircraft was stopped by the push crew and the left wing walker gave a hold brakes signal with his wands as the captain waited for the driver to advise "set brakes." We then noticed the tug driving away and the aircraft appeared to be rolling forward.   Shortly after this the driver said "Captain brakes brakes."  The Captain immediately stopped the aircraft from rolling and set brakes.  Then he notified them that the brakes were set and they were cleared to disconnect the interphone.  To us what had appeared to have happened was the aircraft was still being pulled by the tug driver; but other indications made us question what was happening.  I believe the tug driver was a little shaken from the previous events that had occurred but the error had been trapped and damage/injury was prevented..On taxiout; I researched the publications for tow bar issues and discovered we may have sheared a tow pin and needed an inspection.  We coordinated with ramp to hold in the hard stand and worked with Dispatch; Maintenance Control; ZZZ Ops; ZZZ maintenance; and ramp to setup an inspection.  We proceeded to a new gate for the inspection.  The Captain made an logbook entry and maintenance performed the inspection.  We then proceed with the flight with no further issues and as a crew talked about what had happened and ways to prevent such a miscommunication in the future.Cause: The cause of the event was a miscommunication between the Captain and the push crew.  He did inform them that we were cleared to push but never said that the brakes were released.   I can see why this was confusing for the push crew.  Depending on the situation; Captains sometimes release the parking brake immediately after the brief is received from the push crew but tells the push crew to standby for the push clearance.   Also I'm curious how often the push crews ensure the light is out prior to initiating the push.  If the push crew would have referenced the light this would have been trapped and no error would have occurred."

The FO indicated that he believed it would be a good idea to call them out and assess the situation.I immediately grabbed the hand Mic (as all our belongings had been stowed and some were on the jetbridge) to call ground and ask them to send the trucks out due to a fire that the ground crew had told us about.  I also advised it was the #2 engine that was in question.  Ground asked a passing by jet if they saw any fire from our #2 engine.  The jet confirmed they did see some fire located at the 6 O'clock position of the back of the motor.With still zero visual evidence from the flightdeck of smoke or fire; I proceeded to call the Air Carrier X maintenance Control office to let them know of a possible fire and give them a heads up" of an upcoming Aircraft Maintenance Logbook (AML) entry.  By this time; while on the phone with maintenance; my FO returned to show me a picture he had taken of the fire.  It was; in my opinion; not anything major; but had been now burning for approximately 10 minutes.  I described the fire to the mechanic through the phone as being between the exhaust nozzle and the rear blades.  The mechanic indicated he thought it was a "candle flame".  Right about the same time; I herd the FO say; "They're foaming the engine".  A quick glance out the window; and I could see foam flying by the FO's side window.  When I indicated this to the Mechanic he said that the action of foaming was a big problem and that I needed to find out what type was used for my AML entry. At this point we were nearly deplaned.  I did not make any special PA's to the passengers since most the people were already off and all remaining passengers were in the aisle with their bags in hand.  The two forward FA's were made aware of the situation by the FO.  The cleaning crew that had tried to come onto the aircraft were told; by me; to leave the aircraft.  I had contemplated making a PA but feared at our current point in the deplaning process; the PA could create some unnecessary panic and do more harm than good.  I allowed the deplaning to continue normally which took another couple of minutes.After the passengers were off; I got word from the FO; that the fire chief wanted the APU shut down.  All the passengers were off the aircraft at this time and the FA's were gathering their belongings for their layover.  We did not have any ground power attached; the APU was shut down as if it was the last flight of the day.The FO and I went down to the aircraft to talk with the firefighters.  We ended up talking to the firefighter that sprayed the aircraft.  He mentioned that he had never seen that type of fire and did attempt to spray it with water first; this did not yield the desired result.  I assume this to mean that the fire would not extinguishby water alone.  He then resorted to the foam and mentioned he also foamed the wing as an extra precaution.  When asked the type of foam used for my AML entry; he said it was the "latest and greatest F-3 foam".  Later he indicated the new foam being used was non-corrosive.Having the information we needed and the AML entry complete; the FO and I grabbed our already packed bags and proceeded to the hotel for our scheduled layover.  While walking up the jetbridge I contacted our assigned dispatch at Air Carrier X to make them aware of the aircraft state and that maintenance had been contacted.Cause: During the event a tailpipe fire never entered the conversation.  On our return flight we discussed about the potential being there and that neither of us had really witnessed a persistent tailpipe fire; if one exists.  Myself; I've flown for decades and a majority of that has been in jets.  Pictures of tailpipe fires and possible expansion of QRC to include all steps if this occurs well after engine shutdown."

narrative: While near the end of the ZZZZZX arrival; RWY XX transition; we experienced two uncommanded roll events to the left while autopilot B was engaged. The aircraft was below 10;000' on the segment of the ZZZZZX before the slight left turn at ZZZZZ; on the straight-ahead sequence of fixes between ZZZZZ1 and ZZZZZ when both of these uncommanded roll events occurred. Neither event could be attributed to any change in aircraft configuration; input; or other factor that I can identify; both happened without any identifiable cause. Before the first uncommanded roll event; we were descending via the arrival in LNAV and VNAV with autopilot B engaged. Without warning or identifiable reason; the aircraft suddenly began rolling to the left. The autopilot initially stayed connected; and the autopilot system turned the yoke significantly to the right in an attempt to counter the roll. However; the autopilot was unable to stop the roll; the aircraft continued rolling; an amber 'ROLL AUTHORITY' displayed on the attitude indicator; and an aural alert sounded (this all happened very quickly--I cannot clearly remember what the aural alert was; since at that point I was already reaching for the disconnect to take recovery actions. My captain later said that he recalled it being a 'BANK ANGLE' aural alert). I called out 'my aircraft;' disconnected the autopilot; and applied right aileron and some right rudder to stop the roll and return the aircraft to level flight. Since the aircraft was notifying us that the autopilot's aileron authority alone was insufficient to keep control of the aircraft's bank angle ('ROLL AUTHORITY' annunciation); I determined that some amount of rudder was necessary to ensure we could overcome whatever unusual force was causing this uncommanded roll to the left that the autopilot could not counter with aileron alone. My inputs successfully stopped the roll; and I returned the aircraft to level flight and re-established the aircraft on the flight path. Feeling that the aircraft was now under control; my captain and I searched for any reason why that might have happened and couldn't identify anything. For that reason; we initially suspected wake turbulence. The captain asked ATC if we were following a heavy aircraft on the arrival; but ATC responded that we were following another 737 MAX. We did not think that a fellow MAX miles ahead would cause such an aggressive effect on our aircraft. Since the aircraft was stable and showing no further signs of control issues; we elected to re-engage autopilot B to monitor its response. Shortly thereafter; the same thing happened: an uncommanded continuous roll to the left that the autopilot could not counter with aileron input. I was already prepared to disconnect the autopilot quickly at the first sign of a recurrence; so I did so; applying the necessary inputs to stop the roll and re-stabilize the aircraft. In both instances of this uncommanded roll; it felt as if the autopilot had been commanding some sort of continuous control input that then released when I disengaged the autopilot; because the aircraft was responsive to my control inputs and recovered without difficulty after the autopilot was disengaged each time. Since the aircraft annunciated 'ROLL AUTHORITY' on the attitude indicator; indicating that 100% of the autopilot's roll authority was insufficient to control the aircraft's roll; I wondered if perhaps the aircraft had experienced an uncommanded rudder deflection that the autopilot was unable to overcome with ailerons; which then released when the autopilot was disconnected. However; that is just a possibility that crossed my mind; we could not identify any cause; nor did I feel any sort of yawing or rudder pedal movement prior to each event. After two uncommanded roll events in a row on autopilot B; we were convinced that we had a genuine problem with something in the autopilot system; as two events in a row like that did not seem like a wake turbulence encounter with anaircraft of the same type that was miles ahead. At that point; we were about to make the turn to ZZZZZ2 to join the ILS course to runway XX; so I continued to hand-fly the aircraft to a safe and otherwise uneventful landing. I experienced no control issues while hand-flying the aircraft. The captain made a logbook entry and notified dispatch after gate arrival; in accordance with company SOP.Cause: Causal factors unknown. Recommend thorough maintenance investigation.

The captain flew the airplane while I ran the QRC and QRH. The QRH lead us to the source selector panel and changing the air data source to 2; which created a plethora of red Xs on the captain side Primary Flight Display (PFD). The plane briefly climbed through our assigned altitude of 10;000 feet at this point (reaching 10;400) so the captain disconnected the autopilot and hand flew the plane back down to 10;000 and stayed at 250 knots. I asked air traffic control for present heading and present altitude while we troubleshoot an issue. The captain handed me the airplane; transferred flight directors; and ran the QRH themself; leading to the same issue. The end of that checklist led us to the air data failure QRH which led us to the unreliable air speed QRH. It was at this point that we decided it would be best to return to the field. The captain notified dispatch; and then flew the airplane while I briefed the flight attendant on the brief items. We asked ATC for vectors back to ZZZ airport. In my recollection; ATC didn't tell us what runway to expect; so the CA directed me to load the RNAV for XXL in. I started working on setting up the approach and getting landing performance. As we received further vectors; ATC informed us that we can expect runway XXR; so I reloaded the correct approach. At this point; the captain handed me the aircraft while they double checked my work; double checked the unreliable airspeed QRH to make sure there were no signs of discrepancies; and I was given instructions to intercept the approach and a clearance for the visual approach to XXR. Instead of clicking approach mode; I accidentally clicked the speed mode button. This prompted the captain to take controls; disconnect the auto pilot; and hand fly the intercept. It initially looked like the captain was lining up for runway XXL; so I clarified with them; and we corrected to the correct runway; XXR. The captain kept a buffer above Vref as a precaution for unreliable air speed. Once we landed safely and got off the runway; I called operations to get us a gate. Once we were stopped with the parking brake set; the captain delivered a PA to the passengers. A taxi to the gate without issue and had maintenance meet us there.Cause: I believe the lightning strike that the aircraft suffered the day prior may have affected certain systems that led to this failure. However; I'm not certain.'Suggestion: I should've discussed with the captain about declaring an emergency; and taking a little bit more time up in the air to set up the aircraft properly and calmly before commencing the approach. I should've also flown the airplane the entire time while the captain managed the aircraft and the situation. Tunnel vision and adrenaline were running high in this situation and I failed to speak up and instead deferred to the captain for decision-making.
narrative1: Got a Left Caution Pitot message at 3;000 I had the First Officer run the QRC and the QRH while I continued the climb. He did and it led us to turning the ADC to 2; when we did it killed everything on my side and disconnected the autopilot. We blew through 10;000; I corrected manually and notified ATC we needed present heading and 10;000 ft we needed to trouble shoot and that I was correcting back to 10;000. We ran the Left PITOT caution QRH again and it did the same thing;  I had coupled everything to the First Officer's side so it would knock the Auto Pilot off. We ran the next QRH for ADC failure which then lead us to the unreliable airspeed QRH. At this time I told the First Officer to notify the Flight attendants that we would be returning to the field for a small flight control issue and to remain seated no emergency. I told ATC I wanted Vectors back to ZZZ airport. We were not an emergency at this time but we were returning to field. We got vectors for the approach; we had XXL loaded got switched to XXR reloaded that as we were being vectored. We double checked the unreliable airspeed QRH and we didn't see any signs of unreliable airspeed with the pitch but I flew cross panel off the first officers side and the standby for reference and kept us 10 kts faster from VREF just to make sure I had a buffer. On intercept of course the First Officer accidentally hit my speed mode. This caused my side to black out and clear everything and I clicked off Autopilot and deselected both Flight Directors then hand flew the approach. The First Officer made sure we were lined up with the correct runway XXR since we never really intercepted the course so we corrected to XXR and landed safely. I believe quite a few items got fried which lead to our situation.

narrative: I was piloting a hot air balloon on a passenger flight. We launched from a field just west of ZZZ; and our flight path took us approximately 8 miles to the northwest.I was flying a Cameron Z105 with passengers.Weather was clear with visibility greater than 10 miles. I approached a large open grass field (approximately 7 acres) to land near the driveway leading from the road to the house. I was approximately 5 to 10 feet above ground level; moving about 6 mph toward the driveway. The passengers and I scanned the area for power lines and poles but did not see any in the field. We did see and discuss the power lines along the road; and we agreed the area between us and the driveway was clear.As we approached the driveway; a passenger and I noticed two single-strand power lines running from the road on our left to another pole north of the house. The lines were about 80 feet in front of us.  This occurred at about XA:40 PM; sunset was XB:43 PM.  Factors affecting the visibility of the power lines would have been background clutter with the background field and trees.   The balloon chase crew was also turning onto the driveway at the same time and called out the power lines over the radio.  This occurred just seconds after the pilot and passenger noticed the power lines.  I immediately opened the parachute valve to put the basket on the ground short of the power lines and allow the balloon envelope to lay over the lines. This is considered a 'rip out' situation as described in the flight manual and the FAA Balloon Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-11B). This is the safest maneuver to perform when contact with power lines is inevitable. If not performed; the basket could have contacted the power lines and injuries; or further damage could have occurred.There were three electrical arcs with two power lines. On the third arc; the fuse on the street power pole opened. The basket came to rest on its side; and all occupants were uninjured. We were able to exit the basket on our own. The balloon remained draped over the power line. There were no injuries to the pilot or passengers.A power company removed the balloon envelope.  The power was restored to one residential property.   The balloon and equipment were packed and transported to our storage facility. The next morning; I inspected the aircraft.  Four panels within the first 10 feet of nylon fabric had burns and holes. No load tapes or structural members of the aircraft were damaged. Per the Continued Airworthiness Manual; the holes were not required to be repaired because they were below the first 10 feet of nylon fabric.I plan to develop a near-miss presentation to share with fellow pilots and balloon crew members.The envelope has been repaired by an authorized repairman and returned to service.   The event arose from late identification of two single-strand power lines along the intended landing path. The balloon was already very low and moving toward the driveway when the lines were recognized; leaving limited time and distance to fully avoid contact.Contributing factors-	Low-visibility hazard: The wires were single-strand and therefore harder to see.-	Background clutter: Trees and the field behind the wires reduced contrast/visibility.-	Operating environment: Landing near a road/driveway/house increases the likelihood of utility spans and service runs that are not as obvious as roadside distribution lines.-	Expectation/attention: Attention was drawn to and discussion occurred about the roadside power lines; reinforcing the assessment that the area between the balloon and driveway was clear.-	Time/distance constraints: Wires were detected at close range (~80 ft) during a low-altitude; high-workload phase of flight.The wires were discovered visually on short final when the pilot and a passenger noticed two single-strand lines spanning from the road to a pole north of the house; approximately 80 feet ahead. The chase crew also called out the lines over the road seconds later as they turned onto the driveway.Corrective actions-	Immediate operational action: Pilot opened the parachute valve to execute a stop-short landing ('rip out' procedure) intended to keep the basket short of the lines and reduce occupant risk.-	Utility coordination: Local power company responded; removed the envelope from the lines; and restored power to one residential property.-	Recovery and inspection: With permission; balloon and equipment were packed and transported to storage.-	Maintenance disposition: Damage assessed; envelope repaired by an authorized repairman and returned.-	Lessons learned dissemination: Plan to develop a near-miss presentation for pilots and crew members.Human performance considerations-	High-workload phase: Approach and landing require continuous control decisions while scanning for obstacles; time available to detect/confirm thin hazards can be limited.-	Attention management: Visual attention may narrow toward the touchdown zone; making small; low-contrast hazards (single-strand wires) easier to miss until close.-	Team scanning and shared assumptions: Having passengers assist with scanning can increase coverage; but agreement that the area was clear can also reduce continued challenge/verification.-	Lighting/angle considerations: Late-day conditions and low sun angle can reduce contrast and increase glare risk (sun angle noted in the report).

The flight was now even shorter; so I did the same as the previous flight: snacks and drink orders on the ground. This time around I hadn't seen my partner fall asleep.
