They told me that we didn't have any steering; would have to reset on the ground or be tugged away but didn't declare an emergency. In that moment I immediately began mentally preparing for an emergency while also completely the 2nd row of drinks. As I was pouring drinks; I pulled my flight attendant device and opened the Flight Attendant Manual to ensure my memory served me correctly in this potential emergency. Before I could take the second row of drinks to the passengers the flight deck called again and stated that ATC is providing priority handling. The flight deck had called back to back within 2 minutes- if that. In that time I looked to see if my partner was on the phone but she wasn't anywhere to be found. I finished up my drinks and immediately began to double check the galley and cabin to secure anything that wasn't secured. The flight deck called again third time to ask for specials and give me a time update. We hadn't had any listed specials so I just relayed that message where they then told me it was 15 minutes left. Once the flight deck told us the time; I finally then heard my partner respond okay into the receiver. I always keep my phone timer on so I can also be aware of time just incase. My time was aligned with their time. Less than a minute later my partner came to the galley and asked me to repeat what was going on. I relayed the information to her and told her it's priority handling; so be prepared if it turns into something more. She shook her head as if she understood. She told me she missed the first two calls because she was in the bathroom but knowing that I've seen her asleep in the jumpseat and the bathroom sign NOT illuminated; I don't think she was telling the truth. Before the gear could come out and the sit-down chime went off; I had locked the bathroom and was seated. She was not in her brace position but very relaxed in her seat. As we landed I did a partial announcement by stating to remain seated with the seatbelts on and personal items stowed. I didn't want to give the standard announcement because I knew the captain would make an announcement almost immediately being as though we wouldn't turn off the runway. They then told the passengers what was going on. Making the taxi a bit longer than usual. Once we got to the gate is when I could finally breath. During the takeoff roll we didn't notice or feel any abnormalities beside the runway being very rough and bumpy (which is normal for ZZZ). After rotation and during climb out I noticed that I could feel a slight vibration from the airplane engine and looked at the VIB indicator and notice it was sitting around 3.9. We initially followed immediate action items (non involved); then I called for the QRC; then captain assigned me to continue PF duties while he conducted the QRH. While we ran the checklist I asked ATC to level off at 12;000 feet and stay there while we were troubleshooting. Once I brought the thrust levers back to a normal 250kt cruise speed the engine vibs returned to a normal green range; we continued with the checklist and it directed us to continue with the flight while monitoring the engine vibes. We both agreed that declaring an emergency didn't seem appropriate since the engine was operating normally at lower thrust settings. We communicated with dispatch and came to the agreement to return to ZZZ. The rest of the flight we asked ATC for 'speed our discretion'. We flew back to ZZZ without any other abnormalities. During the landing we didn't feel anything abnormal and even during the taxi to the gate. When we arrived at the gate XX we heard a ramp truck report to ramp control that the aircraft he was looking at had a blown tire. We asked ramp to confirm if it was our aircraft he was talking about; and he confirmed it. During the walk around I saw that the inboard left main tire had blown; I also noticed dents and tire marks on the underside of the wing and flap. The engine showed indications that tire debris had entered the engine. We then notified ground control of potential FOD on runway XXL and XXR.Would have been helpful if someone had noticed our tire blow out during departure. We had no indications that a tire had blown.
narrative1: Tail swapped into Aircraft X for unknown reason. Push back; engine starts; taxi all normal. During takeoff we assumed runway was poorly textured. During rotation FO called out N1 fan vib at 3.9; he called for QRC and QRH. After completing necessary immediate action items we followed QRC and QRH procedures. I instructed him to continue flying while also maintaining radios as I completed the procedures in QRH; coordinated with dispatch; and the FAs. Sometime below 10;000 (I believe around 6;000) the aft FA called and was unable to communicate with the flight deck. The aft FA had to communicate using the fwd fa telephone in order to tell us that he heard a loud bang and vibrations from the left side of the aircraft. After we decided to return to field; dispatch also got in contact with Mx (Maintenance) who agreed that we should return. We determined that we could safely contain the vibration in CRZ setting and deemed that declaring an emergency was not necessary; however had priority to the field. I communicated with FAs; dispatch; then made a PA to the passengers telling them that due to the 'loud vibrational noises from Aircraft left; we would be returning to ZZZ out of precaution'. Completed the rest of the flight as routine standard; landed safely; coordinated gates and specials with operations. We fully taxied to the gate before a ground person told ramp that our left main inboard tire was completely blown and it was communicated to us. We deplaned; contacted maintenance; dispatch coordinators; scheduling; and the chiefs. This resulted in 3 write ups from us directly. We did notify ATC about the tire issue for possible FOD on the runway (either on takeoff or landing); ground called us back to say yes; FOD was found on XXR.Would have been nice to know we had tire damage before parking; but it seems like nobody was around to see it and we didn't believe to have had any indications stating otherwise.

narrative: Flight purpose was to regain proficiency after not flying for several months. Checked fuel quantity using sight gauges and found 2 gallons in the right tank and 5 gallons in the left tank. I expected to use about 4 gallons during the flight. Other aircraft were parked at the fuel pump; so I decided to fill up after the flight.After some airwork and practice landings at another airfield; I headed home. As I was initiating the descent from 3000 MSL (about 2000 AGL); I got a fuel pressure warning from the Dynon system. The fuel pressure indication was fluctuating widely. I decided to stay at my present altitude until within easy gliding distance of my home airport. Roughly a minute later; the Dynon system gave me an engine speed warning and the engine stopped.I glanced at the glide ring on the Dynon system and my home airport was right on the edge. Knowing that the glide ring was based on conservative glide data; I was tempted to continue to my home airport. Then I thought about the reason that I had used conservative glide data (because I might encounter sinking air) and decided that a farm field nearby was a better option. After an uneventful landing in the field; I contacted a neighbor and had him bring fuel to the field. We added five gallons to each tank and I made an uneventful flight home.After getting home; I reviewed the POH. It states that the pilot should alternate between the left and right tank. I had been in the habit of setting both fuel valves to open assuming that; if one tank became empty; fuel would flow from the other one. The POH stated that is not guaranteed with both valves open. In the future; I will follow the POH recommended practice for setting the fuel valves.

The conflicting traffic was not visually acquired during the maneuver. Subsequent post-flight review of ADS-B data indicated that Aircraft Y was operating in the vicinity at approximately 2;500 feet. A handoff was put on Sector XX which left 0 people in the break list for such a high stress; high volume situation. Holdover overtime was used where possible; but eventually staffing declined more; with 7 positions open with 7 controllers available. This includes 2 of the mid workers that came in. We could no longer support a handoff on Sector XX which absolutely needed one. The controller on Sector XZ asked and said he needed to have a DSide; but we had no staffing to provide one. The controller on Sector XY also said he needed help; but we did not have help to offer him. We had 2 RSide's that were trainees; and 1 DSide trainee that could not work Sector XZ Dside as we had to combine Sector XZ with XA because of the lack of bodies. The traffic volume was some of the highest I have seen; especially that late in the evening. I was later informed that the Command Center had gone home and left us all to fend for ourselves with no outside help besides controllers to controllers. This is an insanely unacceptable situation and one of the more dangerous I've witnessed in my career. There was a lack of experience in the area. A lack of anything being done by Command Center. A lack of adequate staffing. Extremely high and complex workload while controllers are forced to suck it up and deal with it for hours on end without breaks. Controllers were put in an extremely risk heavy and dangerous position; asking and voicing their need for help and D Sides; and yet we are unable to provide them with any help what so ever. The controller on Sector XA; being slow but necessary to have been split off; was essentially acting as a 'handoff' or 3rd set of eyes for the sectors above them. This is TOTALLY UNACCEPTABLE. The FAA is constantly knowingly putting it's controllers in harms way and throwing them to the fire. Late last night we entered a situation that was forecast well in advance. Command Center did nothing to alleviate or spread traffic out effectively and left to essentially put the entire workload on controllers that are perpetually over worked. Controllers needed DSides and Handoffs and yet due to staffing it wasn't possible. I am not aware of a staffing trigger that evening. We were hung out to dry last night by an administration that fully knows about these issues that occur all the time; and nothing is being done. This was a total failure of outside leadership.We cannot work hours on end sectors that have 40+ aircraft for hours on end. This was a forecast situation in which Command Center had en entire shift to come up with a plan better than 'Let them all go through one gap and let the controllers figure it out'. Any aircraft transiting the airspace down over IRW heading up to the north west should've come through that gap.Any aircraft diverting around the weather going to points out west or southwest; should have been routed down over ADM and out into Sector XZ. Then; right as we're in the thick of it; Command Center decides to go home. We had multiple controllers in the Center here go over 10 hours last night; and almost everyone was held over and working without a break in sight. Command Center can stay and help try to figure something out.

I was flying and working the radios; but I believe the PTU was turned off and possibly the yellow engine pump. After our plans were settled I requested priority handling and notified ATC of our intentions; souls; and fuel on board.  ATC began vectoring us for an ILS to XYC. We discussed our ability to taxi in but were hesitant due to the brake temp and we had been made aware that a fluid was now leaking from the belly of the aircraft.  A tug arrived and we decided out of an abundance of caution that we would be towed in.  This took a while.  Mx (Maintenance) arrived and asked for the gear pins. narrative1: Departing ZZZ on our third flight to ZZZ1; climbing out of 1000 feet we had yellow hydraulic reservoir low ECAM. Additional messages came up with that failure. I was the pilot monitoring; and I informed ATC that we needed too level off at 5000 feet to work a problem. I asked the FO if he was comfortable flying and working  the radios so I could run the checklist; and he was. He turned on the autopilot and continue to fly and work the radios. We ran through the procedure together; verifying everything was done correctly. At that point I tried a call me message for a frequency with dispatch and Maintenance Control. Since we were at 5000 feet; we had a hard time hearing dispatch and I've ended up telling them our plan was to return to ZZZ; the dispatcher was phenomenal and getting us landing data and information we needed for landing.  We advised ATC. We set up for a return to ZZZ and briefed the plan. I then called the flight attendants and advised them of the situation as well as notified the passengers. We were aware of the possibility of an overweight landing and had a discussion on burning the fuel or just going into land. We elected to land as we were down one hydraulic system. The landing was incredibly smooth and uneventful. Being that we were overweight and heavy; we had the fire trucks meet the airplane as a precautionary measure. Once off the runway; the fire trucks notified us that we did have hydraulic fluid leaking out of the belly; it was described as a slow drip. I communicated with dispatch and Maintenance Control on the ground for the safest course of action with hot brakes. I'm not sure who; but somebody sent us a tug so we thought we would use the tug to get back to the gate. Unfortunately; in the midst of the chaos; I could not find the gear pins in the flight deck as that back closet was dark and the gear pin holder was a dark color. This is no way in excuse that I could not find them; just telling you the real time situation as I was trying to communicate with everybody and find gear pins for the tug in. At this point; the brakes had cooled down enough that we discussed with maintenance and they thought it would be better if we could just taxi in so that's what we elected to do. (once maintenance arrived at the airplane. We did shut the engines down in preparation for being towed in). We started the engines back up and order a taxi back to the gate uneventfully. We coordinated with operations to chock us ASAP as the checklist says that the brake accumulator may not hold the aircraft in position. Maintenance personnel met us at the gate where we continued the discussion of what happened.

narrative: Abnormal Aileron Control Feel. During preflight; the First Officer and I reviewed the logbook and noted a previously closed write-up stating: 'Noticed excessive yoke movement up to 2 units without aileron response.' The write-up was discussed during the departure brief. Control checks after start were normal. During departure from ZZZ; during departure while hand flying in moderate turbulence; the First Officer noticed an abnormal aileron control feel. During right aileron input; resistance was sometimes normal; sometimes significantly lighter than normal; and at times initially normal before abruptly becoming very light. Left aileron inputs were initially normal. The First Officer advised me of the condition and elected to continue hand flying while we discussed what he was experiencing. I subsequently hand flew the aircraft and immediately experienced the same abnormal and inconsistent aileron control feel the First Officer had described.Throughout this period; the aircraft responded appropriately to all control wheel inputs. However; the feel or resistance of the ailerons was highly variable; at times heavier than normal; at times lighter; and occasionally transitioning from heavy to very light during a single control input. We elected not to use the autopilot and to continue the climb to FL300 (planned FL370) to evaluate the condition; and coordinate with Dispatch and Maintenance before making further decisions and determining the safest course of action. There is no published QRH procedure that directly addressed the abnormal aileron control feel. The Jammed or Restricted Flight Controls QRH was reviewed as the closest reference; although it did not precisely match the condition observed. In accordance with our plan strategy; I transferred aircraft control and radios to the First Officer; who is very experienced and had a good feel for the aircraft. I contacted Dispatch and Maintenance Control via Crew Phone. Maintenance Control stated they were not aware of known issues with the aileron system that would produce the symptoms described and advised that the aileron system does not share characteristics with elevator systems that typically experience bearing-related feel issues. No additional guidance was provided. The abnormal aileron feel persisted; remaining variable.After further discussion; and considering the current condition in combination with the recent prior closed aileron write-up; we determined that although the aircraft remained controllable; we could not ensure an adequate margin of safety to continue to destination; nor could we be confident the condition would not worsen. We notified ATC and elected to divert to ZZZ1 which was previously coordinated with Dispatch. ZZZ1 was chosen to allow sufficient fuel burn to reach landing weight with minimal maneuvering; favorable weather; long runways; and crew familiarity. We started the APU; and initially remained at FL300/275 KIAS and did not change airspeed. To continue assessing controllability while burning fuel; we later descended to FL260 and further slowed to 250 KIAS to stay in smooth air and then later descended slowly to 16;000. Airspeed changes were then made in 5 knot increments; closely monitoring control feel with each change. The abnormal aileron feel remained variable throughout all speeds. We extended the landing gear and began configuring early to assist with fuel burn and continue evaluating controlabillity. As a precaution; we elected to limit bank angle to 15 degrees and elected to land Flaps 15 to maintain higher approach speed and roll margin. The aircraft was hand flown for the remainder of the flight; as we were unsure how the autopilot might respond given the abnormal aileron control feel.Below 10;000 feet; continuous light turbulence required frequent control inputs. The aileron feel remained abnormal and variable; however; aircraft control remained effective. The Non Routine Landing Considerations QRH was completed. We requested theILS Runway XXC at ZZZ1 and requested ARFF to observe the aircraft after landing. Descent and before landing checklists were completed; with continuous updates provided to the flight attendants and passengers. The landing was normal. We remained on the runway for a post landing Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) inspection; no abnormalities were observed. ARFF accompanied us during a normal taxi to the gate. The shutdown was normal. Passengers were reaccommodated onto another aircraft. After completion of the flight; both pilots discussed that we did not feel fit to continue flying. The ZZZ1 Chief Pilot assisted in removing us from further duty.  Threat and Error Management (TEM) was used throughout the event; including the decisions to notify ATC; divert to ZZZ1; restrict bank angle; slow and configure gradually; and land Flaps 15 to preserve controllability and safety margin.Cause: The following day I noticed a maintenance write up for this aircraft that air was suspected in the hydraulic lines. That would be a condition I believe would be consistent with what was felt on the controls.  However; that was not something considered during the flight as our attention was more about safe recovery of the aircraft.
synopsis: B737-800 Captain reported abnormal right aileron control responses during climbout.

narrative: The First Officer was flying a normal approach to Runway XXR. As the aircraft settled on to the runway; FO said that the braking felt a little weird and that the aircraft was not decelerating correctly. FO disconnected the AUTOBRAKES via brake pressure; and I said let's go to the next high speed [exit taxiway] 1 because I did not want to try and stress the brake system more. I took control of the aircraft and finished the rollout to 1; made a left turn and the aircraft brakes appeared to be grabbing; and letting go. I then made another left on to taxiway 2 and began taxing EAST on 2. I slowed for a second to gain a better understanding of what was going on. FO asked if I wanted him to tell ATC that we were having brake problems; I asked him to hold off until we got EAST of the next turn off taxiway 3 going eastbound because that was a NORMAL turn off and I wanted to get EAST of it before the next aircraft landed. After I past [taxiway] 3; we called ATC and told them we may need to taxi slowly because of brake problems. As the ground speed dropped below ANTISKID engagement speed; 27 MPH; the aircraft began to roll normally. NO more wobble; no more grabbing; so we continued.The tower asked if wanted different taxi routing because of the brake problem. I told them NO; I then explained to FO that I did want to heat the brakes up any longer on the longer route. I then said; FO; I'm not sure what is going on so we will leave both engines running for idle speed; control and avoid braking.ATC immediately cleared us across RWY XXL so we didn't have to stop; then taxied to 4; 5 and ramp on the bridge. I asked FO to input an ELB (Electronic Log Book) for the anomaly and he did. As I turned on 5; FO then got a clearance for parking via 5; 6 to the alley for gate X. I asked FO to contact maintenance because we need to have a discussion with them and because it was an international flight; I needed them to catch us before we went on to customs. On initial contact with Maintenance; they informed us we had a wheel FIRE; we notified RAMP to dispatch ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) to our location. FO asked if I wanted to evacuate and I said no we simply did not have enough information to that. I stopped the aircraft and made an announcement to the passengers and crew and told them we were not on the gate yet; and Fire rescue will be inspecting the rear tires. After a few minutes; I engaged with MX (Maintenance) Control and Ramp to find out where the ARFF was on the field and an ETA. Numerous employees gathered and took pictures from afar; but no one could tell me if it was getting worse. I made another announcement to the pax reassuring them that we were safe and the ARFF would be pulling up shortly.  Each announcement had to be translated for our passengers by the flight attendants. I made announcements every 5-7 minutes.ARFF arrived and got on the RAMP frequency; asked us to shut down the RIGHT engine; so they could inspect the right wheels; we complied. The Left  Engine was still running; the APU was running. FO asked about shutting down the LEFT engine; we did; and now the packs were running off the APU bleed air. We spoke with ARFF on ramp frequency for a minute and no one said an ACTIVE FIRE was present. As we sat there for about 5 minutes; no communication with ARFF; they elected to spray fire retardant on the brakes; 1st the RIGHT SIDE; then the LEFT side brakes. This forced Smoke and fumes into the cabin because the retardant struck the hot brakes; formed a smoke and the South wind blew it right into the PACK INTAKE system. As soon as it happened I reached up and turned off the packs; and made an announcement to the passengers and crew to remain seated. I later found out the Flight Attendants were getting ready to evacuate until they heard my announcement. This whole sequence of events took less than 20 seconds.I called MX on radio one and notified them I was no longer communicating with ARFF and that they just created a problem with smoke in the cabin. Poor communications between ARFF and the crew.Then ARFF told me to taxi into the gate; I told FO to tell them MX would be towing us; both engines were shut off. After a few minutes; I elected to turn the PACKS back on; made an announcement and asked the passengers to be patient.Numerous vehicles airport ops; MX; baggage handlers; police; etc.; were around the aircraft; but NO ONE was telling me about an active fire. Then MX showed up and requested that I through down the gear pins. RIght then I knew we were NOT on fire; and MX was going to set the gear pins for pull in to the gate. Again; no verbal confirmation from anyone.Ground personnel finally showed up; some frequency communication problems with them; then they pulled us into the gate about :40 total time from the fire notification by MX (Camera - not sure how they knew) and in at the gate. The passenger deplaned; I contacted MX again and requested a face-to-face with someone so I could give them a quick debrief. Someone came up; took my statement. I was informed right then… for the 1st time by the MX guy that we DID NOT HAVE a fire; only the hub cap melted. Good thing we didn't evacuate on just a report of a fire and not confirmation. I wanted to go down to the ramp but Customs had not released the aircraft yet. FO and I proceeded to customs; cleared customs got on the bus and called the Chief Pilot from the employee parking lot.

narrative1: At the gate in BZE during the departure briefing we again discussed the threat of the number of small aircraft traffic and would mitigate that with looking outside and using caution on taxi and takeoff.  We were given push clearance from stand XX onto 'B' taxiway which meant we were pushed almost directly straight back.  As we were clear of our stand two smaller aircraft rapidly taxied through our vacated spot; joining taxiway 'A' towards runway 07.  Shortly thereafter we requested taxi clearance. As we reached the holding point for runway 07; the second of the smaller aircraft was given takeoff clearance and a turn to the north.  We watched them takeoff and start their turn north; well clear of our initial departure path to the east.  Tower asked if we had the traffic in sight; which we did.  We were given takeoff clearance; had a normal takeoff; and switched to Goldson Approach.  Following the LNAV; reaching BZ910 we started the turn to the north. Shortly thereafter we entered the clouds.  Sometime while we were in the clouds Goldson Approach pointed out traffic which we did not have in sight due to IMC. We then saw the target on TCAS to our left (west of us). We agreed it was probably the traffic that took off ahead of us; presuming they were continuing northbound as we didn't hear otherwise.  We were not in the clouds long when we climbed above them becoming VMC again.  It was at that time the captain (PM) visually acquired the traffic; TCAS target turned amber then immediately red with a commanded descend RA.  I aggressively pushed the nose down and realizing that wasn't enough pushed again as I pulled power back.  Once clear of the conflict; I resumed the climb and departure.  ATC was notified of the TCAS RA response by us.After getting our bearings again; the captain called the FAs to make sure they and the passengers were okay.  They did comment on the perceived negative G's but that everyone was ok.  We initially attempted to contact dispatch however neither of us could get the desk numbers to populate.  The captain then notified dispatch using ACARS. As Maintenance Control could not immediately see if the aircraft had been overstressed in the maneuver; we elected to continue to destination as any diversion short of destination would result in an overweight landing and potentially further overstress the aircraft. A logbook entry was made regarding the event.Cause:  The high volume of smaller light aircraft; the fast pace they operate (ie short approaches; short landing and takeoff roll; fast taxi speed); and the sometimes indecipherable communications from those pilots sometimes make it harder to keep situational awareness of where everyone is. We were asked if the traffic was in sight and it was until after takeoff and climbing through the clouds.  We had no way of knowing though what their intentions/clearances were after proceeding northbound and if being complied with. Ultimately ATC should have kept both aircraft well clear of the other either by extending our upwind off the departure path or not allowing the other aircraft to turn east across our path until we were further north. Also; as per the Jeppesen page; the stated IFR departure information was not followed assuming the proceeding aircraft was IFR as they climbed through a cloud layer.We practice responding to TCAS RAs every recurrent. After this experience I feel those are very benign and perhaps a more aggressive and faster paced scenario would be better served. We weren't afforded the luxury of time to watch the scenario build. Add to it that we were in an initial climb profile with pitch and power and when the event started below 3000 feet AGL. Aggressively transitioning from a high pitch and power to nose down; pointed down to the ground still initially with climb power causes a secondary startle effect in the 'float' feeling from the dramatic pitch change.  We can't replicate that part in a sim but the aggressiveness required to respond could be possible; decreasing that startle factor.
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported that while climbing through 2;500 feet; ATC alerted them of traffic at their 11:00 position and 3;000 feet. They got an RA to descend and took evasive action to avoid a possible collision.

We asked ZABQ how people are doing the RNAV app road into ABQ with no GPS and he said to do the RNAV visual.  We said we're not doing a night visual around mountains.  We asked for an early switch to ABQ approach to see what other people are doing.  Switching to ABQ approach two aircraft were in the same predicament we were in. The second aircraft did the same ILS 8 approach and reported them same.  I elected to do the same. We briefed the approach and I briefed the FO.  We flew the approach as advertised at 300 get the tail wind died off.  This caused our indicated airspeed to jump about 10kts at 300 for a brief moment the. Quickly captured back to on speed.  Landed and taxi in was uneventful.Cause: WSMR (White Sands Missile Range) regularly conducts jamming.  If this is known ahead of time we should add fuel and an alternate for a situation where the only approach to the runway in GPS.  Center and approach control need to communicate better to each other and aircraft inbound.  Center seemed to not think this was a big deal; approach was overworked with four inbound aircraft all unable to shoot the approach do to jamming; weather and all other runways beside 08/26 being closed."
narrative1: Immediately prior to top of descent into ABQ as we were setting up the cockpit for the RNAV (RNP) Z Rwy 26 approach we discovered that that our GPS was being jammed and operating in a greatly reduced capacity only receiving between 3-5 satellites at any given time with an operating mode of AIDED instead of NAV. This completely precluded us from preforming the approach to runway 26 which was the only runway open at the time with winds being reported as 270/8 kts and winds aloft being out of the west at approximately 30 knots until 300 feet above the ground. This put added pressure into preforming a tailwind approach in challenging conditions at night using the only available approach. As we crossed the mountains just east of the airfield I observed GPS 1 receiving only a single satellite and GPS 2 receiving no satellites. Multiple aircraft were adversely affected by this GPS jamming at and around our arrival time. This is a major safety of flight issue in ABQ when the winds are out of the west as this completely inhibits us from using any approach to runways 26 or 21. If the winds would have been above our max tailwind component we would not have been able to legally land anywhere as we were not filed with an alternate and did not have the fuel to make any airport without dipping significantly into our fuel reserves. We assessed after the fact that the closest company airport to us would have been ZZZ and at 200 miles away would have used up a significant portion of our remaining fuel. In my estimation if we would have had to divert there we would have arrived with around 30 minutes of fuel remaining onboard the aircraft given we arrived with around 70 mins of fuel in ABQ and assuming the approx 40 minutes of flight time to cover the 200 miles down to ZZZ. In the end we conducted a tailwind approach within limits to runway 8 however there is in my opinion a significant risk of aircraft flying to ABQ with jamming in progress not carrying the fuel for an alternate and not being able to land in ABQ because of tailwinds on the only useable approach as we were only between 2 and 7 knots of wind; depending on the exact aircraft; away from being unable to legally land in ABQ without using emergency authority.Cause: White sands missile range GPS jamming creating a significant threat to aircraft approaching ABQ with no filled alternate under clear weather in particular at night. It is my belief that as long as GPS jamming is underway at white sands every aircraft arriving at ABQ should have a filed alternate and carry sufficient fuel to reach it. In particular aircraft operating at night when winds are forecast to be out of the west.
synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported GPS jamming during cruise and approach phase; which caused the RNAV approach to be unusable; requiring approach and landing on runway with tailwind.

narrative: CA PM FO PFWe were cleared for the visual approach XX backed up with the ILS. The FO had briefed me that he was just off low-time hours in type. We had done one leg together which I flew. On the approach we identified the traffic to follow and proceeded inbound. The FO was delayed in calling for configuration as we became established on the LOC. I am not the type of CA to micromanage speed reductions and flap configurations as long as it does not affect stabilized approach criteria. However; I prompted that we need to begin configuring as we are getting close to the aircraft ahead and do not know their ground speed. I believe we were at flaps 3 gear down when ATC notified us of a 60kt overtake and that S-turns to the right were approved. We slowed to final landing configuration and were stabilized at 1000'. I told the FO to perform S-turns and he proceeded; reaching 1000 fpm momentarily and getting low - hitting 3 red lights on the PAPI before he rejoined the course and corrected - but otherwise we continued to remain stable through 500'. ATC told us at about 200-300' to go around and the FO hit the TOGA button but I did not hear him make the call-out as he was a very soft-spoken individual. I looked down to make sure the throttles were in TOGA detent and made the call-out myself then retracted the flaps to position 2. We performed the gear retraction properly and at that time ATC told us to climb 2000' and turn heading (I believe) 270. I bugged the panel and selected Heading and was monitoring the FO hand flying when I prompted him to take the Autopilot (AP) to reduce our workload; which we engaged. It is hard to remember the exact sequence of events that followed because of the momentary stress but after I engaged the AP; we received another instruction to climb 3000' and turn heading (I believe) 330. It was at this time I noticed our speed reducing and realized we missed the FLCH 210 call out and were still bugged at our Vap of 131. I noticed the speed around 140kts approaching 131 quickly and because we were in a turn; the low speed tape was higher; buffering Vap speed. I called out Speed 210 Speed 210" as the speed turned amber and instead of spinning the speed bug the FO disconnected the AP and pushed the nose down; which threw me off since I was not expecting the action and now I was back to manipulating the control panel. We did not receive a stick shaker. I spun the speed to 210 and at the same time I saw we were in a nearly 40-45 degree bank and approaching 3000' with a high rate of climb. I told the FO "altitude" "bank". I pressed forward on the controls and we managed to level and the FO reduced the bank angle. I engaged the AP once more and we continued to speed up and clean up the aircraft. We came back for a second approach without incident and landed uneventfully. We parked and debriefed the event. It was the FO's first go-around. We discussed fixation which led to the omission of speed on both our ends and the importance of aviate-navigate-communicate. We discussed the speed tape and how at higher bank angles it can lead to accelerated stalls and that there was no need to turn to the heading so aggressively. I also encouraged him to call for AP early in order to reduce workload."

narrative: Preflighted the aircraft normally and performed initial start up and run up checklists as usual. No unusual readouts or abnormalities. On takeoff and climb out all indications were normal. Outside of the airport environment I had my student put on the goggles and directed us to a gps fix for some simulated IMC practice. Upon leveling out at cruise I took controls and had my student remove the foggles; handed control back and had him run through his initial checklist for maneuvers. We loaded in the nearest fields frequency and made a call that we would be maneuvering 15nm NW of the field at 5;700. I demonstrated a set of steep turns and then we went over the importance of running our cruise checklist and scanning all instruments every time in between. Student attempted a set of steep turns and requested to practice another set. We ran through the cruise and instrument scan and noted no abnormalities. We went over the importance of finding good visual reference points; and he attempted a steep turn to the left. After completing and leveling back off; I re-scanned the instruments and noted the Ammeter read out was low (around 2 or 3). I looked to the annunciator panel and noticed there was no illumination and the engine instruments digital screen was flickering and dim. Upon noticing this I took controls and had my student get his checklist to check the alternator low / inop checklist. At this time the Primary Flight Display (PFD) gave an AHRS failure notification and inop readouts for our attitude indicator and heading. Simultaneously both of our G430s went black and our PFD /Multi-function Flight Display (MFD) flashed off and back on. We ran the troubleshoot checklist and verified circuit breakers had not popped; they hadn't; attempted to reduce the load by shutting off the fan; shutting off lights; tried turning battery master and alternator off and back on; turned on the power for the standby attitude indicator and it worked alright for a couple minutes before flagging that it was inop. Nothing worked; and at this time we were a little over what looked like 10nm from the closest airport ZZZ. I made the decision to head to ZZZ and as it was an untoward field and G430s were black screened; I squawked 7600 for loss of comms and attempted to transmit in the blind. Called that we were approximately 10nm NW of the field and inbound for a landing with no electrical power. ZZZ center responded asking if we could hear them; if we needed assistance; and informing us we were transmitting on guard. I responded with our location and intentions and that was when we lost our standby attitude and our PFD / MFD went black. ZZZ center asked if we were able to swap and transmit on the local CTAF. I responded unable as we still did not have the 430s. A nearby aircraft also on guard called center and offered to transmit on our behalf on the local CTAF. Center agreed and we continued inbound to ZZZ prior to landing we lost all electrical. We landed; taxied to the ramp; secured and post flight inspected the aircraft. The only abnormality we found was a significant drop in oil level. In pre-flight it was 6.5 and in post flight it was 5.5 at most

narrative: I was on short final at ZZZ for runway XX. It was sunset. The entire runway was in shadow. The sun was in my eyes from the sunset at my right. I had repeatedly tried to activate the PAPI using 5 clicks on the radio; but it was not activating and was discussing with my pilot/passenger in the right seat why it was not activating. I did not realize that I was on the wrong frequency and not on ZZZ CTAF. I made a call that I was on final runway XX at ZZZ about 3 miles out. I did not see any other aircraft on ADSB north of the field; and I'm not sure I looked south of the field on the map to see if there was anyone on ADSB. The wind was calm; so either runway was a candidate for takeoffs and landings. At about 500 feet AGL/MSL my right-seater and I both noticed at the same time an aircraft's landing lights on the runway. I was doing a short field landing; so was slow; and so I carefully broke off to the left without adding G loading; adding full power; and gently entered a climb with full flaps; gradually working the flaps out. The aircraft must have just landed on runway XY without me hearing them on the radio because I was on the wrong frequency; and without realizing I was on final for XX because they didn't hear my transmission; and they probably didn't notice me on ADSB; if they even have it. Once I was in a stable climb; I realized I wasn't on frequency and changed to CTAF and heard the other pilot calling me. I replied explaining it was entirely my fault because I had been on the wrong frequency; and the other pilot was gracious about the situation. I'm assuming the other plane must have taxied off the runway and to the ramp because I didn't see them after that. We set up for another landing; which was uneventful.The problem was that I don't have a correct-frequency check as a checklist item; and skipped verifying that I was on the correct CTAF. This was compounded by the runway being entirely in shadow and the sun in my eyes. The PAPI not turning on should have alerted me to the fact that I was on the wrong frequency. The short field landing I was doing also had me in a nose-high attitude behind the power curve; which made it slightly harder to see down the runway. I was also focused on maintaining the plane at a low airspeed; lined up for landing; during the slow approach; which is a bit more demanding and may have been an additional distraction from the issue unfolding. The plane that had just landed on XX may have turned on their landing lights on the runway to alert me of their presence; because neither my right seat pilot/passenger or I noticed them until the plane appeared halfway down the runway. To avoid this in future I plan to add a frequency check to my checklists; make sure I run my checklists every time; make sure my landing lights are on for takeoffs and landings; and consider what else may be wrong when I notice something 'weird' like a PAPI not activating.

What they didn't know was that we were very busy dealing with the checklist and ATC concurrently. When we heard the DOOR DOOR DOOR audio; FO performed the immediate action item for the flight deck door and pressed the HARD LOCK switch. We were able to eventually advise them that we were very busy and that we'd contact them when we get a chance. After completing up to step 17 of the CABIN ALTITUDE Warning non-normal; we discussed diverting to ZZZ. We informed dispatch of our issue and our intentions to go to ZZZ. They eventually replied and asked if we requested priority handling and we informed them that we did. I slowed the aircraft to 250 KIAS at 10;000 ft as to not feel rushed dealing with our issue. The FAs were contacted and the brief was performed. The passengers were also briefed of our issue and our intentions to divert to ZZZ. Everyone was also informed about the emergency equipment on standby and they were going to be there as a precaution. The divert* function had been completed; aircraft re-cruised and set up for the arrival into ZZZ. Since we were landing overweight; we calculated our landing distance utilizing the LANDING DISTANCE NORMAL CONFIGURATION - FLAPS 30 (800) table. We were given vectors for ILS XXL and conducted a FLAPS 30/AUTO BRAKES 3 landing. After landing; we exited runway XXL and came to a complete stop so Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) could inspect the aircraft exterior for any damage. After none was noted; they departed the scene and returned to their base of operation. We eventually taxied to the gate. After we completed the parking checklist; we spoke to one of the maintenance technicians. They were debriefed. Afterwords; I contacted the Chief Pilot and advised him that we were ok to continue. Electronic Log Book entries were made for the cabin altitude (occurrence altitude and cabin altitude indication noted) and overweight landing (smooth landing and weight noted (…approximately 8200 lbs overweight). Outside the flight deck; we had to opportunity to conduct a thorough debrief. We discussed aspects of how we handled the situation (workload management and situational awareness) and the fact that we were able to cover all the steps dealing with our issue and safely divert to ZZZ. Communication is what could've gone better. We discussed how the warning horn was a distraction before cutout was selected; establishing communication with masks on; ATC callingus while we were doing checklists and the FAs immediately trying to contact us numerous times as well. The primary issue though was how we both missed the pressurization switch in the manual position. We discussed about the possibility of confirmation bias regarding the switch position; but we also discussed ways to prevent a repeat of undesired outcome of events.
narrative1: On climbout to FL320 at approximately FL270 the CABIN ALTITUDE warning light illuminated and warning horn started sounding.  We accomplished our immediate action items(O2 masks on; establish communications; and seatbelt sign on); and I asked ATC for a descent to 10000' stating we had a pressurization issue.  The CA; PF; initiated an immediate descent.  The CA called for the 'CABIN ALTITUDE Warning or Rapid Depressurization/Descent' QRC.  As I was accomplishing the QRC and got to item 6 I noticed the pressurization controller switch was already in manual and the MANUAL green light was illuminated.  I looked at the cabin altitude and saw approximately 11000'.  Also at this time the FAs began trying to call the cockpit. I attempted to establish communication with them but was unable initially; and was prioritizing the checklist and communication with ATC.  This quickly escalated to banging on the flight deck door and sounding of the 'door; door; door' alarm.  I pushed the hard lock button and attempted again to get in contact with the FAs.  I was able to very faintly hear them over the speaker and advised them we had a pressurization issue; we were descending to 10000' and to stand by. With the O2 masks on and with how busy we were I was unable to discern if they had heard me very well at this point.  I continued with the QRC and eventually the QRH.  We leveled at 10000'; took the O2 masks off and I established better communications with the FAs; restating the situation and asking if they passenger O2 masks had dropped; they had not. 	Level at 10000' at 250 kts and with the masks off and the QRH completed to the deferred items;  the CA spoke with the passengers about the situation and we discussed options between ourselves and with dispatch; eventually concluding to divert to ZZZ. ATC had already asked for souls and fuel onboard but we confirmed with them that we were a priority aircraft.  I then checked the LANDING DISTANCE NORMAL CONFIGURATION - FLAPS 30 (800) table in the Flight Manual (FM) for an overweight landing at 155.6lbs.  After confirming the runway length required we completed the deferred items checklists and the CA made an uneventful landing at ZZZ.  Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) was standing by and checked the aircraft out after we exited the runway with no findings.  We then taxied to gate XX. We debriefed the event as a crew thoroughly; the CA called the Chief Pilot and we put in Electronic Lob Book report for the CABIN ALTITUDE warning; and the overweight landing.   	On the descent while accomplishing the QRC was the first time that either of us noticed the pressurization switch to be in manual.  Both the CA and I remember verifying the pressurization panel was in the correct configuration during the initial flow; the preflight checklist; and the before takeoff checklist. Whether it was confirmation bias and the switch was in fact in the wrong position prior to takeoff or the switch was bumped during flight we are not entirely sure.

narrative: Contacted MIA ground for taxi. Controller advised expect Rwy 8L for takeoff and to taxi via Txy K to holding point for Rwy 8L. When tower contacted us; they directed us to cross runway 8L and hold short Rwy 8R and expedite for traffic on 5-mile final. As we crossed the hold short line for Rwy 8L; tower advised us to proceed onto hold for Rwy 8R.  I advised that we would need a few minutes to run checklists.  Tower replied with hold short Rwy 8L and the CA applied brakes; but we were past the hold short line by about 50 feet.  I advised tower and he said to then expedite and hold short Rwy 8R; traffic on 2 mile final. CA advanced throttles; but we did not clear Rwy 8L in time and traffic on final was directed to Go Around.  Holding Short of Rwy 8R we completed all the runway change items one last time and rest of departure was uneventful.Cause: Change of Runway assignment followed by expedited instructions to cross and then on to the new runway and hold before crew could run required checklists.  I also should have been more vocal about our requirements before attempting to cross Rwy 8L; but with the hold short instructions initially provided for the other side; I thought we would have time while holding short of Rwy 8R.Suggestions: When workload is high and expedited instructions are received to cross an active runway; request hold short of that runway to ensure all requirements are completed to prevent conflicts.
narrative1: Our preflight was normal.  We had the aircraft set up for a departure off of runway 08R and also had the numbers for 08L.  We blocked out early.  Upon receiving initial Taxi clearance we were told to taxi via K to runway 08L and expect 08L for departure.  We immediately reconfigured the aircraft for 08L and had the runway change checklist completed before crossing taxiway K7.  Around approximately taxiway Z the ground controller had us switch to tower and monitor.  We were approximately abeam the beginning of taxiway K1 when the tower controller said 'Aircraft X; cross runway 08L hold short runway 08R traffic five miles out I need you to expedite.' We proceeded to cross 08L and were waiting to reconfigure for 08R until we were stopped and holding short of 08R.  All numbers and  power settings were exactly the same.  We had discussed and noted this before initial taxi. We just had to select runway 08R; reenter V speeds;  and repeat the runway change checklist. As we were crossing the runway 08L hold short line the tower controller said 'Aircraft X Line up and wait runway 08R.'  We responded we'd need a minute to change the numbers and run the checklist.  The controller then said 'Aircraft X hold short  runway 08L.' We responded 'Unable we have already crossed the hold short line.'  The tower controller then said 'Then I need you to expedite crossing 08L and hold short 08R traffic two mile final.' We had stopped when he initially told us to hold short and were now trying to expedite again. At that moment I immediately observed the aircraft on final begin their go around.Cause: When receiving our initial taxi clearance the controller initially gave us 08R then said 'hold on ….'  there was about a three to five second pause then he came back and said 'Taxi via K to runway 08L.'  I believe during that pause the ground controller likely checked with the tower controller or someone else and asked if it was ok to give us 08L. We did not ask for this however I think they were just trying to be accommodating. I think there was some sort of miscommunication between ground and tower and that translated into the tower controller giving us 08R when the ground controller had given us 08L.  In the moment the tower controller got audibly agitated with us as I felt he thought we weren't prepared.  In reality we were fully prepared for either runway and were set up for the runway given.  I just should have refused to cross runway 08L at the initial instruction until we were fully set up again.  In past experience I have also had them do almost the same thing previously to me. The previous time I stopped prior to 08L; reconfigured for 08R; then they eventually came back and reassigned us back to 08L prior to takeoff.Suggestions: In hindsight when the controller initially issued a runway different than we were expecting I should have just held short of runway 08L and told him we were going to have to change numbers and run the runway change checklist there.  I was trying to make it work in the wrong place.  Going forward I that's what I will do.

narrative: After completing the training flight with the student; we were was taxiing the aircraft back to the hangar to be parked. The student was on the control taxing. There is a light pole by the fuel pumps at the flight school that we have to clear on the right side for a turn. There is usually cars parked along on the left side that we also have to clear; but due to the timing of the lesson; there were less cars. This is a tight spot the aircraft has to clear. During this time; there were conversations in the flight deck which caused a distraction to both the student and instructor resulting the right side of the wing running into the light pole.There is structural damage towards the end of the wing. Maintenance observed the damage and reported that the dented parts will need replacement. No spars were damaged but would need to inspect to see if there are internal damages along with the root of the wing as there were small wrinkles observed.The student is a current commercial applicant that is also training for their commercial multi-engine training at the same time. To prevent this; instructor should never get complacent with any student and what rating they hold. Also need to make sure to follow the taxi lines to ensure the clearance and not have expectation bias as aircraft wing spans all differ. During taxi; should always still practice sterile flight deck while engine is still on.
narrative1: After completing the training flight; the instructor and I taxied the aircraft back toward the hangar on the school parking lot; with me at the controls. The area requires careful maneuvering due to limited clearance. During taxi; both the instructor and I became distracted by another aircraft on final performing a power-off 180 approach at what appeared to be a steep angle. Weather conditions was clear; with visibility greater than 6 statute miles and wind gusts exceeding as high as13 knots from the north. Concerned that the aircraft might undershoot and was descending rapidly; our attention shifted away from taxi operations; resulting in the right wing striking a light pole near the fuel pumps on the right side; which must be cleared during the turn. The aircraft was taxiing at a minimal speed with both engines at idle power.The wing skin near the tip of the right wing was damaged. The maintenance team assessed the issue and determined that the dented sections will require replacement. While no spars appear to be affected; a more detailed inspection is necessary to check for any internal damage; particularly around the wing root; where minor wrinkling has been noticed.I am a commercial pilot candidate currently undergoing multi-engine training. As I operate multiple aircraft with varying wingspans; it is essential to strictly adhere to taxiway centerlines to maintain proper clearance and avoid assumptions driven by expectation bias. To mitigate similar situations; I should actively scan for obstacles while maintaining precise centerline tracking during the taxi. A sterile cockpit environment must also be maintained during all taxi operations while the engines are running. This experience provided a critical learning point that I will carry forward for the rest of my career.
synopsis: Tecnam P2006T flight instructor and student reported right wing striking a light pole during taxi. Maintenance assessed damage.

narrative: I was flying aircraft x from EUL for solo training under part 91. I departed EUL and flew westbound in a continuous climb to 12500 MSL approximately 15 miles south of ONO. After maneuvering at 12500; I began a descent eastbound to 08500 MSL approximately 12 miles west-northwest of EUL; where I performed several standard maneuvers. Upon termination of those maneuvers; I began a descent on a 090 heading from 07500 MSL to a planned altitude of 03400 MSL with intent to join the 45 entry to the runway 30 right-downwind at EUL. During this descent I made standard radio calls on EUL CTAF MHZ including my callsign; type; location; altitude; heading and intentions. No radio calls were received which would have indicated conflicting traffic. At an altitude of 05700 MSL; I noticed a traffic alert on my EFB. The traffic was located at my one o'clock; 300 feet low; opposite direction; climbing; at approximately 1 NM range. I immediately applied full power; initiated a climb; and briskly rolled the aircraft into a 35 degree right-hand turn. Upon taking evasive action; I visually identified the conflicting traffic. The conflicting traffic was observed visually and via ads-b in an approximately 30 degree left-hand climbing turn. Observing the conflicting traffic in a left-hand turn; I increased my angle of bank to 45 degrees in the climbing turn. After observing traffic pass below me; I continued the right-hand turn to re-join my original course. During the evasive action; I climbed to a maximum altitude of 06200 MSL. The minimum observed vertical separation from ads-b data on my EFB was 200 feet.An attempt to raise the conflicting traffic was made on CAF and UNICOM MHZ after the conflict was resolved. No response was received.At the time of the incident; my aircraft was equipped with ads-b in and out; and I was utilizing an EFB with live ads-b traffic data from the aircraft superimposed over the sectional chart. At the time of the incident I was relying on visual traffic scanning and pilot-to-pilot radio communications to avoid other traffic. I was not actively scanning my EFB for traffic. If I had used my EFB more proactively during this descent; I likely would have noticed the conflict sooner and been able to avoid the conflict without aggressive maneuvers. During this incident; the conflicting traffic utilized non-standard collision avoidance technique by initiating a left-hand turn and continuing a climb to avoid opposite direction; higher altitude traffic. Because of this; a collision hazard existed throughout the evasive maneuvers; and altitude alone prevented a collision.During this incident; I do not recall hearing radio calls which would have indicated a collision hazard from the conflicting traffic. I was also unable to raise the conflicting traffic on the EUL CTAF after the incident. This serves as a reminder to actively listen to the CTAF when operating in the vicinity of an airport; and to make standard radio calls regarding your position; altitude and intentions.The conflicting traffic is owned and operated by a flight school. This raises questions of traffic awareness and avoidance while instructing; and ensuring that a competent person is actively looking for traffic.
synopsis: GA pilot reported an NMAC while descending towards the airport pattern requiring evasive action to avoid a possible collision.

narrative: Returning to CXP after a discovery flight with multiple ac in the pattern and transiting the area north and south at CXP. we approached the field from the south to enter the 45 for runway 27. We entered the 45 with  Aircraft Y turning left downwind. we established and made frequent radio calls x 2 on the 45 at 3 miles and two miles; at left downwind midfield and abeam the numbers 27. sometime and almost 'stepping on another radio call I heard 'I'll be slow' assuming the call was associated/from Aircraft Y. not aware of what class or type Aircraft Y is; I interpreted ' I'll be slow' as I need to slow ourselves down or create space. I radioed that I would extend our down wind; I slowed ac further by lowering more flaps than normal and waited for Aircraft Y to pass my left wing (they were on final) and waited another 3-5 seconds to turn base. as I turned left base I also was slightly high. I then turned final to see comfortable spacing between our ac and Aircraft Y. We were about 0.5 to 1 mile from the numbers; Aircraft Y appeared almost halfway down the runway.  I was a bit high and utilized a slip to establish on glideslope; as soon as I saw pink(red) over white I removed the slip; maintained a stabilized approach.  with good spacing I felt we could continue to landing. Aircraft Y appeared to be at least if not more than half way down the runway and landed with what appeared slow to no movement. less than 5-10 seconds the spacing became uncomfortable and a go around was performed. full power with carb heat off nose pitched for increasing as. The ac didn't feel as thought it was increasing speed or climbing as it normally does; I performed a flow check and found the flaps still full. The flap setting was set to 10 degrees and the as and eventually the altitude increase. As the we climbed out two radio transmissions announced concern for the proximity of my ac. we performed the go-around in the pattern and landed without further events. I did attempt to find the Aircraft Y pilot  for  purposes of a debrief without success. I believe was ignorant to the type of Aircraft Y and how slow it really can be; and its normal taxi operation. I could have asked but the radio traffic was heavy enough I felt pressured to be short and succinct. I also believed I had enough spacing initially. I could have given more spacing than I thought I needed or performed a go around immediately. I felt I hesitated on my decision due to perceived spacing; the extended time needing to enter the traffic pattern. Possibly 'get there itis' was a factor due to another reservation behind ours; and we were running late due to the heavy traffic and maneuvering required. narrative: On descent into IXD we were given the option by ATC  to fly the ILS 36 approach or fly a visual approach. We had briefed the ILS prior; but having the field insight I elected for the visual. We were cleared for the visual and told to contact tower. We switched frequency and cleared to land. I glanced at the approach plate and saw the glide slope intercept at 1580. Being visual I asked for 1500 in the ALT select. I began my a gradual descent and adjusted my heading to intercept final. As we leveled at 1500 I noticed that we appeared much lower than anticipated and further away than I initially believed. I elected to stay at 1500 and intercept the glide slope as we got closer in.As we were looking outside at the field as we got closer; the terrain actually was beginning rise; triggering the aircraft to alert Landing gear; Landing gear. I asked for the gear. The gear was selected and I began requesting flaps. Flaps 1 and 2 were selected as we began to configure to land. As we were configuring I looked down at the PFD (Primary Flight Display) just in time to see the terrain turn yellow and get a terrain proximity alert then a pull up command.Cause: After shutdown; we debriefed the incident. After reviewing the approach plate I saw I had mistakenly seen and requested the altitude at ZIXAT not the altitude at the FAF SKINI. Complacency stemming from a nice early morning flying into a scenic area. Not reacting to multiple clues of rising terrain. No additional advisories from approach or tower to check altitude. Not excusing my mistakes or complacency; but may have triggered us to take action sooner.I pitched up adding power to climb. I leveled off still at roughly 2000 were I waited to intercept the glideslope before continuing descent on the approach. Once on the glideslope I continued the approach to land.Suggestions: Moving forward if an approach has been programmed and briefed; given the option to fly the approach or take a visual I will elect to continue on the approach as the difference would have been a few additional vectors to final. With regard to visual approaches I will continue to back them up with vertical guidance when available and be more cognizant of both information available to me on approach plates; airport information; and visual cues.

narrative: During takeoff from ZZZ in VMC conditions and LNAV deselected due to vectors from ATC; the CA nav display and Flight Director (FD) lost heading guidance. I (CA) was flying. Following completion of the After Takeoff checklist and once at a safe altitude; it was determined that the FO had full FD and NAV guidance; so controls were transferred and COMMAND B selected while I referred to the QRH. There were no FAULT indications on the overhead; and no procedures in the QRH to address the loss of heading guidance. No Circuit breakers were tripped. I assumed control of the aircraft to allow the FO to search the QRH for an applicable procedure with the same negative result.I transferred control back to the FO; did a thorough scan of the overhead and discovered that that the Inertial Reference System (IRS) 1 selector switch was in ATT vice NAV. With concurrence from FO; decided to switch the IRS to NAV mode; which led to a complete loss of navigation data on both sides and autopilot disconnect. We had attitude guidance and altitude guidance from the FD; but were down to magnetic compass for heading. Notified ATC; and let them know we were trouble shooting the issue. There were no procedures in the QRH or AOM to restore the NAV. We coordinated through Dispatch with Maintenance Control (Crew Phone was down due to loss of WiFi); but Maintenance Control only asked if there were and circuit breakers tripped and had no alternative solutions. We decided that proceeding to our destination without navigation was a poor choice so requested priority handling and diverted to ZZZ1; which was reporting VMC. With vectors from ATC; we hand flew the aircraft to an ILS/visual intercept where we regained FD guidance for the approach using raw data and landed without incident.Cause: The major factors that we identified as a crew that led to this were the inadvertent selection of ATT during preflight by the FO; not catching the lack of Flight Mode Annunciator 'HDG SEL' annunciation; lack of FD guidance at TOGA during the takeoff roll and selection of NAV inflight after the original issue was identified. There is a procedure in the AOM for inadvertent selection of ATT during pre-flight on the ground; but nothing for discovering the condition once airborne. In retrospect; without guidance we should have left the switch in the ATT position with the good data on the FO side; but it would be helpful if there were procedural guidance for this condition inflight.

There were no fault indications; no procedure addressing loss of heading guidance. No circuit breakers tripped. CA took aircraft back to be PF; and I also verified QRH for appropriate procedure. I agreed with CA not seeing an applicable procedure.CA transferred aircraft back to Fo to be PF again. CA did a review of overhead panel Inertial Reference System (IRS) 1 was on ATT not NAV. The final approach fix altitude was 1600 feet; and the first officer selected 1600 as the next altitude while arming the ILS XXR approach. However; when the autopilot captured the ILS signal; it turned away from the runway and paralleled the course instead. It was then that I realized that the ILS signal must have still been set to runway XYL. The ILS frequency for both XXR and XYL were the same; and I had not seen the IDENT displayed on the Primary Flight Display (PFD). The other issue was that the PAPI for that runway was out of service; so it was difficult to determine our glide path. The first officer disconnected the autopilot and tried to return the aircraft to the centerline while I disengaged the flight directors. While I was trying to find an RNAV approach to quickly load into the FMS; ATC alerted us to our low altitude; and I saw we were at 1000 feet and still outside the final approach fix. We attempted to regain altitude to salvage the approach; but ATC offered to vector us back for another approach; and we agreed. At this point; we had already been configuring for landing; and we had the gear down and the flaps were at config 3. As we continued to climb; we were slow to reconfigure; and the aircraft was still at approach speed (160-170 knots) when I instructed the first officer to select TOGA; and we were finally able to climb to 2000 feet and reconfigure the aircraft. On the next approach; I noted the correct IDENT on the PDF for runway XXR; and we were able to successfully land. In hindsight; I should have known something was wrong with the ILS signal when I did not see the IDENT displayed. I also should have been monitoring the approach better and corrected the altitude deviation sooner; or at least commanded a full go-around once ATC alerted us.Cause: It has been many years since I've seen a situation where the ILS frequency is the same for both runways. To our surprise they continued taxing out toward the runway and we called them on ground to inform them that they had hit us.  They said they didn't realize they had hit us; and we asked if they saw us motioning them to stop.  They said that they saw us motioning but their marshaler signaled them to go.  They aborted their taxi and returned to the ramp.We shut down our aircraft and tended to our passengers.  No one was injured.Suggestions: Suggest that the FBO use wider spacing with no overlap when positioning aircraft.  It is already a tight ramp with a high incidence of collisions.  Crew of Aircraft Y should use wing walkers when necessary and confirm wingtip clearance before moving. narrative1: Arriving at FBO X; we were tugged and placed in front of Aircraft Y. Loaded pax (Passengers); briefed and started engines. We gathered our taxi clearance; upon checking left and right; copilot brought Aircraft Y to my attention. From the cockpit it did appear fairly close and at an odd angle; nose pointing slightly towards us; more so than it did on my walk around; where I felt we should clear easily since they were parked behind us. We were discussing how to taxi; either immediately tillering to the left and slowly advancing or calling for extra wing walkers. During this brief discussion; Aircraft Y started moving and attempted to swing hard to their right to try and squeeze out from behind us. Copilot and I were shocked watching them attempt this though recovered and both threw our arms up in an X; universal sign to stop. The crew did stop momentarily; though continued to taxi while we continued to hold our arms in an X in an attempt to stop them. As their wing slid underneath ours; it lifted our wing slightly and dropped it back down as their wing slid clear. The owners saw the event unfold and were as shocked as we were; Person A (one of our passengers) called out the tail number to me as he had a clear view. I hailed Aircraft Y over ground frequency and told them not to take off; that they just struck our wing. They acted surprised. I asked them if they saw my partner and I yelling stop and folding our arms in an X; they replied that they did see us but that the marshaler waved them on so they continued. I believe I responded with 'ok' at that point; I was pretty stunned. I cut the engines; and went back to check on the owners and ensure them a recovery would be in the mix soon. Afterwards; met with authorities; gave a succinct written statement; a verbal statement to the police and met with the FAA shortly. After coordinating with the Chief Pilot and maintenance; applied the AOG and buttoned the jet down.Suggestions: One thing that struck out was the police telling us this happens far too often at TEB. I was unaware of that; at FBO Y south ground ops does a far better job of parking aircraft. FBO X should utilize more marshalers and should use wider spacing when parking aircraft. I can't speak for the crew of Aircraft Y but I would hope they are receiving additional training on spatial awareness and aeronautical decision making; this incident could have been avoided if they slowed their pace.

He found the speed and verbalized it. At that moment; we received a caution obstacle alert. I scanned the Primary Flight Display (PFD); and we were at 1080 MSL crossing ZZZZZ2. The crossing restriction was 1500. At the same time; tower called with a 'Low altitude alert; please check altimeter 29.76'. I responded '29.76; Aircraft X'. narrative1: As pilot flying we were landing GPS XX in ZZZ. When clear for the approach; I armed NAV and set Decision Descent Altitude (DDA) and started down to intercept the snow flake. One that was done I glanced outside and we looked low. At this point we were around ZZZZZ on the approach. I looked down and saw we were on the glide path. I decided to pull off the autopilot and level and further analyze what happened and get back on the visual glide path as I already had the runway in sight and was in VMC. As I pulled off the autopilot I ran the altitude we were at vs required altitude for the next fix and we were below it. As this happened all at once we for a too low Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System (EGPWS) alert and ATC alerted of a low altitude alert and said check altitude. I also noticed the snowflake shot up and showed the glide path was above us and showed us low. I correct and flew the rest of the approach visually and off the PAPIs. The rest of the approach was uneventful.

narrative: I was flying Aircraft X on an IFR flight plan from ZZZ to IWS. My initial clearance was radar vectors/as filed (which was direct from ZZZ to IWS); and shortly after takeoff was cleared direct to West Houston Airport and climbed to my filed altitude of 9000 ft.; which was above the clouds. The ceilings were around 4000 - 5000 ft. for the entire flight; although the visibility was somewhat poor at IWS but still above 3 miles according to the unofficial AWOS that the airport has. The direct route from ZZZ to IWS puts traffic almost directly above 89TA. I used to tow and occasionally fly gliders; so I was familiar with their operations and local frequencies. On this particular day; IAH was landing east and therefore traffic had to be lower than the jets on the east finals. I was given a descent to lower altitudes and I had been hand flying these descents; but my ATP rated passenger (although not familiar with the Century 4 autopilot) stated the autopilot could do the descents. For some reason it kept keeping us around a 300 - 400 fpm descent rate. After struggling with the autopilot for the descents; ATC advised for us to pick up the rate of descent. We then tried to get the autopilot to expedite the descent; at which time I decided to hand fly the descent as I had almost every time flying this plane in the past. As we started coming down; ATC advised multiple targets (possibly gliders) in the area. I then switched to the local Soaring frequency; 123.3; on the secondary radio and made traffic reports for us. At around 4500 ft.; we went VMC through the clouds and immediately in front of us was a glider without ADS-B/transponder as it would normally show up on the display. I took evasive action by leveling off with a turn to the east; knowing that it was likely there were more gliders just below the clouds (likely the legal 500 ft. below; but still in the 3500 - 4000 ft. range). ATC then started getting on us about how we needed to descend. I told them I was leveling off due to glider traffic; and they started giving us vectors to the east and north to take us away from IAH finals while pushing us to descend. It was difficult to comply with the clearances while also trying to maintain visual contact with the gliders. Eventually we descended away from the glider field then landed safely at IWS.I believe the issue is that the glider field is right in the way of descending IFR traffic to IWS and SGR. I looked at procedures in the Houston area and the only arrival available to IWS/SGR is the SNDAY1 arrival that keeps traffic 15 NM west of the 89TA Soaring operation. Flying IFR traffic between 2000 - 4000 ft. within a 3 NM radius of 89TA is not safe due to the gliders being towed anywhere up to 4000 ft. in that area. I would therefore highly recommend not flying IFR traffic over the top of 89TA with altitudes below 5000 ft. on Saturdays and Sundays during daylight hours. I am filing this report for the information of ATC and also in the event that I did not comply with a clearance in the interest of flight safety.
synopsis: General aviation pilot reported having to avoid gliders in the area and stated that glider activities near 89TA conflict with IFR traffic descending to IWS and SGR.

The captains airspeed was again the lower airspeed indicator. narrative1: We pushed back and started normally. After engines were started; checklists complete; and aircraft began to move;  we received a EICAS message HEAT P/S CAPT .  Did the non normal; then called Dispatch and Maintenance Control; the conversation resulted in a Back to Base.Once in the blocks; maintenance ran tests and determined it was the Captains pitot static probe had failed. The deferral was under 30-XX-X-X; in addition to 35-XX-X-X-X.We blocked out again; this time the captain briefed we would watch closely for any anomalies.  On takeoff roll thrust was set. The Relief Pilot mentioned that the captains airspeed was not responding to the movement. As I looked over the captains airspeed jumped up to about 40 kts. At 80 kts the Captains airspeed was trailing the FO and Stby by about 20 knots. The captain said lets see what it looks like at 100 kts. I agreed .  At 100 kts the airspeed on Captain side was within 2-3 kts of FO and STBY.  The Captain elected to continue.In climb and cruise the Captains airspeed was within 1-2 kts.On arrival into ZZZ1 the speed was within 2 kts until touchdown. The captain decided to write up the deviant airspeed indicator.Unfortunately we could only put pieces together once airborne. Looking back; we all recalled that the Left Pitot tube was being unsealed and removed as we were leaving to go to the break room.  Somewhere in a that hour they decided to just defer the Aircraft.  So what happened to the work that was done?  The same part was put back on the plane; was it pressure tested?  It is my belief that had they not touched the airplane; and just deferred it; that the airspeed would have been fine.

We agreed to that plan but once we had pushed back from the gate the smell was still present so we returned to the gate. As far as symptoms go; I had a headache pretty much as soon as I stepped on the aircraft. After taxing out the FO and I both had a strange sensation of a metallic taste which later the #1 FA also commented she had. Upon return to the gate the #1 FA also said she felt slightly nauseous.
