I called the emergency line first who then directed me to call a medical advisory service. The medical advisory service asked about my symptoms during the event and that of the crew members which I explained in detail. Then the medical advisory service asked if any of us were still experiencing symptoms which none of us were. Then the medical advisory service said that in their professional opinion since no one was still having symptoms they would like to medically clear us to fly and continue on the sequence. I explained that we would still be seeking medical care. It took about 20 min with each crew member answering questions before they directed us to go to the Hospital. I was removed from the rest of the sequence and deadheaded home although my schedule does not reflect that at all. It simply shows me ending in ZZZ with no way home. I was told by my chief pilot that it was as if I were removed due to a family emergency. I explained that my schedule was altered due to a company failure to maintain its aircraft; not because I called in sick or with a family emergency. However; due to the lack of contractual language I learned I will not be getting paid for the extra day of the trip. This is a known problem with airbus and the mechanic should have recognized it and backed me up in writing it up. In the future I will immediately deboard if I smell anything even slightly abnormal.

narrative: Aircraft X was delivered to the FBO for annual inspection. After initial completion of the annual inspection; a pre-return to service run-up about a month later revealed a fuel leak on the right engine. Both engines' throttle controls and fuel assemblies; because they were the same vintage; were removed and sent to Company X for overhaul. Both throttle controls and fuel assemblies were overhauled and reinstalled; and the aircraft was returned to service on Day 0. I arrived at ZZZ to pick up Aircraft X on Day 8. After an extended pre-flight; I executed a runup to the tarmac. All engine indications were normal; oil pressures; oil temperatures; cylinder-head temperatures (CHT); fuel flows and exhaust gas temperatures (EGT). The runup was as usual with appropriate indications of oil-pressure and RPM drops as the propellers were exercised. I requested a taxi for full-length of the Runway XX; but changed to an intersection take-off at Taxiway 1. Take-off procedures were normal; i.e.; brakes held until released and engines' indications in the green. Take off roll was normal with full RPM's; manifold pressures; and fuel flows. I extended my upwind flight along the runway center to 500' AGL; then entered a turn crosswind. That is a point at which I normally start another check of the engine instruments; starting with the EGT on the far right of the panel and working left across the RPM; throttle; and mixture in the middle of the panel; then to the lower left for the triple gauges and oil pressures; oil temperatures; and cylinder head temperatures; briefly before a normal RPM reduction to 2500 RPM at traffic pattern altitude or about 1000' AGL. That check showed the left engine EGT spiking to maximum temperature. I called ZZZ Tower for a return to the runway stating I had an instrument problem. The crosswind turn required additional right rudder to correct a slight roll; which keyed me to check the other indications for the left engine. They showed low RPM; low MP (Manifold Pressure); and zero fuel flow. I then automatically pushed all engine controls forward; which they mostly were anyway at that stage of flight. Because of the aircraft's known single-engine climb capability at ZZZ's elevation; I was able to obtain 800' AGL to 1000' AGL on downwind. After executing the emergency checklist; I adjusted the downwind-to base and base-to-dual turns to accommodate the critical engine out; extended the landing gear and flaps and landed on Runway XX; rolling out to Taxiway 1 and eventually taxiing to Taxiway 2 to exit the runway. The aircraft is undamaged and no one sustained an injury. Another aircraft on Taxiway 2 reversed and exited the taxiway as ZZZ personnel and the fire truck arrived. After shutting down both engines and securing the aircraft; I was handed paperwork by the ZZZ airport personnel; which I filled out. The maintenance shop was notified and came out to tow the aircraft back to the shop. Post event; the maintenance shop found a loose connection on a left engine fuel system hose which may have admitted air enough to disrupt normal mixture control. Further; after the event and after additional runups; the left engine boost pump was found to exhibit low pressure and is being replaced. Currently the aircraft is still in the shop awaiting the new left engine boost pump. An additional flight test upon return to service is anticipated. On the human performance considerations; a positive factor is my more than 1000 hours in this aircraft and regular participation in type; make and model specific re-currency training programs. These programs over the years made my responses to this event practically automatic.

narrative: Climbing through about 34;500 MSL; we felt a sudden jolt and then pretty severe airframe vibration. We initially thought it may have been a flight control issue. Engine instruments were normal until we scanned down to the Vibration (VIB) gauge and noted it was pegged at 5.0. There was definitely a startle factor to the whole thing but upon noting the VIB; we both said we needed to reduce thrust on the left side. I started pulling the power back slowly but the VIB stayed high until I got all the way to idle. Then it settled around 1.8. We noted an odor but it fairly quickly dissipated. I asked the captain to ask for a lower altitude and he found the engine out page in the FMS to get our driftdown speed and altitude. Once we had it I set that in the Mode Control Panel and set max continuous thrust on the right engine. I think at this point I had the autopilot off because it had gone into Control Wheel Steering (CWS) at some point so I just took over until I could get it set back up. We decided to go back to ZZZZ1 so we coordinated that with ATC. We elected to go there because the captain and I both fly in there a lot so we are very familiar; and because we have Air Carrier X ops there. The right engine had all normal indications. We briefly discussed ZZZZ which was almost directly under us; but felt more comfortable going back to ZZZ1. That would also give us more time to run checklists and get set up without rushing through things. Around this time I took over the radios and the captain got into the QRH for engine vibration. I believe he sent a quick message to dispatch that we were turning back to ZZZZ1 and had also answered a call from the FAs. I got us all set up for our approach and landing in ZZZZ1; and after running the VIB checklist we decided to request priority handling so we would have Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) standing by. We discussed brake temps and our planned overweight landing and that we were unsure what was going on with the engine or how much damage it had. At this time we also decided to put on our oxygen masks for the remainder of the flight. I think this was after speaking with the FAs and asking if there was any odor in the back and they said there was a little bit. The initial odor we smelled up front lasted for less than a minute and then we were kind of distracted by the immediate issue of the vibrations and possible damage. Then the smell dissipated. But since the FAs said there was an odor and to play it safe; we donned our masks and established communications; and the captain ran the one engine approach and landing QRH. We never shut down the left motor as the vibration stayed below 2.0 at idle. He asked if I was comfortable landing it and I said I was as long as he would back me up with any info from the Head-up Display (HUD) as far as trends. We discussed the high ref speed due to flaps 15 at just above max landing weight. We completed that checklist and flew the RNP XX. Landed without incident just a few knots above ref; rolled down to the end of the runway and had ARFF check our engine and brake temps before taxiing back to a hard stand. After shutdown; mechanics came up to the flight deck and said there was severe fan blade damage. It appeared that a piece of the spinner hub broke off and was ingested by the engine. It damaged about 5 fan blades and took a quarter sized chunk out of the trailing edge of at least one of them. To prevent in future: Maybe mechanics should be checking for metal fatigue in these older 737-800s. I know we also have engines that run at a high VIB level but below 4.0 and we're requested to let maintenance know about that but just continue operations. Sometimes it's audibly noticeable like your old prop sync is out of whack and I've even had flight attendants call saying it sounds abnormally loud in back. I guess in hindsight we sort of treated this like 'engine severe damage' initially and ran the memory items for that rather than getting the QRH out for high vibration first. Maybe this was the right call and we saved the engine from shredding itself by leaving it at high RPM for too long. I don't think we ever attempted to increase the power on it again after going to idle. The sudden jolt we felt seemed to indicate that something had broken internally and I know we briefly discussed that out loud. We probably should have donned our oxygen masks right away and in the future I would do that as soon as an odor is noted. If it had not almost immediately dissipated I'm sure we would have donned them sooner and I realize that we should have because a fume could've still been lingering in the air. Other things we could have done better - probably should've started the APU in flight and had it ready to use in case the left motor fully seized at some point.

narrative: Flight event was for night currency at SRQ.  I needed three takeoffs and landings by myself; before I could legally complete a later flight event with a crewmember to reestablish Night Vision Goggles (NVG) currency. Knowing runway 4/22 is difficult to see/use at night; when I called ATC (all positions combined on tower) for clearance; I requested runway 32 for closed traffic with full stop/taxi backs.  I was immediately asked by the controller if I could use the short runway instead.  Since I didn't hear anybody else using 4/22; I reluctantly accepted.  They also confirmed the type of aircraft I was.  Clearance was given with a reduced pattern altitude at or below 1;100'.  Taxi and runups were uneventful; however; traffic at the airport started to increase with a small surge of arriving practice approaches/night currency aircraft and airliners on runway 32.Upon being cleared for takeoff I was told to enter left closed traffic.  I thought this was odd because I would be operating towards incoming approach aircraft.  Takeoff and initial upwind leg was uneventful.  Right as I was leveling off on upwind; before turning crosswind; the controller called and I heard the instructions of 'make sure downwind is over approach end 32 please.'  I read back 'downwind over approach end 32'.  Workload was high with level off; configuration changes; check lists; turns; etc all happening quickly at the same time.  It is also worth noting this location and flight direction is difficult at night due to facing the blackness of the intercoastal/bay and gulf.  I was relying heavily on the GPS 530 and Horizontal Situation Indicator (HSI) to make sure upwind and crosswind leg headings were correct and instruments to make sure I was level.  Upon turning crosswind; approximately 2.3 miles away from runway 32 centerline; I couldn't see the runway edge lights.  I knew the general location but couldn't identify the beginning of the runway.  The lights for the runways are pretty directional and there are numerous buildings as well as trees on the west/southwest; so visibility from that position was pretty hard from that sideways angle.  Additionally; runway 32 has a long displaced threshold and the sequenced flashing lights (rabbit) is blocked by trees just southwest of their location.  Until you get south or high enough; especially when they are on low intensity; they can be difficult to see.  I finally got sight of the rabbit off my left and started my turn downwind.  After rolling out on downwind; I could see that I was slightly south of the southernmost rabbit light.  A few seconds later; I started putting in flaps when ATC called; 'Aircraft X yeah………turn heading 090 NOW'.  This was about 2 miles from crossing the centerline of runway 32.  I thought this was odd as they were turning me head on into approaching traffic.  I quickly executed an aggressive sharp turn to the right.  The introduction of flaps; sharp turn; and not being trimmed for this new configuration/input contributed to an inadvertent balloon above assigned altitude that I corrected as fast as I could.  After reading back 090; they then angrily responds back 'I have advised you to have the uh…your downwind over the approach end -numbers- for runway 32; traffic at your 1 o'clock; two miles; is Aircraft Y descending out of 1;400'.'  I can't remember if I responded. I believe I read back simply 'looking' as I was trying to identify the correct traffic and get the airplane trimmed for level so I could safely be eyes outside.  They called back to immediately descend at or below 500 immediately now.  They then pointed me out to Aircraft Y at 1;200' and told them to maintain at or above 1;600.  I had pulled power back to idle and dropped the nose aggressively to level off at 500'.  They called they were going missed (on training instrument approach) and had traffic in sight below them.  I also called back that I had traffic in sight as well.  I do not believe the Garmin 530 had issued a TA at any point; but I was diving and eyes outside; so I can't recall if I saw or heard it.At this point it was becoming clear from their previous transmission that they and I were working on different instruction expectations/situation awareness.  I had heard approach end 32 and they had claimed to have said approach end numbers 32.  My readback also did not include it; which was not noticed or challenged.)  The controller then responded back upset 'Aircraft X; you can expect a full stop after this one'.  Trying not to be confrontational and make a bad situation worse after having gone through a roller coaster ride; I simply responded 'Sorry about that'.I was then given instructions to enter the left downwind runway 22.  At this moment I was not stabilized in the pattern (45 degrees diverging away); low at 500'; and runway 4/22 is still hard to see at night unless you are pointing at it.  On my readback; I advised them that I might need to extend out to see the runway.  Their response was 'Yep; that's okay; uh were you confused on the instructions to keep your downwind over the approach end numbers runway 32?' At this point I am behind trying to fly the plane; reenter the pattern and not start any kind of disagreement over the radio. I responded back; 'I heard approach end; but I didn't hear numbers.'  Their response was 'yeah; that wasn't approach end though.'  Again; with the high workload and not wanting to argue; I simply responded back 'Roger'.I was then cleared to land on runway 22.  On final they notified me that there was traffic on 1-mile final runway 32.  I slowed down as much as I could and asked them on short final if spacing was good.  They called for me to do a go around and to extend upwind.  They told me to make right closed traffic this time and advised of traffic that was transiting the intercoastal at 500' that I would be pointing at.  Right as I crossed behind the traffic they gave me a turn for crosswind.  To keep them happy; I proactively kept the pattern tighter than I'd like (~1.1 nm) and made an uneventful approach/landing.  Upon slowing they cleared me to exit and taxi to the ramp.  During taxi in; they didn't mention anything further about what had happened on the flight.  I didn't attempt any further flight events and called it a night.Reviewing and digesting the data on the ground; I feel I was pretty much set up for failure.  In the air and in the moment; based on the conditions previously mentioned; I was not able to identify this.  Had they had given me a distance instead on their initial instruction; I might have been able to promptly decline; negotiate; or adjust my turns accordingly (assuming reasonable request).  Looking at centerline distances from runway 4/22; their last-minute request of flying downwind over the numbers of runway 32 would have put me on a 0.46 nm downwind cross track.  I am familiar with steep turns in this aircraft so to make that work; I would have to bank on both upwind/downwind and downwind/final turns nonstop at about 50-55 degrees.  This is obviously impractical and unsafe in the pattern for a turboprop multiengine Aircraft X.  Even if they had given the approach end of runway 32; as I had heard/perceived; this was still unreasonable as it was at 0.89 nm cross track from the farthest southernmost sequencing (rabbit) light.  Looking at my actual upwind/crosswind turn; using normal 30-degree bank; I rolled wings approximately abeam of this 0.89 nm distance point.  I still needed the extra distance to regain sight of the runway and turn downwind.  The reality is even if I had kept the turn going from upwind straight to downwind; I couldn't have complied with that request.  Assuming on my turn to downwind that night that I made no correction attempts after going wings level and just paralleled runway 4/22; I would have been on a 1.6 nm downwind.Additionally; it is worth noting:Due to company pressures; I flew again the next night to finish my night currency takeoff and landing requirements.  The same controller was working all frequencies again.  Before I called for clearance; an aircraft called for pattern work for runway 22.  I then called and requested pattern work for runway 32; which was granted.  I noted the controller told the other pilot to make sure their downwind leg was 1 nm.  While I am happy they used distance this time and not a ground fix in the dark; it really stuck out to me how unrealistic their expectations were of my aircraft/performance the prior night in comparison.Night currency flight was uneventful.  Subsequent NVG currency flight was also completed without any issues.  After both flights; I reviewed the downwind data for both pilots; and our downwind legs averaged 1.3 nm - 1.8 nm cross track distance using standard turns and procedures.Moving forward on future pattern night currency flights; I will be on higher defense to prevent events like this from happening again.  Additionally; due to poor lighting and visibility I will probably never accept night pattern work on runway 22 again for safety and liability concerns.  I will only accept runway 14/32 or go to a different airport.

It can become habitual to say the callout without fully verifying all of the stabilized approach criteria.Going forward; I will focus on preventing distractions and fixation during critical phases of flight; and I will verify all of the stabilized approach criteria at the 1000 foot call. narrative: A complex go-around created by an ATC landing/take-off conflict led to an undesired aircraft state in which the PM perceived safety was in jeopardy and took control of the aircraft.The flight began eventfully with a passenger and service animal issue that caused a delayed departure. Once resolved; the taxi out through initial approach was unremarkable. The workload and complexity began during the latter stages of the arrival and clearance for the approach.The weather was approximately OVERCAST010 to FEW050 and there was a NOTAM for our landing runway (XXR) that advised 'Special Authorization Cat 1 (ILS) procedure Not Authorized; unless advised by ATC that cranes are down.' As we were cleared for the approach and above the glideslope (~2000' AGL); I directed the PM to inquire on the status of the cranes. We were informed multiple times that the 'cranes are up' and there was an unfamiliarity from ATC about this NOTAM; but eventually a declaration that 'we are authorized for the approach.' Meanwhile; I had disconnected the autopilot and autothrottle; accelerating about five knots; but intercepted the glideslope configured gear/F15; slowing from 165kts to target speed at the FAF/1500' AGL. We briefly discussed that we felt safe continuing the approach; completing the landing checklist prior to 1000' AGL and entering IMC. This phase was the first element of complexity during this approach.Upon breaking out of the weather at approximately 800' AGL; I observed an airplane on the runway and queried the PM if he saw the same thing. He confirmed there was an airplane there; followed by ATC providing instructions to it and the preceding aircraft. Next; we verified stable at 500' AGL and were discussing the probability of a go-around as the aircraft was slow to begin the takeoff roll. ATC instructed us to go around at approximately 300' AGL; but with noticeable closure on the impending lift-off of the other aircraft. I initiated the go around in accordance with the SOP; while offsetting to the right (away from the other runway) and remaining under the weather layer; keeping the departing aircraft in sight. I was unable to verify any of the PM go-around actions as I was primarily concerned about flightpath deconfliction with the other aircraft and verbally said 'what does he want us to do' as I estimated our distance to the other aircraft nearing 3000' nose-tail separation. ATC then gave us a left turn to 060 (nearly across the taking off aircraft's flight path) and climb to 3000' MSL; and after a slight delay; I complied with that instruction; beginning the climb back into IMC. This phase was the second element of complexity during this approach.As we climbed into the weather and I transitioned to instruments; I observed the aircraft passing through approximately 1200' MSL at approximately 12 degrees nose high pitch; but with an airspeed of approximately 190 KIAS and decreasing rapidly with the trend arrow approaching 160 KIAS. I immediately lowered the nose towards 5 degrees nose high as I scanned across the other side of the cockpit to analyze the poor aircraft performance. During this time; I believe I said '(check) Flaps' or possibly 'level change; set Climb Speed (CMS); Flaps 5;' but more attention was narrowly focused on determining the throttle setting/engine performance and aircraft gear/flap configuration. I continued to lower the flight path towards level flight; advanced the throttles slightly; and did observe increasing airspeed; as well as a momentary sink rate of approximately 500' FPM. There was comm from both ATC and the PM during this point that I did not fully interpret while focused on precisely controlling the flight path; while also still attempting to diagnose the performance degradation. At this point; without any Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System (EGPWS) aural warnings; the PM perceived 'red terrain' on the Navigation Display and said 'climb' and then 'I have the aircraft.' Obviously; this was also startling; but I released control of the aircraft and tried to make the mental shift to gain Situational Awareness (SA) as the new PM. I did not immediately notice any 'red terrain'; but did perceive a significant increase in pitch attitude. Still without certainty of the flap position; I begin moving the flaps to a lower setting; neither the FO nor I can definitively say who moved the flaps to 5; though we know he did press LVL Change and set CMS at some point in this immediate sequence of transitioning PF/PM roles. While still gaining SA; I observed 'yellow terrain' on our nose starting at approximately five nautical miles and made a request to ATC that 'we need a turn away.' ATC subsequently provided a frequency change; the new PF also said things during this time that I did not fully comprehend. I observed the aircraft continuing to accelerate; nearing 250 knots and I raised the flaps to UP; the 'FLAPS; FLAPS' aural warning also sounded at some point during this sequence of me functioning as the PM. The PF at some point engaged Command B and we cleared the weather back into VMC. This phase was the third element of complexity during this approach.Now on top of the weather with a stable aircraft and on a good vector and altitude; we were able to restore normal CRM; and executed the after take-off checklist. We double checked each other and the aircraft; returned to the original PF/PM roles; completed a descent check; and uneventful landing and taxi-in (though there was still concern/uncertainty regarding the NOTAMs referencing the cranes; but we had not noticed any on the previous approach).  Due to being late; we only very briefly debriefed in the airplane after completing the parking checklist and I said we would discuss prior to the next flight. The FO left the jet as I stayed to wish passengers farewell and apologize again for the inconvenience. Upon exiting; I saw the CA of the next flight on the jetbridge and we discussed the passenger service animal and NOTAM issue for several minutes. I arrived to the next aircraft and began a deliberate debrief with the FO; recognizing that we will probably be late departing. During our discussions; it became apparent to me that we may have oversped the flaps; I then left the middle of our debrief to go back to the other aircraft to inform the Captain of our suspicion; stating that it was less than 10 knots; for less than 10 seconds; at Flaps 5 or less at ~2000' MSL. I returned to satisfactorily continue our debrief; double checking on the fitness of both the FO and my own fitness for duty for the next flight. He stated that he was; I agreed with his assessment; and did not have concerns regarding my fitness. The next flight was conducted uneventfully.To recap and summarize; the slightly varied and out-of-sync SA among the PF; PM; and ATC resulted in multiple missed/delayed comm and lack of shared mental model on the flight deck (degraded CRM); ultimately producing a poorly executed go around.

narrative: Company Chart 10-7 for BCN in the Jeppesen manual is no longer correct and requires an immediate update. It should read as follows:All current 24L RNAV SIDs state; Maintain runway heading to 410... The initial turn shall begin no later than upon reaching 500." The State Rules and Procedures; 10-1 pages no longer include any of the verbiage referenced in 10-7.I would further recommend the entire section under "Turn Compliance" be deleted or completely rewritten. The current wording states we "must" violate our OpSpecs and begin the turn below 400 feet. ATC does not require this and this circumstance does not meet the other 2 exceptions to our minimum turns after takeoff (FOM).Furthermore; there's a superfluous statement: "Hand fly or autopilot engaged (minimum of 200 feet)." Is there another way to fly an airplane?As one who has regularly flown this departure; it is unnecessary to fly this departure in heading if hand flying. By leaving LNAV engaged and beginning the turn at 410 feet; LNAV magenta path will automatically update directly to the first fix on the departure. It's far simpler and less likely to be flown incorrectly. A far more useful suggestion would be to verify all speed and altitude restrictions on the SID. I have yet to load any of the SIDs at BCN that didn't require manually entering at least one speed restriction not coded in the database. In addition; at the weights we usually depart BCN some of the altitude restrictions are difficult if not impossible to make; especially at higher ambient temperatures. Under these conditions use of Noise Abatement Departure Procedures 1 (NADP1) is required. Lastly; this station frequently publishes variable wind direction in the body of the METAR; often resulting in a tailwind component that prevents us from using the shorter Runway 24L/06R. Many crew members seem unfamiliar with the calculations necessary to ensure Performance Data performance. Perhaps a training module would help?I assume the information on the page was written some time ago and never updated resulting in low altitude turns and overly complicated and unnecessary departure "technique.""

I then look at the MFD (Multi-function Flight Display) and see they are 400 feet below. Immediately we get a TCAS RA to climb. I disengage the automation; go full power and comply with the RA per the procedure in our 737 AOM. When we were clear of conflict I reengaged the automation and continued our climb to FL370. The other aircraft also got a TCAS RA to descend. Then given clear back to ZZZ [VOR].Cause: The climb to 370 was not that imperative-we could have just waited for the other aircraft to pass and climb then. Also there was a SIGMET on the weather app for MOD turbulence up to 350 shortly after Top of Climb. To get above it faster for flight attendant safety and passenger comfort I flew the climb at max rate on the VNAV page which was 256 indicated and that become .752 MACH when we started our climb to 370. Typically we fly 280-300 and then .76-78 so if the conditions allowed a faster climb perhaps I could have had more speed to bleed off to get to FL370. Also with the price of fuel I know we are really paying attention to ECON speeds and everything where our usual 300 and .78 may not be the more desirable speed anymore-but that could have given me more speed to bleed off.

narrative: While performing a normal take off for a flight to ZZZ1 oil sprayed onto my windscreen. At the time I was unsure of what the issue was so I began to prepare to land straight ahead. My passenger; another pilot; assisted me by stating that we still had good oil pressure and that perhaps we should go around and land on the same departing runway XX. I agreed; increased power to full; climbed to pattern altitude and told tower that I'd like to land XX. They asked me if I was requesting priority handling and I responded that I was; and that I had oil spray across my windscreen. I was cleared to land on XX; and I landed on XX. Other traffic on final to XX was directed to clear out of the way. I landed; exited via Taxiway 1 to the ramp and taxied back to the hangar. I was met by airport fire / rescue. Upon inspection after shutdown it was found that the oil filler cap wasn't secured or came loose during takeoff / flight. SOP procedures are currently being updated to stop the practice of taking the cap off after flight to allow the crankcase to exhaust. The positives of this practice seem to me to be far outweighed by the negatives. I also have altered my procedures to never fly an airplane that I haven't physically checked that the oil cap and any other removable caps are secure. I've also discussed with CFIs to update my abort briefing to be adjusted that I only land straight ahead or turn back to land in the event of a power plant failure. If I am able to still safely climb; I will do that and return to land on the departing runway.

She explained to us that a older male pax was on our emergency O2 since his personal O2 was depleted. With the distraction of the radio and heavy turbulence we herd that the O2 bottle has a 15 minute supply on it. With these factors in play I decided to immediately request priority handling and proceeded to ZZZ asap. We advised ATC as well as Dispatch and requested EMT personnel to meet the aircraft at the gate.ZZZ approach cleared us for a visual approach to RWXX. However; they them advised us to turn in order for them to squeeze in one aircraft ahead of us. This did not make me happy to say the least. During this approach we received a Terrain followed by Pull up GPWS which is described in my previous report. Upon landing we quickly got to the gate and the EMT came onboard to check on the PAX before the rest of the plane deplaned. I was told the PAX was ok and he was take into the terminal via wheelchair. After this event ended; I called maintenance and MEL'd the portable oxygen bottle as it was used and still indicating 1000 psi.Once we returned to ZZZ1. I had enough time to talk with our flight attendant. She described the situation and told me how the passenger had two portable oxygen (batteries) that are personal. The first tank was depleted on his previous flights and the tank used for our flight became depleted because of the turbulence and his heavy breathing during the flight. our flight attendant described the actions she took and I think she did a fantastic job in addressing the situation. She was filling out her medical form to provide us. However; the turbulence was so strong. It was not feasible to complete that task or for us to reach out to medlink. There were no medical professionals onboard the aircraft.During this flight we had previously requested priority handling. We had the field in sight and cleared for the visual to RW XX. I had selected 2100 which was the faf altituded and was pointing the plane towards the fix to land asap due to situation. ATC gave us traffic to follow and instructed us to turn right an additional 15-30 degrees. We were in a decent at 1000fpm and the 'Terrain Terrain' caution alarmed followed by a warning 'Pull Up'. We were visual with the ground so I disconnected autopilot and climbed to 3000. The alert went away. This occurred about 10 miles east of the final approach course. I then hand flew the rest of the approach and landed without any further issue.Cause: PAX O2 supply became depleted due to heavy breathing with associated turbulence. The C130 operator had not advised us of his intention to make a short approach. Due to the close proximity and high approach speed of the C130 I chose to stop and remain where we were and advise the C130 our nose was just passed the hold short line. The C130 made a radio call on the common traffic advisory frequency to say they were on left base. In the interest of safety and out of an abundance of caution; I chose to allow the C130 to execute his procedure first before taking the runway. The C130 accomplished a touch and go in front of us and then afterwards we departed without incident.Suggestions: It's incredibly important; especially in an uncontrolled airport environment to be aware of the type of aircraft sharing the airspace. This particular C130 was a firefighting tanker out doing practice maneuvers. The aircraft commander of the C130 never indicated to us the type of aircraft they were or the nature of their fighter pilot type of approach that they were planning on accomplishing. The aircraft descended very quickly from 1600 feet above the runway on a downwind in a hard left bank straight to the runway threshold. This type of approach caught us off guard as we assumed a normal approaching landing which would have given us more than enough time to depart safely without conflict. I'm thankful to the first officer for having his head on a swivel and calling out the closure rate of the surprise maneuver.

After going missed; we vectored Aircraft X and another aircraft toward Rwy XY at ZZZ. Aircraft X was then giving instructions to fly to ZZZZZ direct ZZZZZ1 direct ZZZ for the RNAV X Rwy XY. Procedurally; if you do the approach over ZZZZZ; then there is no procedure turn authorized. Well; Aircraft X did the procedure turn! And as we had another aircraft right behind him; the complexity shot through the roof. I tried to handhold my trainee because I think I have a solid amount of experience and could help him through the situation. I think I did a pretty good job. So I was speaking to my trainee during most of his transmissions. I told my trainee to cancel the back aircrafts approach clearance; maintain 130 thousand; and make him do a left 360 for spacing. As soon as my trainee gives that clearance; Tower calls us to switch the runway again! Which in turn; brings more complexity to the situation. My trainee cancels the approach clearance of Aircraft X. Once that happens; the back aircraft requests something that we dont quite hear; and thats when I step in. I tell the back aircraft that Tower just switched runways on us; and to fly back to Runway XX; and climb him to 140 thousand knowing that my next move would be to climb Aircraft X. Then Aircraft X asks if he should be on a heading. He was currently climbing through like 123 thousand; and flying through a 120 thousand MIA box; but was going to momentarily be in a 129 thousand MIA box. My Trainee told Aircraft X to fly heading 070 which I knew wouldnt be good in a moment. So I keyed up and told Aircraft X reaching 130 thousand to fly heading 270 which would get him away from the other aircraft and be good with terrain. Aircraft X never turned to the heading my trainee gave; and technically did go into the 129 MIA box at 128 thousand briefly before reaching 130 thousand and turning northwest bound. Based on indications; we anticipated progression to L HYD SYS PRESS.The leak appeared slow; and after reviewing the L HYD SYS PRESS non-normal checklist; we assessed that continuing to destination was acceptable. We contacted dispatch via SATCOM; requested Maintenance be advised; and asked for concurrence on continuing. Dispatch confirmed preference to continue to ZZZ.We advised Dispatch that we would likely request priority handling in the terminal area and anticipated the need for a tow off the runway. Requested they notify ZZZ operations.Approximately 30 minutes later (about 90 minutes from ZZZ); we received L HYD ENG PUMP. We accomplished the associated non-normal checklist and secured the engine-driven pump within approximately 90 seconds of the EICAS message.Approximately 5 minutes later; we received L HYD SYS PRESS. We accomplished the associated non-normal checklist and secured the electric pump within approximately 60 seconds.  Dispatch was updated and confirmed all parties had been notified.We requested priority handling with ZZZ Center upon check-in and were vectored toward ZZZ. We requested direct ZZZZZ (final fix on the ZZZZZ arrival) to support our configuration planning.The First Officer and I developed a configuration plan; including Flaps 1 at ZZZZZ. Subsequently; ATC issued a STAR change to ZZZZZ1 arrival; and we requested direct ZZZZZ1; which supported our plan.We were initially advised to expect the ILS XXL and completed the approach setup and briefing. Approximately 20 NM from the airport; ATC reassigned us to ILS XXR. I initially declined due to workload; but advised ATC we could accept XXR if doing otherwise would disrupt the ZZZ operation. After being cleared for the ILS XXR; we were unable to obtain a valid localizer ident or glideslope. Upon query; ATC advised the ILS was out of service and offered the RNAV approach. Due to proximity to the airport and workload; we declined the RNAV and advised we would need to execute a missed approach with the gear remaining down the rest of the flight. ATC issued a  heading and climb to 3000 ft. ZZZ Approach then offered the ILS XXL; which we accepted. The remainder of the approach was uneventful.The First Officer performed the landing. I assumed control at approximately 100 knots for rollout. Rollout was uneventful. A company tug met the aircraft and towed us clear of the runway to parking.The CRM training we received was extremely helpful to us in navigating the challenges we faced as a crew. We were task loaded with a complicated non-normal checklist. We had multiple changes by ATC  on the arrival.  Specifically; reviewing the checklist before executing it; developing a what if plan such as considering an unanticipated missed approach with the landing gear down and the flaps in the alternate configuration; and using our resources such as ATC and dispatch to obtain support in the terminal area.  The company procedures also prepared us well for this challenge.  A recent intensified focus on fuel planning led to an enhanced awareness of our fuel status; which became critical on the missed approach. We both experienced this situation in the simulator many times so we felt very well prepared for this event and felt we; as a crew; maintained good situational awareness.For an aircraft operating under distress with a complex non-normal checklist; the number of late changes (arrival and runway assignment) significantly increased our workload. narrative: At just past XA:00 on Day 0 I was returning from ZZZ to LOM and requested RNAV 6 from PHL Approach Control (123.8) for practicing my IFR flow (the field was visual). A request that was accepted by PHL Approach. I was directed to the LASBE (IAF-RNAV 6) and cleared for the approach. On turning to the final approach course; I told PHL approach that I had visual of the field. They advised me that there was no traffic observed. At this time; I canceled my IFR. I switched to CTAF and made a 9-mile final call on the CTAF; followed by a 5-mile final call; followed by a short final call. I did a quick scan of the runway on short final; and everything looked good to land.As I touched down; I see a plane on 24 at the opposite end of the runway; and that is the first time I heard him. His call was to warn me of his presence on the runway. He had just rolled on to 24 and was fortunately stationary at that end. There was no danger of any collision since I stopped within 1500 feet or so of touchdown and taxied off the runway. Once the runway was clear; the other plane departed as soon as I was off the runway. When I walked into the FBO (there is a speaker tuned to CTAF); the people there told me that they heard my 3rd call - the short final call; but not the first two (or did not pay attention). They said they never heard the other plane till he piped up to warn me of his presence when I had already touched down and I was on my landing roll. What did I learn? When I am on a short final; I am generally focused on the touch down point; typically the numbers at LOM; and once I pass the threshold and begin my level out and flare is when I raise my eyes to the end of the runway. I think that is what I did on this landing as well and by the time the presence of the plane at the other end registered with me; I was on the ground and slowing down. It was too late to go around. I should not assume that the runway is mine even if I have been making calls; scanning and hearing nothing on the radio. I should always be more watchful and continue scanning the entire runway environment; including at this late stage in my landings.

I told Aircraft X that traffic had him in sight and would maintain visual separation when Aircraft X was about 4 mile final and there was about 2 miles between him and Aircraft Y. I had heard the controller working Aircraft Y tell Aircraft Y to maintain visual separation and caution wake turbulence which is how I knew that Aircraft Y reported Aircraft X in sight.I noticed that Aircraft Y was flying a shallower downwind than was usual and was doing about 120 kt. on the downwind which is considerable faster than what similar aircraft do on the downwind. I told the controller who was working Aircraft Y to 'watch for the slop over' because of the way Aircraft Y was flying. I then observed Aircraft Y turn base wide and 'slopped over' or veer into the path of Aircraft X. I could not tell who was in front or behind from my perspective; but I then saw Aircraft X turn sharply to the right as if he was afraid that Aircraft Y was going to impact his left side. I then told the controller that Aircraft Y was too close to Aircraft X. The controller then proceeded to instruct Aircraft Y to start a climb and go around. Aircraft X then said that Aircraft Y was way too close to which I just replied 'Roger.' About 30 seconds later Aircraft X said he was executing missed approach so I issued the standard missed approach instructions which is heading 195 and climb and maintain 3000.I would strongly recommend to suspend all flight training at SNA. The runways at SNA are 500 ft. apart which is extremely close. We are depending on low time or student pilots to turn the base in such a manner as to avoid colliding with airlines and jet traffic inbound on Runway 20R. The AFD instructs pilots to do a 15-degree offset dog leg for base to final turn. That is a lot to ask a pilot who is training or who just got the license. It's a complicated maneuver to begin with but it is a vital necessity due to the proximity of the runways.I see it constantly where the pattern workers on Runway 20L will slop over and veer into the final for Runway 20R. It happens constantly and no matter how many times we tell pilots not to do it or correct the pilots; it happens on a regular basis. Luckily when there has been slop over; either nobody is on final for Runway 20R or the inbound traffic is far enough in front or behind the pattern worker to take enough corrective action. It is my own personal belief that someday a small aircraft will slop over and collide with an airliner or business jet inbound on Runway 20R. In my mind; if flight training is allowed to continue; it's not a question of 'IF' but a question of 'WHEN' a catastrophe will occur. Mixing commercial jet traffic and VFR pattern workers who are either learning or have low time at SNA is a recipe for disaster that will cost a lot of people their lives. There are a number of neighboring airports where the student pilots can go and do their flight training without putting the lives of airline passengers at risk; I believe that right to live of 200 plus passengers on an airliner supersedes the right of a student pilot to learn to fly at SNA.

Runway 20L is the primary traffic pattern / light GA runway here at SNA at 2;887x75. Aircraft Y turned final to Runway 20L off the left wing of Aircraft X; but overshot the centerline of Runway 20L; flying too-wide of a turn; and nearly cutting off Aircraft X; who had to take an evasive turning maneuver to avoid an NMAC. Aircraft X executed a go-around. John Wayne Orange County Airport (SNA) is a very busy Class C airspace air carrier airport in Southern California. The airport handles about 11.5 million passengers per year; while handling a high volume of arrivals and departures daily between XA:00 and XQ:00. The airport has two parallel runways (see above); and is situated on a 500-acre plot of land. The airport has a large terminal that has 22 regularly used airline gates. It also has a ramp just south of the terminal used for air cargo operations. The airport has 3 FBOs on the field with a very high volume of corporate and private jet traffic.Through the years; there have been several close calls between pattern working light GA aircraft and airliners. There have been many light GA airplane incidents that have been attributed to wake turbulence. In my years at SNA; I have witnessed several very close calls between airliners and small aircraft conducting flight training. As a controller; and as one who worked this high volume of traffic daily; I am baffled by the pressing need by these local flight schools to conduct flight training here at a busy air carrier facility. It is not uncommon to have 6 or 7 low time student pilots in the traffic pattern; right next to arriving and departing large and heavy aircraft. The airspace and airfield is so limited in space that it is a requirement for departing GA aircraft off Runway 20L to conduct an immediate left 15-degree offset turn to avoid "drifting" into departing jets off Runway 20R. The margin for error here at SNA is virtually none. Airline pilots and passengers should not be put in this dangerous situation day to day. It is a common occurrence here to see student pilots soloing for the first time; in close quarters with airliners.I rarely feel the need to file a report regarding anything that will hinder the flying public in any way; but I've seen enough here at SNA to prompt me to do something to look out for peoples' lives. Furthermore; to increase safety here; I recommend that Runway 20L be permanently decommissioned and recommissioned as a taxiway. Furthermore; I recommend that an EMAS be installed at the departure ends of Runway 20R and Runway 02L. I would also recommend that a displaced threshold be built at the approach end of Runway 20R in order to increase the length of takeoff rolls for larger aircraft. The current 5;700-foot runway; in my opinion; is not enough of a safety margin when the land space currently exits for a displaced threshold for departures."

narrative: On Day 0; I taxied to take off from Runway 33 LHW in Georgia. The hold short line is extremely faded; and is several hundred feet from the beginning of the runway. I overstepped it by about an airplane length. I stopped; called the Tower and apologized. The Tower cleared me for takeoff and instructed me to turn right to a heading less than one mile after Departure End of Runway (DER). I was distracted by the passing of the line; the non-standard takeoff procedure; but believed all was OK.Immediately after takeoff; when I looked at the engine parameters screen; I noticed something was unusual; but it was not immediately clear what that was - all indicators were in the green; but something seemed different than my usual picture. I was already in the air; committed to completing the takeoff; and under the instructions of very short turn clearance. I continued the climb and planned on identifying the issue and dealing with it once stabilized on the climb; after the turn; however; at that point I turned left instead of right. The Tower directed my attention to the issue but gracefully said that there was no need to correct.The irregularity turned out to be higher than normal oil temperature indication. Once that was clear; I performed a precautionary landing. It was an incorrect indication problem.Lessons and conclusion: The initial hold short line crossing was irregular and got me a bit unsettled; and worried about consequences. In conjunction with the irregular indication; I made the second mistake. The conclusion is that I must make sure that I am 100% back to myself before accepting a clearance.Another lesson is that the markings (throughout the field) in LHW are truly bad; and in my mind at an unacceptable level. Signs are unlit; pavement markings are very faded; and the location of signs is improper. I would like to suggest that placing hold-short line locations on taxi diagrams is a good idea; especially when the hold-short line is so far from the actual runway (I estimate at least 250 ft.). I think that the average pilot will look for a hold-short line much closer to the runway and when the line is so faded will easily miss it. This however clearly does not release me from missing it.

narrative: The Jeppesen 10-26 new revision for AWO 10-9 Chart" (dated Day 0 effective Day 6) now has potentially hazardous misleading information note depicted and published; reference the Runway 16/34 GRASS RUNWAY. However; note that the misleading information note may not necessarily be due to any Jeppesen error; and may instead be traced back to either misleading airport published information; or misleading FAA published source data? Nonetheless; the depiction and related note may contain potentially hazardous and misleading information. The problem: The three Runway 16/34 grass runways to the east of main Runway 16/34 referenced by Jeppesen in the note on the 10-9 diagram are actually 3 separate colinear grass runways that CANNOT be used as a single runway. It is NOT a single 3450 ft. x 145 ft. runway. Note that there are deep terrain grading depressions now located between each of the three separate runways... due to (the arguably inappropriate) surface re-grading that was conducted years ago at AWO. Those grading depressions now preclude any aircraft from rolling at high speed from one grass runway to the next. It is only possible for any aircraft to transit those depressions at very slow taxi speed; as with a glider towing behind a golf cart. Some powered aircraft; could now even risk a prop strike. Note that the original Navy design of the AWO airfield since WWII (before the arguably inappropriate grading between those grass runways) was a much safer design; and actually originally allowed for aircraft contingency use; to safely roll across the crossing taxiways; in any non-normal situation; such as an overrun or underrun. However now; any grass runway overrun or underrun between those three grass runways would likely cause a serious accident. Further; the new (inappropriately) revised geometry of the Runway 34 departure threshold taxiways now places pre-departure holding-area aircraft obstructions in the immediate pre-threshold area of the first Runway 34 grass glider runway when landing to the north; further shortening that grass runway's usable length. The usable Runway 34 grass runway available distances and locations for each of those three separate grass runways should be depicted; and published; separately and individually."
synopsis: Glider pilot reported the Jeppesen chart has misleading information regarding three grass runways located east of Runway 16/34 at AWO.

While scanning instruments and then looking at the Ipad for traffic to safely conduct the ELP the instructors eyes then transitioned to the right and at this point observed a high wing aircraft at the same altitude; going the opposite direction; within 500 ft of the instructor's aircraft. Instructor performed evasive maneuvers while the other aircraft maintained their original heading. No calls were made by the other aircraft on CTAF and the aircraft was not on ADS-B. Corrective actions would be requiring all aircraft to be on ADS-B. Most mid air collisions happen on clear days below 3000ft within 5 miles of an airport. All participating aircraft using ADS-B-out would vastly aid in collision avoidance. The only other corrective action is using the see and avoid doctrine and diligently scanning in a figure 8 pattern 60 degrees to the left and right and 10 degrees up and down of the aircraft. A lapse of the scan pattern for 10 seconds while talking to a student and glancing at an Ipad can mean the difference between a collision and an NMAC.

It was too late for an aborted takeoff as it appeared we would pass barely underneath the the C182. A rotation at that instant would have caused impact with the C182. I felt the safest option was to delay the rotation and remain on the runway for a couple of seconds as the traffic passed over us. It happened very quickly and we rotated and resumed the climb away from the runway. The remainder of the flight was normal and uneventful. The incident occurred due to lack of situational awareness resulting from a lack of radio communication. I was unaware visually of another aircraft positioned at RW XY prior to beginning the takeoff roll. This incident could have been avoided by pilots verifying correct Unicom/ CTAF frequencies in use at uncontrolled airports. narrative1: Our aircraft was departing on runway XX. I made CTAF calls taxiing out of the FBO via 1 and made a call once on runway XX ready for takeoff. No response was heard from any other aircraft in the area; including the aircraft we narrowly missed.Once landed at our destination in ZZZ1 we called airport personnel via cell phone to determine if they could hear our calls on the radio. narrative: In regards to the incident of a hard landing at ZZZ.This report is being written by the Pilot in command of Aircraft X at the time of the accident. The trip was intended to be a day trip into ZZZ; we had departed earlier that morning with a VFR request from ATC to give us vectors in route to ZZZ1. This request was canceled shortly after the plane was no longer under control of ZZZ1's Class C Airspace. The intention behind this action was simply to take a more well defined route down the coast which we would follow south to ZZZ.The exact time of the event is not clear to me; I know that when I was roughly 25 miles to the North East of the field I had received the ATIS and information 1 was in effect. It stated that the active runway was Runway XX and the winds were coming from 060 at 11kts; gusting to 18kts.Upon contact with ZZZ Tower; it was communicated the active pressure in inches of mercury and that I was to advise when I was established on a right downwind for Runway XXPrior to my advancement into the downwind the controller in the tower had called asking if I was setting myself up for a straight in approach into Runway XY; as far as I was aware I was not only far east to the runway but also east of the tower that sits on the east of the runway. The tower communicated that from their perspective; I was in position for the unactive Runway XY; however I was still at pattern altitude and at least a mile away from being lined up with the centerline for Runway XY. I continued my approach into the right downwind and advised with midfield; everything seemed in order and even still; turning to base appeared normal; it wasn't until I had turned to final that it was clear to me that I had not adequately accounted for the wind correction due primarily to the gusts at 18kts. I was blown off to the west by roughly 0.5sm - 1sm; and with the gusts now coming in on the headwind; losing attitude on final proved itself to be a challenge; to the degree where this first approach resulted in missed/go around actions being taken. ZZZ Tower at this point advised me to turn back into the right downwind for Runway XX; however it was not advised that this turn was to be made while midfield with the runway; this required a sharper turn of of the runway heading; while working against the gusting 18kt headwind. My initial plan through this missed approach was to clean up the plane's flaps and trim while maintaining the runway heading until 700ft AGL. This request from the tower; while not the primary cause of the hard landing; was in some key details a reason behind the unstable final approach that lead to the events regarded to in this report. I made the needed adjustments to clean up the plane; however I was only up to 800ft AGL throughout the pattern instead of the pattern altitude of 1000ft AGL. upon this second attempt at a right downwind I extended my downwind to allow for more room for adjustments on base and final. The turn to base was standard and by this point I had only applied 10 degrees of flaps and no trim. Upon my second attempt for a final approach I had started off with 10 degrees of flaps but soon realized that I needed to lose more altitude than anticipated. This is because I knew I was below pattern altitude so I held off on the 500ft decent following the plane being abeam the runway numbers. By my approach into final the plane was still roughly 800ft AGL; this prompted me to add in 20 degrees of flaps; however the trim stayed neutral. The plane was well pitched for 65-70kts on the decent because of the heavy use of flaps and everything was steady on the approach until around 150ft - 200ft AGL the turbulence and gusts had rapidly gotten more intense. This pushed the plane back and while I was able to maintain a steady angle of attack until around 100ft AGL; I was just barely crossing over the runway threshold when a final gust pushed the plane on an uneven angle and slowed it into a stall; the final airspeed I rememberseeing was 38kts right before the stall. This happened so close to the runway that I was unable to go around again or glide comfortably to the runway. Aircraft X impacted with the runway and rolled in the grass between the runway and taxiway 1. It stopped in the grass and the mixture was leaned to idle before pulling out the throttle and turned off all electronics to the plane. The plane was swiftly evacuated and rescue crews arrived on the scene. No damage to property or injury to any body involved was found. The only known damage to be found was a chip to the front wheel's rim which was still able to hold air and the windshield had shattered leaving only half of the glass remaining in frame.

Once below 10000 we removed masks and continued running the EICAS generated non-normal checklists (Cabin Altitude; Bleed 1; Bleed 2; Bleed 3; Bleed 4; Packs 1+2+3; Cabin alt auto; Outflow valve r/l; Suprnmry oxy on; Pack mode 2; Pack mode 1; Pack mode 3). narrative: While descending into CYYC on the EBGAL 7 arrival RWY 36R; I was PM; and the first officer was PF.  We had been held up due to traffic below us; and once cleared to descend to 9;000 feet via the arrival; the PF chose to descend in open descent mode.  We had a restriction to cross EBGAL below 14;000' and TIDUK at 9;000.  I felt that descending in managed descent would have been more appropriate; but did not articulate that notion; because the altitude of 9;000 was in the altitude preselect window; and the FMS showed that we would cross EBGAL below 14;000. We requested the RNAV Y 35R with approach control and they cleared us for it via the TIDUK transition.  At that point the PF set 5200' in the altitude preselect window; and I reminded PF to select APPR mode. When PF selected APPR I noted that column 3 on the Flight Mode Annunciator (FMA) annunciated APPR NAV in green and column 2; line 2 showed ALT FINAL in blue. What I did not notice was that we were still in Open Descent in column 2; line 1.The PF chimed sterile at 13;600; and got the exterior lights at 10;000.I was reviewing my charts when I looked up and realized that we were at about 5;800'. I immediately instructed PF to climb back to 9;000' for the crossing restriction at TIDUK; which we did make.  We were not in dangerous proximity to the ground at that time; and in fact were in VMC; but we actually were between 200-500 feet below MEA on that segment of the approach. After climbing to 9;000'; the remainder of the approach was flown correctly and we landed safely at CYYC.Cause:  I feel that while checking the FMA was appropriate; my missing the Open Descent annunciation in my scan is what allowed this event to occur.  I understand that Open Descent ignores constraints; but I did not realize that selecting APPR would not cancel the Open Descent and capture the vertical path as I anticipated it would. We should have selected managed descent before arming APPR.

narrative: I was contracted to photograph the property at Location X.The property was at the lateral border of class D airspace over ZZZ [Airport]. That border cuts through the parking lot of the property I was photographing. My research in advance had showed the area as LAANC enabled for instant approval up to 400 feet; and only part of the potential operation zone was in restricted airspace. I didn't request that authorization in advance because I was conducting four flights across a 100 mile radius that day and didn't think I could accurately predict my arrival time.This was my fourth and last property of the day for this client; most of which were smaller portions of larger building complexes. The actual amount of land owned by the client at Location X ended up being much smaller than I had anticipated; and so was my operating zone. I picked my takeoff location and pulled up the Aloft air control app; which said that LAANC was not enabled for my operation. I misunderstood this to mean that my operation was outside of the zone requiring authorization as long as I stayed below the legal ceiling of 400 ft.I took off and conducted the flight; and halfway through I received a notification from DJI that I had entered a warning zone. I used the DJI map to navigate away from that area; take a few more shots outside of it; and land a few minutes later. I checked the Aloft map again after landing and realized that there was a temporary flight restriction in place for the entire class D zone around ZZZ; and that I had entered that zone for maybe 1-3 minutes.Primary cause is Pilot Error (Hazardous attitude; inexperience and misinterpretation of maps and restrictions)-The operation zone I discovered when I arrived differed somewhat from what I had researched and planned in advance. -I was licensed several years ago; but I've only conducted about 6-10 commercial flights since then; and none in controlled airspace until Day 0. I had submitted my first LAANC request in Location Y earlier that morning. I wasn't familiar with how the map displayed temporary flight restrictions; I failed to reference the legend; and I misread the situation.-I covered multiple properties in a 100-mile radius that day; and this was the last of the day; leaving me somewhat fatigued and impulsive. I should've rescheduled the property when I realized I was confused instead of proceeding with my best; most convenient guess.Secondary cause may be LAANC software ambiguity. The language for LAANC authorization not being available vs not being required is similar with the app I was using.This was my first experience with LAANC and I have enough first-hand knowledge of the procedure now to significantly reduce my confusion in the future. I won't hesitate to reschedule in the future if I can't be sure I'm in compliance.

narrative: Flight ABC from ZZZ to ZZZZ. Flight was late off the gate because of a tire change in the hangar then cleaning and catering once it got to the gate. Pretty chaotic off the gate; so much so that someone mentioned it felt like a training exercise. There was also a delay in our final weights as we were taxiing due to an error with the initial weights we were pushed. Something to do with an electric wheelchair.Captain's leg; I was pilot monitoring. Climb and level-off were normal. Relief pilot calculated breaks and left for his rest period. Received and OK'd ETOPS WX. We had sent a message but were waiting on reply.Almost exactly two hours after takeoff at XA:38; cruising at 35;000 feet; about 110 miles almost due north of Location X; the amber R ENG OIL PRESS caution popped up and I pointed it out to the captain. Looked at oil indications and right pressure was red; showing pressure of 0. I pulled up the FM Non-normals for ENG OIL PRESS L(R). Pressure indication at or below red line limit: Go to the Engine Failure or Shutdown checklist." What!? A little bit of disbelief and surprise as I process the fact that this is an actual problem. The captain pulls up the non-normal emergency checklist on his side and verifies the issue. He directs me to request priority handling with ZZZ center and request lower altitude.I requested priority handling and get receive descent to 290. Captain then directs me to take over flying duties so he can work the checklist engine shutdown. We transfer controls and I start down in VNAV. I inform ZZZ of 170 SOB and 7+48 fuel on board while CA shuts down right engine. He then calls FA to wake relief pilot and have him report to the flight deck immediately. I am speaking with ZZZ; descending; and receiving vectors to the south while the relief pilot joins us and CA works checklist and coordinates with Dispatch and FAs. I notice the R Engine Temperature indicator in the red. I feel the yaw in the plane but; admittedly; took too long to remember that I needed to step on the left rudder pedal since the right engine had been shut down. Now in trim.A report from the cabin let us know a passenger noted flames coming from the right engine; though we had no indication of fire in the flight deck. The fire handle was decidedly pulled out of sequence from checklist but no extinguishing agent was discharged.I was working the radio and descending. I was trying to VNAV down to 290; then 200; then 6;000 feet; when I realized that was too many steps. I chose V/S out of FL200 because it was right in front of me on the panel. I realize after that I should have done FLCH; but it did what I needed done at the moment. Kind of a frenzied blur of a descent but at some point coordinated for divert to ZZZZ1; put it in the FMC as alternate; CA activated ILS approach RWY XX; coordinated with dispatch; and FAs; and Control for ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting). Through 10;000 feet I was fast but recognized it and started slowing to 250 knots while continuing down. I was aware of but not focused on my distance from the airport and knew that I was high and fast. I was coming up on 6;000 feet; but I was still at 250 knots and high. I was cleared to 3;000 feet and direct to ZZZZZ (IF) for straight in to RWY XX; and shortly thereafter cleared for approach to RWY XX. Still high and 250 kts; though. The single biggest mistake of the night was my not arming APP mode here when cleared for the approach. This led to me being below glide slope on final which was trapped at 1000 feet but could have been avoided had I armed when cleared for approach.We completed the checklist and had a quick brief. There was a question if I felt comfortable performing the landing. I was comfortable but offered if the captain wanted to take it. We stuck with SOP; and I was going to make the landing and he was going to continue monitoring the situation. Relief pilot was an invaluable extra set of eyes and mind offering timely advice and mental support. We were coming up on 3;000 feet but hadn't fully restored our PM and PF rolls. I was worried about ALT CAP at 3;000 because I misinterpreted the approach chart thinking the glideslope started at ZZZZZ. This error was not trapped and 700 was put into the altitude window because we were at ZZZZZ and cleared for the approach. Altitude should have remained at 3000 since it was a level segment until GS intercept but definitely not lower than 1900 per the approach plate. This error when unrecognized and I ended up below GS with the runway in sight. Gear went down around 3;000 feet to help slow the plane and flaps were configured as we slowed through the flap speeds. The "Glideslope" EGPWS warning went off and I shallowed my descent to catch the glideslope. At 1000 AGL it was caught that I needed to level off to intercept the glide slope. I disconnected the AP; leveled off; and armed the approach. LOC was captured right away; I stayed level and moments later intercepted the GS and then continued to follow it to the runway. I got right of course initially with A/P disconnect but worked my way back to the left for a stable approach at 500 ft and a 'buttery' landing; if not a little left of center line.Pulled off the runway; got checked out by ARFF; and coordinated a gate. All cleared and taxied in for an otherwise normal shutdown."

narrative: Scheduled flight was ZZZ1-ZZZ. The Wi-Fi was discovered to be inoperable on this flight and was not previously written up. Dispatch was notified about this and did an excellent job of keeping us informed with the changing conditions and helping build our situational awareness. Enroute to ZZZ; the flight experienced a rapid onset of moderate clear air turbulence which caused the airspeed to rapidly increase above VMO by 10-15 knots for about five seconds. The captain told the flight attendants to be seated immediately. The PF maneuvered the aircraft further away from enroute storms and the turbulence became consistent moderate. Once the turbulence died down; the captain told the flight attendants to take their jump seats; followed by a check in. There were no injuries. ZZZ was calling for thunderstorms; hail and tornadoes at the ETA. Flight held over ZZZ [VOR] at FL310 in smooth air to allow the storm to pass. After about an hour of holding; once the extreme precipitation was north and east of the field as reported by ATC and verified by the weather radar; the crew decided to begin the approach to runway XX. On the descent; at approximately 11;000 ft MSL the aircraft was struck by lightning and immediately showed an Eng 1 Reverse unlocked ECAM message. The approach was aborted; the PF leveled off at 10;000 and made a right turn direct to ZZZ2. Priority handling was requested and the ECAM was actioned; resulting in bringing the eng 1 thrust lever to idle; where it remained for the rest of the flight. There was no buffeting so the engine was not shut down but it was treated as a single engine approach. The captain accomplished the brief with the flight attendants. The crew received vectors for the ILS XYL at ZZZ2. On approach; with flaps one selected; a momentary overspeed occurred due to gusty wind conditions. The overspeed lasted less than five seconds and exceeded VFE by approximately five kts. Emergency equipment was standing by. A normal landing was accomplished followed by an uneventful taxi to the gate. Postflight inspection revealed lightning strike damage to the left engine nacelle; right inboard trailing edge flap; and right sharklet and static wick.
narrative1: We departed ZZZ1 for ZZZ anticipating the need for holding due to lots of severe thunderstorms enroute and near our destination. We had no WiFi on board which limited our ability to monitor everything; but we notified dispatch of our limitation so they could help keep us informed. Our first issue occurred at 37;000 feet enroute to ZZZ. We hit instant moderate-severe clear air turbulence and our airspeed increased by 25-30 knots and we oversped the jet for about 3-5 seconds. The ecam appeared for less than 1 second. After the initial entering of the turbulence; it stabilized to continuous moderate. We coordinated with center to descend and turn away from the storms to try and improve our ride; which worked. When hitting the turbulence the captain told the flight attendants to be seated immediately. After we exited the turbulence; he had them check in and confirm there were no injuries. We relayed that to ATC and continued on to ZZZ.Getting closer it became apparent that we would be unable to continue our approach into ZZZ due to the severe storms. We coordinated for holding at ZZZ [VOR] for about an hour while we worked with dispatch and center to monitor ZZZ. The WiFi was inop on our aircraft so our situational awareness was limited on what was going on at the airfield and around it. We received reports that the conditions were improving and with dispatch made the decision to shoot the approach. We were informed that the area had light thunderstorms with light to moderate rain and up to moderate turbulence. A RJ had gone in 15-20 minutes prior and had reported lightning and moderate chop before discontinuing the approach. We checked the weather again with approach and conditions still appeared to be improving. The 319 weather radar showed only light-moderate rain around the airfield as well. We were told the airfield still had gusty winds but high ceilings and we were told to expect the visual approach to runway XX. This clearance reaffirmed our belief that conditions were improving; so we elected to continue the approach. Around 11000 feet we were struck by lightning. We instantly got an eng 1 reverser unlocked ecam. We leveled off at 10000 feet and coordinated with approach to turn away from ZZZ and head to ZZZ2. All engine conditions were normal; so we started the turn and then ran the ecam. It directed us to pull the power on 1 to idle and leave it there. We then treated it as a single engine aircraft and declared an emergency. The capt did a brief with the FAs and informed the passengers that we were diverting to ZZZ2. We set up for an extended final for the ILS to XYL and ran all Checklists. ZZZ2 also had gusty winds and light to moderate rain; and on approach we oversped the slats at flaps 1 by 2-3 knots for 2-3 seconds. Aside from that we landed normally and emergency vehicles followed us into the gate where we shut down engines and terminated the flight.
synopsis: A319 flight crew reported a lightning strike while on initial approach resulting in an Eng 1 Reverse Unlocked ECAM message. The flight diverted to an alternate airport and after landing; damage was identified to the nacelle; flap; and static wick.

narrative: While operating Flight ABCD from ZZZ1 to ZZZ on Day 0; at approximately XA:22; we were cleared direct to the Final Approach Fix (ZZZZZ) by ZZZ Tower for the visual approach and cleared to land on runway XX. Visibility at the field was reported to be 10 statute miles and weather was VMC. We verified the ILS frequency and course were tuned for Runway XX at ZZZ. With preview selected on the guidance panel; the First Officer selected Approach mode with the autopilot still coupled and while still in magenta lateral and vertical modes. Prior to the aircraft intercepting the localizer; the lateral and vertical modes both turned green and with the autopilot not yet captured on either the localizer or glideslope; autopilot performed an uncommanded descent from the assigned altitude and what appeared to be a smart turn inside the final approach course. The aircraft descended to approximately 800 feet AGL. We heard the 'one thousand' aural altitude alert; which prompted immediate disconnect of the autopilot and the First Officer climbed back to the charted altitude of the ZZZZZ (1;600'). We suspect the aircraft may have inadvertently captured a false glideslope and the combination of PREV mode active with APP armed prior to localizer/glideslope capture may have caused the autopilot to respond to spurious vertical guidance.Upon hearing the 'One Thousand' alert; the pilot flying disconnected the autopilot and initiated an immediate climb back to FAF altitude (1;600'). Shortly thereafter; Air Traffic Control issued a low altitude alert. As PM; I acknowledged and noted that we were correcting.No terrain conflict; obstacle contact or loss of separation occurred. The remainder of the approach was well within company standards and the landing was completed uneventfully.Cause: APP mode selected prior to localizer and glideslope capturePotential false glideslope signal in the vicinity of the FAFPossible smart turn intercept prior to localizer captureEmbraer 170/175 autopilot susceptibility to spurious ILS signals prior to valid course captureAutomation dependency Automation responded to vertical guidance signal before established on the published ILS pathSuggestions: Consider company training emphasis on delaying Approach mode selection until fully established on both localizer and glideslope; even when cleared direct to FAF for situational awarenessConsider training emphasis on direct-to-FAF clearances where autopilot and localizer/glideslope anomalies are most commonplaceConsider encouraging RNAV approaches whenever cleared for visual approaches to avoid mode confusion (both on the part of the aircraft automation as well as on the part of the pilot)
