narrative: We were assigned Aircraft X to fly from ZZZ. When we arrived at the aircraft l was met by the FO that had flown it in. He advised me they had received an EICAS message about the Cargo Fire Extinguishing system and that line maintenance was onboard working on the write-up they had made for the message they had received on landing. We continued to complete our preflight duties while line maintenance cleared the message and the aircraft was cleared by maintenance. We departed and all was normal operations until approximately 30 minutes into the flight at 34;000 feet when we received a EICAS message CRG AFT FIREX HI ARM" Advisory. The message was displayed for just over a minute and then extinguished. During that time we referenced the QRH for direction and it stated this was a "Crew Awareness" message. Immediately after the "CRG FIREX HI ARM" message extinguished a second advisory message briefly appeared "CRG FIREX LO ARM" and was quickly replaced by a "CRG FIREX HI DISCH" status message. The QRH states that this message means that the "Cargo high-rate discharge fire extinguisher bottle has been discharged." We did not see any other indications of a Cargo Smoke warning (lights or EICAS messages). At this point in the flight I opted to send an ACARS message to dispatch to advise maintenance control that the Cargo high-rate bottle had discharged into the cargo compartment and asked them (dispatch and maintenance) if they wanted us to return to ZZZ. Our thought being that we still had over 90 minutes remaining to fly to our destination; but we were now only approximately 30 minutes from ZZZ. I opted to establish a SELCAL phone patch with dispatch shortly after sending the ACARS message to expedite the communication that we needed to have due to the complexity of the possible decision to divert. While establishing the phone patch through Company radio we received the message "MAINTENANCE SAYS ITS CREW DIFEREABLE".Once the phone patch was established with dispatch we discussed the message we received; what I thought was now the state of the compromised cargo fire suppression system; and some possible options with our dispatcher. The dispatcher again restated that maintenance said that we could continue to our destination and defer the cargo fire suppression system there. I told our dispatcher that this would mean we probably would not be able to carry cargo out of our destination. When a Cargo bottle is used to respond to a "CARGO FWD (AFT) SMOKE" warning message and the contents are discharged the QRH states to LAND AT THE NEAREST SUITABLE AIRPORT. While we DID NOT have a CARGO SMOKE indication (Cargo Smoke push lights; or EICAS messages) our high rate bottle had been discharged and our ability to respond to any future CARGO SMOKE messages during the flight was compromised. Upon further discussion I opted to return to ZZZ to address the issue.My concerns regarding this particular in-flight event are the lack of safety minded real time decision making support from the team (dispatch and maintenance control) on the ground. A statement like "Do what your QRH directs" does not help in this situation. Especially considering the fact that the EICAS messages we were referencing in the QRH did not expressly state what to do given this particular set of circumstances. If we had opted to continue to our destination we would have flown for over 90 minutes with a compromised Cargo compartment fire suppression system to a destination that could probably not service (repair the system or replace the halon) on the aircraft while dealing with contract maintenance in a foreign country. According to the FAA; inflight lithium battery fires and smoke incidents on domestic flights now occur at a rate of roughly two incidents per week. A fact that I was made aware of while attending recurrent ground school less than a month ago. We were carrying cargo and according to the EICAS messages present we did not have a high rate bottle option available to fight a fire in either cargo compartment. Guidance to continue to a foreign country destination and overlook the possible inflight risks; as well as deferring equipment that removes or seriously impacts the ability to carry cargo is at a minimum a bad business decision; or worse; our company is left trying to explain to the families of our passengers or the FAA why we opted to continue if we had an actual cargo fire happen without the possibility to fight the fire in the remaining flight. The decision to RETURN TO ZZZ should have been made as a consensus by all parties involved. After returning and landing safely in ZZZ we were advised by line maintenance that this aircraft has a history of these types of messages occurring. A side note to this incident; after being reassigned another aircraft and completing the flight several passenger thanked us for getting them safely to their destination; despite arriving a couple of hours late."
synopsis: EMB-175 pilot reported receiving a cargo fire extinguishing system message during cruise. Flight returned to departure airport.

narrative: Upon blocking in at gate XX; I set the Parking Brake In Accordance With (IAW) SOP's and the Triple Indicator showed normal Brake and Accumulator Pressure.  I then took my feet off the toe brakes and the aircraft began to roll forward.  The FO promptly called 'We're Rolling!' just as 'Brake System Fail' and multiple other ECAM messages populated with aural alerts.  I immediately applied maximum braking to stop the aircraft and noticed that the Brake Pressure indications in the Triple Indicator were at Zero; with normal accumulator pressure.  The airplane stopped abruptly as the ground personnel ran away from it.  Thankfully; the airplane stopped prior to impacting ground equipment; the jet bridge; or personnel.  I estimate we were a MAXIMUM of 5' from impacting equipment in front of the airplane.  I held the brakes until communications were established with ground personnel; the aircraft was chocked; and the tug was connected.  At that time; both engines were shut down and the aircraft was pushed back by the tug to the appropriate parking position.  Shortly after the aircraft was pushed into the appropriate parking position and after the last engine spooled down; normal Brake Pressure indications returned to the Triple Indicator and the ECAM faults cleared.  A detailed Discrepancy was entered in the logbook software. Maintenance was called and I personally described the problem to the responding mechanic.  NOTE:  I did discuss the situation with Union Safety and the Committee volunteer who handled my call stated that this same problem had occurred with another Airbus in the previous few days.Cause: I have no idea what the causal factors were - there was clearly some issue with brake system of that particular airplane and based on my discussion with union Safety; there MAY be an issue with the fleet. Regarding mitigation; I sincerely hope Maintenance; Union Safety; Company Safety; Flight Ops; and all other relevant departments investigate this situation THOROUGHLY.  As mentioned in my narrative above; the airplane was a MAXIMUM of 5' from impacting anything from ground equipment to a jet bridge; to a person.  Had the FO not immediately noticed the unexpected forward motion of the airplane; we would be dealing with an accident; a damaged airplane; and almost certainly injured personnel / passengers.
narrative1: After normal flight at gate arrival; crew taxi'd into gate XX.  After park brake set; each pilot started their flow for shutdown when as pilot monitoring I saw ground crew scattering and noticed aircraft was still rolling forward with the brakes set.  I said we're rolling forward and called for brakes as we jumped over the chocks and were picking up speed.  CA as pilot monitoring hit the brakes bringing us to a stop.  We noted no pressure in the hydraulic gage except for the accumulator and the brake handle was still in the set position.  Then a slew of brake failure cautions presented with no audio ding.  We held the brakes until ground crew connected the tug.  Once the engines were shutdown and the last engine stopped spinning. all cautions corrected themselves and the brake system returned to normal.we were tugged bake into position at the gate.Cause: Complete brake system failure. Recommend review of aircraft data and awareness to flight crews that this can happen during shutdown.
synopsis: A321-NEO flight crew reported the aircraft rolled forward after setting the brakes at the gate because of a brake system malfunction.

narrative: Crew received taxi instructions from ramp control while positioned in the ramp area at ORD. During the initial transmission; the instructions were delivered rapidly and included multiple routing elements. The First Officer; who was relatively junior; missed portions of the readback; and the controller requested the instructions be read back again.The revised taxi instructions were understood as follow another aircraft; taxi on the east side of the Y; taxi via Taxiway SE; hold short of Taxiway A; and contact Ground Metering.While complying with the instructions; the crew encountered several aircraft positioned on Taxiway SP immediately ahead. Additionally; Aircraft Y and Aircraft Z were oriented southeast on Taxiway SP; limiting available maneuvering space and requiring the aircraft to continue further south on Taxiway SP.As the aircraft proceeded; the crew attempted to identify the hold short point for Taxiway A. However; the crew was unable to positively identify the transition point between Taxiway SE/SP and Taxiway A due to limited signage and the absence of a clearly depicted Taxiway SE on available company taxi charts.Uncertain whether the aircraft had stopped at the correct location; the crew contacted ramp control for clarification. Ramp control advised that the aircraft had proceeded too far and instructed the crew to hold position and contact Ground Metering.After contacting Ground Metering; the crew was advised they were not expected to be in that location and were instructed to contact Ground Control. The primary contributing factor was confusion regarding the taxi routing and hold short location in a congested and operationally complex ramp environment. Several factors contributed to the event:The routing issued differed significantly from normal and familiar procedures commonly used in that area in recent months. Historically; crews typically remained on either side of the Y and contacted Ground Metering prior to taxiing northwestbound on Taxiway SP while monitoring 131.3. The routing issued during this event differed substantially from that normal flow. Taxiway SE was not clearly depicted on available company airport charts available to the crew. Signage and markings in the area did not clearly identify where Taxiway SE or SP transitioned into Taxiway A.Multiple aircraft positioned in the area created congestion and reduced maneuvering clarity.Rapid communication cadence and repeated radio exchanges increased cockpit workload during a critical phase of taxi operations.Despite the confusion; the crew operated conservatively; taxied slowly; sought clarification when uncertain; and attempted to maintain clear and professional communication throughout the event.To help prevent similar events in the future; the following improvements should be considered:Improve airport signage and surface markings in the southeast ramp/SP/A taxiway transition area to better identify taxiway boundaries and hold short locations.Ensure all active taxiways and routing terminology used operationally are accurately depicted on company airport charts and electronic flight deck references.Promote standardized taxi routing practices whenever possible to reduce confusion caused by frequent procedural changes.Encourage clear; concise; and measured communication between controllers and flight crews; particularly during periods of high workload and congestion.Consider additional coordination between ramp control; Ground Metering; and ATC to ensure consistent expectations regarding aircraft positioning and routing in this area.The crew believes the event resulted primarily from unfamiliar routing; unclear taxiway identification; and a congested operating environment rather than any intentional noncompliance with ATC instructions.

narrative: While enroute; we had a system 3 hydraulic malfunction that required us to land at the nearest suitable airport. We found a spot on the ramp after exiting the runway. We contacted operations to send a tow team to tow us to the gate. In anticipation of the tow team's arrival; we shut down both engines. After waiting about 20 minutes for the tow team; suddenly the aircraft started to roll forward and then stopped. narrative1: During taxi in to gate XX in ZZZ; a miscommunication occurred and the aircraft moved without concurrence or expectation from the ground crew. This was briefed prior to arrival and we discussed possibly needing a tow into the gate if the turn couldn't be successfully accomplished at idle thrust.  It could not in our case; and we stopped about 50 feet short of the stop bar. The tow  in procedure was initialized by us and the ground crew and we shut down the engines. The incident occurred during the hook up of the tug unit. The tug and ground crew approached the aircraft; and being under the aircraft only briefly; the captain said out loud; ok brakes released" and the captain did so; to which I was alerted as being too soon in the normal sequence. I looked up and around the aircraft and saw the aircraft quickly yawing to the left and said; "whoa; no no no"; and began to depress the brake pedals from my side as I was trying to confirm my belief that this was premature. The captain stated; "I have the brakes released hand signals! They're towing us!" And I responded; "no; no you don't!"; the captain joined me on the brakes and I saw multiple ground crew from my window with the now-visible tug giving us the 'stop' signal; and relayed what I saw to the captain. We realized the aircraft had swung nose-left uncommanded/unintended and put the ground crew at very high risk.  The distance the nosewheel rolled I estimate to be about 10-15 feet.  The ground crew plugged in their headset and they confirmed brakes were set; and the captain asked if everyone was safe and ok; which the ground crew confirmed.  We froze the scene; discussed what happened; and ensured and agreed we could safely continue.  We; the flight crew; realized the ground crew already had the nosewheel bypass pin installed when the aircraft rolled; and the reason the aircraft yawed was the nosewheel free castering under the weight of the unbraked aircraft. This was accomplished safely and the aircraft was pulled into the gate and proceeded normally after that.  We debriefed the event very thoroughly between ourselves and with the ground crew. narrative: The flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 started off uneventful. Everything was going smoothly and as expected. During our climb to FL330; at FL320 I noticed a faint amount of smoke coming from the PTT button panel. There was also a noticeable burning plastic smell. The smoke did not stick around very long and was gone in roughly 20 seconds. The burning smell did remain throughout the flight though. Captain was the pilot flying when we noticed the smoke and smell. Captain transferred controls to me and requested priority handling with ATC. It was a very small amount of smoke; but it was still smoke. So we did our smoke fire and fumes memory action items. We established communication but the Captain was slightly hard to hear with the masks on. Captain tried making another call to ATC but they could not understand anything he was saying due to the mask not being clear. We transferred controls back to him and I took over communications and checklists. I cleared up confusion with ATC that was present from Captain not being understood. We established we were a priority aircraft and would like to divert to ZZZ2. We were told to descend and we could expect vectors for the ILS XX into ZZZ2. While we started a fast descent; Captain sent a message through ACARS to dispatch that we were diverting. I got out our QRH after confirming our memory action items from the QRC. I started the Smoke Fire or Fumes QRH. While going through this checklist I did get interrupted a few times. I needed to relay to ATC our situation. I told them our fuel on board and the souls on board. I needed to make this call a couple times as they did not hear clearly the first time. Once that was clear we called back to the flight attendant that we were diverting and seeing if he had any smoke in the cabin. He could not understand the Captain and after a couple attempts; I told him we were diverting and learned he did not have any smoke in the back. While this conversation was happening ATC was giving us instructions to swap frequencies and to keep descending. I believe we got swapped to approach at roughly 14;000 MSL. Approach gave us a heading to fly as well for the ILS XX. While we were descending; and I was handling communications; the Captain got the approach loaded and frequencies set up. Communications were set up and the approach was loaded. I continued the QRH and got to the point of executing an emergency descent; at this point Captain said to pause that checklist as we needed to focus on preparing for landing. We were also at roughly 10;000 MSL so we did not need any more of an emergency descent as we had acted quickly about getting lower. On our descent I called the FA for a briefing. I told him there was smoke and we are landing in ZZZ2. I told him he had roughly 5 minutes or less until landing. No special instructions as we should be going to the gate as normal. No bracing signal. I had him report that back and he did so perfectly. Continued our descent; we broke out of IMC at roughly 8;000 MSL if I recall correctly; after having being in IMC up until this point through the issue. Captain gave a briefing on the approach. Afterward; I ran the Cruise; Descent; and Approach checklists. Both of us verifying items were complete and accurate. After running the approach checklists; I checked our weight and told the Captain we would be over max landing weight. We got swapped to tower and continued our approach. I ran the overweight landing checklist and we utilized the new landing distance that we were still in compliance with. We were cleared to land by tower on runway XX. With the landing; Captain came in slightly below glide slope to have some time to arrest our descent. He did so very well and we touched down very smoothly. Tower told us we could stop on taxi way 1 after exiting the runway but we elected to get to the ramp. While we taxied I gave a passenger announcement that we were in ZZZ2 due to a precautionary event and we would give them an update when we have one.I apologized about the inconvenience of the diversion and for not addressing them in the air as we were quite busy. Tower gave us instructions to cross runway XY on 2. We got to the ramp and a fire truck was parked in front of the intersection; 3; that we took. The Captain came to a stop as it seemed two firefighters were approaching us and wanted us to stop. The firefighters came up to the plane with both engines running. They did not appear to see anything abnormal as they were very calm. They wanted to communicate and gave us some hand motions to their ears. The Captain and I opened our windows and I tried shouting to them that we could still smell the burning plastic. I had the goggles and mask still on which made this hard. They handed up a note pad to the Captain and we coordinated to taxi to a gate with passing the note pad back and forth. I told the Captain that we can still smell the smoke and mentioned evacuating there. He said no; it will be much better getting passengers off at the gate and I agreed. We did not confirm with the FA that everyone was seated before we started moving again. Later; FA did tell me that everyone was seated when we started moving. We did not contact company ops in ZZZ2; which looking back could have made the ground operations a bit smoother for us. While we taxied to the gate I addressed the passengers and apologized again about the inconvenience and thanked them for their understanding. While addressing the passengers I did not use an alarmed tone or emergency terminology. We parked the plane and continued to run all of our check lists on the ground as normal. The passengers started to deplane and while everyone was exiting; they were very grateful for keeping them safe. Many expressed their thanks to our entire crew. No passengers reported any sort of illness or injuries. Firefighters came aboard and utilized their heat camera and said they did not see anything triggering it. We assumed the source of the smoke was confirmed to be out. We talked with dispatch and maintenance and got everything situated for the day. The crew took a deadhead back to ZZZ.Suggestions: I would suggest that during training there be a little more emphasis of what to do with issues when safely on the ground. Our situation was time critical but did not constitute an emergency evacuation that would have drawn much more attention to the situation. The communications on the ground were lacking as well. I had assumed tower would have gotten a spot set up for us to go to when on the ground but they seemed very laid back with the mentality that we can go wherever we want.

At this point in the approach; the PF noted that a small amount of increased right aileron input was required to maintain control. While abnormal; it was easily controllable. From this point on; both pilots focused on landing the aircraft safely. During touchdown and rollout the aircraft performed normally. Automatic spoiler deployment occurred upon touchdown and the aircraft decelerated normally on autobrakes 3. Manual braking was applied shortly after touchdown by the PF. The transfer of aircraft control to the Captain occurred at approximately 70 knots. Initially; nose wheel steering was operational and we cleared the runway on taxiway Charlie cautiously and at a slow taxi speed. Upon the completion of the turn on to taxiway Charlie; the nosewheel steering failed. Once clear of the runway the parking brake was set. At this point we determined that we had a complete loss of system A hydraulics. We informed Tower that we needed to hold position to address a hydraulic leak.  We did not declare an Emergency; as the aircraft was on the ground and under control with the parking brake set.  The Captain then directed the Loss of system A" QRH and the FO read the checklist and we accomplished the applicable items. Communication was established with the Flight Attendants by the Captain and they confirmed that the situation was normal in the cabin.  Since the checklist calls for the gear pins to be installed prior to taxi; we determined the safest course of action would be to shut down the aircraft on the taxiway; have a ramp crew come out to the aircraft; install the gear pins; and tow us to the gate.  The Captain made a PA announcement explaining the situation to the passengers and informing them that we would be towed to the gate and all was under control.  When the tow crew showed up; they plugged in to the intercom and we devised a plan to pin the gear and tow the aircraft to the gate; escorted by airport operations.  We were advised us that they did not have gear pins available.  We then briefed a plan to shut down the aircraft engines; and remain on APU power.  Once safe to approach the aircraft; we would drop the gear pins out of the flight deck window; then clear him to pin the gear.  Once the gear was pinned; we were towed to the gate by the ground crew.  Upon post-flight inspection it was noted that hydraulic fluid was leaking from the number one ground spoiler actuator on the left wing. Also; Airport Operations said that there was hydraulic fluid on the runway.Recommendations to mitigate the riskAfter debriefing as a crew we discussed some other options.  Option 1:  We could have gone around to run the checklist and to devise a plan. However; with the gear stuck down; we had a higher fuel burn rate and no alternate fuel (there is a warning in the checklist about this).  We would have had to maneuver without the use of half the flight spoilers.  We both believed that this option would have prolonged a dangerous airborne situation.  We had the proper configuration for landing; adequate brake pressure; excess runway available (8700' avail).  This option is worth discussing; but we both believed in this particular situation it was better to land.  The difference between a normal landing and a non-normal with loss of A hydraulics is only 400'.Option 2: Stop straight ahead on the runway; pin the gear; get towed to the gate.  We both agree that this may have been a better option.  However; we would have been on an active runway at night;  closing down the runway to other traffic.  That being said; it would have been the most conservative action. Option 3:  Coordinate with ATC to have ARFF available on site and follow us to the gate; since we had a hydraulic leak.  At the time; we did not consider this.  In retrospect; we believe it would have been a more conservative option. If we had accomplished the Non-Routine Landing Considerations QRH; it would have reminded us to do so."

narrative: On Flight ABCD from ZZZ to ZZZ1 on Day 0; we encountered multiple areas of turbulence along our route of flight associated with convective and ride activity depicted on our weather and Sky Path information systems. Prior to departure and throughout the flight; the First Officer and I actively monitored ride reports; weather depictions; and turbulence forecasts in order to mitigate exposure to passengers; flight attendants; and the aircraft.After departure from ZZZ on the ZZZZZX Departure; we initially experienced intermittent light to moderate turbulence during climb and cruise. Based on turbulence depictions along our route; particularly over portions of States X and Y near the ZZZ VOR area; I briefed the flight attendants in advance that we would likely require them to remain seated for an extended period in accordance with turbulence mitigation procedures.As we approached the area near ZZZ; we requested ride reports and altitude advisories from ATC in an effort to identify smoother ride conditions; however; ATC advised that aircraft in the area were reporting similar ride conditions at multiple altitudes. During this phase of flight; we encountered periods of light to moderate and occasional moderate turbulence; intermixed with smoother ride segments. Due to the continuing ride conditions and forecasted turbulence ahead; I directed the flight attendants to take their jump seats and repeatedly advised passengers to remain seated with seat belts fastened.While operating east of the river and north of the ZZZ area; both the First Officer and I began observing abnormal lateral/directional aircraft response characteristics during otherwise routine light to moderate turbulence encounters. Specifically; the aircraft began exhibiting a Dutch roll-type oscillation following even minor turbulence inputs. We noted that the oscillations appeared to amplify with time after turbulence encounters rather than dampen normally.The First Officer; who was Pilot Flying; remained prepared to assume manual control if necessary while I continued monitoring aircraft systems; ATC communications; and cabin coordination. During this time; I made additional passenger announcements emphasizing the need for all passengers to remain seated due to ongoing turbulence. Flight attendants also reported continued passenger movement in the cabin despite repeated announcements.Shortly north of ZZZ2; we again encountered light to moderate turbulence during which the aircraft's lateral oscillation increased further. The autopilot disconnected; and the First Officer smoothly assumed manual control of the aircraft while intentionally avoiding abrupt control inputs in order to minimize unnecessary aircraft motion and provide the best ride possible for the cabin. During this event; the aircraft experienced an altitude deviation of approximately 600-700 feet while in turbulence. I immediately requested and received a block altitude clearance from ATC between FL350 and FL360 to safely manage aircraft control and ride conditions. Other aircraft on frequency were simultaneously reporting similar turbulence-related issues and requesting altitude blocks in the same area.The First Officer stabilized the aircraft promptly; and we returned to our assigned altitude shortly thereafter. While monitoring aircraft systems; I observed the Yaw Damper switch in the OFF position with the associated Yaw Damper light illuminated. I checked the annunciator panel and noted no associated FLT CONT annunciation. Based on system knowledge and QRH guidance; I reengaged the Yaw Damper switch; at which time the Yaw Damper light extinguished and the aircraft's flight characteristics returned to normal. The First Officer concurrently referenced and completed the applicable QRH non-normal procedures while I monitored aircraft performance and flight path.After the aircraft returned to normal handling characteristics; I contacted the flight attendants to assess cabin conditions. The flight attendants advised that there were no injuries among passengers or crew; although several passengers in the aft cabin and one flight attendant experienced nausea associated with the lateral oscillation and ride conditions. At no point did the aircraft experience severe vertical acceleration or abrupt up-and-down movement; the primary ride issue involved lateral oscillation and rolling motion that was particularly noticeable in the aft cabin.Following coordination with ATC; stabilization of aircraft systems; and confirmation from the flight attendants that there were no injuries; we elected to continue the flight to ZZZ1. An ELB (Electronic Logbook) message was sent in flight to advise Maintenance Control of the event and to facilitate maintenance evaluation upon arrival. For passenger comfort; we subsequently reduced cruise speed to Mach .75; and ride conditions improved significantly as we progressed north of State Z. Once conditions permitted; the flight attendants resumed cabin duties; and I made a passenger announcement apologizing for the turbulence and advising passengers that multiple aircraft in the area had experienced similar ride conditions.Upon arrival in ZZZ1; we coordinated with maintenance personnel to debrief Maintenance Control regarding the event and aircraft behavior observed during the turbulence encounter.
narrative1: While cruising at flight level 360; the aircraft began to respond with rhythmic yoke movement after encountering continuous chop and turbulence events. All appropriate actions to sit the FAs and customers were completed prior to encountering this area of turbulence. Both pilots discussed concerns with the airplanes rhythmic movements. We checked for any anomalies on the annunciator panel as well as the overhead panel. As the pilot flying I chose to request a heading to disengage the LNAV function in an effort to see if this was causing the rhythmic response. As we encountered more turbulence; the movements became more abrupt at which point in time the autopilot disengaged as the aircraft entered into a progressively building dutch roll. I immediately confirmed the auto pilot was disengaged and asked the pilot monitoring to request a lower altitude as I began to turn into the tail role slightly and then maintaining a steady profile with the wings while engaging in a slight descent to counter the roll force. I then asked the pilot monitoring to slow my bugged speed to .75 from .77 which correlated initially with N1 speed recommendations for the environmental conditions. After approx 30 to 45 seconds of dampening the aircraft's movement utilizing flight controls; thrust and speed reduction the aircraft settled into a level profile. During this time we were approved off of heading and into a block between 350 and 360 feet. Once reestablished we climbed back to 36;000 feet and engaged initially the heading function followed by the LNAV function; direct to our next checkpoint and on course; then finally the autopilot flight control systems. At that time we noticed that the Yaw dampener light on the overhead was illuminated; and the magnetic switch was in the off position. Checking again the recall there was no associated flight control light or the master caution annunciator. In accordance with the QRH; we performed the action procedures listed to reengage the yaw damper. There are no further actions or anomalies for the remainder of the flight. The captain completed the appropriate write-ups while we debriefed the scenario. Of note the encounter with turbulence as well as the rhythmic rolling motion; which led to the auto pilot disengaging; and what appears to be the disconnection of the yaw damper; resulted in numerous sick passengers as well as flight attendants in the back half of the airplane. These items were also addressed in accordance with the reporting profiles outlined in the FOM by the CA.
synopsis: B737 crew reported Dutch Roll; lateral and altitude control issues during cruise in areas of turbulence. Crew observed Yaw Damper had disengaged and proceeded to destination after reengaging same.

narrative: I was completing the competition landings flight for short field landing competition.Everything seemed as normal throughout the flight. I completed my first attempt at landings as the 3rd aircraft in a heat of 4 airplanes. I had noted on my second climb out that my location with the second position aircraft had become less spaced out than on the initial lap in the pattern. To remedy this; I spaced on my upwind leg significantly so there would be no traffic conflicts on approach. I had waited until position one of the heat had made their mandatory base call to turn crosswind. From this point; I continued downwind as normal; remaining vigilant of the two aircraft ahead of me. As I was on the first quarter of the downwind leg; I heard position 2 call their base. I observed an aircraft head of me turning base to final at this time. I reduced power as normal; added flaps and turned base once I was 45 degrees off of the approach end. I cleared left and right final before commencing my turn. Upon turning final; I had the Runway XX numbers in sight and pitch for 70mph and added flaps 40. Once I had been established on final for about 20 seconds; tower called and said 'Position 2 and 3 you guys appear to be pretty close.' At this time; I looked ahead on runway XX to the aircraft taxi off the runway at 1 and beleived the controller was referring to this.Seconds after the initial call; I heard 'Position 3 go around.' I immedietly commenced the go around procedure. Tower had asked if I had the aircraft in sight to which I responded 'I have them in sight now; apologies for not seeing them sooner.' I beleived he had been referring the aircraft I had seen taxiing off the runway. I then responded 'Will this next lap count as my second attempt?' beleiving since tower called my go around I would be alloted another compeition landing attempt.After taxing back to the shutdown box; I was met by the Cheif Judge of competion who greeted me with 'Hey.' I then said; 'Hey; tower called my go around' to inform the To inform the judges to count my second attempt of landings after the go around. He then responded; 'Tower did not call your go around; the judges did. Do you have any idea why?' Confused; and with the prior aircraft taxi off the runway in mind; I responded; 'Spacing?' He then responded sharply and said; 'You came within 100 feet of another airplane.'Shocked and confused; I stood next to the aircraft and was escorted over to speak with a pilot of another aircraft with the chief judge. The pilot had informed myself and the judge that I was so close; the pilot could see me through their sky light. I spent the rest of the evening confused and shocked until I heard more perspective from eye-witnesses. From what I understand now; the pilot in position 2 had extended their downwind base and final legs significantly. In fact; so far out that they had exceeded the competition pattern limitations by nearly 2.5 times. By the time I had turned based to final; they had extended so far out and were so low that they had become completely obscured to spectators on the ground; and invisible to myself in the aircraft. Based on eyewitnesses; on final approach leg; I had become positioned over top of the position 2 aircraft within 50 feet. I assume they became completely obscured at this portion of the pattern as the aircraft cowling was blocking them. I believe at this point; I had mistaken the position one aircraft's location which aligned perfectly with when position 2 had called their base. Competition landings operations are limited. For landings operations as a heat; only the lead aircraft is squawking and repeating clearances. This puts following aircraft at a disadvantage to identify the building of a near mid-air collision especially when aircraft competing leaves the published pattern limits which all competitors are thoroughly briefed on. This also limits tower's ability to identify this risk as well since only squawking aircraft appear on their scope. In a meeting with competition representatives; I brought up the possibility of having judges equipped with devices to allow a secondary location reference of aircraft other than visually. This would allow them to communicate with trailing aircraft when a aircraft ahead of them departs from the stringent pattern limits which would degrade not only an approach to landing; but safety in general. It is reiterated to pilots to space on the upwind leg; however this does not accommodate for aircraft who complete final leg segments twice the size of their upwind leg.

narrative: It was my take off out of ZZZ. Right as we were about to hit 100 knots or the high speed regime we got a master caution for and right side IRS (Inertial Reference System) fault. Captain said continue so I did. We rotated as normal. However as I started transitioning from flying visually to inside I looked down and realized I had the VERT HDG AND ATT flags as well as no flight director guidance. I glanced over and saw the captains instruments and flight director were there and working. Being a more critical phase of flight I didn't say anything to the captain yet due to not wanting to startle him more than necessary and I knew I could fly based of his instruments and visually. Once we got through 1000 ft and I knew we were safely away from the ground I stated that I didn't have any of that guidance. The captain said well let me take the plane and radios so you can run checklists to try to fix the issues. Once we transferred the controls I started looking through the non normals. I started by trying to look for any checklist relating to my instrumentation failure. I looked and read through display failure but we both stated this didn't make sense cuz the display was fine. After talking we said the first indication was the IRS FAULT light so let's start there. I started reading through that checklist and performing the actions it stated. It was around that time I realized we had performed a bleeds off TO and we hadn't switched the bleeds to the engines yet. So I performed that action before we got into any type of unsafe situation. Continuing that IRS FAULT checklist it had me turn the IRS selectors switch to both on left. As soon as I did that my side had all instrumentation and guidance once again. At this point we had leveled off at 270 because neither autopilot was working and they wouldn't let us into rvsm airspace without a working autopilot. I had sent a message to Maintenance Control stating our failures so that we could try to get the best guidance possible in trouble shooting. We transferred the controls back to me so he could talk to dispatch and manage the situation. Due to being 10000 ft lower than planned we weren't sure we would make it to ZZZ1. So we made a plan to go to ZZZ2 if needed based on how our fuel burn was going. We also made a plan to change controls back and forth so neither of us get too tired due to having to hand fly. We realized after a while we hadn't updated the cruise winds. Once we did that we realized we were right above bingo fuel. Then after flying a little while long we got below bingo so the decision was immediately made to go to ZZZ2. This entire time we were conferring with dispatch and they agreed. On the descent into ZZZ2 every time we started descending my vertical guidance went out on the flight director. So I again just used other instruments to back up my descent and every time we leveled off the vertical guidance came back on my flight director. Once we got on the approach both my vertical and lateral guidance went out. I was comfortable with flying it raw data and visually so continued flying to landing. Due to the added stress of everything that had gone on the entire flight and having to hand fly for over 4 hours by the time we got to the gate both of us felt somewhat fatigued and weren't sure if we really felt safe to continue. I talked to maintenance to add the failures on decent and approach to our list of failures we had already reported. While I did that captain called the chief pilot about everything and why we needed to do now. The manager asked how we felt and he said we are both on the fence. He went through the fatigue questions and he said based on those answers you guys aren't fit to fly and you are fatigued and will not continue. I don't think we did anything wrong on the flight in any way and I think we worked together well to divide or manage the workload. All of that added stress to flying and having to do so much more work than normal I know drained me which lead to me being fatigued.
narrative1: During the van ride to the airport; the FO and I reviewed the flight plan. The dispatcher notes included 'WILL NEED RWY XXL FOR TAKEOFF IF CALM WINDS OR WINDS FAVOR RWY XXL' and 'PLANNED BLEEDS OFF FOR T.O.' It was also noted in the release that the First Class Cabin outlets were inoperative. We mentioned the noise abatement as a possible reason for the opposite direction takeoff; or better weight/climb performance. Upon reaching the airport; we walked straight from security to the aircraft. Rather than stopping for coffee on the way to the aircraft; the FO decided to return to the terminal for coffee after stowing his bags on the aircraft. After briefing the flight attendants; to include the potential wait of an opposite direction departure and the First Class outlets; the FO had not yet returned to the aircraft. In the interest of time; I completed the entire initialization of the FMC; with the exception of requesting takeoff data. One of our ACARS messages had revealed a weight restriction; so despite the close proximity between the reserve and REMF (Remaining Fuel); I opted not to add additional fuel; and decided to wait until fueling was finished to request more accurate takeoff data. The FO returned with his coffee and then performed the walk-around. While on the walk-around; the gate agent brought down the reconciliation; and I briefed the passengers about today's flight. Upon returning; the FO began his preflight flow; and I went to the bathroom. When I got back; he then went to the bathroom. The flight attendants had completed their checks and were ready to close the cockpit door; but needed to wait until the FO was finished to do so. Once he returned to the flight deck; the door was closed. At this point; I realized that the autothrottle was not engaged; and so I checked the TAKEOFF page in the FMC and realized that neither of us had sent for the appropriate data yet. When asked; the FO stated that he had requested it; but our current weight was sending back an error for RWY XYR. As a result of his lack of initiative; I suggested that he send for numbers on XXL; as dispatch had requested. He did so; and it also returned an error for being overweight. The suggested value; was roughly 300lbs below our current weight; and due to the line of aircraft that had formed for a XYR departure; I was willing to accept this weight since our wait for an opposite direction departure would likely; burn enough fuel. He believed the weight for XYR was close; and so I permitted him to send it again. The required weight for a XYR departure was roughly 1000 pounds below that for a XXL departure. I told him to send for numbers at the maximum weights specified in the error; and if we got below the number for XYR before our opposite direction departure is permitted; we can do that. I also acknowledged that this weight would be extremely close to our required reserve fuel. Once he sent for a successful solution; I reviewed it and realized that the auto function for the bleed air was recommending a bleeds on solution. I then had him send for takeoff data forcing a bleeds off takeoff; at which point our current weight returned a valid solution for RWYXXR. We were past our scheduled departure time at this point; so we quickly briefed the departure; noting the threats of complacency from day-4; the bleeds off takeoff; and the line of aircraft we would be waiting in. Despite acknowledging these threats; I permitted the first error to be introduced by not requesting a more thorough brief of the clearance and SID; or verifying that the selected altitude was correct. It was not. 3000 feet was still selected from the arrival crew; despite our being cleared to climb via the SID; and the top altitude of the ZZZZZX being 13;000 feet.After completing the before push checklist; we notified the ground crew and pushed off the gate approximately 5 minutes late; and a line of approximately 8-10 aircraft had already formed. The ground crew advised us toturn on our lights; at which point the FO turned on two light switches. I did not verify which switches. During our taxi; the ground controller asked us to re-cycle our transponder. The FO had not turned on the transponder during push; and turned it on now. All checklists and callouts were accomplished satisfactorily through our clearance for takeoff on RWY XYR. During the takeoff roll; approaching 100 KIA; a Master Caution illuminated corresponding to an IRS (Inertial Reference System) annunciator. I extinguished it and verbalized continue; followed by the 100 knots; V1; and VR callouts. Once airborne; the FO directed me to retract the flaps and perform the after takeoff checklist. During final flap retraction; the FO verbalized that he had lost some of his displayed instrumentation. I assumed he meant his Flight Director; and opted to take the aircraft as my displays were operating normally. I continued to fly the departure and climb. Approaching 3000 feet; the Flight Director commanded a level off; as this was the altitude selected in the MCP (Mode Control Panel). I began decreasing power and leveling off as I recognized the VNAV ALT in the FMA (Flight Mode Annunciator) and cross checked the MCP to deduce that this was not due to the departure. I grabbed the printed PDC and quickly located the clearance to climb via SID. I then resumed the climb noting the next 5000B restriction at ZZZZZ1. Due to the timing of this mistake; it resulted in neither pilot accomplishing the After Takeoff or No Engine Bleed Checklists. This small error that was not repaired during the briefing permitted additional errors to occur; contributing to a lower fuel state.As we continued the climb; the FO continued to troubleshoot his displays and I eventually became aware that in addition to losing the Flight Director (FD); the FO's ADI and HSI were black; with yellow ATT; HDG; and VERT annunciations; but accurate speed and altitude was still displayed. He began searching for a non-normal checklist associated with the malfunctioning display. At this point; I opted to take the radios in addition to flying the aircraft. Passing 10;000 feet I switched the sterile light; 'double dinged' the flight attendants; checked and verbalized that the cabin was pressurizing; and attempted to turn on the autopilot. However; the sterile light was apparently in the wrong position; so instead of turning it off; I inadvertently turned it on. I typically engage the autopilot at this time; but it failed to engage on either the A or B channel. I cycled the FO's FD switch; to make my source the master; and attempted to engage the autopilot again. It did not engage; so I continued to hand fly the aircraft. To prevent myself from overwhelming the FO; who was still searching for an appropriate checklist; I decided not to inform him that the autopilot was not functioning until it became pertinent. The FO reviewed several non-normal checklists and we deduced that they were not the correct checklists. At one point; the Flight Attendants called the flight deck. The FO took the call; as I had my hands full. They were asking why the sterile light had been turned on; and he notified them of our predicament; and I turned the light back off. This was the consequence of yet another error that was not repaired on the ground; adding additional complication to this situation. The flight attendants also informed us that in addition to the outlets being inoperative in the First Class Cabin; they were inoperative in the entire aircraft; all of the screens at the seats were inoperative; and there was no internet connectivity. During this time we passed FL180; and set 29.92 inHg at which point I chimed in that it is possible to use one of the reversionary switches to simply force my display onto his. In reviewing the overhead panel; the FO discovered that the bleed air was not appropriately set. He quickly performed the procedure to set the bleed panel without referencing the No Engine Bleed Checklist. He then set the gear; auto-brakes; and igniters to complete the After Takeoff Checklist. Thankfully the APU was still pressurizing the cabin despite being above 17;000 feet; and maintaining an approximately 5;000 foot cabin altitude. Although we repaired this error before it became an undesired aircraft state; we simultaneously introduced another error as the appropriate checklist was the No Engine Bleed Checklist. Therefore; the APU continued running.Returning his attention to the overhead panel; I attempted to help guide him to the appropriate switch while keeping my eyes on the gauges because I was hand-flying. I then mentioned that there are also reversionary switches on the dash; and perhaps it was one of those. He did move several of these switches but only the upper and lower DU'S (Display Units) changed; so he returned to the overhead. He eventually actuated several of those switches; and again got no positive resolution. As a result; I guided him back to the original indication - the IRS Master Caution. On the overhead panel; the R IRS FAULT and ALIGN lights were illuminated. He located the IRS FAULT checklist. During the climb; ATC eventually cleared us to an RVSM altitude. Knowing that autopilot is a required piece of equipment; I declined that altitude and was cleared to FL270. At this point; I filled in the FO that the autopilot was not functioning. After performing the checklist steps; the FO's instrumentation was restored; but the autopilot still would not engage; and the #2 transponder displayed a fault; so the #1 was selected. We interfaced with Maintenance Control via ACARS for any additional assistance. With the FO's display functioning correctly; I asked if he felt good enough to fly. He confirmed that he was; and I handed aircraft control over to him. We agreed to trading off who would fly every 30-60 minutes to avoid fatigue. At this point; I started my timer and began interfacing with dispatch about our options. This included requesting to transit RVSM airspace as a non-RVSM capable aircraft; which was denied multiple times. While at cruise in ZZZ Center's airspace; we discussed divert options with dispatch and opted to continue as the FMC computed FOB at ZZZ1 was 5.7; which was above the required 5.5. I also sent multiple ELB (Electronic Logbook) reports for the various issues we encountered. We also discussed the possibility that this was a larger electrical malfunction; as opposed to simply an IRS FAULT. I then realized that I had not requested new winds for our lower altitude. After doing so; our calculated FOB decreased. However; dispatch revised the alternate which decreased the required fuel to 5.1; which we were above. As a result of some storms in the area; we needed to use the Engine Anti-Ice; again decreasing our FOB calculation; now below the required 5.1. Shortly thereafter; the center tanks were emptied; the center fuel pumps were turned off; and dispatch notified us that an alternate was no longer required. The required fuel was now 4.4; and the FMC calculated to have 4.7 FOB at ZZZ1; so we continued. As a result of the inadvertent APU usage; the use of ENG ANTI-ICE at cruise; the variations associated with hand flying; and common fuel system anomaly associated with a decreasing FOB after turning off the center fuel pumps; our fuel total slowly decreased below the 4.4 FOB requirement. At this point; the decision was made to divert to ZZZ2. During our descent; the FO's instrumentation began further degrading. During descents in VNAV; LVL CHG; and V/S; the FO would lose his vertical Flight Director; but it would reappear at the level off altitude. I offered to fly as my display was functioning correctly; and he declined. I made sure to keep an eye on our flight path; and the FO was doing a great job without my interference. We were cleared to fly the visual approach to RWYXZR at ZZZ; and backed it up with the ILS. We discussed the possibility of his Flight Director malf
synopsis: B737 flight crew reported loss of multiple avionics and auto systems resulted in fatigue; a higher fuel burn and divert.

Traffic on final is difficult to see especially if said traffic overshoots from base to final and or are low on the approach. narrative1: While on vectors for the RNAV RWY 34 approach at HPN; leveled at 3;000 ft MSL; I observed traffic at our 12 o'clock position; approximately 400 ft below us. The First Officer and I maintained visual contact with the traffic to ensure separation. At approximately 5 NM; we received a TCAS Resolution Advisory (RA) -- MONITOR VERTICAL SPEED." As the Pilot Flying; I complied with the RA and continued to monitor the traffic visually. The traffic passed without further conflict and the RA resolved. Shortly after; New York Approach advised us of helicopter traffic to our right; 400 ft below; which was the same traffic we had been monitoring. We advised ATC that we had received an RA due to that traffic. No further incidents occurred. We continued the RNAV RWY 34 approach and landed without further incident.Cause: TCAS RA triggered by helicopter traffic during radar vectors on approach. We began our descent on the VNAV profile. As we began the turn from base to final; the glide path was captured which I believe created a pitch down moment. Immediately after level off; we stopped receiving the GPWS warning. narrative: I was operating from ZZZ as the First Officer and pilot flying. The aircraft was an Airbus A319.  It was the first flight of the day. Upon arriving to the aircraft; the plane had been powered up (assuming by maintenance); however APU was off; Pre-Conditioned Air (PCA) hose unplugged and tangled up by aircraft nose. The three temperature sensors in the plane read; CKPT 90; FWD 94; AFT 98". This became a top priority to try a cool the airplane prior to boarding. With the APU Bleed on; we were able to cool the aircraft and no issues noted. All things considered normal up until after engine start. We noticed Pack 1 was still showing a fault; but both myself and the Captain agreed it was probably a "sticky valve" and once we added a little bit of engine power; that issue would go away. Prior to calling for taxi clearance; the fault went away and everything was normal. However; when taxing out to the runway; the fault came back; but would go away when engine thrust was added and would come back again when thrust was brought to idle. This process repeated itself for about 3 cycles until we decided to tell Ground Control we'd like to pull over and troubleshoot the fault. The CA worked with dispatch and maintenance to eventually MEL Pack 1. Maintenance gave us the MEL 21-XXX "Packs Pressurized Flight (A319) X. Option 2 - (Limited Effectivity) (Speed Brakes Operative)". The main takeaway for this MEL is that the aircraft altitude is limited to Flight Level 370. The day prior; the same CA and I flew another very similar A319 with an inop APU and a MEL'ed Pack 1. The MEL associated with that flight was 21-XXY ""Packs Pressurized Flight (A319) Y. Option 1 - (Limited Effectivity) (Speed Brakes Inoperative)"; with the main takeaway from that; was it had a max altitude of Flight Level 310. Our filed flight plan for our flight was Flight Level 350. We had some discussions on what the differences were and why on one flight we had Y and this one we had X. We discussed the two different altitudes and noted our flight level was right in between them and would monitor the cabin altitude. But according to the MEL that maintenance gave us; FL350 was still legal and we pressed on. On the climb out the aft cabin was "ok" with temperature; but the front was high 70s/low 80s and the cockpit was 90°+; with the aircraft not cooling down on one Pack. While still in the climb to FL350; I started having the discussion on different possibilities to resolve this issue. We were in the process of reaching out to Dispatch via ACARS to send us a fuel plan with a much lower altitude so we could potentially use the APU Bleed to cool the plane off. During that time; we were passing FL330 in which the CA mentioned the cabin altitude passing ~8;000'; which then prompted him to immediately request a level off; then a lower altitude. Our descent started somewhere in the mid FL340s heading back down initially to FL330; never reaching our filed FL350. That's when we received the Master Warning and the "CAB PR EXCESS CAB ALT" ECAM. We donned the oxygen masks; established crew communication and continued the ECAM steps. I took the aircraft and the radios and requested a descent down to 10;000' and a westbound heading to get us heading back over land (our flight path was in a Northeast heading out over the water). The CA was busy with checklist; dispatch; flight attendants and passengers; so I initially elected direct ZZZ1 to have something to aim for. I'm not sure the exact altitude the cabin got to; but it was less than 14;000' because there were no issues or indications of a pressurization issue in the back since the passenger oxygen masks did not deploy and the Flight Attendants had no idea any issues were going on up in the flight deck. Once at 10;000'; the cabin altitude was back to normal (300' or so) and we were able to take our masks off; regroup and come to a logical solution for what would be next. Dispatch requested us to head back to ZZZ; which we deemed was safeand appropriate. We landed back in ZZZ with no further issues and taxied to the gate. Our debrief questions that we wanted answers for; 1. Was there any correlation at the start of the morning trying to cool off an extremely hot airplane; and essentially overworking the packs? 2. We still never received an explanation for the 2 different MELs and why they would have 2 different max altitudes?Cause: The temperature of the aircraft was unacceptable; especially with the plane already being powered up; a working APU (that was off) and working PCA which the hose was disconnected. It set the tone of the morning with; "here's something else we have to deal with." -Recommendation: With summer pretty much here; and with locations that are known for hot summers; planes need to be cooled prior to crews getting there.Having a fault while on taxi out is distracting; especially when running checklist and dealing with Ground ATC. To then have a fault that affects the cooling of the aircraft; which again was already an aggravation for the entire crew (flight attendants included). The cockpit temperature was extremely distracting; and it took away some of our situational awareness away with the Pack 1 MEL and the cabin altitude.Having essentially the same aircraft the day prior with the same issue(s); yet a different max altitude per a different MEL has huge expectation basis. Having a better understanding of what and why maintenance is giving us that MEL as well as addressing our concerns about the max altitude would be very beneficial. It's practically impossible for our specific situation where the CA is dealing with all of that while I'm monitoring ATC frequencies. No blame or fault to the CA; again for the reasons listed; but all of my questions came after he was done talking to maintenance and answers were left to interpretation of how we were reading the MELs."

narrative: I was cleared for a straight in landing on runway 22 due to approaching the airport from the east. The active runway at the time for other arrivals was runway 12. I have flown to TUS a lot in the past. Normally after touchdown tower will instruct me to do a 180 on the runway and back taxi to alpha and contact ground / proceed to the FBO. Or sometimes I will be instructed to make a left on delta 3 and contact ground. In this case the controller was busy transmitting to another aircraft by the time I had slowed down so I made the first available exit which happened to be taxiway alpha 2. After vacating onto alpha 2 I realized I was now directly in the approach path / area of runway 12 with Aircraft Y on a few mile final for this very runway. I decided to hang another left and get clear of the area on taxiway delta to prevent a problem before contacting tower who then handed me off to ground. The ground controller did not mention anything about an incursion and instructed me to taxi along delta to the ramp as usual.The situation still felt weird to me after the fact however because while I taxied on delta to the ramp I crossed over a red marking on the pavement that said 30-12" that would imply I was just on an active runway without a clearance even though the taxiway turnoff that brought me here didn't say anything. After looking through other safety reports I am not the first person to get confused by the taxiway layout at this specific intersection despite having lots of experience operating here. When you are rolling out on runway 22 taxiway alpha 2 looks like a completely normal turn off. No special markings on the runway and no red signs for an intersecting runway approaching. Alpha 2 is also depicted like any other taxiway on the airport diagram on initial glance. Once you are on alpha 2 however you are on runway 12 and that becomes apparent when you vacate runway 22 and now see runway 12 right in front of you. When you then make either a left or right onto delta you cross over a pair of hold bars that read in red letters on the concrete "30-12" again implying you are / were on a runway even though the taxi diagram depicts it as a taxiway and there are yellow stripe markings on the ground. narrative: On Day 0 and Day 1; I made 5 UAS flights totaling approximately 35 minutes from Location X. During this time; I was not aware of a TFR that was in place. I was attempting to fly directly up and hover my UAS over Location X for recreational pictures and videos. I checked the map in the DJI Fly app used to control the UAS and it appeared to show only a restricted flight zone for ZZZ Airport; which I was just outside of. The status indicator in the top left corner of the DJI control app showed green indicating good satellite connection and showed the message 'Takeoff Permitted'; which I believed confirmed that no flight restrictions were in place. I maintained line of sight; kept the UAS over private property; remained below 400 feet and believed I was following all FAA UAS operational rules. I was not aware of the TFR until the final flight when I was approached by law enforcement personnel.Reviewing my DJI app flight log shows the following:On Day 0; I made one flight for approximately 2 minutes and landed without incident. On Day 0; I made another flight for approximately 7 minutes and landed without incident.On Day 1; I made one flight for approximately 23 minutes and landed without incident.On Day 1; I made another flight for approximately 2 minutes; lost connection and the UAS returned to the take off point.On Day 1; I made another flight for 3 minutes. As the UAS was hovering I was approached by several law enforcement personnel. They informed me I was inside a TFR and directed me to land the UAS. I immediately landed the UAS and complied with all instructions. They informed me I should use an FAA approved mobile app to monitor for current TFRs and that the manufacturer's proprietary drone application was not sufficient. This issue was caused by inexperience; insufficient understanding of how TFRs work and the incorrect assumption that the UAS manufacturer's control application showed both temporary and permanent flight restrictions; which I now do not believe it does. I have no experience operating this UAS or other types of flight experience and should have waited but I was excited and wanted to try it out.In order to prevent this from occurring again I have downloaded the FAA approved AutoPylot app to remain aware of all NOTAMS and TFR's and I have completed the FAA WINGS safety course ALC-42: Airspace; Special Use Airspace and TFRs (Know Before You Go: Navigating Today's Airspace).To prevent this in the future; I believe training certification should be required to purchase and operate all drones. The extremely small size; low cost and ease to purchase my DJI drone gave me entirely the wrong idea about how serious the regulations are for its operation and I had no idea I could get into such trouble for its use.  In conclusion; I regret flying my drone before I fully understood its possible implications. I should have had a better understanding of the FAA rules and restrictions. Thank you for taking the time to read this and I hope it contributes toward something useful for the future.

narrative: My student began to set up for eights on pylons; a commercial single-engine ground reference maneuver. The objective was to have her practice explaining and demonstrating the objective; tolerances; and execution of the maneuver. Her pylon selection was satisfactory. However; she was going to begin the maneuver noticeably low at about 1100' MSL where pivotal altitude today was closer to 1400' MSL. She was reminded of this and she climbed to 1400' MSL using the pivotal altitude table. She began the first turn a few minutes later which was performed well. She recovered to 1400' MSL and began setting up for the second turn in the maneuver. But in doing so; a combination of turbulence and overbanking caused my student to get too low. Overbanking in this maneuver causes pylons to seem to move forward; resulting in an illusion that the aircraft is higher than actual altitude. This prompts the pilot to push forward on the controls when otherwise unnecessary. My student was inadvertently overbanking the airplane (not keeping the bank fixed); resulting in a large descent to which I did not intervene in time. She was reminded to keep the bank angle fixed. In the process of instructing her to do so; we descended to 681 indicated altitude which I believe is below 500' AGL; prompting this report. Besides greater vigilance on behalf of instructors like myself who may find themselves too low; it is important to draw the line higher such that students do not get anywhere near the 500' AGL limit. Fixation on pylons and bank angle may be beneficial to the maneuver itself but can cause a loss of altitude awareness which has resulted in controlled flight into terrain in past general aviation accidents. I plan on drawing the line higher for students performing this maneuver; especially for students who are new to the maneuver from the right seat or students who have not flown the maneuver for some time.
synopsis: General aviation instructor reported a loss of altitude awareness during a training flight while performing a ground reference maneuver; resulting in a descent below an altitude limit above the ground.

narrative: I was the Pilot in Command of Aircraft X operating from ZZZ to ZZZ1. Approximately 25 minutes into an otherwise uneventful flight; while established in cruise at FL320; we experienced a right engine failure.The event was immediately apparent to the entire crew. We heard two distinct and extremely loud bangs that were consistent with compressor stalls and were accompanied by significant airframe vibration. The severity of the noise and vibration left little doubt that we were experiencing a major engine-related event. Immediately following the bangs; numerous EICAS messages populated the displays. The most prominent message was a Right FADEC FAIL indication; which was followed by High ITT; Low Oil Pressure; and indications consistent with a rollback of the right engine.At the time of the event; I was serving as the non-flying pilot and immediately began running the applicable checklist associated with the Right FADEC FAIL message. As we worked through the checklist; the aircraft indications and system responses were consistent with what we were observing; reinforcing our assessment that we had experienced a significant engine malfunction.Given the loud compressor stall events; severe vibration; and multiple engine-related indications; our initial assessment was that we may have suffered a catastrophic engine failure rather than a simple FADEC malfunction. At that point; our primary focus became aircraft control; system management; and determining the safest and most expeditious airport for diversion.As we transitioned from ZZZ Center to ZZZ1 Center; communication difficulties introduced additional challenges during an already high-workload situation. Although we had been communicating on the ZZZ1 Center frequency for several minutes; when I advised ATC that we were operating as a priority aircraft; the initial response was a question regarding whether we were attempting to pick up an IFR flight plan. This response led us to believe that there was a significant lack of awareness regarding our situation.I immediately restated that we were requesting priority handling and required a diversion to ZZZ2. ZZZ1 Center then requested our position and destination; further indicating that they did not yet have a clear understanding of the nature or urgency of our circumstances.From a crew resource management perspective; this lack of situational awareness created additional workload at a time when both pilots were heavily engaged in checklist execution; aircraft systems monitoring; diversion planning; and threat assessment. Rather than being able to focus exclusively on managing the situation; we found ourselves dedicating valuable attention to ensuring that ATC fully understood the seriousness of our condition.To remove any ambiguity and ensure immediate recognition of our status; I selected transponder code XXXX and transmitted to ATC on the frequency. My intent was to clearly communicate the urgency of the situation; obtain priority handling; and expedite vectors toward ZZZ2. Following these actions; ZZZ1 Center recognized the nature of the situation; coordinated appropriately; and provided the assistance necessary for us to continue the diversion and prepare for landing.As the flight progressed and we began preparing for a single-engine approach into ZZZ2; we became aware of additional system abnormalities involving Hydraulic System 2. We received a FLT SPOILERS FAULT message and observed multiple yellow cautions on the flight controls synoptic page. The indications suggested that the flight spoilers were deployed and were not returning to their normal trail position.To verify the indications; both pilots visually inspected the wings from the cockpit. We observed that spoiler panels 3 and 4; as well as panels 7 and 8; appeared deployed on both wings. These observations matched the indications displayed on the aircraft systems pages and confirmed that we were dealing with an additional flight control anomaly beyond the engine failure.We completed all applicable checklists associated with the hydraulic and spoiler indications. These procedures included actions intended to restore Hydraulic System 2 functionality through electric pump operation. Despite completing the prescribed procedures; the spoiler panels remained deployed and the associated cautions persisted. No corrective action restored the system to a normal configuration; and the aircraft continued to experience the associated aerodynamic drag. It was then as PIC I took control of the flying and the SIC (Second in Command) took control of the radios.As we approached ZZZ2 and entered the downwind for Runway XXR; it became evident that we would be landing with a combination of degraded aircraft performance factors: a failed right engine and substantial additional drag from spoilers that appeared to be stuck in the deployed position. This additional time allowed us to evaluate aircraft handling characteristics; verify performance expectations; review landing considerations; and effectively 'learn how to fly' the aircraft in its current degraded state before committing to the approach.The approach and landing were ultimately completed without further incident. Following a normal touchdown and rollout; we taxied clear and completed the appropriate shutdown procedures. The aircraft was subsequently towed to the FBO ramp where emergency response personnel met the aircraft. Firefighters conducted a visual and thermal assessment and reported no evidence of fire; overheating; or external engine damage following landing.During the post-flight inspection; no visible external damage to the right engine was observed. However; after all hydraulic systems were powered down; the flight spoilers remained physically stuck in the deployed position; confirming that the spoiler anomaly persisted beyond aircraft shutdown. The condition of the spoilers appeared consistent with the indications we had observed in flight and likely contributed significantly to the increased drag experienced during the diversion and landing.While the crew successfully managed the event and landed safely; the combination of an apparent engine failure; subsequent hydraulic and flight spoiler anomalies; and initial communication difficulties with ATC created a complex and rapidly evolving situation.

Suddently; I relized that my left wheel was dropping off the left edge of the concrete runway into; what turned out to be; very soft (cultivated) soil. What followed happened in the blink of an eye but takes a while to describe hereinafter. The left wheel slowed down due to the massive drag in the very soft soil; causing the aircraft to veer 90 degrees to the left. The right wheel subsequently entered the soil; and; with the 90 degree angle of the aircraft to the runway; it dug in as well. The speed at that point was probably quite slow; 3-4 kts perhaps. The aircraft tipped to the right and the right wingtip made contact with the soft soil. My right shoulder bumped into the right plexiglass window and broke it (no injury to me). The aircraft came to a stop and the right wing came back up to its normal position. I turned off the engine and all switches and got out. A walk around inspection indicated that nothing broke off the aircraft and the propeller never made contact with the ground. The right wingtip was dirty; with some dirt on top of the wing as well. The right wingtip showed some signs of contact with the ground and the wingtip light was still intact. The extent of the damage could not be ascertained at that point. The owner helped me to push the aircraft back to the runway and I taxied it back to the hangar building on the north side. While I am not at all proud about how this landing turned out; there may be some useful learning points to take from it. A lot of what I am stating below has the benefit of hindsight. First; I wish I would have used a booster cusion to get my head and line-of-sight as high up as possible. If I had seen over the nose the entire time; I would have noticed my drift to the left and stopped it. The sitting height I was at was totally adequate for landing at an airport with a runway that is wider and/or has center line and edge line markings and elevated runway lights. It is also an ok sitting height when landing in wider grass fields or grass runways where lateral position is not as critical. I am used to landing on narrrow runways with this aircraft; such as for example at ZZZ3. However; that concrete runway transitions smoothly into a wide strip of mowed grass on each side of the runway and the outer extent of that mowed grassis marked with edge lights. All of this provides a pripheral vision cue that is completely sufficient for lateral alignment corrections. The runway at ZZZ is new concrete but it has no grass on either side and; in fact; there is a bit of a step down into very soft cultivated soil that; in fact; is so soft that a person could dig their hands in down to 6-10 inches without resistance. I could not ascertain that situation from the airport data during my preflight or during the recon pass I made. Physiologically what happened was that when the tail settled on the ground; I lost all forward view of the runway (this is normal) but also all peripheral view (this is not normal) because the sight triangle from my eyes; across the lower window edge ended up in the uniformly colored soil to the left and right of the runwway. Thus; due to the narrowness of the runwway; all I could perceive on the left and right was uniform soil from a uniformly cultivated field on both sides of the runway. This provided me with no ability to perceive lateral drift cues and it happened quickly. The small step from the concrete to the soil acted like an accelerant to pulling the left wheel off the runway; once it reached the edge during the drift to the left; with no recourse to get it back up on the concrete. Unlike the mowed grass overrun that other narrow runway airports have (like ZZZ3); this airport had very soft (cultivated) soil immediately to the left and right of the firm concrete runway. I could not ascertain that information during preflight and the recon pass. The softness of the soil provided an unforgiving environment that immediately bogged the left wheel down; while the right one was still on hard concrete. This resulted in the sudden veering turn to the left.Second; and of course with the benefit of hindsight; I wish I would have opened both windows and the right folding door. This would have improved my sight triangle to the ground and I might have noticed the drift. Third; I wish I could have foreseen the sudden loss of peripheral alignment cues during the tail low portion of the landing. Uniformly cultivated fields abutting directly onto a runway are not suitable to provide pilots who are unfamiliar with a particular airport.
