narrative: Flight Following from ZZZ to ZZZ1 coordinating with ATC following the coast and keeping clear of convective weather; as I also avoided clouds. At XA:45pm aircraft started to experience turbulence and a strong desire to climb above 11k'. Once I brought us back down to 10500 and stabilized us; at about XB:05pm a heavy mist blew in from the S and overtook my visibility. We were sucked up into a climb more much more quickly and violently than before. I turned R to the N toward the coast; and tried descending us to get out of the mist/cloud and back to VFR conditions. It was a very light rain; but total white out. During my descending turn to the N it felt like the aircraft was pushed by a strong gust of wind; the right wing lost lift; and we went into a spiraling dive/spin. As I worked to regain control of the aircraft; I think it was a combination of me recovering from the spin and the atmosphere rapidly changing condition (we were experiencing up and down drafts) that led to the aircraft shooting straight up in the air until stalling. My passenger and I were unsure of what was happening at that point; as all the up; down; and turns had us disoriented. All of our instruments were spinning in circles one way one second; then spinning the other direction the next second. All this in white out conditions. We experienced weightlessness; then increasing gravitational forces. ATC came on asking if we were ok because they had us 'losing altitude rapidly.' Not having any control over the aircraft; all instruments spinning erratically; and total white out visibility... I responded: 'Requesting priority handling; we are not ok. Please stay with us.' My passenger pointed out the VSI got to 9 o'clock by going 'down' and I saw the airspeed indicator increasing in the yellow arc. We were in a power on vertical dive. I saw the airspeed approaching 185mph and I struggled through the g forces to pull the throttle back to idle. I then crushed the right rudder to the floor. I believe this deflection to the side of the fuselage was what slowed our straight vertical dive (maybe we were spinning in the dive too). Either way; the Attitude Indicator then became stable and indicated a diving left bank. Knowing not to pull back on the yoke hard; I gently and intermittently gave the yoke right and back pressure inputs. The g forces lessened; and the instruments all began stabilizing. We became level; but were still falling. Like a parachute. In total white out still. After a few seconds of that; we gently fell below the cloud layer; like coming down an elevator. I put the power back in; and we were on our way. ATC came on asking if we were ok. I said something like 'I love you. Thank you so much for being there for us. Please get me an airport to land at as soon as possible.'I never exceeded the 214mph Vne of my Piper Arrow II; and I do not believe I reached the positive load factor of 3.8 G. Regardless; before my next flight I called my home airport aviation mechanic and performed a visual and tactical inspection of the aircraft with him via video call. I would not have flown my aircraft again if I had any doubt about her airworthiness. Regardless of not hitting the structural limitations of the aircraft... in an abundance of caution; I am having it professionally inspected by my aircraft mechanic.  Although I aimed to remain 20 miles away from the convective weather; I believe it was the outer edges of the cell that caused us to experience the updrafts; downdrafts; and strong wind gusts that caused us to lose control of the aircraft. I kept power in thinking I could keep control of the plane against the winds that way; but in hindsight I think I should have decreased power sooner. Losing altitude and diverting N was difficult because there were other clouds to avoid beneath us; intense air traffic coming and going from all the airports in that area; and lots of different airspace; including military airspace that I was trying to remain clear of for safety. I thought my altitude and heading would keep us safe from the weather; heavy traffic in the area; and the airspaces. In hindsight; maybe I should have asked ATC if it was ok for me divert more N. There was a storm that had just come over the shore from the S to the N that I was trying to stay below as well though. So there was a lot going on. It also looked like small cells; but heavy precipitation over the airports I would have liked to divert to before the event happened. I kept hearing of the 12k' ceiling above me; and ceilings at different airports at 2500' and 4500'. I didn't want to get stuck in IMC trying to descend to land at an airport to avoid the weather; only to end up in it so close to the ground. I wanted altitude for safety; and it was a major factor in why I was able to recover. Not only am I going to make sure my aircraft is just as good as it was before the incident; but I am also intensifying my weather knowledge; and I am going to pursue Spin Training and Aerobatics. These are 'advanced pilot techniques' that I think should be taught to every Private Pilot. Especially since inadvertently getting caught in IMC conditions is such a killer of GA pilots.What could ATC have done differently... I don't think their equipment showed me getting 'too close' to the danger zone that day. A lesson we can learn is how dangerous a tightly formed cell with heavy precipitation consuming its growth can create extreme wind shear around its outer perimeter. The radio was very busy that day with aircraft diverting due to rapidly changing weather conditions. I was very grateful ATC came on to let me know I was losing altitude rapidly. As tossed around as we were; this was helpful in the moment. I was hoping they would call out my altitude repeatedly as it changed; and hoping they would call it out as I was losing or gaining it. Any information they could have given me like that could have helped. I understand they are not pilots; and probably shouldn't give the pilot in an unknown flight condition piloting advice; but the altitude and possibly heading call outs could help in a situation like that. I have no complaints. ATC did a great job handling the weather and workload they had that day. I have a new respect for weather; and this will make me a better pilot; and sharing my experience with others hopefully will help them stay safe. I want to be in compliance with all that is expected of me as a pilot. I want to be an incredible pilot. Please let me know if anything else is expected or needed of me. Thank you for the time you devote to our safety.

I debriefed the situation with the student and made sure to emphasize the importance of maintaining vigilance in the traffic pattern and scanning for traffic. I made it known that I wasn't upset with them and that it was a huge lesson for me and for the student as well. As an instructor; I am trusted to stay vigilant; pay full attention to every radio call and ask ATC for clarification if unsure. I have done a lot of reflecting on this occurrence and went back and listened to the ATC audio recording to figure out how all of this happened. I was pretty shaken up afterwards and still keep asking myself 'How can a 1;000 hour pilot let something like that occur?' I believe a large contributing factor to this incident was fatigue and inadequete nutrition and hydration. I had spent the entire day before (Day 0) volunteering for a non-profit as a pilot. That day had been long and involved extensive waiting on the ground for thunderstorms with insufficient food and water. I believe that had lingering effects on me that night and into the next day (the day of the occurrence). I woke up the next morning feeling a little tired; but thought I felt well enough to fly and work. Feeling rushed that morning; I also did not pack a lunch that morning like I normally do. I refilled my water once that day; but I don't think I was drinking enough. Knowing it was a 90 degree day and I had multiple activities scheduled; I should have taken extra care to hydrate and make sure I was getting enough food. Over all this occurrence has been very eye-opening for me and has taught me huge lessons. One is the paramount importance of remaining vigilant during traffic pattern instructional flights. I take full responsibility and realize the seriousness of the situation. I wish to use this as a learning moment for myself and my student. Moving forward; I plan to take at an absolute minimum 1 day off of flying completely every week so that I can rest and ensure I am completely present for each and every flight operation and prevent anything like this from ever reoccuring.

ATC climbed us to 3;000 feet to give us room to work.The First Officer was the pilot flying. Once we reached 3;000 feet; I requested priority handling; stating our fuel and souls on board; and advised that we would need about 20 minutes to work through the various checklists. Knowing these procedures can be lengthy; I felt comfortable because the weather in ZZZ was perfect and we had plenty of gas; including an alternate of Indianapolis; so I was not pressed for fuel and knew we could take our time.I opened the QRH to 'Trailing Edge Flap Asymmetry.' We had no abnormal lights in the flight deck; but the flap indicator showed a slight split with the needles stuck between 0 and 1. The checklist directed us to return the flap handle to UP. As we began that checklist; the flap indicator stopped showing a split. We realized we no longer had an asymmetry; and since that checklist would have required a landing at an extremely high speed which we felt wasn't appropriate for the situation we opted to look for other QRH options.We settled on 'Trailing Edge Flap Disagree.' We felt this was the correct procedure; so we extended the flaps via the alternate flap extension method. Everything progressed normally with no asymmetry or abnormal lights; and we prepared for a flaps 15 landing as directed by the QRH.Once stabilized; I called the flight attendant to brief her on the situation and confirmed it would be a normal landing. I then sent a message to dispatch stating we had requested priority handling; explained the issue; and confirmed we were about to land. I made a PA to the passengers to explain we had a malfunction that required us to work through checklists; and that they should not be alarmed by the presence of emergency vehicles upon arrival. I requested that ATC have ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) standing by and that they follow us to the gate as a precaution.At this point; it was a routine flaps 15 landing. The First Officer was doing a great job; given his previous experience flying this aircraft in the military; I felt comfortable letting him continue the landing while I monitored from a high level. I think the main confusion was around what constituted as flap asymmetry; it was not very clear reading the QRH conditions and objectives header.  Could we look at  putting  some bullet points to consider in the QRH to help clarify.

narrative: This report is my best recollection of an altitude deviation that occurred during the OYODA TWO RNAV departure from Henderson Executive Airport (HND).I was operating Aircraft X single-pilot. Due to high summer-like temperatures; the aircraft was operated at a moderately light weight and once airborne; exhibited strong climb performance. Prior to departure; the OYODA TWO RNAV departure was loaded into the G1000 NXi flight management system; and the initial altitude of 6;000 feet was set.The takeoff and initial departure were normal. The aircraft was climbing at approximately 170 KIAS with a climb rate exceeding 2;000 feet per minute. As the aircraft passed through approximately 5;500 feet MSL over the mountainous terrain southeast of Henderson; it encountered a sudden onset of moderate-to-severe turbulence.During the turbulence encounter; my left hand was forced from the control yoke and inadvertently came down on the autopilot disconnect button; resulting in an unexpected autopilot disengagement. At the time; the aircraft was trimmed for a steep climb. I immediately took manual control and applied forward pressure on the yoke while simultaneously reducing power and commanding nose-down electric trim.Despite these corrective actions; the aircraft's climb rate initially increased rather than decreased. At one point; I observed the vertical speed indication at around 3;000 feet per minute. The turbulence required significant attention to aircraft control. It is possible that the aircraft encountered a localized area of strong rising air; although this could not be confirmed.Within approximately 20 seconds; the aircraft climbed through the assigned altitude of 6;000 feet and reached an estimated maximum altitude between 6;600 and 6;800 feet before I was able to arrest the climb and begin descending back toward the assigned altitude. During this period; the aircraft also deviated somewhat from the published lateral departure track as my primary focus was maintaining aircraft control and recovering from the upset.The turbulence remained significant while I worked to reengage the autopilot and reestablish both the assigned altitude and lateral course. Before I could return to 6;000 feet; the departure controller issued an altitude alert. Shortly thereafter; I was instructed to continue climbing to 7;000 feet.The entire event occurred over approximately one minute. I was surprised by the magnitude of the altitude excursion and by my inability to arrest the climb sooner despite immediate corrective action.In retrospect; I should have advised ATC immediately regarding the turbulence encounter. Doing so would have provided important context for the deviation and would have allowed ATC to warn other aircraft operating in the area. My focus on regaining aircraft control; reestablishing the departure path; and complying with assigned altitudes caused me to overlook making that report.
synopsis: General aviation jet pilot reported severe turbulence during the climb; resulting in an altitude and heading deviation. The Captain recovered the aircraft and returned to the clearance.

narrative: On Day 3 at approximately XA:00; I was operating a DJI Mavic 3 Enterprise under 14 CFR Part 107; conducting a commercial construction-site progress flight at 165 ft AGL. During my planning-stage airspace check three days prior; on Day 0; I observed a published TFR covering the area up to 400 ft AGL; scheduled to become effective Day 1; but not yet in force at the time of my check. I did not log the pending restriction or set a reminder for its effective date; and by the day of the flight I had forgotten it existed.On the day of the flight; my third-party mission-planning software (DroneDeploy) displayed a summary airspace status of 'No Authorization Required' for the planned flight area. I relied on that green status indication and launched. I did not separately verify active TFRs and NOTAMs through official FAA sources before launching. A portion of my planned flight area overlapped the outer edge of the TFR boundary. The operating area is Class G airspace and is normally unrestricted; which contributed to my reliance on the summary status.During my flight; a local law enforcement officer arrived on scene; informed me that an active TFR covered the area; and instructed me to land the aircraft. I landed immediately and complied with all instructions. The airspace incursion was unintentional; and I did not knowingly operate within restricted airspace. The officer issued a verbal warning.Contributing factors: This was primarily a human factor (memory) failure. I learned of the pending TFR during my planning-stage check but did not log it or set a reminder for its Day 1 effective date; and by the flight date I had forgotten it. On the day of the flight; I relied on the third-party application's summary status indicator; which is not an FAA-approved airspace source; rather than verifying through official FAA sources -- so nothing in my day-of process surfaced the restriction or prompted my recollection of it.Corrective actions: Going forward; I will log any pending TFR or NOTAM observed during planning; with its effective date and a calendar reminder; at the time I first see it. I will verify active TFRs and NOTAMs directly through official FAA sources (tfr.faa.gov and the B4UFLY app) immediately before every flight; regardless of any third-party application's status indication. I have added a mandatory day-of official-source TFR/NOTAM check to my preflight checklist. I will not operate at this site for the duration of the TFR period unless authorized through the FAA's Special Governmental Interest (SGI) process.

narrative: C90 STARS system continues to alert controllers via forcing a yellow full or limited data block on arrival scopes any aircraft that is deemed an early decent on an ILS/RNAV final between selected altitudes of approximately 6200-6800 feet outside the 7000 crossing fix on all approaches into ORD. Since implementation this system has created more false alerts than identifying real problems for me. It continues to create distractions and unnecessary nuisance alerts to other controllers; often unrelated to the operation at hand.  Controllers are trained and conditioned that yellow aircraft (yellow data blocks) are special; point outs; or otherwise needing special attention. This is not useful during flow changes; configuration changes; or single/dual runway arrival situations where aircraft can legally and procedural be at those flagged altitudes.  Displaying aircraft unnecessarily as special aircraft via yellow highlight will soon cause controllers to get fatigue from the constant yellow alerts and start ignoring it; and become complacent. We have already seen this throughout the field with the nuisance CA (Conflict Alert) alerts. Specifically; during a two runway arrival operation when the high runway controller can use 5-11000 to join their final/localizer; it is entirely possible an aircraft will (and should) be joining the final at 6000 or higher to allow a base turn ahead of the wider traffic at 5000 for positive separation. Positive separation without nuisance alerts should be absolutely possible.  It should also be noted that random miscellaneous VFR aircraft also show up yellow. But only between the flagged altitudes. This could easily lead a controller to miss other VFRs not within the altitude filter or EDAA box because they are expecting them to be yellow.   Aircraft X was being vectored for an approach to runway 10C in a two runway operation. The W controller was using their assigned altitudes in their assigned airspace but the entire arrival line received a false warning that Aircraft X had descended early while at 6700 feet. This alert was a false positive.  Disable the EDAA entirely as it is an unnecessary distraction in the operation.

Later; after giving a pilot's discretion descent to 150; the pilot asked how low I could descend them. I indicated that 110 would be the lowest until ZZZZZ; and that if they proceeded direct to the airport after ZZZZZ; I could descend them to 100. There was a little back-and-forth; and I felt the need to reiterate to the pilot that they would need to proceed direct to the airport after ZZZZZ in order to be able to descend to 100.I did give an instruction to proceed to the airport after ZZZZZ (not as an official clearance; that had supposedly been done already by another controller at an earlier point in time). At no point did I say 'descend and maintain 100;' only indicated to the pilot that I'd be able to descend them to 100 after ZZZZZ. The pilot read back 110; and the aircraft leveled off at 110 a few miles ahead of ZZZZZ. I took care of some other tasks. I gave a Low Altitude Alert with an instruction to climb and maintain 110. When I unkeyed; it sounded like someone else was just finishing a transmission too; so I repeated myself. With no response after a few seconds; I changed transmitters and repeated myself once again. Amidst all this; Aircraft X stopped their turn on a heading that was about 10 degrees left of a course direct to the airport... a heading that matched the RNAV-A approach; and which quickly approaches higher terrain.Finally; after the third attempt at a Low Altitude Alert; the pilot responded questioning that they had been cleared to 100 after ZZZZZ. narrative: The ongoing prohibition of parallel visual approaches at the San Francisco Airport has escalated from an operational inconvenience to a critical safety hazard. The resulting daily Ground Delay Programs (GDP) introduce two unmitigated risks into our system: chronic flight crew fatigue and unpredictable; near-minimum fuel operations.The SFO GDP frequently spans to XA:00 to XQ:00; causing domestic delays ranging from 45 to over 90 minutes. This systematically pushes flight crews to the limits of their Flight Duty Period (FDP); transforming a standard 8 to 10 hour duty day into exhausting 10 to 12 hour marathons. Pilots are regularly forced to fly complex arrivals into a high-density environment after being delayed - sometimes for multiple hours - where fatigue becomes a major factor.This threat materialized on day two of our pairing. Our schedule consisted of a three leg sequence: ZZZZ - SFO; SFO - ZZZZ; and a return to SFO. Both segments into SFO were hit by GDP delays exceeding one hour. The second GDP would have pushed us past our legal 13-hour FDP limit. While the crew desk was able to proactively remove us from the final turn - at considerable financial cost and inconvenience to our customers - many other crews had not timed out. Instead; they are being forced to fly into SFO fatigued; having already exhausted their mental and physical reserves waiting out ground delays.The current SFO configuration also severely compromises fuel planning predictability. Because a GDP of over an hour does not guarantee a clear path upon arrival; clear weather (CAVOK) days now yielding traffic saturation risks usually reserved for low-visibility operations.The severity of this breakdown was demonstrated on our flight from ZZZZ to SFO. The weather at SFO was pristine; endless blue skies with standard westerly winds. Normally; a remaining fuel of 1 hour 15 minutes is sufficient fuel to conduct an approach; handle a go-around; and land with a comfortable 60-minute reserve. Recognizing the SFO volatility; we planned a conservative gate fuel giving us an increased remaining fuel of 1 hour 45 minutes.The fuel preservation effort began immediately on the ground in ZZZZ; where our wheels-up time meant a 15-minute wait at the runway end. We proactively taxied on one engine and shut down the motor during our wait to preserve our margins. However; as we approached SFO our situation deteriorated. While on the BDEGA Arrival; ZOA assigned us a published hold at BGGLO due to traffic saturation on the SFO final approach.We immediately slowed the aircraft and began coordinating our fuel status with dispatch. I determined a bingo fuel of approximately 7;500 lb. before we needed to divert to SMF (1 hour remaining fuel of 5;100 lb. plus 2;300 lb. burn to SMF). We entered the BGGLO hold at 8;900 lb. After just one circuit our fuel had dropped to 8;300 lbs. Recognizing that a third circuit would push us below our diversion threshold; I informed ZOA that the second lap would have to be our final circuit; we either needed to press to SFO or immediately divert to SMF.Fortunately; ZOA released us from the hold with 7;700 lb. remaining. narrative1: During a routine flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ we received a runway change from XYR to XXR. This is a short flight and as a result we were working quickly to switch the runways/obtain landing data/rebrief/etc. This led to task saturation in a busy environment during the arrival/approach phase of flight. We were also managing fuel as we were going to be close to max landing weight so the PF was trying to get flaps/gear/spoilers extended early to help increase our burn. As a result; we ended up starting our descent on the visual approach slightly late. The PF increased their descent rate to try and get back on a 3.0 degree glide. At this time we became distracted in making sure our landing weight was acceptable with the fuel on board. This led to us descending below a 3.0 glide; the PF noticed and disconnected the autopilot and began correcting the glide path. Shortly after we started correcting we received a low altitude warning from ATC. This occurred around ZZZZZ on the approach to XXR. The published altitude is 7;000' and we were around 6500'. At this point we were still flaps 30 so we began final configuration and the before landing check. We completed these tasks around 800' AGL and continued the approach and landing uneventfully.Cause: The cause of this event was task saturation combined with a distraction during a critical phase of flight that led to us not availing first. This resulted in getting low on a visual approach and not meeting the stabilized approach criteria at 1;000'. As PM I failed to call a go around at 1;000' and allowed the aircraft to continue. Another contributing factor was the short flight combined with a fuel load bringing us close to max landing weight. We attempted to burn fuel enroute with an increased speed but were not able to do so due to turbulence. Ultimately us fixating on the fuel during the final descent led to the deviation below glide path.Suggestions: Prior to the approach beginning we should have asked ATC for more time to get setup for the runway change to help manage our task saturation and mitigate rushing through those tasks. A mother of an infant onboard removed all of the baby's clothing as she feared the infant was overheating. One FA in the back was dripping with sweat. Another FA in the back had to sit down for a couple minutes as he began to feel faint. Several customers started asking for water. I started feeling very nauseous. We got everyone on and seated and very quickly closed the overhead bins. Due to this pressure to board so quickly; FA A hurt his bag rushing to assist a customer who was dropping a bag. We made him an ice pack for his back and I checked on him throughout the flight. Nonetheless; we got all bins closed within about two minutes per the captain and were ready to close. Then we had to wait on AFT catering; then we had to wait on Maintenance. I kept being told; 'a couple more minutes' which in reality was about 10-15 minutes. It was pure chaos and misery. I kept being told different things by different people. People kept telling us it would cool down. One person; even said the plane would cool when the cabin door was shut. We shut the door hoping to finally have some relief. This was the opposite of the truth. It just kept getting hotter. The pilots said we couldn't start the engine yet due to Maintenance. Every concern I had just kept getting completely brushed off and ignored. It was so dangerous and my crew and I genuinely felt helpless. I didn't even know what to keep telling the customers as it was NOT getting cooler. We finally pushed back and it was still so hot. The pilots said it was around 85° in the cabin. narrative: I am a recently instrument-rated private pilot with approximately 450 total flight hours operating a turbocharged Piper PA-32 single-engine piston aircraft not approved for flight into known icing. I departed ZZZ1 VFR with flight following; returning to ZZZ; a non-towered airport.Afternoon convective activity was present. Prior to departure; I completed a weather briefing and planned a route north of the convective activity with the intent to cross in an area that appeared less active before turning south toward ZZZ.After departure; I proceeded northwestbound and cleared the ZZZ1 Class B. Based on visual observations and available weather information at the time; conditions appeared to permit a crossing while remaining clear of cloud; and I requested an IFR pop-up clearance to cross the ridge. ZZZ Center approved the clearance. I climbed in orbits to FL240 and was subsequently cleared direct to my destination.While proceeding westbound; it became apparent that convective build-ups were developing along my route. I received ATC approval for multiple heading deviations; including a larger left deviation; to remain clear of weather. As I approached the ridge at FL240; the visual corridor between cloud formations narrowed and I no longer observed a clear path forward that would allow me to remain clear of clouds.At that point; I decided to request to reverse course toward Area X and made two radio calls requesting a turn-back and vectors. Neither transmission was acknowledged. After the unanswered calls; I became concerned that communications may not have been effective and was preparing to squawk 7600.At approximately the same time; while near the ridge at FL240; I encountered a significant downdraft and became unable to maintain assigned altitude. The aircraft began a rapid descent. I lowered the nose to maintain airspeed and made a small heading adjustment to remain clear of a nearby convective build-up.During this descent; ZZZ Center transmitted instructions to maintain FL240 due to traffic behind and below me on a similar route of flight. I responded 'unable.' ATC subsequently issued traffic avoidance instructions to the trailing aircraft. Based on ADS-B In observations; closest proximity appeared to remain approximately 5 to 6 miles laterally with vertical separation maintained.I continued the descent through a visual opening into VMC; remained in communication with ATC; cancelled IFR descending through 18;000 feet; and proceeded to an uneventful landing at ZZZ1. No injury; aircraft damage; or loss of control occurred.Contributing factors included afternoon convective activity over high terrain; acceptance of direct routing rather than continuation of my original planned route north of the weather; operation at high altitude with aircraft performance considerations; the need to remain clear of cloud due to icing concerns; and a period in which my radio transmissions requesting a turn-back were not acknowledged by ATC.Lessons learned from this event for me include maintaining more conservative margins for mountain crossings in convective conditions; adhering to pre-planned routing around weather rather than accepting more direct options when conditions are deteriorating; and communicating changing circumstances to ATC earlier when weather avoidance or aircraft performance begins limiting available options. I have debriefed this flight in detail with experienced CFIIs and mentors and am incorporating these lessons into future weather assessment; route selection; and mountain flying decision making.

The aircraft touched down smoothly on the runway centerline without incident and the landing gear initially supported the aircraft normally. Because this was a touch-and-go landing; the student retracted the flaps and applied takeoff power. During the transition to the go portion of the maneuver; the nose landing gear suddenly collapsed. The student immediately closed both throttles; and I immediately moved both mixture controls to cutoff. I assumed control of the aircraft and elected not to apply brakes or rudder inputs to avoid aggravating the situation. The aircraft veered approximately 10-15 feet left of the runway centerline and came to rest between Taxiways 1 and 2. I informed the tower that we had experienced a nose gear collapse; and the tower advised that airport rescue and firefighting personnel were responding. As we got on with ZZZ ARTCC; we heard the Center issuing expect holding instructions to aircraft behind us. Based on this; we inferred that we would likely be among the last aircraft to land at ZZZ; and this was later confirmed by ATC.Prior to arrival; we set up and reviewed for the ILS Runway XXC approach; discussing the associated threats and weather conditions. We also reviewed our plan of action in the event of windshear or the need for a missed approach. My captain asked me if I felt comfortable taking the landing; and I said yes. To help mitigate the weather threat; we both had our WX radars up to monitor its movement. ATC informed us that the storm was still a couple of miles from the airport and aircraft were still landing at ZZZ.While being vectored for the ILS Runway XXC approach; we were cleared to intercept the localizer at 4;000 feet MSL. The Captain again asked whether I felt comfortable conducting the approach given the weather conditions and the potential for windshear. After I thought about the conditions; associated risks; and considering my limited experience operating in potential windshear environments; I determined that the most safety-conscious decision was to transfer pilot flying duties to him for the approach and landing. We completed a positive exchange of controls and received our approach clearance after that. The approach controller stated the winds at the field; which at the time no longer had a gust factor like the ATIS. However; we elected the safest course of action was to leave the gust factor in there due to the weather.Upon checking in with Tower; we were advised of a windshear alert in the vicinity of the runway. We elected to continue the approach after considering all the information; including the fact that another  company aircraft was directly 4 miles ahead of us on the same approach; it was still not raining at the airport; and the weather conditions looked safe enough to continue the approach. I observed that company aircraft land and exit the runway without reporting any windshear encounter or other abnormal conditions. Based on the information available at the time; we continued the approach while remaining prepared to execute a go-around if conditions worsened.At approximately 1;000 feet AFE; we began encountering windshear; including rapidly increasing airspeed and updrafts. To my recollection; we gained 100-200 ft and 10-15 kts of airspeed.  We determined the approach could no longer be continued according to our stable approach criteria. Seconds before initiating a go-around; the amber WSHEAR (Wind Shear) annunciation appeared on the PFD (Primary Flight Display). Additionally; a modified ground checklist protocol will be implemented to require a strict physical and audible verification of the throttle; mixture; and ignition controls prior to rotating the propeller. narrative: Summary: A near stall/spin accident on the base to final turn that didn't involve poor airspeed or attitude awareness.About the plane: The RV-6A is a side by side experimental airplane. It has a stall speed of about 55 kts; approaches are flown at 70 kts and the maximum flap extension speed is about 85 kts. It has dual controls with the sticks between the legs of the pilot and passenger about 6' behind the front of the knees. There is limited room for the stick and both the pilot and passenger must bow their legs to allow full motion. The flap control can either be electric or a Johnson bar manual control between the pilot and passenger seats. This plane has manual flaps. The pilot and passengers hips are in near contact and it requires reaching between the pilot and passenger legs to pull the flaps. The control is relatively short and the forces make it very difficult to apply full flaps with engine power applied or at any speed above 80 kts.About the flight: The winds were light; sky clear and daytime. I was taking a friend for his first flight in a small airplane as well as his first experience in the cockpit. It was a short flight from my local control towered airport to a nearby uncontrolled field (ZZZ). I did my typical brief as I go with a passenger. I made sure he knew how the seat belts worked as well as how to open the canopy. During the run-up when checking the controls for 'free and correct' I made a point to mention that he should stay clear of the stick between his legs while I was taking off or landing. As I flew to the nearby airport; my friend was enjoying the flight as well as doing some minor maneuvering with his stick.About the incident: I approached ZZZ by entering mid field downwind and started to slow down. I applied the 1st of 2 notches of flaps on downwind. The first notch of flaps doesn't require much effort on my part; but I do have to dig my hand between our legs to get access to the handle. At 1 notch; the end of the flap handle protrudes a little bit above the legs. As I was turning base to final I reached down to apply the 2nd notch of flaps. My friend felt me reaching near his knees decided to helpfully shift his legs away from my hand forcing the stick to the right and locking it in pitch. Note; I'm 5'10' 135#; my friend is 6' and over 200#. I noticed the un-commanded roll to the right. The airspeed was slowing and the AoA alert beeped briefly. I said something to the effect of 'you've got to give me the stick' and he quickly straightened up. I finished the turn and landed safely.How this could have gone bad: If my friend hadn't quickly responded to my request; the intercom wasn't working for some reason or if I had been tongue tied or he hadn't understood the ambiguous request this could have resulted in a stall/spin. Furthermore; to post crash analysis; this would have looked like poor airspeed or attitude awareness even if the logged data was examined.Lessons learned for me: * The terms taking off and landing are ambiguous even to another pilot. I should have announced the phases as I went. Before takeoff; 'stay clear of the stick till I let you know'; start of cruise; 'ok; don't worry about bumping the stick for now'; approach to land 'stay clear of the stick until I let you know'; etc.* I should modify my approach to landing to apply full flaps while still at altitude and in a relatively low workload phase when flying with a non-pilot passenger. * Our passenger stick is locked in with a clevis pin secured with a safety pin. If there is any concern I should always remove the stick for takeoff and landing. Replacing the stick for cruise if I want to let the passenger to try out flying.Suggestions: * During our build; Van's sent a service bulletin to bolt the passenger stick into its socket to prevent it accidentally being pulled out by a pilot flying in the right seat during a critical flight phase. This appears to be trading one risk for another. If used for flight training;the bolt seems entirely appropriate. The stick unsecured may actually be safest if the passenger is only going to do cruise maneuvering.* A statistical analysis of accidents involving between-the-legs sticks as compared to yokes or side sticks would be interesting. An analysis of manual vs. electric flapped equipped RVs may be worthwhile for this particular accident scenario; but there are hopefully not a statistically relevant number.

narrative1: Coming in on the ZZZZZ arrival at 6000ft on the down wind. ATC told us to slow to 190kt and to descend and maintain 4000 feet. I started a descent. On the Multi-function Flight Display (MFD) it looks as if we would intercept right around the FAF fix. We were still flying at 190kt maintaining the airspeed to keep a good descent rate. Captain requested a 120 heading to give us a little more time. We turned back left slightly and continued the descent. ATC then advised us; that due to the new turn that we are now below the Glideslope and that the next fix on the approach is 3000ft. I selected V/S and reduced the vertical speed to -200 ft./min. Captain selected 3000ft in the Mode Control Panel (MCP); but also selected ALT HOLD to try to assist in a very busy period. I saw the 3000ft in the MCP; but did not recognize the ALT HOLD selection. At which point I looked at the MFD to gain situation awareness of the approach; and the Aircraft began to pitch up to return to the altitude that was captured for ALT HOLD. The Speed Brakes were still out and the thrust was at a lower setting; and so airspeed bled off quickly. Once I recognized what had happened; I immediately grabbed the controls to push the nose forward and increase the thrust. Due to the surprise of the sequence of events; I only managed to select the Autopilot disconnect once. After a few moments though; I got the auto pilot horn off; and I stowed the speed brakes. The aircraft sped up; and after a some adjustments; stabilized to a normal attitude and airspeed. We brought the gear down; and set final approach speed. The speed continued to decrease towards target; and we were stable by 1000ft and 500ft. The landing; touchdown and rollout were uneventful.

narrative: I was the remote pilot in command of a 14 CFR Part 107 small UAS operation conducted under a LAANC authorization with a maximum altitude of 100 feet AGL.  The operation was located approximately 3 miles Northeast of ZZZ at approximately XA:00 on Day 0.  The purpose of the flight was to capture video of a private construction project nearing completion.My prior Part 107 experience in controlled airspace has primarily involved DJI Phantom and Mavic aircraft used for construction mapping and site progress photography; often on automated missions. This operation used a homebuilt first-person-view (FPV) small UAS. I was operating with a visual observer who is also an experienced FAA Part 107 remote pilot.Before the first event; my visual observer reported that he did not observe any aircraft in the vicinity of the operation. I initiated a high-rate climb. Shortly after the climb began; the GPS-derived altitude displayed in my FPV goggles indicated approximately 172 feet AGL; or approximately 72 feet above the 100-foot LAANC authorization. I immediately initiated recovery by reducing throttle; rolling the aircraft inverted; and commanding a descent back toward the operating area.During the recovery descent; the aircraft's FPV perspective indicated that it was descending; but the displayed GPS altitude continued to increase and briefly indicated approximately 272 feet AGL before becoming inconsistent and then decreasing. Because the altitude indication was GPS-derived and appeared to lag or behave unreliably during the high-rate climb and recovery; I cannot determine the aircraft's actual maximum altitude with certainty. However; I believe the aircraft exceeded the 100-foot LAANC authorization; and I immediately continued the descent and landed. The altitude exceedance appeared to last approximately five seconds. After the aircraft returned to low altitude; my visual observer again reported that he did not observe any aircraft in the vicinity.I did not intend to deviate from the LAANC authorization; and I took immediate corrective action as soon as I recognized the altitude exceedance. Contributing factors included unreliable or delayed GPS altitude indication during a high-rate climb; limited visual altitude references in the open area; and my underestimation of the climb performance of the FPV aircraft relative to the 100-foot authorized ceiling.Corrective actions have already been taken. I configured audible altitude warnings and altitude callouts on my radio transmitter. Before future operations I will review and set those warnings with a significant buffer below the authorized ceiling. For 100-foot LAANC authorizations; I will use a substantially reduced personal maximum altitude rather than operating up to the LAANC ceiling. I will also avoid high-rate vertical climbs in low-ceiling LAANC airspace.A second altitude exceedance occurred later in the same operation; several battery packs later. I activated the GPS Return to Home / GPS Rescue function in the same open operating area to observe its routing behavior. During the automated return; I realized the aircraft was climbing toward and then above the 100-foot LAANC ceiling. I attempted to override the automation with stick inputs; which changed the aircraft attitude but did not stop the climb. I then deactivated the return function by switching back to full manual control. I observed a maximum displayed GPS altitude of approximately 128 feet AGL; or approximately 28 feet above the authorized altitude. I immediately descended and landed. This altitude exceedance also appeared to last approximately five seconds. My visual observer reported that he did not observe any aircraft in the vicinity.During debrief; I realized this second event likely occurred because my GPS Return to Home / GPS Rescue function was configured to return at the maximum altitude recorded during the flight session. I had configured it this way to avoid an incorrectly preset return altitude. However; I misunderstood how the Betaflight flight controller defined a flight session. I had kept the flight controller and GPS powered during main battery changes using a USB battery pack so that GPS lock would be retained. I now believe the flight controller treated the later battery pack as part of the same flight session; meaning the return altitude was based on the maximum altitude recorded earlier in the operation rather than only the current battery pack or arming cycle.Although I chose the open field because it reduced collision risk with ground obstacles; I did not adequately account for the risk of testing an automated flight aid under a low LAANC ceiling in controlled airspace. I will not test GPS Rescue; Return to Home; failsafe behavior; or other autonomous flight functions within LAANC-controlled airspace or other altitude-sensitive airspace unless the full test profile remains safely below all applicable altitude limits. Future testing of these functions will be conducted in suitable airspace with a larger altitude margin.These events highlighted gaps in my understanding of my aircraft's altitude indication; climb performance; flight controller session behavior; and automated rescue configuration. The most important lesson for me is that open terrain on the ground does not mean the airspace risk is low. I will use these lessons to improve my preflight planning; altitude margins; automation testing procedures; and overall aeronautical decision-making to better protect the airspace and the people living and working beneath it.

Upon reaching our cruising altitude of 17;000 ft both the CA and I simultaneously smelled a strong odor of something electrical that was burning (noxious and acrid). It was only a second or two before it became very strong and we immediately donned our oxygen masks; established crew communications; and followed the instructions in the QRC. We re-established that I would remain the PF and the CA would handle the radios; QRH; etc. The CA then advised ATC and reported a burning odor in the flight deck and requested a diversion to ZZZ1. I agreed with that decision given the weather we had just left in ZZZ and the weather we were dealing with at the time; and I remembered that during our pre-departure briefing we had both pointed out that the weather near ZZZ1acuse (to the east) was better than in ZZZ or to the south.The CA worked on communicating to ATC and Dispatch (via ATC); as well as to the FA and the passengers while I continued flying the aircraft. ATC began giving us descents and headings to bring us onto the approach to runway XX. It was difficult to establish meaningful communication with the FA because the oxygen masks are so loud; as well as the fact that the noise from heavy rain on the windshield was quite loud as well. We had trouble hearing him and he had trouble hearing us; but we were able to at least communicate that we were diverting to ZZZ1 and that there was no smoke in the passenger cabin.The CA continued working through the QRH during the descent toward the airport in heavy rain; IMC; and moderate turbulence. We jointly decided not to depressurize the cabin given the fact that there was no reported smoke or fumes there.We accomplished our remaining checklists and were eventually vectored onto the approach for runway XX; whereupon we broke out of the weather; picked up the runway lights; and landed in heavy rain without incident. Emergency vehicles met us on the taxiway and followed us to the gate; where firefighters entered the aircraft to inspect for smoke and we were able to deplane. EMS wanted the CA and I to deplane first for treatment; but both the CA and I were uncomfortable with leaving the aircraft before the passengers so we waited until the plane was empty to leave the flight deck. EMS then treated me and the CA and said we both had high blood pressure and heart rates; which is to be expected after a stressful event like this. We were both nauseated and somewhat light-headed as well; but again that was to be expected given the odor and the stress of the situation. Several passengers were seen by EMS as well for anxiety.In the end; I believe the CA and I handled the situation correctly and professionally; that we followed our training; and I am thankful for the safe outcome for everyone involved.Root cause narrative: Acrid; burning odor which smelled like something electrical was burning.
narrative1: A few mins after reaching our cruise altitude of 17;000 Feet; the FO and I smelled an acrid electrical odor on the flight deck that quickly became stronger and overpowering. The FO continued flying the aircraft and I followed the QRC steps to don our oxygen masks and establish communication over the speakers. Once communication was established between us; I advised ZZZ Center. We had 51 souls and 5500 lbs of fuel on board the aircraft. I looked at divert options. The ZZZ airport was about 60 behind us with marginal weather and heavy rain showers. ZZZ1 was slightly closer and had better weather and a longer runway; so I informed ZZZ Center to give us direct to the ZZZ1 airport; which they did. I also asked them to contact our dispatcher/operations and let them know of the divert. I contacted the FA through the cabin emergency mode of the intercom; but because the oxygen masks were so loud; we were having trouble hearing him. I asked several times if the FA had any smoke or odor in the cabin. Finally; the FO heard the FA say no smoke or odor. We were initially cleared down to 11;000 feet. The FO continued flying and I gave him the radios while I ran the QRH. I accomplished the initial steps on the QRH but stopped short of depressurization because I didn't feel it was warranted; with no odor in the cabin and no visible smoke of any kind. I also decided not to isolate the electrical system or turn off any generators as we were in heavy rain showers and IMC and I did not want to compound the issues; given it was an odor and we were not dealing with smoke or fire.At this point we were given 4;000 feet and handed to ZZZ approach. We descended below the weather shortly after this and took the ILS into RXX. Emergency vehicles met us on the taxiway and followed us to the gate where we met firefighters. They tested the air quality on the flight deck and we deplaned using the main cabin door. The FO and I felt nauseous and were checked by EMS and released with no further symptoms other than elevated blood pressure. Several passengers were quite anxious and also evaluated and released.
synopsis: Embraer 145 flight crew reported a burning electrical odor upon reaching cruise. The flight diverted to an alternate airport and landed.

narrative: Hot Summer day leaving ZZZ on Aircraft X. We were heavy with fuel because of needing a precautionary alternate. There were long lines of thunderstorms through the northeast en route and at the destination. We had to run numbers for passengers and bags due to weight restrictions. In order to takeoff  we needed to burn fuel off to make takeoff weight restrictions. We were also calculating out through landing weight restrictions. For the first leg I was pilot monitoring and the captain was pilot flying. During the takeoff roll at approximately 80 knots the engine indicating system for Interstage Turbine Temperature (ITT) engine one went red. I let about 3 seconds pass debating on calling for the reject before V1. I observed the ITT go back to normal temperatures and decided not to call reject before reaching V1. On climb out after the takeoff checklist and getting the auto pilot on I informed the captain of what I had observed. On review of SOPs I realize I should have verbalized the indication immediately but hesitated due to there being no annunciation. Throughout the flight we continued to monitor the ITT temperature gauges. We noticed engine 1 ITT consistently 40 degrees higher than engine 2. When the pilot selected climb one we observed ITT 1 nearing overheat so we backed off the throttle to climb 2. Nearing the top of climb we similarly observed ITT 1 nearing limitations reaching FL280. Similarly after leveling off and beginning to accelerate to 290 temperatures began spiking and nearing limitations. We slowed to cruising at 270 to avoid an exceedance. After landing in ZZZ1 the landing exceedance warning pops up and we ran the QRH. After getting to the gate in ZZZ1 we write up the excedence and maintenance (MX) come out to perform an inspection. After the inspection maintenance said the operations check was good. Leaving ZZZ1 the captain and I discussed threats leaving and the plan with another potential ITT 1 excedence. We speculated hot temperatures in ZZZ and near max weight as being causes and since we were lighter and If temperatures were lower it would be less likely. We tried to coordinate for a takeoff on XX for runway length in case of a rejected takeoff but ATC had difficulties coordinating it with staffing. We accepted XYL for takeoff. We also decided to do the TO with no flex to increase runway remaining if needed. I was pilot flying from ZZZ1 on this flight. During the takeoff roll we observed ITT 1 turn red exceeding temperature limits again at around 80 knots.  The Captain called the reject and took controls. We notified ATC and returned to the gate. Maintenance came out to the aircraft and perform and another inspection. Stated the exceedence were within limits and ops checked it clearing it for flight. We refused the flight since no other mx was done and they would not perform a run up of the engine.
synopsis: Embraer 170 First Officer reported an engine temperature exceedance during takeoff and intermittently on the previous flight leg as well. The Captain rejected the takeoff and returned to the gate and then refused the aircraft.

Knowing we had just experienced an engine loss; the captain advised ATC and coordinated an immediate descent. I clicked off the autopilot and began handflying the descent. I noticed on my display that ZZZ was almost right underneath us; and before I could recommend that I believe ATC offered it as a landing site. Captain agreed and we started planning. Everything felt controlled and smooth; granted there was a sense of urgency given the situation and we had no idea what had caused the engine to fail randomly. I kept flying and took over the radios so the captain could coordinate with the FA's; notify the passengers of the situation; and started running QRC and emergency checklists. They were using XXR at ZZZ so the captain set me up quickly for that runway in the FMS and the radios. Later ATC told us to plan for XXL; so we set up for that runway instead. I configured the aircraft earlier than I usually would so I could make sure it was trimmed and stable well before we got too close to landing. He set the parking brake and had CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) look our right engine over and make sure there was nothing going on with it before taxiing. We'd had no high temperature abnormalities or fire indications in the air so we were fairly confident it was fine; but in the interest of safety we wanted verification before clearing the runway and taxiing to the gate.

narrative: Due to low staffing numbers AVP; radar positions have been combined to the tower cab outside of mid-shift hours. This has been expected of us by upper management to facilitate operating the facility with 50% staffing. During the winter months when traffic volume is low is quite a different situation than now in the summertime when traffic volume is high. We've done this for years; as it was common practice when I arrived to the facility. The current SOP allows the practice but has requirements for notifications to management outside of the building if it is done outside of mid-shift hours. District management was advised this would have to become standard practice until staffing numbers increase and has elected to forego the phone call and consider a daily log entry as sufficient.On the date and time above; I was instructed to work a session on North in the tower cab. It was early afternoon and a typical busy time. Traffic was moderate and complex with sequencing to the primary airport; a mix of IFR and VFR overflights; plus Aircraft Y and Aircraft Z flying around the airspace sightseeing. I also had multiple flight school airplanes in the practice areas. I don't recall if I had any practice instrument approaches at that time. At least SERMNs (SWAP (Severe Weather Avoidance Plan) Escape Routes - Metro New York Area) or PHLYRs (Philadelphia area weather avoidance routes) weren't active. I don't think I stopped talking for the 90 minutes I was on.I was busy enough and uncomfortable enough that at one point I grabbed another CPC who was not on position at the moment and just told him to keep an eye over my shoulder. He assisted with landline coordination and making amendments for me as Ground Control (GC) was defaulted to covering Arrival Data (AD) functions; something that isn't covered by SOP. The trainee in question is certified on both GC and AD but is otherwise not a CPC. I was forced to manually coordinate routing for one or two aircraft because the trainee wasn't able to complete amendments I needed correctly and in a timely manner. It took him close to 10 minutes to amend a VFR's altitude so that I could hand off to the correct sector. I have no clue what the exact issue was with that; or what other traffic he had on Ground at that exact time. AVP was busy as a whole so there were definitely airplanes that required attention outside of the window. Working arrival data is a heads-down position and completely contrary to what a ground controller should be doing. This particular day was unique in that AVP was using both of our intersecting runways due to winds and traffic.To further complicate the session; while I was working with frequencies directly in my ear; many times I had trouble hearing pilots talking to me because of other speakers in the cab. There were low clouds moving in from the west forcing most of my VFR traffic that was flying westbound to continue to descend lower and lower to maintain VFR; which only put them in the middle of our arrival and departure corridors.Upper level management almost expects us to combine to the tower in order to operate the facility and accomplish training. I understand that realistically the ONLY way to get out of the staffing crisis is to train and certify controllers. I feel we've reached the point where doing this is inherently unsafe. The safety of day to day operations rest solely on the shoulders of the small handful of FPLs (Full Performance Level) on the shift. We're outnumbered daily by partially qualified and newly position-certified trainees. There are often times where an FPL on radar has had to correct a situation on local; or the Controller in Charge (CIC) has had to step in; or even an FPL who is on technically on break has to step in.When combined to the tower cab; we are forced to sacrifice a lot in terms of redundancy and basic safety. There is no voice switch bypass for radar frequencies in the tower cab. This has been brought up to tech operations foryears already. There is only one Interim Voice Switch Replacement (IVSR) that radar controller can use and no spare that someone can plug in and help coordinate in a pinch. GC is defaulted to work AD functions and when training is underway on a new trainee that adds undue burden on both the trainee and the trainer as they don't even have a concept of what is happening in the airspace. The Tower Display Workstation (TDW) is 1/3(?) of the size of a Terminal Controller Workstation (TCW); is washed out as soon as someone bumps a window shade open.In the moments we're told to train then it feels like the trainee and I could share a chair. The small scope means I need to stand nearly in their lap to be able to even see the scope. Meanwhile; the doubling of people required to train crowds the room quickly. There have been many instances where we're training on all 3 positions at the same time. Sure it looks great on the Cru-ART (shift log); but at what cost. What is the benefit of teaching new people bad practices from the start? What is the benefit of working without a basic backup to our radios? What is the benefit of doubling the heads-down workload of a trainee who should be looking out the window? What is the benefit of forcing a trainee to complete AD functions when they haven't even received classroom training on it? What is the benefit of putting all the above-mentioned responsibility on the shoulder of the few FPLs on the shift?Recommendation: At this point I don't know what would be the most effective change to implement. We need more than 50% staffing. We can't continue to be pushed to exhaustion by 60-hour workweeks just to have basic staffing in the building. We can't be expected to work radar combined to the tower until further notice. We should not be forcing trainees to endure decades of bad decisions while they struggle to learn to separate airplanes.Adding a full TCW has been brought up in the past but adding just installing a new screen without an addition IVSR or even so much as a bypass for the voice switch is a waste [of] time and money. Splitting off AD from GC won't work because we don't have enough IVSRs or so much as enough counter space.Forcing trainees to sit on position even if there's no traffic but also rushing them to check out sooner continues to rob them of the quality training.
synopsis: AVP Controller reported that due to low staffing; TRACON and Tower have been combined during certain shifts and having to train and manage trainees without proper communication equipment have made operations unsafe.

narrative: After a moderate to heavy volume of arrivals; Aircraft X was one of the last in the sequence. They were coming from the south-southwest; and had the field in sight about 18 miles out for AVL. I cleared them for a visual approach to Runway 35. A moment later; Aircraft Y; who never called Approach for services (we looked up the callsign that was tied to the ADS-B to find out the information on the aircraft) departed 0A7 northwest bound and then turned to the left and was climbing at a good rate. Thankfully for everyone involved; I had not shipped Aircraft X to the tower yet as they were descending in for the visual approach. Since I've seen this exact scenario play out numerous times; I cancelled the Aircraft X's visual approach clearance and had them continue on present heading followed by a right turn; and right when they crossed the 051 MVA boundary; I had them maintain 050 because I had another aircraft in the right downwind for Runway 35 at 060. Aircraft Y continued to climb; oblivious to the fact that they were flying right through our final for AVL at a dangerous altitude. Aircraft X was cleared for the visual approach 35 after passing behind the VFR aircraft.Plenty of luck was involved here that avoided any major deals or potential midairs. If I had simply shipped the Aircraft X to the tower when they were 13 miles out; which is not unreasonable; the potential for a midair collision would have been significant because Aircraft X would have been in frequency transition during the critical moment; and Aircraft Y had no need to or desire to call Asheville Approach for services because they were legally outside of Class C airspace still. Luck was involved with me not descending the aircraft on the right downwind to 051; which would have been a standard thing to do. If Aircraft Y had decided to depart a few minutes earlier; when my traffic volume was much greater; including many VFR aircraft flying around in and around downwinds that I had to maneuver all of my arrivals around; I may not have noticed their departure as quickly as I did now.Recommendation: Similar reports to this have been filed multiple times over the many years that I've worked here by many different controllers. The AVL Class C needs to be changed to not allow 0A7 departures to fly under the Runway 35 final approach course at dangerous altitudes. As it stands; it is LEGAL for VFR aircraft to cross UMUXE at 040 and not violate the Class Charlie; which is EXACTLY the published altitude for crossing that fix on the RNAV 35 and the ILS 35. The FAA has been made aware that this is a HIGHLY DANGEROUS situation on numerous occasions and the only feedback the FAA has ever given the controllers at AVL is that changing the Class Charlie would require an act of Congress" AKA it is too hard/too much effort for management to do. The FAA spends plenty of time monitoring and figuring out how to reduce CPC breaks and other useless behaviors; there is plenty of time for them to do ACTUAL WORK and fix the AVL Class C airspace. One day; if nothing changes; all of the wrong luck will happen in this KNOWN AND WELL REPORTED ON UNSAFE AIRSPACE/PROCEDURE that will cost people their lives. If that ever happens; let it be known that this safety issue was reported on numerous times and something could have been done about it."

narrative: In Month 6; prior to conducting a flight operation in Class E airspace; a Remote Pilot in Command (RPIC) performed a routine review of the documentation required for waivered flight operations. During this review; the RPIC discovered that the aircraft registration sticker was not attached to the drone and the registration card was missing from the drone case.The RPIC then verified the aircraft's registration status through the FAA DroneZone portal and determined that the registration had been marked as 'Cancelled' effective Month 0. As a result; the RPIC immediately suspended the planned flight operation and did not operate the aircraft.To prevent further use; the RPIC placed the drone and its remote controller into storage; labeled both the drone and its case as 'UNREGISTERED;' and removed the aircraft from service pending further investigation.The subsequent investigation revealed that the drone had been operated despite the cancelled registration. The aircraft registration was cancelled in Month 0 and was in storage until Month 3. Starting in Month 3; three different RPICs had conducted a total of 204 flights accumulating 67 flight hours using the aircraft over a period of approximately four months. The majority of these flights occurred in Class G (uncontrolled) airspace; while several flights were conducted in Class B (controlled) airspace after obtaining proper authorization through the Low Altitude Authorization and Notification Capability (LAANC) system. Although all required airspace approvals and clearances had been obtained for operations in controlled airspace; the aircraft's FAA registration was not in compliance during this period.The aircraft was initially operated by an experienced RPIC with several years of company drone operations experience. The drone was subsequently transferred in Month 4 to a new RPIC for their first inspection assignment. In Month 6; the drone was later handed off to another experienced RPIC. That RPIC performed maintenance but did not check registration documents upon receiving the aircraft. After approximately one week of operation; the final RPIC recognized that the aircraft's external FAA registration-number sticker was missing and initiated a review that ultimately identified a missing registration card and the cancelled registration status.The investigation determined that the registration had been cancelled in error due to a mislabeled drone case. A retired and damaged drone had been stored in a case incorrectly labeled with the identifier of an active operational drone. As a result; the FAA registration associated with the operational aircraft was mistakenly cancelled.The investigation also identified weaknesses in the drone registration management process. Registration documents were typically stored inside drone cases and were not readily visible during routine equipment checks; making it unlikely that a missing registration card would be immediately detected. Additionally; while the FAA registration sticker was missing from the aircraft; a company issued Drone Identifier sticker remained affixed to the drone. The presence of this identifier created the appearance that the aircraft was properly labeled; causing the absence of the FAA registration number sticker to go unnoticed during pre-flight inspections and routine use.Apparent Cause 1 Mislabeled drone case containing a damaged drone led to the cancellation of the registration of an operational active drone.Apparent Cause 2Registration cards are often kept inside drone cases underneath equipment to keep them secure. The registration cards are not readily visible to the RPICs leading UAS crews to inadvertently overlook the missing registration card.Corrective Actions:1) Conduct a safety stand-down to verify inventory and confirm all active drones have valid FAA registration.2) Update Uncrewed Aerial Systems (UAS) Fleet Management document to include recommended procedures for retired drones.3) Amend the Preflight Checklist to require drone registration validation and part of daily pre-flight checks.4) Attach a durable external registration tag to all active drone cases.5) Require all UAS crews to verify their assigned drone registration is present and current.6) Contact FAA regarding possible DroneZone inventory management improvements.7) Designate a single individual responsible for drone inventory management.8) Require maintenance log including drone registration verification be complete before operation in the field upon transferring drones between operators.9) Verify all active drones have FAA registration number sticker properly displayed on external surface of the aircraft.
callback: Reporter stated the serial numbers of the two UAS were very close; which was an additional contributing factor that led to the accidental cancellation of the UAS registration.

narrative: I secured local university permission to fly UAS/UAV on the university campus in advance of flights for XA:00 to XC:00/XD:00 on Day 0.  This is part of weekly planned flights on campus for flight practice/training hours for one student and learning in an independent study for another student. In addition to the educational outcomes; we fly to collect video and images for various business purposes on campus. On this particular day only one of the two students was present and flying as part of the planned flight; Person A. While Person A was manipulating the controls at the time with the Mavic 2 Pro; I was serving as Remote PIC. In addition to the Remote PIC; I also served as the Visual Observer.  Partly to assist with keeping an eye on the UAS/UAV; to assist with people who may be approaching nearby to the flight; and also to answer questions when individuals approach (common on a university campus). We typically meet at XA:00 and do pre-flight checks inside the office and then go out to fly. This particular morning; I was running late to meet at the office and this particular human factor led to me forgetting to do the TFR check as part of the pre-flight checklist.  I also did not ask if my student had checked. Come to find out; this turned out to be a very good learning experience for both of us and I doubt that either of us will ever forget to do that check again.  Our series of flights started at Location X on campus; then we flew in the area around Location Y and the area around Location Z. Our final flights to capture video and images for a campus project were to fly the east end of Location Z and Location A. We were approached multiple times during all of our flights and we paused flight; grounded the UAS/UAV; and ensured the safety of all passerby's whether walking or biking on campus. Flights were planned to be fairly low (below 100 feet and some at average height level of a human. The highest flight that we planned to fly was no more than 400 feet AGL and that was simply to ensure that the student had the experience of what that type of height is like from an observational experience. Our highest flights were along Location Z at 397 feet for less than 1-2 minutes. The drone at all times was above myself and the student manipulating controls; we didn't fly it beyond our line of sight and manually straight up from take off location(s) at the ends of Location Z. We were approached by several people during our flights that day asking questions from curiosity to technical questions. I handled most of the questions while Person A collected the images/video and maintained line of site. We were never further apart than about 10-15 feet and could communicate by voice without any issue. Both of us were in high visibility safety vests.  While not required; we find it's best to ensure others know we are flying our UAS for university business purposes as students are not allowed to fly on our campus unless part of a class or another business purpose.  At roughly XC:00; just after bringing the Mavic 2 Pro down from the west end of Location Y safely (literally we hovered in the air to ensure several families and people with dogs passed by before we landed); we began walking and preparing for the next flight -- the backside of Location A.  We were approached by an individual. He asked if we were with the university. I turned toward him with my name tag on and stated yes and explained our learning purpose and university business purpose of shooting videos. I thought he was a typical tourist asking questions or maybe a hobbyist or other Part 107 pilot. He then asked if we had checked the TFRs for the day and location and I realized I had not before we left. He then introduced himself as a law enforcement officer and flipped out his identification wallet.  I immediately opened my phone and app and realized we had unknowingly been flying just inside of a TFR.  The law enforcement officer acknowledged that they were aware of ourprevious flights that were just outside of the TFR and that we were brought to their attention only with our last flight that was just inside the edge of the radius of the area covered by the TFR. We immediately stopped all flights and began to put away the UAS. We discussed how this will be a good learning experience for my future classes and how I am often asked the question 'who enforces TFRs?'.  It truly was a mistake and we were not intending to break any TFRs when we set out for the filming and flights. We now have a printed checklist that must be checked through before leaving the office to ensure situational awareness.  Both Person A and I will NEVER forget to check TFRs.  I also notified our campus police (the entity that approves flights on our campus) and let them know that for the rest of that week the TFR was in place and flights should be avoided in the area we were in plus several of the university areas that are more administrative/facilities related.  This will be a discussion topic for our next drone committee meeting on campus; as we may want to use our UAS/UAV listserv to remind folks about active TFR's in the area of the university.
narrative1: I was flying a UAV (DJI Mavic 2 Pro) between XA:00 and XC:00 on Day 0 on campus; where I am a student. I was flying with Person B. Person B was serving as the remote PIC and visual observer; while I was the person manipulating controls. We were taking photo and video for the university to use in various business purposes on campus.While preparing to fly that day; I made the mistake of assuming that Person B had checked for TFRs; and as a result I neglected to do so myself; focusing on batteries and other set up duties. We made several flights around campus; covering Location X and Location Y. We mostly stayed under 100ft; but on our last flight we took the UAV up to 397ft AGL for practice and to get some more panoramic shots of campus. At that point we realized that we had both forgotten to. We packed up for the day.As a new pilot; this was a valuable learning experience. I understand now that I need to personally check TFRs before flying rather than rely on anyone else to do it. After this incident; I've made a checklist of items I need to perform before each flight and I plan to refer to it before each flight to ensure I don't miss anything.
